3. 'Nirjara' refers to the preventive stoppage of the inflow of new karmic particles through self-restraint, whereas 'Samvara' refers to the active purging and shedding of previously accumulated karma through austerity (Tapas).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A defining hallmark of Jain philosophy is its strictly materialist conception of Karma as subtle atomic matter (Karma-pudgala) that encrusts the soul when lubricated by passions (Kashayas). Liberation (Moksha) requires the two-stage process of Samvara (blocking new karmic influx) and Nirjara (burning away existing karmic deposits via Tapas).

exp.why: While Buddhism, Yoga, and Vedanta treat Karma as non-physical moral impressions (Samskaras, Vasanas, or Adrishta), Jainism uniquely conceptualizes Karma as real, ultra-subtle physical matter (Karmana-pudgala) filling cosmic space. These material particles literally invade the soul (Jiva), form a karmic body (Karmana-sharira), weigh it down in Samsara, and obscure its innate infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy (Ananta-chatustaya).

Among the Nine Tattvas (Jiva, Ajiva, Punya, Papa, Asrava, Bandha, Samvara, Nirjara, and Moksha), vibrational activity (Yoga) of mind, speech, and body creates channels through which karmic particles flow into the soul, a process called 'Asrava' (influx). When the soul is moistened by the four passions (Kashayas: anger/Krodha, pride/Mana, deceit/Maya, and greed/Lobha), this inflowing matter sticks and binds to the soul, which is termed 'Bandha' (bondage).

This statement swaps the technical definitions of Samvara and Nirjara. 'Samvara' is the preventive stoppage or blocking of the channels of karmic influx (the reversal of Asrava) achieved through mindfulness (Samiti), restraint of mind/speech/body (Gupti), and observance of vows. 'Nirjara' is the exhausting, burning away, and shedding of already accumulated karmic matter from the soul (the reversal of Bandha), accomplished primarily through internal and external austerities (Tapas).

ref: Tattvartha Sutra Ch. 6–10; Padmanabh Jaini, The Jaina Path of Purification, Ch. 4

stem: With reference to the doctrine of the Three Jewels (Triratna) in Jainism, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Jain canonical literature, the 'Triratna' denotes the institutional refuge taken by a lay or monastic follower in the Tirthankara, the Canonical Law (Agama), and the Four-fold Monastic Order (Chaturvidha Sangha).

2. Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra opens by declaring that the path to liberation (Moksha-marga) consists in the unified confluence of Right Faith (Samyak Darshana), Right Knowledge (Samyak Jnana), and Right Conduct (Samyak Charitra).

3. Unlike philosophical schools that treat intellectual gnosis (Jnana) alone as sufficient for salvation, Jainism holds that none of the Three Jewels can independently produce liberation without the simultaneous perfection of the other two.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike the Buddhist Triratna (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha), the Jain Triratna is an ethical-epistemological triad comprising Samyak Darshana, Samyak Jnana, and Samyak Charitra. As codified in the opening aphorism of the Tattvartha Sutra, all three jewels must operate simultaneously as an indivisible unity to achieve Moksha.

exp.why: This statement conflates the Jain Triratna with the Buddhist Triratna (refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha). In Jainism, institutional refuge is four-fold (Chatuhsharana: refuge in the Arihantas, Siddhas, Sadhus, and the Kevali-proclaimed Dharma), whereas the Jain 'Triratna' refers strictly to the internal spiritual triad of Right Faith (Samyak Darshana), Right Knowledge (Samyak Jnana), and Right Conduct (Samyak Charitra).

The Tattvartha Sutra (Moksha-shastra) of Acharya Umasvati—the foundational Sanskrit treatise accepted as authoritative by both Svetambaras and Digambaras—begins with the famous sutra 'Samyag-darshana-jnana-charitrani mokshamargah' (1.1), defining the path to liberation as the collective unity of Right Faith, Right Knowledge, and Right Conduct.

In contrast to Sankhya or Advaita Vedanta, where liberating knowledge (Jnana) by itself dispels ignorance and effects liberation, Jainism insists on a strict synthesis of faith, cognition, and ethical action (Jnana-Karma-Samuchchaya). Using the classic medical analogy—trusting the physician (Darshana), knowing the pharmacological prescription (Jnana), and actually consuming the medicine while following dietary discipline (Charitra)—Jain philosophers emphasize that the absence of any one jewel renders the other two powerless to achieve Moksha.

ref: Tattvartha Sutra 1.1; Upinder Singh Ch. 6; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-I

stem: With reference to the doctrinal and historical divergences between the Digambara and Shvetambara traditions of Jainism, consider the following statements:
items: 1. According to the Digambara tradition, an ascetic who has attained omniscience (Kevala Jnana) continues to require physical morsel food (Kavalahara) to sustain the body, whereas the Shvetambara tradition holds that a Kevalin transcends all need for physical nourishment.

2. While the Digambara sect regards the nineteenth Tirthankara, Mallinatha, as a female ascetic who attained liberation in that very birth, the Shvetambara sect holds that women must first be reborn as men to attain Moksha.

3. Following the twelve-year Magadhan famine and the southward migration led by Bhadrabahu, the Digambara tradition maintains that the original eleven Angas and fourteen Purvas were progressively lost, whereas the Shvetambaras preserve the eleven Angas compiled at Pataliputra.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The schism between the Digambaras (led by Bhadrabahu) and Shvetambaras (led by Sthulabhadra) crystallized around four principal doctrinal disputes: whether an omniscient Kevalin consumes physical food, whether ascetic nudity makes female liberation (Strimukti) impossible in a female body, the gender of the 19th Tirthankara Mallinatha, and the authenticity of the surviving Agama canon.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the positions of the two sects. The Digambara tradition holds that once an ascetic attains omniscience (Kevala Jnana), the body is sustained purely by spiritual energy and no longer requires ordinary physical morsel food (Kavalahara). Conversely, the Shvetambara tradition maintains that even a Kevalin continues to take physical food until final nirvana.

Statement 2 also reverses the sectarian positions. The Shvetambara tradition holds that women are capable of attaining liberation in their female body (Strimukti) and reveres the 19th Tirthankara, Malli (Mallinatha), as a woman. The Digambara tradition insists that complete ascetic nudity (Achelaka) is indispensable for Moksha; since social and spiritual norms preclude public nudity for women, Digambaras maintain that a woman must be reborn as a man to achieve liberation and that Mallinatha was male.

Statement 3 is correct. After the twelve-year famine in Magadha at the end of the fourth century BCE, the monks who migrated south to Shravanabelagola under Bhadrabahu returned to find that the monks who stayed behind under Sthulabhadra had adopted white robes (Shvetambara) and compiled eleven Angas at Pataliputra. The Digambaras rejected this compilation, maintaining that the original eleven Angas and fourteen Purvas taught by Mahavira were progressively lost.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 14; Padmanabh S. Jaini, The Jaina Path of Purification, Ch. 1

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the codification of Jain canonical literature:
items: Statement-I: The First Jain Council held at Pataliputra around 300 BCE was presided over by Bhadrabahu and resulted in the final redaction of all twelve Angas into Sanskrit, which were accepted as authoritative by both the Shvetambara and Digambara sects.

Statement-II: The Second Jain Council held at Vallabhi in the sixth century CE under the presidency of Devardhigani Kshamashramana systematically committed the surviving Shvetambara Agama canon to writing in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit, while acknowledging the permanent loss of the twelfth Anga (Drishtivada).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Shvetambara Agama canon was orally compiled at the First Council of Pataliputra (c. 300 BCE) under Sthulabhadra and finally redacted into written Ardhamagadhi Prakrit at the Council of Vallabhi (6th century CE) under Devardhigani Kshamashramana. The Digambara sect rejected both councils, holding that the original canon was lost.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect on three counts: first, the First Jain Council at Pataliputra (c. 300 BCE) was presided over by Sthulabhadra, not Bhadrabahu (who was absent in Nepal or South India); second, only eleven Angas were compiled there in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit (not all twelve Angas in Sanskrit), as the twelfth Anga (Drishtivada) containing the fourteen Purvas could not be fully reconstructed; third, the followers of Bhadrabahu (Digambaras) rejected the authority of this Pataliputra canon.

Statement-II is correct. Fearing the erosion of oral memory due to famines and the passing away of senior monks, the Second Jain Council at Vallabhi (Gujarat) in the early sixth century CE, presided over by Devardhigani Kshamashramana, reduced the surviving Shvetambara Agama literature (including the eleven Angas, twelve Upangas, Prakirnakas, Chedasutras, and Mulasutras) to writing in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit, formally recording that the twelfth Anga (Drishtivada) had been lost.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 6; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I

stem: With reference to the sacred and philosophical literature of Jainism, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Acharanga Sutra : First of the Shvetambara Angas laying down the code of monastic conduct and ascetic discipline
2. Bhagavati Sutra (Vyakhyaprajnapti) : Fifth Anga containing an encyclopedic exposition of Jain metaphysics in the form of dialogues between Mahavira and Indrabhuti Gautama
3. Shatkhandagama : Revered Digambara scripture on the doctrine of Karma compiled in Prakrit by Acharyas Pushpadanta and Bhutabali
4. Tattvartha Sutra : Shvetambara Chedasutra composed in Ardhamagadhi by Acharya Kundakunda that is rejected by the Digambara tradition
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: While the Shvetambara Agamas (headed by the Acharanga and Bhagavati Sutras) and the Digambara Shatkhandagama and Kundakunda's Prakrit treatises represent distinct sectarian canons, Umasvati's Sanskrit Tattvartha Sutra (Mokshashastra) uniquely bridges both traditions as the foundational compendium of Jain philosophy.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The Acharanga Sutra (Ayaramga) is the first of the twelve Angas in the Shvetambara canon. It prescribes the rigorous rules of monastic conduct (Achara), non-violence, and ascetic austerity, and preserves the earliest biographical account of Mahavira's twelve years of penance.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. The Bhagavati Sutra (formally titled Vyakhyaprajnapti) is the fifth Anga of the Shvetambara canon. Structured predominantly as a series of 36,000 questions and answers between Lord Mahavira and his chief disciple Indrabhuti Gautama, it covers cosmology, ontology, karma theory, and Mahavira's interactions with contemporaries like Makkhali Gosala.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Rejecting the Pataliputra Agamas, the Digambara tradition accords quasi-canonical status to the Shatkhandagama ('Scripture in Six Parts') composed in Sauraseni Prakrit by Acharyas Pushpadanta and Bhutabali (c. 1st–2nd century CE) based on the surviving oral fragments of the fifth Purva (Agrrayaniya) transmitted by Acharya Dharasena, alongside Gunabhadra's Kasayapahuda.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. The Tattvartha Sutra (also known as Tattvarthadhigama Sutra or Mokshashastra) is neither a Chedasutra nor composed by Kundakunda in Ardhamagadhi. It is the first systematic Sanskrit aphoristic treatise on Jain epistemology, metaphysics, cosmology, and ethics, composed by Acharya Umasvati (Umasvami), and is uniquely revered as authoritative by both the Shvetambara and Digambara traditions. Acharya Kundakunda was a seminal Digambara philosopher who composed Prakrit mystical treatises such as Samayasara, Pravachanasara, and Panchastikayasara.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 6; Paul Dundas, The Jains, Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the medieval reform movements and sub-sects within Jainism, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both the Sthanakavasi sect within the Shvetambara tradition and the Taranpanthi sect within the Digambara tradition reject idol worship (Murtipuja) on the ground that the ancient scriptures do not sanction temple rituals.
2. Both the Shvetambara Terapantha and the Digambara Terapantha are strictly non-idolatrous (aniconic) monastic orders that prohibit the installation or veneration of Tirthankara images in temples.

3. Unlike the Digambara Bispanthis, the Digambara Terapanthis reject the religious authority of traditional Bhattarakas and refrain from offering fresh flowers, fruits, or lit lamps (Arati) during temple worship to avoid violence against one-sensed living beings.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although the name 'Terapantha' appears in both major branches of Jainism, their ritual characters differ fundamentally: the Shvetambara Terapantha (founded by Acharya Bhikshu) is an aniconic offshoot of the Sthanakavasi tradition, whereas the Digambara Terapantha is an idol-worshipping temple reform movement that purged Bhattaraka mediation and offerings of living plant matter.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In the 15th century, the Gujarati scribe Lonka Shah initiated an aniconic reform within Shvetambara Jainism by arguing that the Agamas do not mention idol worship (Murtipuja); this lineage gave rise to the Sthanakavasi sect in the 17th century, whose monks reside in prayer halls (Sthanakas) rather than temples. Similarly, in the late 15th/early 16th century, Tarana Svami founded the Taranpanthi (Samaiyapanthi) sub-sect within the Digambara tradition in Bundelkhand, which repudiates idol worship and instead venerates sacred scriptures (Shastras) placed on altars.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it conflates two distinct movements bearing the same name. The Shvetambara Terapantha, founded by Acharya Bhikshu (Bhikhanji) in 1760 CE as a breakaway from the Sthanakavasis, is indeed strictly non-idolatrous (aniconic) and centralized under a single Acharya. However, the Digambara Terapantha, which emerged in 17th-century North India under reformers like Banarsidas and Amra Bhaunsa, is an idol-worshipping (Murtipujaka) sect that continues to venerate Tirthankara images in temples (Mandirs).

Statement 3 is correct. Within the Digambara tradition, the Bispanthis accept the authority of clerical pontiffs (Bhattarakas), worship tutelary deities (Yakshas and Yakshinis such as Padmavati) alongside Tirthankaras, and perform Arati and offer fresh flowers, fruits, and green betel leaves. The Digambara Terapanthis reformed temple practice by rejecting the authority of Bhattarakas, worshiping only Tirthankara idols (not Yakshinis), and substituting dry, inanimate substances like sacred rice (Akshata) in place of fresh flowers, fruits, or lit lamps so as not to injure plant-bodied or fire-bodied souls (Ekendriya Jivas).

ref: Paul Dundas, The Jains, Ch. 8; Nitin Singhania, Indian Art and Culture

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the social philosophy and occupational structure of Jainism:
items: Statement-I: Over the course of Indian history, the lay community (Shravakas) of Jainism predominantly gravitated toward trade, commerce, and banking rather than agrarian cultivation, even while the religion continued to function within the broader framework of the Varna social order without calling for its total abolition.

Statement-II: Jain metaphysics holds that even earth, water, fire, air, and plants possess living souls (Ekendriya Jivas) that suffer fatal injury during ploughing and harvesting, while explaining an individual's birth into a particular Varna as the consequence of past Karma rather than divine creation.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Jainism's radical extension of ensoulment (Jiva) to single-sensed earth-bodied and plant-bodied beings made agriculture ethically problematic due to unavoidable violence (Himsa) during tillage, steering lay Jains toward mercantile professions. Simultaneously, Jainism rationalized birth into a high or low Varna through the law of Karma while rejecting Vedic ritual privileges and a Creator God.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Historically, Jain householders (Shravakas) increasingly abandoned agriculture and warfare, concentrating instead in trade, commerce, moneylending, and urban crafts. At the same time, unlike radical movements that sought to dismantle social hierarchy entirely, Jainism did not abolish the Varna system in lay society, even though it rejected Brahmanical ritual supremacy and opened its monastic order to spiritual seekers.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains both parts of Statement-I. Because Jain hylozoistic metaphysics attributes souls not only to mobile multi-sensed creatures (Trasa Jivas) but also to immobile single-sensed beings (Sthavara/Ekendriya Jivas) inhabiting earth, water, fire, air, and plants, agricultural activities like ploughing, digging, and pest control entail massive violence (Himsa), compelling pious lay followers to choose mercantile occupations. Furthermore, According to Mahavira, a person is born into a higher or lower Varna due to sins or virtues accumulated in a previous birth (Gotra Karma), though through pure conduct and asceticism anyone can transcend karmic bondage and attain liberation.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 14; NCERT Class VI & XII History

stem: With reference to the ethical code of Jainism for ascetics and householders, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The five great vows (Pancha Mahavratas) in their absolute and unconditional form are prescribed only for mendicant monks and nuns, whereas lay householders observe the same five principles in a modified degree known as Anuvratas, supplemented by three Gunavratas and four Shikshavratas.

2. The ritual vow of Sallekhana (Santhara) may be undertaken at any stage of life by an individual experiencing acute emotional distress or worldly failure as a rapid means of shedding accumulated Karma.

3. Jain canonical treatises such as the Ratnakaranda Shravakachara distinguish Sallekhana from suicide (Atmahatya) on the ground that suicide is driven by passions (Kashayas) and uses violent means, whereas Sallekhana is a passionless, gradual renunciation of nourishment undertaken only when death is imminent due to terminal illness, extreme old age, or inescapable calamity.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Jain ethics differentiates between the absolute Mahavratas binding exclusively on ascetics and the twelve-fold householder code (five Anuvratas, three Gunavratas, and four Shikshavratas). At the end of life, the vow of Sallekhana represents a passionless, gradual withdrawal from food and water under terminal conditions, fundamentally distinct from passion-driven suicide.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In Jainism, the five vows—Ahimsa (non-injury), Satya (truth), Asteya (non-stealing), Brahmacharya (celibacy/chastity), and Aparigraha (non-possession)—are observed as absolute Mahavratas only by initiated mendicants (Sadhu and Sadhvi). For lay householders (Shravakas and Shravikas), complete avoidance of injury to one-sensed beings or total non-possession is impossible; hence they observe the five lesser vows (Anuvratas: avoiding intentional injury to mobile two-to-five-sensed beings, gross falsehood, etc.), along with three subsidiary vows (Gunavratas) and four disciplinary vows (Shikshavratas), making twelve lay vows in total.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Jain canonical and ethical texts strictly prohibit undertaking Sallekhana out of emotional distress, grief, anger, fear, or worldly failure, or when one still has a normal span of healthy life remaining. Terminating life due to emotional turmoil or desire for rewards in the next birth is condemned as a sin of passion (Kashaya).

Statement 3 is correct. Acharya Samantabhadra's Ratnakaranda Shravakachara and Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra explicitly distinguish Sallekhana (Santhara) from suicide (Atmahatya). Suicide is committed under the sway of passions (attachment, aversion, anger, or delusion) and employs abrupt, violent means (poison, weapons, etc.). Sallekhana is permitted only when normal life or observance of vows becomes impossible due to incurable terminal disease, extreme senility, severe famine, or unavoidable calamity (Upasarga), and involves a serene, gradual reduction of solid food and liquids while forgiving all beings.

ref: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaranda Shravakachara; Tattvartha Sutra Ch. 7; Padmanabh S. Jaini, The Jaina Path of Purification, Ch. 6 & 7

stem: In the canonical Jain epistemological framework (Pancha Jnana), knowledge is graded according to the degree to which the soul (Jiva) overcomes karmic veils (Jnanavaraniya Karma) and transcends reliance on physical intermediaries. Consider the following stages of knowledge:
items: 1. Avadhi Jnana (Clairvoyant perception of material objects across spatial and temporal limits)
2. Mati Jnana (Sensory and mental cognition mediated through the physical sense organs and mind)
3. Manahparyaya Jnana (Telepathic cognition of the subtle mental states and thoughts of other sentient beings)
4. Shruta Jnana (Conceptual, verbal, and scriptural knowledge derived from signs, symbols, and authoritative testimony)
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct ascending epistemological hierarchy of the above stages, culminating finally in Kevala Jnana (absolute omniscience)?
core: Jain epistemology divides the five types of valid knowledge (Pancha Jnana) into indirect, sense-mediated cognition (Paroksha: Mati and Shruta) and direct, unmediated perception by the soul (Pratyaksha: Avadhi, Manahparyaya, and Kevala). Unlike Nyaya or Buddhist epistemology, early canonical Jainism classifies ordinary sensory perception (Mati Jnana) as indirect (Paroksha) because the soul perceives objects only through the external instrumentality of physical sense organs and the mind.

exp.why: Avadhi Jnana occupies the third rank in the five-fold ascending hierarchy. It is the lowest form of super-sensory direct perception (Pratyaksha) where the soul perceives material substances (Rupi Dravyas) across distance and time without the aid of sense organs or mind, upon the partial destruction-cum-subsidence (Kshayopashama) of Avadhi-jnanavaraniya karma.

Mati Jnana is the foundational first stage in the ascending hierarchy. In canonical Agamic Jainism, it is classified as Paroksha (indirect knowledge) rather than Pratyaksha, because the soul does not contact the object directly; instead, cognition is mediated through the physical sense organs (Indriya) and the mind (Anindriya/Manas) via four stages: Avagraha, Iha, Avaya, and Dharana.

Manahparyaya Jnana occupies the fourth rank, immediately below Kevala Jnana. It is a higher, subtler grade of direct perception (Pratyaksha) than Avadhi Jnana, enabling a spiritually disciplined ascetic within the human realm (Manushya-kshetra) to directly perceive the subtle mental matter (Manovargana) constituting the thoughts of other minds.

Shruta Jnana occupies the second rank in the hierarchy and is always preceded by Mati Jnana. It encompasses conceptual, linguistic, and scriptural knowledge acquired through signs, words, or Agamic canons, and like Mati Jnana, it belongs to the category of Paroksha (mediated/indirect knowledge). Thus, the ascending sequence from lowest to highest before Kevala Jnana is Mati (2) -> Shruta (4) -> Avadhi (1) -> Manahparyaya (3).

ref: Tattvartha Sutra of Umasvati, Chapter 1 (Sutras 9-12); Outlines of Indian Philosophy by M. Hiriyanna

stem: With reference to the philosophy of the Ajivika sect founded by Makkhali Gosala, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Despite rejecting the efficacy of human free will (Purushakara) and moral-karmic causality, Ajivika monks practiced severe asceticism and bodily mortification.

Statement-II: According to Ajivika cosmology, every sentient soul (Jiva) automatically attains liberation (Samsara-shuddhi) only after completing an immutable, predetermined cycle of 8,400,000 great eons (Mahakalpas).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Makkhali Gosala's doctrine of Niyati (absolute determinism) denied that human effort or penance could alter one's destiny or shorten the fixed cosmic cycle of 8,400,000 Mahakalpas required for liberation. Ajivika ascetics nevertheless practiced extreme austerities not to burn past karma or accelerate liberation, but because they held that their ascetic vocation was itself rigidly predetermined by Niyati.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Both Buddhist (Samannaphala Sutta) and Jain (Bhagavati Sutra) sources record that Makkhali Gosala denied free will (Purushakara), manly strength, and karmic causation, yet his Ajivika followers underwent extreme nakedness, dietary austerity, and fatalistic penances.

Statement-II is also correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. Under the doctrine of Samsara-shuddhi, just as a ball of thread flung out unwinds to its full length and no further, both the fool and the wise must transmigrate through exactly 8,400,000 Mahakalpas before sorrow ends. Because this fixed duration cannot be shortened by penance, this cosmological doctrine does not explain why Ajivikas practiced severe asceticism; rather, they practiced asceticism because Niyati itself necessitated their ascetic state as an unavoidable stage in the soul's predetermined trajectory.

ref: A.L. Basham, History and Doctrines of the Ajivikas; Digha Nikaya (Samannaphala Sutta)

stem: With reference to the historical trajectory and patronage of the Ajivika sect in ancient and medieval India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Emperor Ashoka dedicated rock-cut caves in the Barabar Hills to the Ajivikas, his grandson Dasharatha Maurya discontinued Ajivika patronage and dedicated the Nagarjuni Hill caves exclusively to the Mahasanghika Buddhist sect.
2. Following the collapse of the Mauryan Empire, the Ajivika sect vanished completely from the Indian subcontinent by the Gupta period, leaving no literary or epigraphic trace in South India.
3. In Chola-era Tamil inscriptions, the term Acuvika-k-kasu denotes a tax-free royal land endowment granted by the state for the maintenance of Ajivika monastic settlements.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Ajivika sect enjoyed continuous Mauryan patronage from Bindusara and Ashoka down to Dasharatha Maurya, who dedicated the Nagarjuni Hill caves to Ajivika ascetics. Far from disappearing after the Mauryas, the Ajivikas survived in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka until the 14th century CE, where their doctrines were debated in Tamil epics and their communities were subjected to a special poll tax known as Acuvika-k-kasu.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Dasharatha Maurya did not discontinue patronage to the Ajivikas; immediately upon his accession, he excavated and dedicated three rock-cut caves in the Nagarjuni Hills (Gopika, Vadathika, and Vapiyaka caves) specifically to the Ajivika ascetics (Bhadantas) for their monsoon retreat, continuing the policy of Ashoka (who had gifted the Barabar caves) and Bindusara (whose court patronized the Ajivika fortune-teller Pingalavatsa).

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Ajivika sect did not vanish by the Gupta period; it migrated southward and survived in the Palar basin (Tondaimandalam in Tamil Nadu and Kolar in Karnataka) until the 14th century CE. Tamil philosophical and literary texts such as the Manimekalai, Nilakesi, and Civanana Cittiyar preserve detailed accounts of South Indian Ajivika atomism and determinism.

Statement 3 is incorrect. In Pallava, Chola, and late medieval South Indian epigraphy (from Avani, Kanchipuram, and Tiruvorriyur), Acuvika-k-kasu (or Acuvika-k-katamai) was not a royal grant to Ajivikas, but a burdensome special poll tax or community cess levied by the state upon Ajivikas, which contributed to their eventual socio-economic decline and assimilation into Digambara Jainism and Shaivism.

ref: A.L. Basham, History and Doctrines of the Ajivikas; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 6 & 7

stem: With reference to the epistemology and metaphysics of the Charvaka (Lokayata) school of Indian philosophy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It rejected inference (Anumana) as an independent and infallible source of valid knowledge because universal invariable concomitance (Vyapti) cannot be verified across all unperceived past and future instances.

2. It accepted only four gross material elements (Mahabhutas) as the ultimate constituents of reality, rejecting Akasha (ether) on the ground that it cannot be grasped through direct sensory perception.

3. Under its doctrine of Dehatmavada, consciousness (Chaitanya) is considered an eternal, latent property residing individually within each atomic element prior to their combination into a living body.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Charvaka philosophy is grounded in radical empiricism, accepting Pratyaksha (sensory perception) as the sole Pramana and consequently rejecting both deductive/inductive inference (Anumana) and the imperceptible fifth element (Akasha). Its theory of consciousness (Bhutachaitanyavada/Dehatmavada) is strictly emergentist: consciousness does not exist in the four elements individually, but arises de novo when they combine in a specific organic configuration.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Charvakas argued that valid inference (Anumana) depends entirely on establishing Vyapti (universal, unconditional invariable concomitance between the middle term/Hetu and major term/Sadhya, such as smoke and fire). Since sensory perception can only observe present and particular instances, it can never guarantee that the relation holds universally across all unobserved times and places without circular reasoning.

Statement 2 is correct. Because Pratyaksha is the sole acceptable Pramana for the Charvaka school, only Earth (Prithvi), Water (Ap), Fire (Tejas), and Air (Vayu)—which are directly perceptible by the senses—are admitted as real Mahabhutas. Akasha (space/ether), whose existence other schools establish only through inference from sound, is rejected.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Dehatmavada and Bhutachaitanyavada, consciousness is not an eternal or pre-existing latent property inside individual material elements. Just as individual ingredients of fermentation (flour, water, molasses) possess zero intoxicating power on their own, yet produce intoxicating spirit (Mada-shakti) when combined in a specific proportion, consciousness emerges as an epiphenomenon only when the four insentient elements combine to form the physical body, and it ceases completely upon bodily dissolution.

ref: Sarvadarshanasamgraha of Madhavacharya, Chapter 1 (Charvaka-darshana); S.N. Dasgupta, A History of Indian Philosophy, Vol. III

stem: In the history of Indian philosophical thought, a heterodox tradition denied the existence of an afterlife (Paraloka), critiqued Vedic funerary rites (Shraddha) and animal sacrifices as a mere livelihood devised by priests, recognized only wealth (Artha) and sensual fulfilment (Kama) as legitimate human ends (Purusharthas) while equating liberation (Apavarga) with physical death itself, and produced the 8th-century CE radical-skeptical treatise Tattvopaplavasimha ('The Lion that Destroys All Categories') authored by Jayarashi Bhatta. Which one of the following philosophical traditions is described above?

opts.A: The Ajnanavada school of Sanjaya Belatthiputta
opts.D: The Prabhakara school of Purva Mimamsa

core: The Brihaspatya or Lokayata (Charvaka) school rejected transmigration, karma, and Vedic ritualism, reducing the four Purusharthas to Artha and Kama alone and defining Moksha simply as the dissolution of the body at death (Marana). Jayarashi Bhatta's 8th-century Tattvopaplavasimha is the sole surviving authentic Sanskrit philosophical text affiliated with this radical materialist-skeptical lineage.

exp.why: Option C is correct. Attributing its foundational sutras to Brihaspati, the Lokayata/Charvaka tradition rejected Dharma and Moksha as independent Purusharthas, declaring that Kama (pleasure) is the ultimate end and Artha (wealth) is the means to secure it, while death itself is liberation (Maranam evapavargah). It satirized Vedic Shraddha ceremonies by asking why food offered to ancestors in rituals does not satisfy travellers on a journey. Jayarashi Bhatta's Tattvopaplavasimha (8th century CE) is the only extant original text from the Lokayata camp, extending Brihaspati's critique into a radical epistemological demolition of all Pramanas across Nyaya, Mimamsa, Buddhist, and Jain schools. Option A is incorrect because Sanjaya Belatthiputta's Ajnanavada was an early 6th-century BCE Sramana agnosticism without connection to the Brihaspati sutras or Tattvopaplavasimha. Option B is a Buddhist realist school accepting karma and nirvana. Option D (Prabhakara Mimamsa), though non-theistic, upheld the absolute infallibility of Vedic ritual injunctions (Dharma).

ref: Tattvopaplavasimha of Jayarashi Bhatta; Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya, Lokayata: A Study in Ancient Indian Materialism

stem: With reference to the heterodox Sramana teachers contemporary with Gautama Buddha as documented in the Pali canonical text Samannaphala Sutta (Digha Nikaya), consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Purana Kassapa : Doctrine of Akriyavada (Amoralism asserting that neither virtuous nor violent actions generate karmic merit or demerit)
2. Ajita Kesakambali : Doctrine of Ucchedavada (Annihilationist materialism holding that a person is composed of four elements and perishes completely at death)
3. Sanjaya Belatthiputta : Doctrine of Ajnanavada (Agnostic skepticism utilizing a fourfold negation to avoid definitive metaphysical commitments)
4. Pakudha Katyayana : Doctrine of Caturyama Samvara (Fourfold ascetic self-restraint through which karmic influx is arrested and exhausted)
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Samannaphala Sutta of the Digha Nikaya records the philosophical doctrines of six prominent non-Vedic Sramana teachers addressed to King Ajatashatru of Magadha. It distinguishes Purana Kassapa's amoralism (Akriyavada), Ajita Kesakambali's materialism (Ucchedavada), Sanjaya Belatthiputta's agnosticism (Ajnanavada), and Pakudha Katyayana's eternalist seven-element atomism (Asasvatavada/Sassatavada) from Nigantha Nataputta's ascetic restraint.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. In the Samannaphala Sutta, Purana Kassapa expounds Akriyavada (the doctrine of non-action/amoralism), arguing that the soul remains completely passive and unaffected whether a person performs charity and sacrifices or commits murder and theft along the banks of the Ganga; hence there is neither Papa (demerit) nor Punya (merit).

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Ajita Kesakambali ('he of the hair-blanket') was the earliest known precursor to the Charvaka materialists, preaching Ucchedavada (annihilationism). He held that a human being is built of four elements; upon death, earth returns to earth, water to water, fire to fire, and air to air, while the senses vanish into space, leaving nothing behind after cremation.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Sanjaya Belatthiputta propounded Ajnanavada (radical agnosticism or 'eel-wriggling' Amaravikkhepika), refusing to affirm or deny unverifiable transcendental propositions (such as whether an afterlife exists) by employing a five-part or fourfold negative dialectic ('It is not A; not non-A; not both; not neither').

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. In the Samannaphala Sutta, the doctrine of Caturyama Samvara (fourfold restraint) is attributed to Nigantha Nataputta (Vardhamana Mahavira / the Nirgrantha Jain tradition). Pakudha Katyayana, by contrast, propounded eternalist seven-element atomism (Sassatavada/Asasvatavada), asserting that seven uncreated, immutable substances—Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Pleasure (Sukha), Pain (Dukkha), and the Soul (Jiva)—stand barren and immovable like mountain peaks, so that even cleaving a head with a sharp sword merely passes through the interspaces between these seven eternal elements without destroying anything.

ref: Digha Nikaya, Sutta 2 (Samannaphala Sutta); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the doctrinal and institutional differences between Jainism and Buddhism in ancient and medieval India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Buddhism rejected the existence of an eternal soul (Anatta), Jainism recognized an immortal soul (Jiva) exclusively in mobile biological organisms and regarded earth, water, fire, and wind as soulless matter (Ajiva).

2. Unlike the Buddhist Sangha which functioned primarily as an order of monks and nuns, the Jain Chaturvidha Sangha institutionally integrated the lay community (Shravakas and Shravikas) alongside ascetics.
3. The strict doctrinal conservatism of Jainism and the close supervision of householder ethics by the monastic order prevented its complete assimilation into Puranic Hinduism in India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Jainism differs structurally from Buddhism both in its pan-psychic metaphysical view of Jiva (extending soul-consciousness even to elemental earth, water, fire, and wind bodies) and in its fourfold Chaturvidha Sangha, which bound lay householders and ascetics into an interdependent institutional network that ensured its survival in India.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Unlike Buddhism (which upholds Anatta or non-soul) and even unlike orthodox Brahmanical traditions, Jain metaphysics posits that immortal souls (Jivas) inhabit not only mobile multi-sensed beings (Trasa) and plants (Vanaspatikaya), but also immobile one-sensed elemental bodies (Sthavara Ekendriya Jivas)—namely earth-bodies (Prithvikaya), water-bodies (Apkaya), fire-bodies (Tejaskaya), and wind-bodies (Vayukaya). Dead or inanimate matter (Pudgala) is Ajiva, but the natural elements themselves possess microscopic souls, which explains Jainism's extreme emphasis on Ahimsa.

Statement 2 is correct. Mahavira organized the Jain community into a fourfold order (Chaturvidha Sangha) comprising Sadhus (monks), Sadhvis (nuns), Shravakas (laymen), and Shravikas (laywomen). By prescribing a structured code of twelve lesser householder vows (including five Anuvratas) that mirrored the ascetic Mahavratas, Jainism gave the laity a formal constitutional stake in the Sangha, unlike Buddhism where the Sangha largely remained a monastic institution.

Statement 3 is correct. While Buddhism in India increasingly relied on huge royal land-grant monasteries (Mahaviharas) and converged ritually with Tantric and Puranic traditions—leading to the Buddha being absorbed as an Avatar of Vishnu—Jainism maintained sharp doctrinal boundaries, banned Vedic-style blood sacrifice and creator-god theology, and relied on resilient mercantile lay networks (Sanghas and Gachchhas) that ensured its uninterrupted survival in India.

ref: RS Sharma, Ancient India; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to Jain cosmology and its conception of the cosmic wheel of time (Kalachakra), consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Jain philosophy, the universe (Loka) is an eternal and uncreated entity regulated by universal natural laws without a creator or destroyer deity.

2. The cosmic wheel of time alternates perpetually between Utsarpini, characterized by progressive growth in human lifespan, stature, and ethics, and Avasarpini, characterized by progressive moral and physical decline.
3. According to Jain tradition, the current epoch lies within the Avasarpini half-cycle, during the third and fourth divisions (Aras) of which all twenty-four Tirthankaras of our era appeared.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Jain cosmology rejects creationism (Ishvara-kartritva-vada), viewing the Loka as beginningless and endless, while dividing cyclical cosmic time (Kalachakra) into ascending (Utsarpini) and descending (Avasarpini) half-cycles of six Aras each.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Jain philosophy categorically rejects the notion of an omnipotent Creator God (Karta). The cosmos (Loka) is composed of six eternal substances (Shad-Dravya: Jiva, Pudgala, Dharma, Adharma, Akasha, and Kala) and operates eternally through its own intrinsic nature (Svabhava) and karmic causality.

Statement 2 is correct. A full cosmic cycle (Kalpa) is divided into two endless half-cycles: Utsarpini (the ascending half-cycle in which morality, spirituality, human stature, and longevity progressively increase across six epochs or Aras from extreme misery to utmost bliss) and Avasarpini (the descending half-cycle in which these attributes progressively deteriorate from bliss to misery).

Statement 3 is correct. Humanity currently lives in the fifth Ara (Dukham-kala) of the descending Avasarpini phase. The first Tirthankara Rishabhanatha appeared toward the end of the third Ara (Sukham-Dukham-kala) when natural wish-fulfilling trees (Kalpavrikshas) declined and social institutions (Asi, Masi, Krishi) were needed, while the remaining twenty-three Tirthankaras (from Ajitanatha to Mahavira) appeared during the fourth Ara (Dukham-Sukham-kala).

ref: Tattvartha Sutra Ch. 3-4; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the contribution of Jainism to the growth of Indian languages and regional literature, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the canonical Agamas of the Shvetambara sect were preserved in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit, the early foundational texts of the Digambara sect were composed primarily in Shauraseni Prakrit.
2. Early Tamil literary classics such as the epic Civaka Cintamani and the didactic anthology Naladiyar were authored by Jain scholars.
3. The classical age of Kannada literature was pioneered by the 'Three Gems' (Ratnatraya)—Pampa, Ponna, and Ranna—all of whom composed major Jain Puranas alongside heroic epics.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: By adopting vernacular speech (Prakrit, Apabhramsha, Tamil, and Kannada) to reach the laity before later adopting Sanskrit for pan-Indian scholastic debate, Jain monks became the primary architects of early grammatical, epic, and didactic literature across western and southern India.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Mahavira preached in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit, which became the canonical language of the Shvetambara Agamas finally redacted at the Second Council of Vallabhi. Conversely, the Digambara tradition rejected the surviving Agamas and preserved its oldest sacred literature—such as the Shatkhandagama of Pushpadanta and Bhutabali and the mystical treatises (Samayasara, Pravachanasara) of Acharya Kundakunda—in Shauraseni Prakrit.

Statement 2 is correct. Jain ascetics (Samanars) made foundational contributions to Sangam and post-Sangam Tamil literature. Ilango Adigal authored Silappadikaram; Tiruttakkatevar authored the great Tamil mahakavya Civaka Cintamani (Jivaka Chintamani); and 400 four-line moral stanzas composed by Jain monks were compiled into the Naladiyar (part of the Pathinenkilkanakku).

Statement 3 is correct. In tenth-century Karnataka under Rashtrakuta and Western Chalukya patronage, the 'Three Gems' (Ratnatraya) of Kannada literature championed Jain themes: Adikavi Pampa wrote the Adipurana (on Rishabhanatha), Sri Ponna wrote the Shantipurana (on the 16th Tirthankara Shantinatha), and Ranna wrote the Ajitapurana (on the 2nd Tirthankara Ajitanatha).

ref: Nitin Singhania, Indian Art and Culture; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India

stem: With reference to the royal patronage of Jainism in ancient and early medieval India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The later Mauryan emperor Samprati is commemorated in Jain tradition as the 'Jain Ashoka' for building numerous Jain temples and facilitating the spread of Jain monks into non-Aryan regions of southern India.
2. The Rashtrakuta monarch Amoghavarsha I was a disciple of the Digambara preceptor Jinasena and authored the Sanskrit ethical work Prashnottara Ratnamalika.

3. While the Chedi king Kharavela restored the Kalinga Jina image taken away by the Nandas, the Chaulukya ruler Siddharaja Jayasimha renounced Shaivism to become a Jain monk under Acharya Hemachandra and prohibited animal slaughter across Gujarat.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Royal patronage played a decisive role in shifting Jainism's geographical strongholds from Magadha toward Kalinga (under Kharavela), western India (under Samprati and later the Chaulukya king Kumarapala), and the Deccan/Karnataka (under the Gangas and Rashtrakutas like Amoghavarsha I).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Samprati, the grandson of Emperor Ashoka who ruled from Ujjain and Pataliputra, was initiated as a Jain lay follower by the great Acharya Suhastin. Jain chronicles such as the Kalpa Sutra and Parishishtaparvan hail him as the 'Jain Ashoka' because he commissioned thousands of Jain shrines across Saurashtra, Malwa, and Rajputana and sent missionaries to Andhra and Dramila (Tamil) regions.

Statement 2 is correct. Rashtrakuta Emperor Amoghavarsha I (r. 814–878 CE) revered the Digambara monk Jinasena (author of the Adipurana). Amoghavarsha I was a scholar-king associated with the Kannada poetics work Kavirajamarga and personally composed the Sanskrit catechetical treatise Prashnottara Ratnamalika, repeatedly abdicating state duties for Jain monastic retreats.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Although the Hathigumpha inscription confirms that King Kharavela of Kalinga recovered the Kalinga Jina idol seized earlier by Mahapadma Nanda, the second half of the statement confuses Siddharaja Jayasimha with his successor Kumarapala (r. 1143–1172 CE). Siddharaja Jayasimha remained an ardent Shaiva (builder of the Rudramahalaya temple), even though he patronized Acharya Hemachandra's scholarship. It was Kumarapala who embraced Jainism under Hemachandra's guidance and enforced the Amari edicts banning animal slaughter across Gujarat, though he too ruled as a pious Jain monarch (Parama-Arhata) rather than taking monastic ordination.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7 & 10; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: Consider the following pairs of non-canonical Jain literary works, their authors, and their primary subject matter:
items: 1. Parishishtaparvan : Acharya Hemachandra — Chronicles of early Jain patriarchs and Mauryan rulers
2. Saddarshanasamuchchaya : Haribhadra Suri — Compendium of the major philosophical schools of India
3. Nitivakyamrita : Uddyotana Suri — Prakrit narrative depicting the linguistic and cultural ethnography of eighth-century India
4. Kuvalayamala : Somadeva Suri — Sanskrit treatise on royal statecraft and political ethics modeled on the Arthashastra
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: Beyond canonical scriptures, Jain scholars produced invaluable historical chronicles (Prabandhas and Charitas), non-partisan philosophical doxographies rooted in Anekantavada, ethnographic romances, and secular treatises on polity.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The Parishishtaparvan (also known as Sthaviravalicharita), composed in Sanskrit in the 12th century by the Shvetambara polymath Acharya Hemachandra as an appendix to his Trishashtishalakapurushacharita, records the biographies of early Jain elders (Sthaviras) alongside vital historical accounts of the Nandas and Mauryas (Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka, and Samprati).

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Driven by the Jain epistemological spirit of Anekantavada (intellectual non-absolutism), the 8th-century Shvetambara philosopher Haribhadra Suri authored the Saddarshanasamuchchaya ('Compendium of Six Philosophies'), which systematically and fairly summarizes Buddhist, Nyaya, Samkhya, Jaina, Vaisheshika, and Mimamsa (plus Charvaka) systems.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Nitivakyamrita ('Nectar of the Maxims of Polity') was authored by the 10th-century Digambara Jain scholar Somadeva Suri (not Uddyotana Suri) and is a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, kingship, and political ethics closely following Kautilya's Arthashastra.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Kuvalayamala was composed in Prakrit in 779 CE at Jabalipura (Jalore) during the reign of the Gurjara-Pratihara king Vatsaraja by Uddyotana Suri (not Somadeva Suri). It is a celebrated Campu-kavya (mixed prose and verse romance) famous for recording specimens of 18 regional languages (Deshabhashas) and cultural traits of 8th-century Indians.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 1 & 10; Romila Thapar, Early India

stem: With reference to the principles and evolution of Jain iconography in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Jain sculpture, Tirthankaras are depicted exclusively in either the seated lotus posture (Padmasana) or the standing meditation posture of bodily abandonment (Kayotsarga), often marked with the auspicious Srivatsa emblem on the chest.

2. Because liberated Tirthankaras have transcended cosmic existence and do not dispense worldly favours, Jain temple iconography incorporated attendant Yakshas and Yakshinis as Shaasanadevatas to address the protective and material prayers of lay devotees.

3. To differentiate the identically stylized figures of the Tirthankaras, specific cognizance emblems (Lanchhanas) were carved on their pedestals, with the Conch shell representing the first Tirthankara Rishabhanatha and the Bull representing the twenty-second Tirthankara Neminatha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Jain iconography resolves the tension between ascetic transcendence and lay devotion by portraying all 24 Tirthankaras in uniform meditative detachment (distinguished only by pedestal Lanchhanas or serpent canopies) while pairing each with dynamic Yaksha-Yakshini guardian deities (Shaasanadevatas).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Unlike Buddhist and Hindu sculptures which employ varied narrative postures (such as Tribhanga or Lalitasana) and hand gestures (Mudras), Jain Tirthankara icons represent supreme detachment (Vitaraga) and are depicted strictly in two meditative postures: seated cross-legged (Padmasana/Dhyanamudra) or standing erect with arms hanging freely without touching the thighs (Kayotsarga). From the Kushana period at Mathura onward, the Srivatsa mark on the chest became a hallmark of Jina images.

Statement 2 is correct. In Jain theology, a liberated Jina resides at the apex of the universe (Siddhashila) in omniscient bliss, completely detached from worldly affairs (neither granting boons nor answering petitions). To satisfy the psychological and devotional needs of lay worshippers seeking progeny, wealth, or protection, Jainism integrated semi-divine celestial beings—a male Yaksha and female Yakshini paired with each Tirthankara (such as Dharanendra and Padmavati for Parshvanatha, or Gomedha and Ambika for Neminatha)—as Shaasanadevatas (guardian deities of the Jina's dispensation).

Statement 3 is incorrect because it swaps the cognizance emblems (Lanchhanas) of the two Tirthankaras. Since all Tirthankaras look nearly identical (except Parshvanatha and Suparshvanatha, who have serpent hoods, and Rishabhanatha, who often has hair locks falling on his shoulders), Gupta and post-Gupta art standardized specific Lanchhanas on the pedestal: the Bull (Vrishabha) is the emblem of the first Tirthankara Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), whereas the Conch shell (Shankha) is the emblem of the twenty-second Tirthankara Neminatha (Arishtanemi). Mahavira's emblem is the Lion, and Parshvanatha's is the Serpent.

ref: NCERT Class XI, An Introduction to Indian Art; Nitin Singhania, Indian Art and Culture

stem: With reference to the early archaeological and epigraphic evidence of Jainism in ancient India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri hills opens with a Prakrit salutation to the Arihants and Siddhas, representing the earliest surviving epigraphic version of the Jain Namokar Mantra, and records King Kharavela's recovery of the Kalinga Jina image taken away by a Nanda ruler.

2. While sculpted votive tablets known as Ayagapattas were dedicated at early Jain shrines in Mathura, archaeological excavations at Kankali Tila demonstrate that the architectural tradition of erecting commemorative Stupas was absent in early Jainism and remained confined to Buddhism.
3. The polished stone torso of a Jina discovered at Lohanipur (Patna) is carved in the spotted red sandstone of the Kushana school and bears a dedicatory inscription of Emperor Kanishka.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Early Jain archaeology is testified by the Mauryan-era Lohanipur torso (Chunar sandstone with Mauryan polish), the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela (containing the earliest epigraphic Namokar Mantra formula and reference to the Kalinga Jina), and the Kankali Tila site at Mathura, which proves that early Jains also erected and worshipped Stupas alongside Ayagapattas.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. King Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription (c. 1st century BCE) at Udayagiri hills in Odisha begins with 'Namo Arihantanam, Namo Savva-Siddhanam', the earliest epigraphic attestation of the Jain Namokar (Navkar) Mantra. In its twelfth year record, it also states that Kharavela brought back the revered image of the 'Kalinga Jina' that had earlier been carried away to Magadha by King Nanda (Mahapadma Nanda).

Statement 2 is incorrect. Excavations at the Kankali Tila mound in Mathura unearthed the remains of a brick Jain Stupa (referred to in a Kushana-era inscription as a 'Devanirmita Stupa' dedicated to Suparshvanatha/Parshvanatha) alongside numerous stone votive tablets (Ayagapattas), several of which explicitly depict Jain Stupas being worshipped by celestial beings and lay devotees. Thus, Stupa architecture was practiced by early Jains and was not exclusive to Buddhism.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The famous nude male torso discovered at Lohanipur (Patna) in the posture of Kayotsarga is carved out of buff Chunar sandstone and exhibits the characteristic mirror-like Mauryan polish (dated to c. 3rd century BCE), not the spotted red sandstone of the Kushana school of Mathura, and it bears no inscription of Kanishka.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7 & 8; Epigraphia Indica Vol. XX (Hathigumpha Inscription)

stem: In the context of Jain theology and liturgical practice, which of the following statements accurately brings out the philosophical distinction between an 'Arihant' and a 'Siddha' within the fivefold hierarchy of supreme beings (Pancha Parameshthi) venerated in the Namokar Mantra?

opts.A: An Arihant is a disembodied soul residing at the apex of the universe (Siddhashila) after shedding all eight types of Karma, whereas a Siddha is an embodied teacher who retains physical existence to guide the monastic order.
opts.B: An Arihant is an embodied soul who has destroyed the four destructive (Ghati) Karmas to attain omniscience and expounds the Dharma, whereas a Siddha is a completely disembodied soul who has eradicated all eight Karmas and transcended rebirth.
opts.C: The Namokar Mantra invokes the personal names of the twenty-four Arihants to seek divine grace for the expiation of past sins, whereas Siddhas are excluded from liturgical salutation as they no longer intervene in worldly affairs.
opts.D: Every Siddha must necessarily have been a Tirthankara who founded a monastic community (Sangha) during their final earthly life, whereas one can become an Arihant solely through scriptural scholarship without attaining Kevala Jnana.

core: In the Jain Pancha Parameshthi hierarchy, an Arihant (Jina) is an embodied omniscient being who has eliminated the four destructive (Ghati) Karmas but still retains the four non-destructive (Aghati) Karmas governing bodily existence, whereas a Siddha is a completely liberated, bodiless soul at Siddhashila who has shed all eight Karmas.

exp.why: Option B is correct. In Jain karma theory, an Arihant (also called Kevalin or Jina) has destroyed the four destructive karmas (Ghati Karmas: Jnanavaraniya, Darshanavaraniya, Mohaniya, and Antaraya) to attain omniscience (Kevala Jnana) while still living in a physical body sustained by the four non-destructive karmas (Aghati Karmas: Nama, Gotra, Vedaniya, and Ayushya). Upon physical death (Nirvana), the Arihant sheds the remaining four Aghati Karmas and becomes a Siddha—a completely disembodied, liberated soul residing at the summit of the universe (Siddhashila). Option A swaps the two definitions. Option C is incorrect because the Namokar Mantra venerates the spiritual qualities/ranks of all five supreme beings (Arihants, Siddhas, Acharyas, Upadhyayas, and Sadhus) without mentioning any individual's personal name or asking for material boons. Option D is incorrect because ordinary omniscient beings (Samanya Kevalins) also become Siddhas without having been Tirthankaras, and no one can be an Arihant without attaining Kevala Jnana.

ref: Padmanabh S. Jaini, The Jaina Path of Purification, Ch. 1 & 8; NCERT Class XI Introduction to Indian Art

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the theory of Atomism (Paramanuvada) in Indian philosophical traditions:
items: Statement-I: Both Jainism and the Nyaya-Vaisheshika school hold that ultimate material atoms (Paramanus) are divided into four eternally fixed qualitative classes corresponding to earth, water, fire, and air.

Statement-II: In Jain metaphysics, the aggregation of indivisible atoms (Paramanus) into composite material bodies (Skandhas) occurs autonomously through their inherent properties of cohesiveness (Snigdha) and dryness (Ruksha), without requiring the intervention of an external Creator God (Ishvara).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike Nyaya-Vaisheshika atomism—which posits four qualitatively distinct, immutable classes of atoms (earth, water, fire, air) guided by Ishvara—Jain atomism holds that all Paramanus of Pudgala are intrinsically homogeneous and combine autonomously into Skandhas through inherent degrees of Snigdha (cohesiveness) and Ruksha (dryness).

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. While the Nyaya-Vaisheshika school divides ultimate atoms (Paramanus) into four eternally distinct qualitative classes corresponding to earth (Prithvi), water (Ap), fire (Tejas), and air (Vayu), Jain metaphysics rejects this qualitative division. According to Jainism (e.g., Tattvartha Sutra and Panchastikayasara), all ultimate atoms of matter (Pudgala Paramanus) are qualitatively homogeneous and identical in their fundamental substance; any single atom can transform its sensible qualities (touch, taste, odor, and color) and contribute to the formation of earth, water, fire, or air.

Statement-II is correct. Jain philosophy is strictly non-theistic in terms of cosmic creation and rejects the Nyaya-Vaisheshika postulate that an external Creator (Ishvara) directs atomic combination via unseen moral force (Adrishta). Instead, Jainism explains that Paramanus combine into composite aggregates (Skandhas) autonomously by virtue of their intrinsic physical polarities—cohesiveness/moisture (Snigdhatva) and dryness/roughness (Rukshatva)—whenever the difference in the degrees of these qualities meets specific thresholds.

ref: Tattvartha Sutra of Umasvati, Ch. 5; Surendranath Dasgupta, A History of Indian Philosophy, Vol. I (Jaina Philosophy & Nyaya-Vaisheshika)

stem: With reference to the doctrine of 'Lesya' (psychic coloration of the soul) in Jainism and the doctrine of 'Abhijati' (spiritual classes) in the Ajivika sect, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Jain philosophy, a soul's psychic coloration (Lesya)—ranging from black (Krishna) to white (Shukla)—is permanently fixed at birth by past karma and cannot change within a single lifetime.
2. The six Lesyas in Jainism are generated by the interaction of the soul's activities of mind, speech, and body (Yoga) with the four cardinal passions (Kashayas): anger, pride, deceit, and greed.

3. Although Makkhali Gosala's Ajivika sect also classified humanity into six color-coded spiritual categories (Abhijatis), these categories represented a deterministic hierarchy through which a soul evolved solely by the cosmic law of Niyati rather than voluntary ethical conduct.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While both Jainism and Ajivikism employed a sixfold color spectrum (black, blue, grey, red, yellow/lotus-pink, white) to classify spiritual states, Jain 'Lesyas' are dynamic moral-psychic dispositions shaped by passions (Kashayas) that change continuously through free will, whereas Ajivika 'Abhijatis' were rigid deterministic classes governed by Niyati.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. In Jainism (expounded in the Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Chapter 34), the six Lesyas—Krishna (black), Nila (blue), Kapota (grey), Tejo (red), Padma (pink/yellow), and Shukla (white)—are not permanently fixed at birth. Because Jainism upholds Kriyavada (moral agency), an individual's Lesya is dynamic and constantly fluctuates within a single lifetime depending on the purity or defilement of their thoughts, passions, and ascetic restraint.

Statement 2 is correct. Lesya is the karmic stain or psychic aura produced when the soul's vibrations through mind, speech, and body (Yoga) are tinged by the four cardinal passions (Kashayas): Krodha (anger), Mana (pride/ego), Maya (deceit), and Lobha (greed). The first three dark Lesyas (Krishna, Nila, Kapota) are inauspicious (Ashubha) and driven by intense passions, whereas the three bright Lesyas (Tejo, Padma, Shukla) are auspicious (Shubha) and reflect progressive mastery over passions.

Statement 3 is correct. As recorded in the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya and Digha Nikaya (Samannaphala Sutta), Makkhali Gosala's Ajivika system classified all beings into six color-coded spiritual classes (Chalabhiijatiyo: black, blue, red, yellow, white, and supremely white). Unlike Jainism, Ajivika doctrine held that a person's progression through these classes was strictly predetermined by Fate (Niyati) over 8,400,000 great eons (Mahakalpas) and could not be accelerated by moral effort.

ref: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Ch. 34; A.L. Basham, History and Doctrines of the Ajivikas, Ch. 13

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the socio-economic transformation of the sixth century BCE in the Gangetic plains:
items: Statement-I: The ethical emphasis on Ahimsa (non-injury) championed by Jainism and Buddhism resonated strongly with the expanding agrarian communities of the middle Gangetic basin, as the spread of iron-plough agriculture made the preservation of draught cattle economically indispensable.

Statement-II: The early Brahmanical Dharmasutras looked down upon trade and condemned lending money on interest (usury), which motivated the rising class of urban merchants and bankers (Setthis) to extend generous patronage to heterodox sects.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The sixth-century BCE heterodox movements drew support from two distinct socio-economic groups for distinct reasons: agrarian communities embraced Ahimsa because iron-plough cultivation required preserving draught cattle against Vedic sacrifices (Statement-I), while urban Setthis/Vaishyas patronized these sects because Brahmanical Dharmasutras condemned usury and mercantile pursuits (Statement-II).

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The clearing of the dense alluvial forests of the middle Gangetic plains (Eastern UP and Bihar) and deep ploughing required iron ploughshares drawn by bullocks. The proliferation of Vedic sacrifices (Yajnas) involving the large-scale slaughter of cattle decimated cattle wealth and hindered agricultural expansion. Consequently, the Jain and Buddhist doctrine of Ahimsa directly protected the material foundation of the new iron-plough agrarian economy.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. The Second Urbanization saw the rise of punch-marked coins, long-distance trade, and wealthy merchant-bankers (Setthis/Gahapatis) belonging primarily to the Vaishya varna. Because early Brahmanical Dharmasutras assigned Vaishyas a subordinate social status and condemned money-lending on interest (usury/Kusida), the mercantile class turned to Jainism and Buddhism, which validated honest wealth creation and debt repayment. While Statement-II explains urban mercantile patronage, it does not explain why agrarian communities valued cattle preservation in Statement-I.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 14 (Jainism and Buddhism); Romila Thapar, Early India, Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the classification and critique of rival philosophical schools in early Jain canonical literature, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Sutrakritanga (Suyagadamga), the second Anga of the Svetambara canon, classifies all contemporary philosophical systems into four broad categories: Kriyavada, Akriyavada, Ajnanavada, and Vinayavada, identifying Mahavira's teaching with Kriyavada.

2. The Bhagavati Sutra (Viyahapannatti) portrays Makkhali Gosala as the senior spiritual preceptor of Mahavira who ordained him into the Nirgrantha order before their doctrinal split over the theory of Syadvada.
3. In the Jain canonical classification of heterodox doctrines, 'Vinayavada' refers to the radical materialism of the Charvakas that rejected all forms of ascetic discipline and moral restraint.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Jain canonical text Sutrakritanga categorizes all philosophies into four schools—Kriyavada (Jainism's doctrine of moral agency), Akriyavada (fatalism and materialism denying karmic efficacy), Ajnanavada (agnosticism), and Vinayavada (ritualistic formalism)—while the Bhagavati Sutra records Makkhali Gosala as a former subordinate companion of Mahavira rather than his teacher.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Sutrakritanga (Prakrit: Suyagadamga), the second Anga of the Svetambara Agamas dedicated to refuting heretical doctrines, divides all philosophical schools into four major groups totaling 363 sub-sects: Kriyavada (affirming the soul, moral responsibility, and efficacy of action, championed by Mahavira), Akriyavada (denying the soul or moral efficacy of action), Ajnanavada (skepticism/agnosticism like that of Sanjaya Belatthiputta), and Vinayavada (formalistic adherence to external rules of deference).

Statement 2 is incorrect. Book XV (Saya 15) of the Bhagavati Sutra (Viyahapannatti) does not portray Makkhali Gosala as Mahavira's preceptor. On the contrary, it narrates that Gosala persistently requested Mahavira to accept him as a disciple at Nalanda, wandered with Mahavira as a subordinate companion for six years, and later broke away over the doctrine of Niyati (fatalism) and transformation (Pauttapariharavada) to falsely proclaim himself a Jina at Savatthi.

Statement 3 is incorrect. In the Sutrakritanga and Uttaradhyayana Sutra, 'Vinayavada' (the doctrine of formalistic discipline/reverence) refers to moralists who believed that salvation is achieved merely through blind, external deference and obedience (Vinaya) toward gods, kings, parents, elders, and ascetics, without possessing true metaphysical knowledge (Jnana). The radical materialism of the Charvakas (referred to as Tajjivatacchariravada, the view that the soul is identical with the body) was categorized under 'Akriyavada', not Vinayavada.

ref: Hermann Jacobi (trans.), Jaina Sutras Part II (Sutrakritanga & Uttaradhyayana), Sacred Books of the East Vol. XLV; Bhagavati Sutra Book XV

stem: With reference to Kautilya's 'Saptanga' theory of the State expounded in Book VI of the Arthashastra, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Kautilya's organic conception of the State, the seven constituent elements (Prakritis) are arranged in a descending hierarchy of political criticality, beginning with Svamin (the Sovereign) and concluding with Mitra (the Ally).

2. In his comparative analysis of state calamities (Vyasana), Kautilya places Danda (coercive military force) above Kosha (treasury) and Durga (fortified capital), arguing that fiscal resources cannot be protected without a standing army.

3. Unlike the six internal administrative limbs, Mitra (the Ally) represents the external dimension of sovereignty that bridges the Saptanga framework with the Rajamandala theory of interstate diplomacy.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Kautilya's Saptanga theory treats the seven Prakritis not as a random list, but as a strict hierarchical sequence (Svamin, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda, Mitra) where the calamity (Vyasana) of each preceding element is more grave than that of the succeeding one. Specifically, Kosha precedes and sustains Danda because a rich treasury enables the recruitment, maintenance, and loyalty of the army.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In Book VI, Chapter 1 of the Arthashastra, Kautilya enumerates the seven Prakritis in a deliberate hierarchical sequence: Svamin (King), Amatya (Ministers/Bureaucracy), Janapada (Territory and Population), Durga (Fortified Capital), Kosha (Treasury), Danda/Bala (Coercive Force/Army), and Mitra (Ally). In Book VIII (Vyasanadhikarika), he explicitly defends this sequence against earlier schools of statecraft, establishing that a calamity befalling an earlier limb in the list is more perilous than one affecting a later limb.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Kautilya explicitly places Durga and Kosha ahead of Danda in the hierarchy of Prakritis. Refuting earlier teachers who claimed Danda was more vital than Kosha, Kautilya argues in Book VIII that Danda is rooted in Kosha (koshomulo dandah): without a treasury, the army either defects to the enemy or slays its own master, whereas a full treasury allows the sovereign to raise a new army, secure allies, and maintain fortifications.

Statement 3 is correct. While Svamin, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, and Danda constitute the internal architectural pillars of the sovereign state, Mitra (the hereditary, permanent, and controllable ally) acts as the seventh constituent limb that connects internal state capacity with the geopolitical circle of states (Rajamandala) and the six-fold foreign policy (Shadgunya).

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra, Books VI & VIII; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the comparative accounts of Mauryan society and labour in Megasthenes' Indica and Kautilya's Arthashastra, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Megasthenes' Indica accurately recorded the ritual four-fold Chaturvarna hierarchy of Indian society, while further subdividing the Shudra category into three distinct occupational guilds.

2. Both Megasthenes' Indica and Kautilya's Arthashastra concur that the institution of slavery (Dasa) was completely absent in Mauryan India and that all agricultural and domestic labour was performed by free wage-earners.

3. Under the Dasakalpa regulations of the Arthashastra, an Arya who was pledged as a temporary bonded labourer (Ahitaka) permanently forfeited all rights to personal property, inheritance, and redemption upon entering servitude.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Megasthenes misunderstood Indian social organization by conflating endogamous Jati/occupational categories with the ritual Varna system (listing seven classes instead of four), and erroneously declared that 'all Indians are free and not one of them is a slave' because Indian Dasas and Ahitakas enjoyed legal rights to property, inheritance, and manumission unknown in Greek chattel slavery.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Megasthenes did not describe the four-fold Chaturvarna system. Instead, he confused occupational and administrative categories with hereditary endogamous divisions (meros/genea) and classified Indian society into seven groups: (1) Philosophers (Sophistai, comprising Brahmanas and Shramanas), (2) Cultivators (Georgoi), (3) Herdsmen and Hunters, (4) Artisans and Retail Traders, (5) Warriors/Soldiers, (6) Overseers/Inspectors (Episkopoi), and (7) Royal Councillors and Assessors.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While Megasthenes (as quoted by Arrian, Diodorus, and Strabo) famously asserted that all Indians were free and no Indian was a slave, both Buddhist Pali texts (which refer to Dasa-kammakaras) and Kautilya's Arthashastra (Book III, Chapter 13, Dasakalpa) extensively document the existence of diverse categories of slaves (such as dhvajahrita or war captives, udaradasa or those born into slavery, and atmavikrayin or self-sold slaves) engaged directly in domestic service as well as agricultural production on crown lands.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Kautilya laid down the landmark legal principle that an Arya could never be reduced to permanent chattel slavery ('na tvarya-sya dasabhavah'). Even when an Arya was temporarily pledged in distress as a bonded labourer (Ahitaka), or regarding regular Dasas under the Dasakalpa, the Arthashastra protected them from degrading work, permitted them to own and inherit property independently of their master, and guaranteed their right to manumission upon repayment of the principal debt or ransom.

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra Book III Ch. 13 (Dasakalpa); Romila Thapar, Ashoka and the Decline of the Mauryas; Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the epigraphic history of the Sudarshana Lake in Saurashtra:
items: Statement-I: The Mauryan state deployed provincial governors of diverse social and ethnic backgrounds in western India, with the Vaishya governor Pushyagupta constructing the Sudarshana Lake reservoir under Chandragupta Maurya and the Yavana governor Tushaspha adding irrigation conduits to it under Ashoka.

Statement-II: During the second century CE, the Western Kshatrapa ruler Rudradaman I repaired the breached embankments of the Sudarshana Lake entirely from his personal treasury without burdening his urban and rural subjects with forced labour (Vishti) or emergency benevolence levies (Pranaya).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Junagadh (Girnar) Rock Inscription of Rudradaman I (c. 150 CE) is a vital epigraphic record bridging Mauryan and post-Mauryan history: it confirms both the construction and upgradation of the Sudarshana Lake by Chandragupta Maurya's Vaishya governor Pushyagupta and Ashoka's Yavana governor Tushaspha, as well as its subsequent restoration by Rudradaman I without levying oppressive taxes like Vishti or Pranaya.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman I provides direct epigraphic attestation of Mauryan administrative reach in Saurashtra (Anarta-Surashtra). It records that the Sudarshana Lake was originally constructed by damming streams flowing from Mount Urjayat (Girnar) by Pushyagupta, a Vaishya who served as the provincial governor (Rashtriya) of Chandragupta Maurya, and was later adorned with irrigation conduits (pranalibhir-alamkritam) by the Yavana (Greek/Indo-Iranian) king/governor Tushaspha during the reign of Ashoka Maurya.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. The same Junagadh inscription records that in Shaka year 72 (c. 150 CE), a violent storm breached the Sudarshana embankment. Against the hesitation of his ministers, Rudradaman I rebuilt the dam three times stronger through his Pahlava governor Suvishakha, financing the massive project entirely out of his own treasury (svasmat koshat) without oppressing the Janapada with kara (extra taxes), vishti (unpaid forced labour), or pranaya (emergency benevolence levies). Because Statement-II describes a Saka restoration more than four centuries after the Mauryan construction, it does not causally explain Statement-I.

ref: Epigraphia Indica Vol. VIII (Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman); R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 18 & 20

stem: With reference to the central administrative machinery described in Kautilya's Arthashastra, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A clear institutional distinction existed between the small inner cabinet of high-ranking Mantrins (drawing 48,000 panas per annum) consulted on urgent daily statecraft and the larger deliberative Mantriparishad (whose members drew 12,000 panas per annum).
