2. While the Sannidhata functioned as the Collector-General of Revenue responsible for assessing fiscal yields across the seven heads of income (Ayasharira) such as Durga and Rashtra, the Samaharta served solely as the physical custodian of the royal treasury and state granaries (Koshthagara).

3. The apex tier of the central bureaucracy comprised eighteen key functionaries designated as Tirthas, whose integrity and official conduct were continuously monitored through an institutionalized network of secret agents (Gudhapurushas).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mauryan central fiscal administration separated revenue assessment and budgeting under the Samaharta (Collector-General) from physical custody of treasury and state storehouses under the Sannidhata (Chief Treasurer), while executive policy relied on a two-tier ministerial structure differentiating elite Mantrins from the broader Mantriparishad.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Book I and Book V of the Arthashastra differentiate between the Mantrins (an inner core of three or four top advisers including the Mantrin, Purohita, Senapati, and Yuvaraja, who had passed all four Upadha or integrity tests and received the highest salary of 48,000 silver panas per annum) and the Mantriparishad (a broader council of ministers summoned during emergencies or policy deliberations, whose members received 12,000 panas per annum). Ashoka's Rock Edict III and VI also corroborate the active role of the Parishad.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it swaps the portfolios of the Samaharta and the Sannidhata. The Samaharta was the Collector-General of Revenue who prepared the state budget and supervised revenue assessment across the seven sources of income (Ayasharira: Durga/fortified towns, Rashtra/countryside, Khani/mines, Setu/irrigation works and gardens, Vana/forests, Vraja/herds, and Vanikpatha/trade routes). Conversely, the Sannidhata was the Chief Custodian of the State Treasury and Storehouses, responsible for constructing and managing the Koshagriha (treasury), Koshthagara (granary), Kupyagriha (forest-produce store), and Ayudhagara (armoury).

Statement 3 is correct. Kautilya lists eighteen highest-ranking central officials as the Astadasha-Tirthas (also referred to as Mahamatras), encompassing the Mantrin, Purohita, Senapati, Yuvaraja, Dauvarika, Antarvamshika, Prashastri, Samaharta, Sannidhata, Pradeshtri, Nayaka, Paura, Vyavaharika, Karmantika, Mantriparishadadhyaksha, Dandapala, Durgapala, and Antapala. Their conduct was kept under surveillance by roving and stationary secret agents (Sanchara and Samstha Gudhapurushas).

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra Book I Ch. 12, Book II Ch. 5–6, Book V Ch. 3; Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: In the context of Book II (Adhyakshapracara) of Kautilya's Arthashastra, consider the following pairs of heads of economic departments (Adhyakshas) and their primary administrative portfolios:
items: 1. Sitadhyaksha : Superintendent of Crown Lands and State Agriculture
2. Lakshanadhyaksha : Superintendent of the Royal Mint and Issuance of Stamped Coins
3. Panyadhyaksha : Superintendent of Standardized Weights and Measures
4. Pautavadhyaksha : Superintendent of State Commerce, Price Regulation and Foreign Trade
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Book II of the Arthashastra outlines nearly thirty specialized economic Superintendents (Adhyakshas) who regulated state monopolies, crown agriculture (Sitadhyaksha), coinage issuance (Lakshanadhyaksha) versus currency inspection (Rupadarshaka), state commerce (Panyadhyaksha), and standardized weights and measures (Pautavadhyaksha).

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The Sitadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Crown Lands (Sita). He managed royal estates cultivated either directly through hired labourers (Karmakaras), slaves (Dasas), and convicts, or through sharecroppers (Ardhika/Svaviryopajivins) who received one-half of the harvest if they supplied their own seeds and oxen, or one-fourth to one-fifth if they contributed only physical labour.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. The Lakshanadhyaksha was the Superintendent of the Royal Mint responsible for manufacturing silver coins (pana/rupahrupa) and copper coins (mashaka/tamrarupa) stamped with royal insignia. Alongside him worked the Rupadarshaka (Examiner of Coins), who regulated currency circulation in the market and collected minting and inspection charges such as Rupika (8%), Vyaji (5%), and Parikshika (1/8%).

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Panyadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Trade and Commerce (Panya = commodities for sale), not weights and measures. He monitored demand and supply, regulated prices, fixed profit margins (5% on indigenous goods and 10% on foreign imports), and organized the centralized sale of royal merchandise (Rajapanya).

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Pautavadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Weights and Measures, responsible for manufacturing, stamping, and periodically inspecting standardized weights and balances every four months to prevent market fraud. Conversely, state commerce and foreign trade fell under the Panyadhyaksha.

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra Book II (Adhyakshapracara), Ch. 12, 16, 19 & 24; Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the fiscal and revenue terminology of the Mauryan period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Mauryan fiscal administration, Bhaga denoted the revenue derived exclusively from royal crown lands cultivated under the direct supervision of state officials, whereas Sita referred to the general land tax of one-sixth to one-fourth levied on independent peasant proprietors.

2. Udaka-bhaga was a state irrigation cess levied at graded rates ranging from one-fifth to one-third of the produce, calibrated according to the mechanical method used to lift water from rivers, tanks, or wells.

3. While Pindakara functioned as a lump-sum collective tax assessed on entire villages rather than individual holdings, Pranaya was an emergency benevolence levy that the state could impose only once during a severe fiscal crisis.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mauryan land revenue strictly distinguished between Sita (direct income from royal crown lands managed by the Sitadhyaksha) and Bhaga (the King's customary share—typically 1/6th, or modified to 1/4th or 1/8th as shown in the Rummindei Pillar Inscription—collected from privately cultivated peasant holdings in the Rashtra), supplemented by a graded water rate (Udaka-bhaga) and extraordinary levies like Pranaya.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it reverses the meanings of Sita and Bhaga. In the Arthashastra, Sita denotes the agricultural revenue derived exclusively from royal crown lands managed by the Sitadhyaksha. Conversely, Bhaga (literally 'share', categorized under Rashtra revenue) was the royal share of agricultural produce—ordinarily 1/6th (Shadbhaga), though varied between 1/4th and 1/8th as attested in Ashoka's Rummindei Pillar Edict—levied on privately cultivated peasant holdings.

Statement 2 is correct. Under the Arthashastra (Book II, Chapter 24), cultivators using irrigation water had to pay a separate water cess called Udaka-bhaga, which was strictly graded by the mode of water lifting: one-fifth (1/5) of the produce if water was lifted manually by hand (hastapravartima), one-fourth (1/4) if lifted by bullocks on shoulders (skandhapravartima), one-third (1/3) if lifted by mechanical contrivances (srotoyantrapravartima), and one-fourth (1/4) if drawn from natural channels, rivers, lakes, or tanks.

Statement 3 is correct. As explained by the commentator Bhattasvamin on the Arthashastra, Pindakara was a collective lump-sum tax assessed on an entire village or cluster of villages, paid annually in kind or cash. Pranaya (literally 'gift of affection' or benevolence) is detailed in Book V, Chapter 2 of the Arthashastra as an extraordinary emergency levy imposed by a ruler facing an acute treasury crisis; Kautilya explicitly warns that Pranaya can be levied only once and never twice, and exempts seed-lands and frontier tracts serving strategic needs.

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra Book II Ch. 6, 15, 24 & Book V Ch. 2; Rummindei Pillar Inscription; Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the judicial administration envisaged in Kautilya's Arthashastra, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The Mauryan legal architecture instituted a specialized tier of courts known as Kantakashodhana (removal of thorns), presided over by three Pradeshtris or Amatyas, alongside the regular Dharmasthiya courts presided over by three Dharmasthas.

Statement-II: The expansion of state control over economic production, trade regulation, and public order required fast-track administrative and criminal tribunals to deal with artisan fraud, official malfeasance, espionage offences, and sudden unnatural deaths (Ashumritaka-pariksha), as distinct from private interpersonal disputes.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Arthashastra bifurcated the Mauryan judiciary into Dharmasthiya (civil and personal law courts) and Kantakashodhana (criminal, regulatory, and state-security tribunals) to match the administrative demands of a centralized political economy.

exp.why: Book III and Book IV of the Arthashastra lay down a dual judicial structure: Dharmasthiya courts (presided over by three Dharmasthas proficient in sacred law alongside three Amatyas) and Kantakashodhana courts (literally 'clearing of thorns', presided over by three Pradeshtris or three Amatyas).

While Dharmasthiya courts adjudicated interpersonal disputes arising out of marriage, stridhana, inheritance, debt, deposits, and boundary disputes, Kantakashodhana courts functioned as regulatory and summary criminal tribunals. They protected the state and populace from anti-social elements ('thorns') by prosecuting malpractice by artisans, merchants, and state officials, using secret agents for entrapment of corrupt officers, and conducting forensic post-mortem inquiries into sudden unnatural deaths (Ashumritaka-pariksha). Thus, Statement-II directly explains the rationale behind Statement-I.

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra Books III & IV; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the intelligence and espionage organization (Gudhapurushas) described in the Arthashastra, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the state's intelligence verification protocol, routine reports transmitted by secret agents in coded script (Gudhalekhya) were accepted as reliable for executive action only when independently corroborated by three distinct espionage sources.

2. The Sanstha wing of intelligence comprised roving operatives such as Tikshna (assassins), Rasada (poisoners), and Parivrajika (wandering nuns), whereas the Sanchara wing consisted of stationary agents operating from fixed commercial or domestic covers.
3. Impoverished Brahman widows and female mendicants (Bhikshuki) were systematically inducted into the espionage apparatus to monitor the private households of high-ranking ministers and nobles.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Kautilya's espionage network divided secret operatives (Gudhapurushas) into stationary groups (Sanstha) and wandering agents (Sanchara), operating under strict multi-source verification protocols so that spies did not know one another.

exp.why: In the Arthashastra (Book I, Ch. 11-12), intelligence reports were transmitted via cipher writing (Gudhalekhya). To prevent fabrication or collusion, spies were kept ignorant of one another's identities, and information was treated as verified only when reports from three independent sources concurred (Trayanam ekavakyata).

The categories are swapped. Sanstha referred to stationary spies based in one location under five distinct covers: Kapatika-chhatra (fraudulent disciples/students), Udavastita (renegade ascetics), Grihapatika (householder-farmers), Vaidehaka (merchants), and Tapasa (practicing ascetics). Sanchara referred to wandering/roving spies, including Satri (classmate-spies specially trained in palmistry and magic), Tikshna (desperadoes/bravos), Rasada (poisoners), and Bhikshuki/Parivrajika (wandering nuns).

The Arthashastra explicitly recommends recruiting impoverished Brahman widows (Parivrajika) and Shudra female mendicants (Mundas/Vrishalis) into the Sanchara wing because the wives and inner quarters of high ministers (Mahamatras) revered them, granting them unimpeded access to confidential domestic conversations.

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra Book I, Ch. 11-12; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past

stem: According to the accounts of Megasthenes (as preserved in later Classical Greco-Roman writings), the municipal administration of the Mauryan capital, Pataliputra, was entrusted to a commission of thirty officials divided into six boards of five members each. Which one of the following accurately reflects a distinctive regulatory function performed by these municipal boards?

opts.A: Maintaining a mandatory vital register of both births and deaths to facilitate systematic taxation and demographic assessment, alongside stamping manufactured goods to prohibit the mixing of old and new wares.
opts.B: Minting imperial punch-marked silver Karshapanas exclusively through autonomous merchant guilds (Shrenis) without interference from royal superintendents.
opts.C: Adjudicating religious disputes among Buddhist monastic sects and enforcing the dietary prohibitions of Ashoka's Dhamma within the urban precinct.
opts.D: Collecting a uniform one-fourth share of agricultural produce from crown lands (Sita) surrounding the capital through hereditary military fief-holders.

core: Megasthenes recorded six specialized municipal committees of five members each in Pataliputra responsible for industrial crafts, foreign visitors, vital statistics (births and deaths), retail trade/weights, manufactured goods, and collection of the 1/10th sales tax (Sulka).

exp.why: Option A is correct: As recorded by Strabo citing Megasthenes' Indica, the six five-member boards governing Pataliputra looked after: (1) industrial arts and wages; (2) care, lodging, medical attendance, and surveillance of foreigners; (3) registration of births and deaths so that government levies and demographic records remained accurate; (4) retail trade, seasonal commodities, and verification of weights and measures; (5) inspection and official stamping of manufactured articles so that old and new goods were sold separately; and (6) collection of a tithe (one-tenth) on the value of all goods sold. Option B is incorrect because coinage under the Mauryas was tightly controlled by the royal Mint Master (Lakshanadhyaksha) and Examiner of Coins (Rupadarshaka), not left autonomously to guilds. Option C is anachronistic to Megasthenes (who visited during Chandragupta Maurya's reign). Option D is incorrect as Mauryan officers were salaried cash officials rather than hereditary military fief-holders.

ref: Romila Thapar, The Penguin History of Early India; Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the provincial, district, and sub-district administrative hierarchy during the Mauryan period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Ashoka's Major Rock Edict III, the Pradeshika, Rajuka, and Yukta appear as a functional triad of officers commanded to undertake quinquennial (five-yearly) tours of inspection (Anusamyana) for both administrative audit and propagation of Dhamma.

2. In the rural fiscal hierarchy below the district (Ahara or Vishaya), the Sthanika administered a larger revenue division equal to one-quarter of the janapada, whereas the Gopa functioned under him in charge of the accounts and census registers of a cluster of five to ten villages.

3. Strategic frontier and core provinces (Chakras) such as Uttarapatha (Taxila), Avantiratha (Ujjayini), Kalinga (Tosali), and Dakshinapatha (Suvarnagiri) were governed by royal princes designated as Kumaras or Aryaputras, assisted by a council of Mahamatras.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mauryan territorial administration linked imperial provinces headed by Kumaras to districts overseen by Pradeshikas, Rajukas, and Yuktas, and further down to sub-district revenue tiers managed by Sthanikas (quarter-district) and Gopas (5–10 villages).

exp.why: Major Rock Edict III explicitly directs the Yuktas (subordinate revenue/secretarial officers), Rajukas (rural land survey and judicial officers), and Pradeshikas (overall district/divisional heads) to go out on circuit (Anusamyana) every five years (or every three years in Kalinga and Ujjayini per the Separate Rock Edicts) for administrative inspection as well as instructing the populace in Dhamma.

According to the Arthashastra (Book II, Ch. 35), the Collector-General (Samaharta) divided the countryside (janapada) into four divisions, each placed under a Sthanika. Below the Sthanika, the Gopa serves as the foundational village accountant and registrar supervising five to ten villages, maintaining detailed boundaries, land-use surveys, tax exemptions, and household occupational censuses.

Ashokan inscriptions confirm that royal princes—titled Kumaras at Taxila, Ujjayini, and Tosali, and Aryaputra at Suvarnagiri—served as viceroys of major provinces (Chakras). They functioned alongside provincial councils of Mahamatras, who also received direct imperial communications from the Emperor.

ref: Ashoka's Major Rock Edict III & Separate Rock Edicts; Arthashastra Book II Ch. 35; Upinder Singh Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the ideological character of Ashoka's Dhamma as inscribed in his edicts, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Ashoka's policy of Dhamma in the Major Rock and Pillar Edicts was formulated as a non-sectarian civic and social ethic aimed at harmonizing a pluralistic empire rather than a liturgical exposition of sectarian Buddhist metaphysics.

Statement-II: The Major Rock Edicts explicitly mandate that all householders across the empire must master the Buddhist metaphysical doctrines of the Four Noble Truths (Arya Satyani) and the Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga) as a statutory condition for attaining Nirvana.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Ashoka's personal faith in the Buddhist Triratna is attested in his Minor Rock Edicts (such as Bhabru/Bairat), the Dhamma of his public Major Rock and Pillar Edicts omits sectarian theology (Four Noble Truths, Nirvana) and emphasizes social responsibility and mutual concordance (Samavaya).

exp.why: Historians such as Romila Thapar and Upinder Singh emphasize that while Ashoka was personally an upasaka (lay follower) of Buddhism—explicitly expressing reverence for the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha in the Bhabru (Bairat) Edict and policing schisms in the Schism Edicts—the public Dhamma of his Major Rock and Pillar Edicts was designed as a broad ethical code to weld together a socially, culturally, and religiously diverse empire.

Remarkably, the Major Rock and Pillar Edicts never mention core sectarian Buddhist theological doctrines such as the Four Noble Truths (Arya Satyani), the Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga), Pratityasamutpada (dependent origination), or even the ultimate Buddhist goal of Nirvana. Instead, Pillar Edict II defines Dhamma as having few sins (Apasinave), many virtuous deeds (Bahukayane), compassion (Daya), liberality (Dana), truthfulness (Sacha), and purity (Sochaye), promising the attainment of Svarga (heaven) and happiness in this world and the next.

ref: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas; Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the paternal theory of kingship and judicial reforms articulated in the Ashokan inscriptions, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the Separate Kalinga Edict I (inscribed at Dhauli and Jaugada in place of Major Rock Edicts XI–XIII), Ashoka declared that 'All men are my children' (Save munise paja mama) and cautioned city judicial officers (Nagalaviyohalakas) against arbitrary imprisonment and harshness arising from anger, impatience, or fatigue.

2. Under Pillar Edict IV, the Rajukas were granted autonomous authority in awarding honours and judicial punishments so that they could enforce uniformity in judicial procedure (Viyaohala-samata) and uniformity in punishment (Danda-samata) without fear or favour.
3. Following his remorse over the Kalinga War and commitment to non-injury (Ahimsa), Ashoka completely abolished capital punishment across the Mauryan Empire by imperial decree.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Ashoka reformed Mauryan judicial administration by warning urban magistrates against arbitrary torture (Separate Kalinga Edict I) and standardizing judicial procedure under the Rajukas (Pillar Edict IV), while retaining capital punishment with a mandatory three-day stay of execution.

exp.why: At Dhauli and Jaugada in Kalinga, Major Rock Edicts XI, XII, and XIII (which recounted the horrors of the Kalinga conquest) were omitted and replaced by Two Separate Kalinga Edicts. Separate Edict I articulates Ashoka's paternal kingship ('All men are my children') and warns the Nagalaviyohalakas (city judicial magistrates) against sudden arrest (Akasma-bandhana) or unjust torture caused by envy, anger, cruelty, hurry, or laziness.

In Pillar Edict IV (issued in his 26th regnal year), Ashoka compares the Rajukas (who ruled over hundreds of thousands of people) to skilled nurses caring for a king's child, vesting them with independent discretion in rewards (Abhihale) and punishments (Danda) to establish Viyaohala-samata (uniformity of judicial procedure) and Danda-samata (uniformity of penalties).

Ashoka did NOT abolish capital punishment. Pillar Edict IV explicitly demonstrates that the death penalty remained in force: Ashoka decreed that prisoners convicted and sentenced to death (Vadha-bandhana) were to be granted a mandatory respite of three days (Timni divasani me yote dinne), enabling their relatives to appeal to the Rajukas for clemency or allowing the condemned prisoners to observe fasts and give alms in preparation for the next world.

ref: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. I (Hultzsch); Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to Major Rock Edict XIII of Emperor Ashoka, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To publicly express his remorse before the conquered populace of Kalinga, Major Rock Edict XIII was prominently inscribed at Dhauli and Jaugada alongside the two Separate Kalinga Edicts.

2. Despite his repentance over the Kalinga carnage, Ashoka warns the forest tribes (Atavikas) in this edict that he retains the power to punish and execute them if they do not desist from lawlessness.

3. Among the five contemporary Hellenistic monarchs mentioned in the edict as recipients of Dhamma envoys, 'Turamaya' refers to Seleucus Nicator of Syria and 'Antiyoka' refers to Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Major Rock Edict XIII balances Ashoka's profound moral remorse over the Kalinga War with pragmatic imperial statecraft—deliberately omitting the edict inside Kalinga (Dhauli and Jaugada) out of political sensitivity while sternly warning internal forest tribes (Atavikas) and projecting soft power across five contemporary Hellenistic kingdoms.

exp.why: Major Rock Edicts XI, XII, and XIII were deliberately omitted from the Kalinga sites of Dhauli and Jaugada because reciting the graphic slaughter and deportation of Kalinga's people would have been politically insensitive and painful to the newly conquered populace. In their place, two Separate Rock Edicts (Kalinga Edicts I and II) were inscribed to reassure the subjects that 'all men are my children' (Savve munisse paja mama).

Ashoka's pacifism did not dismantle Mauryan coercive capacity. In Major Rock Edict XIII, he issues a direct warning to the unruly forest tribes (Atavikas) within his empire that 'even in his remorse, the Beloved of the Gods possesses the power (prabhava) to punish them,' urging them to feel ashamed of their crimes lest they be killed.

The identifications are reversed and historically mismatched: 'Antiyoka' refers to Antiochus II Theos of Syria (the Seleucid monarch, grandson of Seleucus Nicator), whereas 'Turamaya' refers to Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt. The other three Hellenistic rulers named in Major Rock Edict XIII are 'Antikini' (Antigonus Gonatas of Macedonia), 'Maka' (Magas of Cyrene), and 'Alikasudala' (Alexander of Epirus or Corinth).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Ashoka's policy of religious toleration:
items: Statement-I: In Major Rock Edict XII, Emperor Ashoka advocates 'Samavaya' (concord among religious sects) and 'Vachaguti' (restraint of speech), observing that whoever disparages other sects out of excessive devotion to their own sect actually inflicts the severest injury upon their own sect.

Statement-II: Through Major Rock Edict XII, Ashoka ceased royal patronage and cave-dwelling endowments to non-Buddhist sects like the Ajivikas and mandated that inter-sectarian assemblies be supervised exclusively by the Buddhist Sangha.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Major Rock Edict XII is the foundational charter of ancient Indian religious pluralism, rooted in the ethical logic that sectarian arrogance harms one's own faith and that true spiritual growth ('Sara-vadhi') requires mutual listening ('Bahu-sruta') and restraint of speech ('Vachaguti').

exp.why: In Major Rock Edict XII, Ashoka appeals for 'Samavaya' (concord/harmony) and 'Vachaguti' (guarding/restraint of speech), urging followers of all sects to become 'Bahu-sruta' (well-informed by listening to one another's Dhamma). He articulates the psychological and ethical insight that praising one's own sect while disparaging another on improper occasions out of sectarian attachment only damages one's own sect.

Major Rock Edict XII explicitly states that the Emperor honours all sects—both ascetics (pravrajitas) and householders (grihasthas)—with gifts and diverse forms of reverence. Furthermore, he notes that Dhamma-Mahamattas, Ithijhakha-Mahamattas (superintendents of women's affairs), and Vachabhumikas work uniformly for the promotion of all sects, and Ashoka himself donated the Barabar hill caves to the Ajivika sect.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. I (Hultzsch)

stem: In the context of the administrative machinery of the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka, specifically as laid down in Major Rock Edict VI, which one of the following best describes the role of the 'Pativedakas'?

opts.A: Ecclesiastical officers instituted in the thirteenth regnal year to oversee the welfare of prisoners and propagate Dhamma among the Yavanas, Kambojas, and Gandharas
opts.B: Provincial judicial and land-settlement commissioners vested with autonomous discretion over rewards and punishments (Abhihara and Danda) across the rural janapadas
opts.C: Royal reporters authorized to keep the Emperor informed of the affairs of the people (Jana-karya) at all hours and in all places, including the inner apartments and royal gardens
opts.D: Frontier wardens stationed along the unsubdued borderlands to conciliate forest chieftains and secure trans-regional trade routes

core: Major Rock Edict VI institutionalizes round-the-clock administrative responsiveness by empowering 'Pativedakas' (royal reporters) to bring urgent public business ('Jana-karya') and ministerial disputes directly to the Emperor regardless of his personal schedule.

exp.why: Option C is correct because in Major Rock Edict VI, Ashoka declares that previously public business (artha-kamma) and reporting were not conducted at all hours, and therefore he has instructed the 'Pativedakas' (reporters) to report the affairs of the people to him at all times and places—whether he is eating, in the inner female apartments (orodhana), in the inner chamber (gabhagara), at the cattle-shed (vracha), in the palanquin, or in the pleasure gardens. Option A describes the 'Dhamma-Mahamattas' (Major Rock Edict V); Option B describes the 'Rajukas' (Major Rock Edict III and Pillar Edict IV); and Option D describes the 'Anta-Mahamattas' (Pillar Edict I and Separate Kalinga Edicts).

ref: NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I, Theme 2; Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the Minor Rock Edicts and Commemorative Pillar Inscriptions of Ashoka, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While most edicts refer to the Emperor by his titles 'Devanampiya' and 'Piyadassi', his personal name 'Ashoka' explicitly appears in the Minor Rock Edicts at Maski, Gujarra, Nittur, and Udegolam.

2. In the Bhabru-Bairat Minor Rock Edict, Ashoka addresses the Buddhist Sangha directly, declares his reverence for the Triratna (Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha), and recommends specific canonical Buddhist texts for study.

3. The Rummindei Pillar Inscription records that during his visit to Lumbini in his twentieth regnal year, Ashoka granted the village a complete exemption from both the religious tribute (Bali) and the royal share of agricultural produce (Bhaga).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Minor Rock Edicts (Maski, Gujarra, Nittur, Udegolam, Bhabru) establish Ashoka's personal identity and personal Buddhist faith, the Rummindei Pillar Inscription provides critical fiscal evidence differentiating two distinct Mauryan agrarian taxes—'Bali' (completely remitted) and 'Bhaga' (reduced to one-eighth).

exp.why: For decades after James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi edicts in 1837, 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' was linked to Ashoka primarily through Sri Lankan chronicles (Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa). The discovery of the Maski Minor Rock Edict in 1915, followed later by Gujarra (Madhya Pradesh), Nittur, and Udegolam (Karnataka), confirmed the identification by explicitly engraving his personal name 'Ashoka'.

Unlike the general public edicts dealing with broad civic morality (Ashokan Dhamma), the Bhabru-Bairat (Calcutta-Bairat) Minor Rock Edict III is overtly sectarian and Buddhist in character: Ashoka salutes the Sangha, professes his faith in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, and lists seven Dhamma-paliyayas (canonical Buddhist passages) for recitation by monks, nuns, and laypersons.

The Rummindei (Lumbini) Pillar Inscription states 'Lumbini-game ubalike kate atthabhagiye cha'—meaning that because the Buddha Sakyamuni was born there, the village of Lumbini was made free of 'Bali' (ubalike, completely exempted from the obligatory tribute/cess) and required to pay only a one-eighth share of 'Bhaga' (atthabhagiye, a concessionary reduction of the regular agricultural produce tax, not a total exemption from Bhaga).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past

stem: With reference to the scripts, languages, and paleographic features of Ashokan inscriptions, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Major Rock Edicts at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in the north-western frontier are composed in the Aramaic language and engraved in the right-to-left Kharosthi script.

2. A portion of the Minor Rock Edict at Yerragudi in Andhra Pradesh exhibits the 'boustrophedon' style, wherein consecutive lines of the Brahmi script are written alternately from left to right and from right to left.
3. The Shar-i-Kuna edict discovered at Kandahar is a bilingual inscription engraved in Sanskrit and Greek to address both Brahmanical scholars and Hellenistic settlers.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Ashokan epigraphy adapted its linguistic and graphic medium to local audiences across the empire: Prakrit in Brahmi across peninsular and gangetic India (with a rare boustrophedon variant at Yerragudi), Gandhari Prakrit in right-to-left Kharosthi at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, and Greek and Aramaic in the north-western borderlands of Kandahar and Taxila.

exp.why: While the script used at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (in modern Pakistan) is indeed the right-to-left Kharosthi script (derived from Aramaic), the language of these two edicts is Prakrit (specifically northwestern Gandhari Prakrit), not the Aramaic language.

At Yerragudi (Erragudi) in Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh, sections of the Minor Rock Edict are engraved in the 'boustrophedon' ('ox-turning') manner—running left to right on one line and right to left on the next—making it a notable paleographic anomaly within Ashokan Brahmi inscriptions.

Sanskrit was never used in any Ashokan inscription. The famous Shar-i-Kuna bilingual rock inscription at Kandahar (Afghanistan) is engraved in Greek and Aramaic (both languages and scripts), catering to the Yavana (Greek) and Iranian/Kamboja populations of Arachosia.

ref: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following pairs of Ashokan Pillar Inscriptions and their distinctive epigraphic contents:
items: 1. Delhi-Topra Pillar Edict VII : Comprehensive retrospective summary of Dhamma measures found on no other Ashokan pillar
2. Pillar Edict V : Recording of donations of mango groves and alms-houses by the Second Queen Karuvaki, mother of Prince Tivara
3. Allahabad-Kosam Queen's Edict : Exhaustive code declaring specific species of birds, fish, and quadrupeds inviolable (Avadhya) on designated lunar days
4. Nigalisagar Pillar Inscription : Commemoration of the Emperor's visit and enlargement of the stupa of Buddha Konakamana to double its original size
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Ashoka's Pillar Inscriptions fall into administrative/ethical Pillar Edicts (PE I–VII) and specialized commemorative/donative inscriptions: PE VII (unique to Delhi-Topra) summarizes his entire reign's welfare works, PE V codifies wildlife protection, the Allahabad-Kosam Queen's Edict records Queen Karuvaki's charities, and Nigalisagar documents early stupa cult patronage.

exp.why: While Major Pillar Edicts I to VI are inscribed across multiple pillars (such as Delhi-Meerut, Lauriya-Araraj, Lauriya-Nandangarh, Rampurva, and Allahabad-Kosam), Pillar Edict VII—composed in Ashoka's 27th regnal year as a comprehensive retrospective review of his public welfare works (banyan trees, mango groves, rest houses, wells at every half-kos) and Dhamma-sadhana—is engraved exclusively on the Delhi-Topra pillar.

Pillar Edict V does not deal with Queen Karuvaki's donations; rather, Pillar Edict V (issued in the 26th regnal year) contains the famous proto-environmental code declaring a wide list of birds, aquatic creatures, and quadrupeds inviolable (Avadhya), forbidding the caponizing of cocks and the burning of husks/forests containing living creatures, and banning animal slaughter on Chaturmasya and Uposatha lunar days.

The Queen's Edict on the Allahabad-Kosam Pillar (originally at Kausambi) instructs the Mahamattas everywhere that whatever gifts are made by the Second Queen (Dutiyaye Deviye) Karuvaki, the mother of Tivara (Tivala-mata)—whether mango groves, gardens, alms-houses (dana-gahe), or anything else—shall be officially registered in her name to earn her merit.

The Nigalisagar (Nigali-Sagar) commemorative pillar inscription in the Nepal Terai records that in his 14th regnal year, Ashoka enlarged the stupa of the mythical past Buddha Konakamana (Kanakamuni) to double its original size, and in his 20th regnal year came in person to offer reverence and erect a stone pillar.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka

stem: With reference to Emperor Ashoka's relationship with the Buddhist Sangha and the administration of monastic discipline, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: In the wake of the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra, Emperor Ashoka assumed the supreme ecclesiastical title of 'Sangharaja' and personally rewrote the monastic code of the Vinaya Pitaka to prevent sectarian splits.

Statement-II: Through the Schism Edicts issued to the Mahamattas at Kaushambi, Sanchi, and Sarnath, Ashoka ordered that any monk or nun who caused division (Sanghabheda) in the united Buddhist Sangha be dressed in white robes (odatani dusani) and made to reside in a non-monastic dwelling (anavasasi).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Emperor Ashoka remained a lay Buddhist (Upasaka) and never claimed ecclesiastical ordination or rewrote the Vinaya Pitaka, he exercised sovereign state authority through the Schism Edicts to enforce existing Vinaya penalties against monks and nuns causing Sanghabheda.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. As recorded in the Minor Rock Edicts and the Bhabru (Bairat) Edict, Ashoka remained a lay follower (Upasaka) who expressed veneration for the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha. He never assumed any priestly or ecclesiastical office such as 'Sangharaja', nor did he rewrite the Vinaya Pitaka. At the Third Buddhist Council in Pataliputra, ecclesiastical proceedings were presided over by the elder Moggaliputta Tissa, who compiled the Kathavatthu (added to the Abhidhamma Pitaka) to refute heretical doctrines.

Statement-II is correct. In the Pillar Edicts known as the Schism Edicts (found at Allahabad-Kaushambi, Sanchi, and Sarnath), Ashoka instructed his provincial and city Mahamattas to preserve the unity of the Sangha. Any monk (bhikkhu) or nun (bhikkhuni) who created a schism (Sanghabheda) was to be stripped of monastic saffron robes, dressed in white garments (odatani dusani) signifying reversion to lay status, and expelled to reside outside the monastic residence (anavasasi).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas

stem: With reference to the rock-cut cave architecture and epigraphy of the Barabar and Nagarjuni hills in Bihar, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Sudama and Karna Chaupar caves in the Barabar hills contain inscriptions of Emperor Ashoka recording their dedication to the ascetics of the Ajivika sect.
2. The three caves in the adjacent Nagarjuni hills—Gopi, Vapiyaka, and Vadathika—were excavated and donated to the Ajivikas by Chandragupta Maurya prior to his abdication.
3. These early Mauryan caves are characterized by a mirror-like polish on hard granite interiors and architectural features replicating timber prototypes.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Barabar and Nagarjuni hill caves represent the earliest surviving rock-cut architecture in India, dedicated to the deterministic Ajivika sect by Emperor Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha Maurya respectively.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In the Barabar hills (Jehanabad district, Bihar), the Sudama (Banyan Tree) cave and the Karna Chaupar (Supiya) cave bear Brahmi inscriptions of King Piyadassi (Ashoka) dated to his 12th and 19th regnal years respectively, recording their gift as rainy-season retreats to the Ajivika ascetics.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The three caves in the Nagarjuni hills (Gopi or Gopika, Vapiyaka, and Vadathika) were excavated and dedicated to the Ajivika ascetics by Ashoka's grandson and successor, Dasharatha Maurya, immediately upon his coronation (abhisheka), and not by Chandragupta Maurya. Notably, Dasharatha also used the royal title 'Devanampiya' in these dedicatory inscriptions.

Statement 3 is correct. Carved out of extremely hard gneissic granite, the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves exhibit the hallmark Mauryan mirror-like burnished interior polish. Furthermore, their structural layouts—such as the circular vaulted chamber of the Sudama cave mimicking a thatched hut and the carved chaitya-arch facade of the Lomas Rishi cave showing wooden lattice rafters—closely imitate contemporary freestanding timber and thatch architecture.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art

stem: In the context of the administrative and economic history of ancient India, the early Brahmi inscriptions discovered on a copper plate at Sohgaura (Gorakhpur district) and a limestone plaque at Mahasthan (ancient Pundranagara)—featuring symbols such as three-storeyed granaries, crescent-on-hill, and tree-in-railing—primarily provide epigraphic evidence for which of the following?

opts.A: Royal charters granting tax-free land endowments (Brahmadeya) and judicial immunity to Vedic hermitages
opts.B: Administrative directives for state-sponsored famine relief through the distribution of grain and cash advances from royal storehouses (Koshthagara) during times of acute distress (Atyayika)
opts.C: The regulation of maritime customs duties and the maintenance of riverine lighthouses along the Ganga-Brahmaputra trade artery
opts.D: The standard weights, alloy purity ratios, and punitive fines prescribed for private merchant guilds minting silver punch-marked coins

core: The Sohgaura copper plate and Mahasthan stone plaque inscriptions are vital early Mauryan paleographic records confirming the state's maintenance of buffer granaries (Koshthagara) for famine relief, corroborating Kautilya's Arthashastra.

exp.why: Option B is correct. Both the Sohgaura copper plate (from Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh) and the Mahasthan fragmentary limestone plaque (from Bogra district, Bangladesh, corresponding to ancient Pundranagara) are written in Prakrit using early Brahmi script of the Mauryan period (often attributed to the reign of Chandragupta Maurya). The Sohgaura plate bears visual depictions of two three-storeyed pillared granaries (Koshthagara) alongside Mauryan punch-marked coin motifs like the crescent-on-arched-hill and tree-in-railing, and orders the Mahamattas of Sravasti to distribute grain from royal storehouses only during seasons of drought or acute distress (Atyayika). Similarly, the Mahasthan plaque instructs the administrator of Pundranagara to advance paddy and cash coins (Gandaka/Kakanika) from the state treasury to the Samvangiyas during an emergency, to be replenished when prosperity returns. Options A, C, and D are incorrect as land-grant copper plates (Brahmadeya) emerged much later under the Satavahanas and Guptas, and neither inscription deals with maritime lighthouses or minting purity rules.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 18; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the monetary system and craft guilds (Shrenis) during the Mauryan period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the administrative framework of the Arthashastra, the salaries of state officials were stipulated in silver punch-marked coins called Panas, and an officer termed Rupadarshaka examined the validity and circulation of currency.
2. The imperial silver Karshapana coins issued by the Mauryan state bore the die-struck portrait of the reigning emperor on the obverse along with bilingual Prakrit and Greek legends.
3. Under the centralized Mauryan economy, artisan and merchant guilds (Shrenis) were stripped of their customary internal rules and prohibited from registering legal agreements.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mauryan monetization relied on uninscribed silver punch-marked coins (Panas/Karshapanas) bearing geometric and natural symbols rather than royal portraits or legends, supervised by the Lakshanadhyaksha and Rupadarshaka.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Kautilya's Arthashastra outlines a monetized bureaucracy where cash salaries were paid in silver Panas (ranging from 48,000 Panas per annum for top officials like the Mantrin, Purohita, and Senapati down to 60 Panas for lowest-tier staff). While the Lakshanadhyaksha served as the superintendent of the royal mint, the Rupadarshaka (examiner of coins) inspected coins in circulation, collected seigniorage/testing fees (Rupika and Vyaji), and detected counterfeit currency.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Mauryan silver punch-marked coins (Panas or Karshapanas, weighing 32 rattis or approx. 3.4–3.6 grams) carried only punched symbols—typically a combination of five marks including the sun, the six-armed symbol (Shadara-chakra), the peacock-on-arched-hill, and the crescent-on-hill. They never bore royal portraits, names of kings, dates, or written legends. Die-struck portrait coins with bilingual Greek and Prakrit legends were introduced into north-western India later by the Indo-Greek rulers.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Although the Mauryan state regulated weights, measures, and market tolls through superintendents like the Panyadhyaksha and Samsthadhyaksha, artisan and merchant guilds (Shrenis or Sanghas) retained significant internal autonomy. In Book III of the Arthashastra, guild laws and customs were recognized in settling disputes among members, guilds were allocated dedicated residential quarters inside fortified cities, and guild heads (Jyeshthakas/Pramukhas) could enter into legally enforceable contracts with state and private actors.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; Kautilya's Arthashastra Book II & IV

stem: With reference to the legal provisions governing marriage, women's property, and social classes in Book III (Dharmasthiya) of Kautilya's Arthashastra, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It permitted the dissolution of marriage (Moksha) by mutual consent on grounds of mutual enmity in the four non-orthodox forms of marriage, and allowed a deserted wife to utilize her Stridhana for household sustenance during distress.

2. In its laws on servitude (Dasa-kalpa), it explicitly included Shudras within the legal category of 'Arya' to protect free-born Shudras from arbitrary enslavement and favoured settling Shudra cultivators in newly established crown villages (Janapadanivesha).

3. It imposed an absolute prohibition on the remarriage of widows and wives of long-absent husbands across all forms of marriage, mandating the permanent escheat of their maintenance to the royal treasury.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike the rigid orthodoxy of later Dharmashastras, Kautilya's Arthashastra adopted a pragmatic legal approach that permitted divorce (Moksha) by mutual consent in non-orthodox marriages, regulated widow remarriage, and protected free-born Shudras from arbitrary enslavement.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In Book III, Chapter 3 of the Arthashastra, Kautilya stipulates that while the first four orthodox (Dharmya) forms of marriage (Brahma, Prajapatya, Arsha, and Daiva) cannot be dissolved, divorce (Moksha) is legally permissible in the remaining four non-orthodox forms (Gandharva, Asura, Rakshasa, and Paishacha) by mutual consent of both husband and wife on the ground of mutual hatred/enmity (paraspara-dveshat mokshah). It also recognized a woman's Stridhana (consisting of maintenance endowment up to 2,000 Panas and jewellery), allowing her to draw upon it to maintain her son, daughter-in-law, or herself if her husband left without making provision or during famine and calamity.

Statement 2 is correct. In Book III, Chapter 13 (Dasa-kalpa), Kautilya explicitly defines a free-born Shudra as an 'Arya-prana' (having the life/status of an Arya, alongside Brahmana, Kshatriya, and Vaishya) and prescribes graduated monetary fines for anyone selling or pledging a minor Arya (including a Shudra) into slavery, declaring that 'never shall an Arya be subjected to slavery' (na tvevaryasya dasabhavah). Furthermore, in Book II (Janapadanivesha), Kautilya recommends settling newly cleared crown lands predominantly with Shudra agriculturists (Shudra-karshaka-prayam).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Far from imposing an absolute ban on remarriage, Book III, Chapters 2 and 4 of the Arthashastra lay down detailed rules permitting the remarriage (Nivesha) of widows as well as wives whose husbands have gone abroad or deserted them for specified waiting periods (ranging from one year to several years depending on whether she has borne children and whether maintenance was provided). A widow only forfeited the bride-price/endowment given by her late husband's family if she remarried outside her father-in-law's consent; her property was not escheated to the state.

ref: Patrick Olivelle, King, Governance, and Law in Ancient India: Kautilya's Arthashastra (Book III); Upinder Singh, Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following pairs of Mauryan archaeological and epigraphic sites and their distinctive discoveries:
items: 1. Kanaganahalli (Sannati, Karnataka) : Limestone relief slab bearing a sculpted portrait of Emperor Ashoka with the Brahmi label 'Raya Asoko' (Ranyo Ashoka)
2. Kumrahar (Patna, Bihar) : Remains of an 80-pillared assembly hall with polished Chunar sandstone columns
3. Dhauli (Khordha, Odisha) : Rock-cut forepart of an elephant emerging from living rock alongside the Separate Kalinga Edicts
4. Panguraria (Sehore, Madhya Pradesh) : Monastic rock shelter bearing a Minor Rock Edict addressed by Ashoka to a royal prince (Kumara) named Samva
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: Major Mauryan and post-Mauryan excavations at Kanaganahalli, Kumrahar, Dhauli, and Panguraria provide material and epigraphic corroboration of Ashoka's historical portraiture, imperial architecture, artistic symbolism, and provincial governance through royal princes.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Excavations at the Mahastupa of Kanaganahalli (near Sannati on the banks of the Bhima river in Kalaburagi district, Karnataka) yielded a unique Satavahana-period limestone sculptural slab depicting Emperor Ashoka accompanied by his queens and female attendants, explicitly identified by the inscribed Brahmi label 'Raya Asoko' / 'Ranyo Ashoka' (King Ashoka)—the only known inscribed stone portrait of the Mauryan emperor.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Excavations at Kumrahar (ancient Pataliputra, Patna) conducted by D.B. Spooner and later A.S. Altekar and V. Mishra uncovered the remains of a monumental Mauryan 80-pillared hall (organized in rows of monolithic polished Chunar sandstone pillars resting on a massive timber substructure and wooden floor).

Pair 3 is correctly matched. At Dhauli (ancient Toshali, on the banks of the Daya river in Odisha), directly above the inscribed rock surface bearing Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts (where Edicts XI, XII, and XIII are replaced by the two Separate Kalinga Edicts), the forepart of an elephant (Gajatama) was sculpted directly out of the living rock to symbolize the Buddha.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. At the monastic rock-shelter complex of Panguraria (Saroo-Maroo, Sehore district, Madhya Pradesh), a version of Ashoka's Minor Rock Edict I is prefaced by a unique royal directive in which the king addresses a prince (Kumara) named Samva while the prince was travelling towards the monastery of Upunitha-vihara in Manema-desha.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; ASI Excavations at Kanaganahalli

stem: With reference to the structural and stylistic differences between the Mauryan pillars of Ashoka and the Achaemenid pillars of Persepolis, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Like the Achaemenid columns at Persepolis, Ashokan pillars were constructed by joining multiple fluted cylindrical stone drums resting upon a stepped square plinth.
2. While Achaemenid pillars functioned as architectural supports for vast palace halls, Ashokan pillars were erected as independent, free-standing monuments in open spaces.
3. The shafts of Ashokan pillars were predominantly carved out of buff-coloured Chunar sandstone and finished with a characteristic mirror-like lustrous polish.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Ashokan pillars are monolithic, smooth (un-fluted), tapering sandstone shafts erected directly in the ground without a stepped base as free-standing commemorative monuments, whereas Achaemenid columns were multi-segment fluted masonry structures resting on bases to support palace ceilings.

exp.why: This statement reverses the structural features of the two traditions. Achaemenid pillars at Persepolis and Susa were built in segments by joining several fluted masonry drums placed upon an elaborate bell-shaped or stepped stone base. In contrast, Ashokan pillars are monolithic (carved from a single block of stone), have a completely smooth, un-fluted, gently tapering circular shaft, and were buried directly into the earth on an underground foundation stone without any visible sub-base or plinth at ground level.

Achaemenid columns were integral load-bearing components of vast hypostyle palace complexes (such as the Apadana hall at Persepolis). Ashokan pillars, conversely, served no load-bearing architectural function; they were erected as freestanding monumental pillars (Dhamma-thambhas) along sacred pilgrimage sites and arterial highways to proclaim imperial edicts and Buddhist symbolism.

Mauryan imperial pillars were quarried primarily at Chunar (near Varanasi) from fine-grained, buff-coloured sandstone (occasionally spotted red and white sandstone from Mathura in the region around Delhi) and were treated with the famous Mauryan mirror-like surface polish (opadarsha).

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 3 (Arts of the Mauryan Period); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7

stem: Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts were strategically engraved along the outer frontiers, coastal ports, and arterial trade corridors of the Mauryan Empire. Consider the following Major Rock Edict sites:
items: 1. Girnar
2. Kalsi
3. Yerragudi
4. Sopara
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of the above sites when arranged from North to South?
core: Ashoka positioned his fourteen Major Rock Edicts at strategic frontier and trade nodes spanning the subcontinent—from Kalsi in the Himalayan foothills of Uttarakhand (~30.5° N), through Girnar in Saurashtra (~21.5° N) and the western port of Sopara (~19.4° N), down to Yerragudi in the Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh (~15.2° N).

exp.why: Girnar (Junagadh district, Gujarat) is located at approximately 21.52° N latitude in the Saurashtra peninsula. It served as the western provincial node near Lake Sudarshana (constructed under Chandragupta Maurya's governor Pushyagupta and furnished with conduits by Ashoka's Yavana governor Tushaspha).

Kalsi (Dehradun district, Uttarakhand) is located at approximately 30.52° N latitude at the confluence of the Yamuna and Tons rivers in the Siwalik foothills, marking the northern sub-Himalayan frontier node of the Uttarapatha trade network among the four given sites.

Yerragudi (Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh) is situated at approximately 15.20° N latitude in the southern Deccan gold-and-diamond bearing corridor (near Suvarnagiri), making it the southernmost Major Rock Edict site on the list.

Sopara (ancient Shurparaka, Palghar district, Maharashtra) lies on the Konkan coast north of Mumbai at approximately 19.42° N latitude, south of Girnar (21.52° N) and north of Yerragudi (15.20° N), where fragments of Major Rock Edicts VIII and IX were discovered at this premier western maritime port.

ref: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Map 7.2 (Distribution of Ashoka's Inscriptions)

stem: With reference to the Mauryan state policy of settling virgin lands (Janapadanivesha / Sunyanivesha) and forest management as prescribed in Kautilya's Arthashastra, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Newly established villages were to be populated predominantly with Shudra cultivators (Shudra-karshaka-praya) transferred from overpopulated regions, and the state was empowered to confiscate land from peasants who failed to cultivate their plots.
2. To expand the agrarian revenue base rapidly, the Arthashastra encouraged private entrepreneurs to clear elephant forests (Nagavana) and convert them into tax-exempt private estates.

3. To promote cultural integration in newly colonized tracts, the Arthashastra mandated the construction of public pleasure gardens, theatrical halls, and monasteries for wandering ascetic orders inside every new revenue village.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Book II, Chapter 1 (Janapadanivesha) of the Arthashastra outlines a tightly regulated agrarian colonization policy in which the state settled Shudra cultivators on virgin lands under strict cultivation obligations, strictly prohibited the clearance of strategic elephant forests (Nagavana), and barred non-Vanaprastha ascetics, theatrical troupes, and pleasure gardens from new villages to prevent any distraction of peasant labour.

exp.why: In Arthashastra 2.1, Kautilya stipulates that new villages (ranging from 100 to 500 families, situated one or two kroshas apart) should be settled predominantly with industrious Shudra agriculturists (Shudra-karshaka-praya) induced to migrate from overpopulated regions or brought from outside. While the state advanced grain (dhanya), cattle (pashu), and cash (hiranya) to be repaid conveniently, lands allotted to taxpayers (karada) were held strictly on condition of cultivation: if a peasant failed to till the land, the state confiscated it and reassigned it to another cultivator or to village labourers (gramabhritaka) and traders.

Kautilya drew a sharp strategic distinction between productive timber/material forests (Dravyavana) and war-elephant preserves (Hastivana / Nagavana) established along the frontiers. Because war elephants were the backbone of the Mauryan military, elephant forests were strictly protected by the Superintendent of Elephant Forests (Nagavanadhyaksha) and forest guards (Vanapala); private clearance was forbidden and anyone killing an elephant was subject to capital punishment.

Far from mandating pleasure gardens and ascetic monasteries inside newly settled villages, Arthashastra 2.1.32–35 explicitly prohibits non-Vanaprastha wandering ascetics (pravrajita), actors (nata), dancers (nartaka), singers, musicians, and bard troupes from entering newly colonized villages, and forbids the construction of public halls for entertainment or pleasure gardens (arama), so that cultivators would not be distracted from agricultural work and treasury replenishment.

ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra, Book II, Ch. 1 (Janapadanivesha) & Ch. 2 (Bhumichhidravidhana); R.P. Kangle, The Kautilya Arthasastra Part II

stem: With reference to provincial administration and internal governance challenges in the Mauryan Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. According to the Buddhist text Divyavadana, the citizens of Takshashila revolted during the Mauryan period not out of hostility toward the Emperor or the royal prince (Kumara), but against the oppression of wicked officials (Dushtamatyas).

2. In his Separate Kalinga Rock Edict I, Ashoka admonished city judicial officers (Nagaravyavaharikas) against arbitrary imprisonment and torture, and instituted the periodic inspection and rotation (Anusamyana) of officials every three years at Takshashila and Ujjayini.

3. Following the disturbances in the north-western province, Ashoka abolished the office of the royal viceroy (Kumara) and placed all frontier provinces under the direct day-to-day supervision of the municipal boards of Pataliputra.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Both Buddhist literary accounts (Divyavadana) and Ashoka's own epigraphs (Separate Kalinga Edict I) confirm that bureaucratic high-handedness in distant provinces like Takshashila was a major structural strain in the Mauryan Empire, prompting Ashoka to institute triennial and quinquennial official circuits (Anusamyana) under the provincial Kumaras rather than abolishing provincial viceroyalties.

exp.why: The अशोकavadana (part of the Divyavadana) records that when Prince Ashoka (during Bindusara's reign) and later Prince Kunala (during Ashoka's reign) were sent to quell rebellions at Takshashila (Taxila), the townspeople welcomed the prince and explicitly stated: 'We are not opposed to the Kumara nor even to King Bindusara, but the wicked ministers (Dushtamatyas) come and insult us.'

In Separate Rock Edict I (at Dhauli and Jaugada), Ashoka directly addresses the Mahamattas and judicial officers of the city (Nagaravyavaharikas), warning them against sudden anger, haste, and unprovoked imprisonment or torture (akasma bandhana-parikilesa). To check administrative abuse, he ordered the Mahamattas to go out on tour (Anusamyana / Niskramana) every five years in the core provinces, while the Prince (Kumara) at Ujjayini and at Takshashila was required to dispatch officers on such tours every three years.

Ashoka never abolished the office of the royal viceroy (Kumara or Aryaputra). Separate Rock Edicts I and II as well as Minor Rock Edict I at Brahmagiri explicitly confirm that royal princes continued to govern key provincial capitals—namely Tosali (Kalinga), Ujjayini (Avanti), Takshashila (Uttarapatha), and Suvarnagiri (Dakshinapatha)—assisted by provincial Mahamattas.

ref: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas, Ch. 4 & 7; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the cadre of Dhamma-Mahamattas instituted by Emperor Ashoka:
items: Statement-I: Following their creation in the thirteenth regnal year of Ashoka, the Dhamma-Mahamattas superseded the Mantriparishad as the supreme military command over the Mauryan standing army and confined their welfare duties to Buddhist monastic establishments.

Statement-II: As recorded in Major Rock Edict V and Pillar Edict VII, the Dhamma-Mahamattas were empowered to operate across all religious sects—including Brahmanas, Ajivikas, and Nirgranthas—as well as among frontier communities such as the Yonas, Kambojas, and Gandharas, and within the households of Ashoka's own royal relatives.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Instituted in Ashoka's 13th regnal year (Major Rock Edict V), the Dhamma-Mahamattas possessed an extraordinary pan-sectarian and social jurisdiction covering the Buddhist Sangha, Brahmanas, Ajivikas, Nirgranthas, western frontier peoples, prisoners, and the royal household itself, but they remained distinct from both the military command and the advisory Mantriparishad.

exp.why: The Dhamma-Mahamattas neither replaced the Council of Ministers (Mantriparishad—which is explicitly attested as an active consultative body in Major Rock Edicts III and VI) nor exercised military command over the standing army. Furthermore, their duties were never confined to Buddhist monasteries; they were explicitly charged with promoting concord, charity, judicial clemency for prisoners with families or advanced age, and ethical conduct across all communities.

Major Rock Edict V and Pillar Edict VII explicitly state that the Dhamma-Mahamattas were occupied with the affairs of all major religious sects (Savva-pasandesu)—specifically naming the Buddhist Sangha, Brahmanas, Ajivikas, and Nirgranthas (Jains)—and worked among the Yonas (Greeks), Kambojas, Gandharas, Rishtikas, and Pitinikas on the western borderlands, as well as inside the inner apartments (Orodhana) and households of Ashoka's brothers, sisters, and other relatives in Pataliputra and outlying towns.

ref: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. I (Inscriptions of Asoka by E. Hultzsch): Major Rock Edict V & Pillar Edict VII

stem: With reference to the diplomatic relations of the Mauryan Empire with the Hellenistic world and the history of the post-Ashokan Mauryas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the treaty of 303 BCE, Chandragupta Maurya ceded the four satrapies of Aria, Arachosia, Gedrosia, and Paropamisadae to Seleucus Nicator in return for a contingent of five hundred Syrian war elephants.

2. During the reign of Bindusara, the Seleucid monarch Antiochus I Soter dispatched Heliodorus as his ambassador to the Mauryan court at Pataliputra, while Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt sent Megasthenes.
3. Following the death of Ashoka, his grandson Samprati repudiated the heterodox Sramana traditions and suppressed Jain monastic orders across Malwa and Saurashtra.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Every statement contains a classical historical inversion: Seleucus Nicator ceded the four north-western satrapies to Chandragupta Maurya in exchange for 500 Indian war elephants; Antiochus I sent Deimachus (and Ptolemy II sent Dionysius) to Bindusara, whereas Heliodorus was a later Indo-Greek envoy to the Shunga court; and Ashoka's grandson Samprati is celebrated as one of ancient India's foremost royal patrons of Jainism.

exp.why: This statement reverses the terms of the Seleucid-Mauryan Treaty of 303 BCE as recorded by Strabo, Appian, and Plutarch. It was Seleucus I Nicator who ceded the four trans-Indus satrapies—Aria (Herat), Arachosia (Kandahar), Gedrosia (Makran/Baluchistan), and Paropamisadae (Kabul valley)—to Chandragupta Maurya, along with a matrimonial alliance (Epigamia), in exchange for 500 Mauryan war elephants that Seleucus subsequently deployed at the Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE).

This statement confuses the Hellenistic ambassadors sent to India across different dynasties. Megasthenes was dispatched by Seleucus Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya. During the reign of Bindusara (Amitrochates), the Seleucid king Antiochus I Soter sent Deimachus of Plataea, while Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt dispatched Dionysius. Heliodorus of Taxila belonged to the post-Mauryan period (c. late 2nd century BCE) and served as the ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to the court of the Shunga ruler Bhagabhadra at Vidisha (Besnagar).

Far from suppressing Jainism, Ashoka's grandson Samprati (son of Kunala), who ruled from Pataliputra and Ujjayini, is revered in Jain canonical and historical texts (such as Hemachandra's Parishishtaparvan and the Kalpasutra tradition) as a great patron of Jainism on par with Ashoka's patronage of Buddhism. Initiated by the Jain acharya Suhastin, Samprati erected numerous Jain temples and facilitated the spread of Jain monks into western and southern India.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7; H.C. Raychaudhuri, Political History of Ancient India

stem: With reference to the political and cultural history of the Sunga dynasty in the Post-Mauryan period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Pushyamitra Sunga performed the Vedic Ashvamedha sacrifice to assert imperial legitimacy, an event corroborated by the Ayodhya stone inscription of Dhanadeva and literary references in Patanjali's Mahabhashya.
2. Owing to the orthodox Brahmanical resurgence under the Sunga monarchs, all construction and architectural expansion of Buddhist stupas in Central India came to a complete halt during their reign.

3. Kalidasa's Sanskrit drama Malavikagnimitram provides a literary account of Sunga political history, including a military triumph over the Yavanas on the banks of the Sindhu river during the viceroyalty of Agnimitra at Vidisha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Sunga period witnessed a vigorous revival of Vedic ritualism and Sanskrit grammar alongside continued artistic and architectural expansion of major Central Indian Buddhist monuments such as Bharhut and Sanchi through guild, lay, and royal patronage.

exp.why: Pushyamitra Sunga, the founder of the Sunga dynasty after overthrowing Brihadratha Maurya, revived Vedic horse sacrifices. The Ayodhya inscription of his descendant Dhanadeva explicitly describes Pushyamitra as 'Dvir-Ashvamedha-Yajin' (performer of two Ashvamedha sacrifices), and the grammarian Patanjali refers to officiating at a sacrifice for Pushyamitra in the present tense ('Iha Pushyamitram yajayamah') in his Mahabhashya.

Despite later Buddhist sectarian chronicles like the Divyavadana portraying Pushyamitra as hostile to Buddhism, archaeological and epigraphic evidence from Central India demonstrates that Buddhist monumental architecture flourished under Sunga rule. The sculpted stone railings (vedika) and gateways (torana) of the Bharhut Stupa (bearing the inscription 'Suganam raje'—during the reign of the Sungas) as well as the stone encasement and enlargement of Stupa I and the construction of Stupas II and III at Sanchi took place during the Sunga period.

Kalidasa's play Malavikagnimitram revolves around Agnimitra, Pushyamitra's son who governed as viceroy from Vidisha. The play records the conflict with Yajnasena of Vidarbha and mentions how Pushyamitra's grandson Vasumitra guarded the sacrificial Ashvamedha horse and defeated a cavalry detachment of Yavanas (Indo-Greeks) on the southern bank of the Sindhu river.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 19

stem: In the context of Post-Mauryan history, consider the following description of an Indo-Greek monarch: He ruled from his capital at Sakala (modern Sialkot) and his philosophical inquiries regarding the Buddhist doctrine of non-self (Anatta) with the monk Nagasena were immortalized in a celebrated Pali text. According to the classical account of Plutarch, such was his popularity as a just ruler that upon his death in camp, rival cities contended for a share of his ashes and eventually agreed to distribute the relics among themselves to erect monuments (stupas) in his memory. Which of the following rulers is described above?
core: Menander I (Milinda), the most celebrated Indo-Greek ruler of the 2nd century BCE with his capital at Sakala, became deeply associated with Buddhism through the Pali treatise Milindapanho and Greco-Roman records of stupa-like relic veneration upon his death.

exp.why: Option B is correct: Menander I Soter (known in Indian Pali sources as Milinda, c. 165–145 BCE) ruled a vast Indo-Greek dominion from his capital at Sakala (Sialkot in Punjab). His philosophical dialogue with the Buddhist sage Nagasena—Wait using the famous chariot simile to explain the absence of an eternal ego/soul (Anatta)—is recorded in the Pali canonical/paracanonical work Milindapanho (Questions of Milinda). The Greek biographer Plutarch (in Moralia / Precepts of Statecraft) records that when Menander died in camp, the cities of his realm disputed over his funerary remains and divided his ashes equally to erect monuments (stupas) over them, closely mirroring the funerary honours accorded to the Buddha. Option A (Demetrius I) was an early Graeco-Bactrian conqueror of north-western India. Option C (Antialcidas) was an Indo-Greek ruler of Taxila known from the Besnagar pillar inscription for sending his ambassador Heliodorus to Vidisha. Option D (Gondophernes) was the famous 1st-century CE Indo-Parthian (Pahlava) ruler associated with the Takht-i-Bahi inscription and Christian traditions of St. Thomas.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part I

stem: With reference to the numismatic developments in the Indian subcontinent during the Post-Mauryan period (c. 200 BCE – 300 CE), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the earlier uninscribed punch-marked coins of the Mauryan era, Post-Mauryan coinage enabled historians to definitively attribute individual coin issues to specific monarchs and dynasties.

2. The Kushanas were the very first rulers in the Indian subcontinent to introduce die-struck portrait coins carrying bilingual legends in Greek and Prakrit, as well as the first to issue gold coins in India.

3. While the Kushanas minted high-purity gold dinaras and the largest volume of copper coins for everyday monetized exchange, the Satavahanas predominantly issued coins in lead, potin, and copper alongside sporadic silver issues.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indo-Greeks revolutionized Indian numismatics by pioneering die-struck portrait coins with bilingual inscriptions and issuing the first gold coins in India, whereas the Kushanas later institutionalized large-scale gold coinage calibrated to Roman weight standards alongside massive copper issues.

exp.why: Pre-Mauryan and Mauryan silver karshapanas were punch-marked coins bearing only geometric, floral, and animal symbols without royal names or dates. In the Post-Mauryan period, rulers began inscribing their names, titles, and effigies on coins, allowing precise dynastic reconstruction.

This statement swaps the pioneering numismatic contributions of the Indo-Greeks with the Kushanas. It was the Indo-Greeks (not the Kushanas) who were the first rulers in India to issue coins that can be definitely attributed to individual kings, the first to introduce die-struck realistic royal portraits with bilingual legends (Greek on the obverse and Prakrit in Kharoshthi or Brahmi on the reverse), and the very first to issue gold coins in India. The Kushanas (specifically under Vima Kadphises) were the first to mint gold coins on a wide, systematic scale with a high purity and weight standard (~8 grams) matching the Roman aureus/denarius.

The Kushana economy was deeply monetized at both ends: high-value gold dinaras facilitated international and silk-route commerce, while vast issues of copper coins (and local imitations called Puri-Kushana coins) served daily retail transactions. Conversely, in the Deccan, the Satavahanas primarily minted coins in cheap base metals—lead, potin (an alloy of copper, tin, and lead), and copper—while reserving silver mostly for portrait coins or restruck Kshatrapa issues.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the Besnagar (Vidisha) Garuda Pillar Inscription, a landmark epigraphic record of the Post-Mauryan era, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It records the erection of a Garuda-dhvaja in honour of Vasudeva (styled Devadeva) by Heliodorus, an inhabitant of Taxila who served as the ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to the Sunga ruler Bhagabhadra.

2. The didactic portion of the inscription rejects the ethical virtues of self-restraint (dama), charity (tyaga), and conscientiousness (apramada), asserting instead that Vedic animal sacrifice alone leads to heaven.

3. Because it was commissioned by an envoy hailing from the north-western frontier city of Taxila, the pillar inscription is composed in classical Paninian Sanskrit and engraved in the right-to-left Kharoshthi script.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The late 2nd-century BCE Besnagar Pillar Inscription of Heliodorus, written in Prakrit in the Brahmi script, provides the earliest epigraphic testimony of diplomatic ties between the Indo-Greeks of Taxila and the Sungas of Vidisha, as well as the assimilation of foreign elites into the ethical and devotional fold of early Bhagavatism.

exp.why: Part I of the Besnagar pillar inscription (near modern Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, c. 113 BCE) explicitly records that the Garuda-dhvaja (pillar surmounted by Garuda) of Vasudeva, the God of Gods (Devadeva), was erected by Heliodorus, son of Dion, a Bhagavata (worshipper of Vishnu/Vasudeva) and resident of Taxila, who came as the Yona-duta (Greek ambassador) of Maharaja Amtalikita (Antialcidas) to King Kasiputra Bhagabhadra, then in the 14th year of his prosperous reign.

Part II of the Besnagar inscription does the exact opposite: it affirmatively proclaims that 'three immortal precepts (trini amuta-padani), when practiced well, lead to heaven (svaga): self-restraint (dama), charity/renunciation (chaga/tyaga), and conscientiousness/vigilance (apramada).' Historians note this verse as a direct epigraphic echo of the ethical philosophy expounded in the Stri Parva and Udyoga Parva of the Mahabharata.

Although Heliodorus hailed from Taxila (where Kharoshthi was widely used), the Besnagar Garuda Pillar Inscription was erected in Central India (Vidisha) and is composed in Middle Indo-Aryan Prakrit and engraved in the left-to-right Brahmi script, not in classical Sanskrit or Kharoshthi.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization, Vol. I

stem: With reference to the political transition in northern India during the 1st century BCE, which of the following statements accurately describes the historical position of the Kanva dynasty?

opts.A: They were a branch of the Mahameghavahana clan who established an independent Jaina kingdom in Kalinga following the decline of the Mauryan Empire.
opts.B: Founded by an Amatya (minister) named Vasudeva who overthrew the last Sunga ruler Devabhuti, their brief Brahmanical rule in Magadha witnessed a severe contraction of central authority before being extinguished by the Satavahanas.
opts.C: They served as feudatories in the Krishna-Guntur region of Andhra and succeeded the imperial Satavahanas with their capital at Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda).
opts.D: They were a lineage of Saka military governors who ruled over Malwa and Kathiawar from their capital at Ujjayini using the title of Mahakshatrapa.
