core: The Kanva (Kanvayana) dynasty (c. 73–28 BCE) consisted of four Brahmanical rulers in Magadha inaugurated by the minister Vasudeva Kanva, marking the final twilight of native Magadhan imperial dominance in the 1st century BCE prior to Satavahana and Mitra regional ascendancy.

exp.why: Option B is correct: According to the Puranic accounts and Banabhatta's Harshacharita, the last Sunga monarch Devabhuti was overthrown around 73 BCE through a conspiracy orchestrated by his Brahmin minister (Amatya) Vasudeva Kanva. The Kanva dynasty ruled for only about 45 years across four kings (Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, and Susarman). During their reign, Magadha's territorial reach shrank drastically as Punjab, Mathura, Kosala, and Panchala passed under independent Mitra and tribal rulers or Indo-Greek/Saka incursions, until the last Kanva ruler Susarman was overthrown by the Satavahanas (Andhras) around 28 BCE. Option A describes the Chedi (Mahameghavahana) dynasty of Kharavela in Kalinga. Option C describes the Ikshvaku dynasty of Vijayapuri. Option D describes the Kardamaka line of Western Kshatrapas.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 19; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the Saka (Scythian) Kshatrapa houses of Western India and their political interactions with the Satavahanas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Saka rulers in India institutionalized the satrapal system of governance, wherein a senior ruler styled Mahakshatrapa frequently ruled conjointly with a junior heir-apparent styled Kshatrapa.

2. Rudradaman I belonged to the Kshaharata lineage of Western Kshatrapas, and it was his vast silver coinage discovered in the Jogalthambi hoard that was captured and counter-struck by the Satavahana ruler Gautamiputra Satakarni.

3. The Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman I is celebrated as the earliest long royal panegyric composed in chaste classical Sanskrit prose and records the restoration of the Sudarshana lake embankment out of his own treasury without imposing forced labour (vishti) or emergency benevolence levies (pranaya).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Western India under the Sakas was governed successively by two distinct Kshatrapa houses—the Kshaharatas (Bhumaka and Nahapana, defeated by Gautamiputra Satakarni) and the Kardamakas of Ujjain (Chashtana and Rudradaman I, who later defeated the Satavahanas and patronized classical Sanskrit epigraphy).

exp.why: The Sakas and Parthians introduced the Achaemenid-derived Satrapal (Kshatrapa) system to India. Under this system of diarchic or conjoint administration, the senior sovereign held the title of Mahakshatrapa while the junior co-ruler (often the crown prince or brother) held the title of Kshatrapa, each exercising minting rights.

This statement conflates the two distinct dynasties of the Western Kshatrapas: the Kshaharatas and the Kardamakas. It was Nahapana (not Rudradaman I) who belonged to the Kshaharata dynasty and whose silver coins (over 13,250 coins found in the Jogalthambi hoard near Nashik) were captured and restruck by Gautamiputra Satakarni—an achievement corroborated by Gautami Balashri's Nashik Prasasti declaring that her son 'uprooted the Khakharata (Kshaharata) race without leaving a remnant.' Rudradaman I belonged to the rival Kardamaka lineage founded by his grandfather Chashtana at Ujjain; far from being defeated by Gautamiputra, Rudradaman I defeated the Satavahana lord of Dakshinapatha (Vashishthiputra Satakarni/Pulumavi) twice, sparing him only because of a close matrimonial alliance.

The Junagadh (Girnar) Rock Inscription of Rudradaman I (dated Saka Year 72, i.e., 150 CE) is the earliest extensive royal inscription in classical Sanskrit prose conforming to Kavyalankara norms. It records how the Sudarshana lake (originally built by Pushyagupta, provincial governor of Chandragupta Maurya, and fitted with conduits by Tushaspha under Ashoka) was breached by a fierce storm and repaired by Rudradaman's Pahlava governor Suvishakha solely from the royal treasury without oppressing the urban and rural populace with forced labour (vishti), emergency taxes (pranaya), or special cesses (kara).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20

stem: With reference to the Western Kshatrapa ruler Rudradaman I and the epigraphic record of public works in ancient India, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: To finance the massive reconstruction of the breached Sudarshana reservoir in Saurashtra, Rudradaman I levied compulsory forced labour (Vishti) and emergency benevolence cesses (Pranaya) on the rural peasantry.

Statement-II: The Junagarh (Girnar) Rock Inscription of Rudradaman I (c. 150 CE) constitutes the earliest long epigraphic specimen composed in chaste classical Sanskrit prose (kavya style) and records the repair of the Mauryan-era reservoir exclusively out of the monarch's own treasury.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Junagarh Rock Inscription (Saka year 72 / 150 CE) of Rudradaman I is both a landmark in the history of classical Sanskrit kavya epigraphy and a crucial primary source for post-Mauryan fiscal terms such as Kara, Vishti (forced labour), and Pranaya (emergency benevolence levies). It explicitly highlights royal welfare ethics by stating that the ruler rebuilt the dam of the Sudarshana Lake from his personal treasury without burdening his subjects with extraordinary taxes or forced labour.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. The Junagarh inscription explicitly praises Rudradaman I for restoring the severely breached embankment of the Sudarshana Lake—despite his council of ministers (Mati-sachiva and Karma-sachiva) advising against the project due to its prohibitive cost—without oppressing the urban and rural population with extra taxes (akara), forced labour (avishti), or emergency benevolence levies (apranaya-kriya).

Statement-II is correct. Engraved on the same Girnar rock that bears Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts (and later Skandagupta's inscription), Rudradaman's inscription of 150 CE is the earliest extensive royal panegyric composed in ornate classical Sanskrit conforming to early kavya aesthetics. It traces the history of the Sudarshana Lake from its construction by Pushyagupta (provincial governor of Chandragupta Maurya) and conduit additions by Tushaspha (under Ashoka) to its repair under Rudradaman's governor Suvisakha using funds drawn entirely from the king's own treasury (svasmad-kosha).

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20 (Central Asian Contacts); Epigraphia Indica Vol. VIII (Junagarh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman)

stem: In the context of post-Mauryan North-Western India, which one of the following rulers is attested by the famous Takht-i-Bahi inscription near Mardan and is associated in early Christian apocryphal tradition with the arrival of St. Thomas the Apostle in the Indian subcontinent?
core: Gondophernes (Guduvhara in Kharosthi inscriptions) was the most prominent ruler of the Indo-Parthian (Pahlava) dynasty in the first century CE, ruling over Arachosia, Kabul, and Gandhara. The convergence of the Takht-i-Bahi stone inscription (dated in year 103 of an era corresponding to 45/46 CE and the 26th year of his reign) with the 3rd-century Syriac text 'Acts of Thomas' provided one of the major chronological synchronisms in early Indian history.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct. Gondophernes (Prakrit: Guduvhara) was the greatest of the Indo-Parthian (Pahlava) kings who succeeded the Indo-Scythians in parts of North-Western India during the early 1st century CE. His historicity is established by his extensive coinage and the Kharosthi stone inscription discovered at Takht-i-Bahi (near Mardan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). Early Christian literary traditions, particularly the 'Acts of Thomas', record that the Apostle Thomas travelled to India during the reign of King 'Gudnaphar' (Gondophernes) before eventually moving to South India. Options (B) and (C), Maues (Moga) and Azes I, were earlier Indo-Scythian (Saka) rulers of the 1st century BCE. Option (D), Kujula Kadphises, was the founder of the Kushana dynasty who displaced the last Indo-Parthian rulers in the Kabul and Gandhara region.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20

stem: With reference to the monetary and religious history of the early Kushana rulers, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Kujula Kadphises, who unified the five Yueh-chi principalities, was the first Kushana monarch to mint an extensive gold currency in India modeled on the weight standard of the Roman aureus.

2. The earliest Kushana coins depicting the deity Shiva alongside his bull Nandi and bearing the Prakrit Kharosthi title 'Mahisvara' (Maheshvara) were introduced by Kanishka I rather than his predecessors.
3. The Kushana rulers adopted the silver drachm of the Indo-Greeks as the primary anchor of their imperial monetary system across the Gangetic plains while discontinuing copper coinage.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A clear chronological progression defines early Kushana numismatics: Kujula Kadphises issued exclusively copper and billon coins imitating late Indo-Greek (Hermaeus) and Roman Augustus portraits; his grandson Vima Kadphises introduced the first extensive Kushana gold currency (dinaras) and explicitly proclaimed his Shaivite devotion (Maheshvara) on his coins. Throughout the Kushana period, gold and copper formed the twin pillars of the currency system, whereas silver coinage was nearly absent across the core empire.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. While Kujula Kadphises unified the five yabgus (tribes) of the Yueh-chi and extended Kushana power south of the Hindu Kush, he minted only copper and low-grade billon coins (including types imitating the portrait head of the Roman Emperor Augustus and the Indo-Greek king Hermaeus). He did not issue any gold coins; the earliest Kushana gold coinage was instituted later by Vima Kadphises.

Statement 2 is incorrect. It was Vima Kadphises—the father and predecessor of Kanishka I—who first introduced the iconic reverse motif of Shiva holding a trident, often accompanied by his bull Nandi, alongside the Kharosthi legend 'Maharajasa Rajadirajasa Sarvalogaisvarasa Mahisvarasa Vima Kathphisasa' (proclaiming himself an ardent devotee of Maheshvara/Shiva). Kanishka I later replaced the mono-cultic Shaivite reverse with a multi-deity pantheon, where Shiva appears under the Bactrian label 'Oesho'.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Unlike the Indo-Greeks and Western Kshatrapas who relied heavily on silver drachms, the Kushana monetary system was bimetallic in gold and copper. Silver coins are virtually non-existent in the standard imperial Kushana series (save for rare local issues in the lower Indus region). Instead, the Kushanas issued massive quantities of copper coins (tetradrachms) that facilitated everyday retail monetization across urban centers in northern India.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8 (The Kushana Empire); NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I, Theme 2

stem: With reference to the Kushana Empire under Kanishka I and its epigraphic evidence, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Rabatak inscription found in Afghanistan, composed in the Bactrian language and written in the Greek script, provides a direct genealogical sequence of the early Kushana emperors from Kujula Kadphises to Kanishka I.
2. The empire under Kanishka I operated through a dual administrative axis anchored at Purushapura in the north-west and Mathura in the Yamuna basin.

3. Epigraphic and numismatic records indicate that Kushana political authority under Kanishka I remained strictly confined west of the Yamuna river and never penetrated the middle Gangetic cities of Kausambi or Pataliputra.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The discovery of the Rabatak inscription in Baghlan province (Afghanistan) revolutionized Kushana historiography by clarifying both the genealogy of the early Kushanas (Kujula Kadphises -> Vima Taktu -> Vima Kadphises -> Kanishka I) and the vast eastern extent of Kanishka's Indian dominions. Together with dated inscriptions from Sarnath and Kausambi, it proves that Kushana hegemony stretched from Central Asia deep into the Gangetic plains.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Rabatak inscription, issued in the first regnal year of Kanishka I, is written in the Bactrian language (an Eastern Iranian tongue adopted by the Kushanas in place of Greek) using the modified Greek alphabet. In recording the construction of a royal sanctuary (Bagolaggo), Kanishka orders images to be made of his great-grandfather Kujula Kadphises, his grandfather Vima Taktu (Soter Megas), his father Vima Kadphises, and himself.

Statement 2 is correct. Kanishka's vast trans-Asian empire was governed through two principal nodal capitals: Purushapura (modern Peshawar in Pakistan), where he erected a monumental relic stupa and vihara, and Mathura on the banks of the Yamuna, which served as the southern imperial capital, artistic hub, and site of the royal devakula (dynastic shrine at Mat).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Far from being confined west of the Yamuna, the Rabatak inscription explicitly records that in Year 1 of Kanishka's reign, his authority was proclaimed across the heartland of India ('Kshatriya' realm), specifically naming the eastern cities of Saketa (Ayodhya), Kausambi, Pataliputra, and Sri-Champa (Bhagalpur) as subject to his will. This is independently corroborated by early regnal-year inscriptions of Kanishka found at Kausambi (Year 2) and Sarnath (Year 3), as well as large hoards of Kushana copper and gold coins across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8 (The Rabatak Inscription, p. 377-379); B.N. Mukherjee, The Rise and Fall of the Kushana Empire

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the religious policy and ideological foundations of the Kushana Empire:
items: Statement-I: Although Kanishka I convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir—where extensive Sanskrit Buddhist commentaries such as the Mahavibhasha were compiled—his imperial coinage depicts an eclectic pantheon comprising Iranian, Hellenistic, Brahmanical, and Buddhist deities.

Statement-II: Following the conclusion of the Fourth Buddhist Council, Kanishka I declared Mahayana Buddhism the exclusive state religion of the Kushana Empire and prohibited royal grants to non-Buddhist shrines along the Silk Route trading hubs.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Kushana statecraft exemplifies deliberate religious pluralism designed to legitimize imperial rule over a multi-ethnic, trans-continental dominion spanning Bactria, Gandhara, and the Gangetic plains. While literary tradition remembers Kanishka I as a great patron of Buddhism on account of the Fourth Buddhist Council, numismatic and epigraphic evidence demonstrates that Kushana emperors simultaneously venerated Zoroastrian/Iranian, Greek, and Brahmanical deities to integrate diverse merchant and regional communities along the Silk Route.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. According to Buddhist traditions, Kanishka I convened the Fourth Buddhist Council at Kundalavana Vihara in Kashmir (presided over by Vasumitra, with Ashvaghosha as deputy), which systematized Sarvastivada doctrines into the Sanskrit encyclopedic commentary Mahavibhasha and catalyzed the rise of Mahayana Buddhism. Simultaneously, the reverse dies of Kanishka's and Huvishka's coins portray over thirty distinct deities drawn from Iranian/Zoroastrian (Miiro/Mithra, Mao, Nana, Athsho, Pharro), Greek (Helios, Hephaistos, Herakles), Brahmanical (Oesho/Shiva, Skando-Komaro, Maaseno), and Buddhist (Boddo, Metrago-Boddo) traditions.

Statement-II is incorrect. Neither Kanishka I nor any other Kushana monarch ever declared Buddhism an exclusive state religion or suppressed non-Buddhist cults. On the contrary, the Rabatak inscription shows Kanishka attributing his kingship to the Iranian goddess Nana and a host of Iranian deities assimilated with Indian gods (such as Mahasena and Visakha). Kushana political legitimacy across Cosmopolitan Silk Route oasis cities and Indian urban centers relied on inclusive patronage of Buddhist, Jain, Bhagavata, Shaivite, and Iranian sanctuaries alike.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to long-distance trade and monetary circulation during the Kushana period, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The Kushana rulers issued a large volume of gold coins (dinaras) of remarkably uniform weight and high purity, underpinned by their strategic control over the southern transit corridors of the Central Asian Silk Route connecting China, Bactria, and the ports of western India.

Statement-II: Because Indo-Roman trade operated at a chronic balance-of-payments deficit against India, Kushana mints had no access to Roman gold aurei and depended exclusively on indigenous gold mines in the Kolar region of South India.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The proliferation and high metallic purity of Kushana gold dinaras were directly linked to two geopolitical and economic mechanisms: the Kushana Empire's stranglehold over the Taxila-Kabul-Bactria spur of the Silk Route (which bypassed hostile Parthian territory to channel Chinese silk to western Indian ports like Barbaricum and Barygaza), and India's massive trade surplus with the Roman Empire, which brought a steady inflow of Roman gold bullion (aurei) that correlated closely in weight (~124 grains / ~8 grams) with the Kushana dinara.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. By uniting the Oxus basin, the Hindu Kush passes, Gandhara, and the Indus-Gangetic plains under a single imperial umbrella, the Kushanas guaranteed security to caravan merchants and collected lucrative transit tolls along the feeder routes of the Silk Road linking Han China with the Roman Orient via Indian Ocean ports.

Statement-II is incorrect because it reverses the direction of the Indo-Roman trade balance. In reality, Indo-Roman trade operated at a massive surplus in India's favour due to insatiable Roman demand for Indian spices, textiles, precious stones, and trans-shipped Chinese silk—a bullion drain famously lamented by the Roman author Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia. The resulting influx of Roman gold coins (aurei), combined with gold acquired from Central Asia (the Altai region), supplied the bullion and inspired the weight standard (approximately 7.9 to 8 grams) for the Kushana gold dinara.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20 (Impact of Central Asian Contacts); NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I, Theme 2

stem: With reference to the political and administrative institutions introduced or popularized by the Sakas and Kushanas in ancient India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Kushana monarchs adopted the lofty imperial title 'Devaputra' (Son of God) and instituted the practice of erecting 'Devakula' shrines housing royal ancestral statues, as excavated at Mat near Mathura.

2. Their polity introduced the system of hereditary dual rule, in which two kings ruled simultaneously in the same kingdom, alongside military governorships designated by the Hellenistic title 'Strategos'.

3. Replacing the decentralized feudatory alliances of the post-Mauryan principalities, the Kushanas established a uniform, hyper-centralized civil bureaucracy across northern India strictly modelled on the Kautilyan Arthashastra.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Saka-Kushana political order combined exalted sacral kingship (Devaputra ideology and Devakula royal ancestor temples) with a decentralized feudatory structure grounded in the Kshatrapa system, hereditary co-regency, and military governors (Strategos).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Kushana kings exalted royal authority by adopting the title 'Devaputra' (Son of God), inspired by the Chinese imperial concept of 'Tien-tzu' (Son of Heaven). To reinforce this divine status, they constructed 'Devakula' (royal shrines) where statues of deceased rulers were installed for veneration, conspicuously evidenced by the headless statue of Kanishka I and the inscribed image of Vima Kadphises excavated at Mat near Mathura.

Statement 2 is correct. The Sakas and Kushanas introduced the peculiar administrative practice of hereditary dual kingship (co-regency), wherein a father and son (often serving as Mahakshatrapa and Kshatrapa respectively) ruled simultaneously over the same territory. They also retained the Indo-Greek practice of appointing military governors called 'Strategos' (and Meridarchs) to maintain martial control over strategic provinces.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Far from establishing a hyper-centralized Mauryan-style bureaucracy, the Sakas and Kushanas strengthened a decentralized, multi-tiered feudatory polity. By adopting titles such as 'Maharaja' and 'Rajatiraja' (King of Kings), Kushana emperors implicitly acknowledged the existence of numerous subordinate tributary rulers, autonomous satraps (Kshatrapas and Mahakshatrapas), and local chieftains who paid homage and tribute rather than being replaced by a salaried civil service.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20 (Central Asian Contact and Mutual Impact); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the epigraphic, numismatic, and political history of the Satavahana dynasty, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Naneghat Cave Inscription : Composed by Queen Gautami Balasri to record the military conquests of Gautamiputra Satakarni
2. Nasik Cave (Pandavleni) Inscription : Issued by Queen Nayanika detailing the performance of Asvamedha and Rajasuya sacrifices by Satakarni I
3. Jogalthambi Coin Hoard : Silver coins of the Kshaharata ruler Nahapana counter-struck by Gautamiputra Satakarni
4. Pratishthana (Paithan) : Imperial capital of the Satavahanas situated on the banks of the Godavari river
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: A precise distinction between early Satavahana epigraphy (Queen Nayanika's Naneghat inscription of the 1st century BCE) and later Satavahana revival epigraphy (Queen Gautami Balasri's Nasik Prasasti of the 2nd century CE) is essential for reconstructing Deccan political history.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. The Naneghat Cave Inscription (Located in the Western Ghats near Junnar, Maharashtra) was engraved by Queen Nayanika (Naganika), the wife of the early Satavahana ruler Satakarni I (and daughter-in-law of Simuka). It records the performance of numerous Vedic sacrifices, including two Asvamedhas and one Rajasuya, alongside lavish dakshina grants of cattle, horses, and karshapanas.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The famous Nasik Cave (Pandavleni Cave No. 3) Prasasti was caused to be engraved by Queen Gautami Balasri, the mother of the later Satavahana monarch Gautamiputra Satakarni, during the 19th regnal year of her grandson Vasishthiputra Pulumavi. It eulogizes Gautamiputra Satakarni's victories over the Sakas, Yavanas, and Pahlavas and his restoration of Satavahana glory.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. The Jogalthambi hoard discovered in the Nasik district yielded over 13,000 silver coins originally minted by the Western Kshatrapa (Kshaharata) ruler Nahapana, nearly two-thirds of which were restruck (overstruck) by Gautamiputra Satakarni with his own dynastic Ujjain and three-arched hill symbols, confirming his decisive triumph over Nahapana.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Pratishthana (modern Paithan in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar/Aurangabad district of Maharashtra), located on the upper Godavari river, served as the principal imperial seat of the Satavahanas and a major hub along the Dakshinapatha trade route.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I, Theme 2

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ideological claims and diplomatic practices of the Satavahana dynasty during the first and second centuries CE:
items: 1. In the Nasik Cave Prasasti, Gautamiputra Satakarni is extolled as 'Ekabrahmana' (the peerless Brahmana) who crushed the arrogance of the Kshatriyas and halted the contamination of the fourfold varna order (chatur-varna-sankara).

2. Following Gautamiputra Satakarni's uprooting of the Kshaharata clan, the later Satavahana monarchs observed an uncompromising ban on matrimonial alliances with the Saka ruling houses of western India to preserve ritual purity.

3. The mountain ranges listed in the Nasik inscription—such as Vindhya, Sahya, Pariyatra, and Malaya—delineate the trans-peninsular geopolitical claim of the Satavahanas as 'Dakshinapathapati' (Lords of the Deccan).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Satavahana royal panegyrics projected the dynasty as strict upholders of Brahmanical orthodoxy who prevented varna-sankara, their realpolitik accommodated matrimonial alliances with the assimilated Saka Kardamaka dynasty of Ujjain.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In the Nasik inscription of Gautami Balasri, Gautamiputra Satakarni claims to be 'Ekabrahmana' (the unique Brahmana) and 'Khatiya-dapa-mana-madana' (destroyer of the pride and conceit of the Kshatriyas), asserting that he stopped the intermixing of the four varnas ('vinivatita-chatu-vana-sankara') and extirpated the Kshaharata (Khakharata) race.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Despite the orthodox ideological rhetoric against 'varna-sankara' and foreign groups (Sakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas), Satavahana political strategy was highly pragmatic. As attested by the Kanheri inscription and Rudradaman I's Junagadh rock inscription, Vasishthiputra Satakarni (a successor of Gautamiputra Satakarni) entered into a matrimonial alliance with the Saka Kardamaka house by marrying the daughter of Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman I—a kinship tie that persuaded Rudradaman to spare the Satavahana ruler despite defeating him twice in battle.

Statement 3 is correct. The Nasik inscription describes Gautamiputra Satakarni as the lord of mountains including Vijha (Vindhya),achhavata (Rikshavat), Parichata (Pariyatra), Sahya (Western Ghats), Kanhagiri (Kanheri), Mahendra (Eastern Ghats), and Malaya, asserting the Satavahana claim as 'Dakshinapathapati' whose chargers drank the waters of the three oceans (tisamuda-toya-pitavahana).

ref: NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I, Theme 3 (Kinship, Caste and Class); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding kinship and succession in the Satavahana polity:
items: Statement-I: The Satavahana Empire followed a matrilineal system of royal succession in which the imperial throne passed exclusively through the female line rather than from father to son.

Statement-II: Later Satavahana monarchs routinely adopted metronymics derived from the Vedic gotras of their mothers, such as Gautamiputra and Vasishthiputra, and royal queens issued major political and donative inscriptions in their own right.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Although Satavahana monarchs bore metronymics derived from their mothers' Brahmanical gotras (reflecting the political importance of royal marriage alliances and perhaps local Deccan kinship substrata), succession to the Satavahana throne remained strictly patrilineal.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Despite the prominent status of royal women and the custom of kings prefixing their mothers' gotra names to their own, the succession to the Satavahana throne was strictly patrilineal and patriarchal. The crown passed through male heirs (father to son or brother to brother), never through the female line.

Statement-II is correct. From the reign of Gautamiputra Satakarni onwards, Satavahana rulers regularly used metronymics derived from Vedic Brahmanical gotras such as Gautama, Vasishtha, and Mathara (e.g., Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Gautamiputra Yajna Sri Satakarni). Furthermore, queens like Nayanika (who acted as regent) and Gautami Balasri exercised substantial political agency and commissioned major royal inscriptions and monastic grants.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 21 (The Age of the Satavahanas); NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I, Theme 3

stem: With reference to the history of land grants in ancient India, consider the following statements regarding the Satavahana charters:
items: 1. The Satavahanas were the earliest Indian rulers attested by epigraphic records to make perpetual grants of tax-free cultivated land and villages to Buddhist monastic orders and Brahmanas.

2. Satavahana land charters frequently surrendered royal administrative rights over the donated plots, including immunity from the entry of royal troops and police ('apavesya') and exemption from the state's monopoly over salt ('alonakhadaka').
3. Unlike later early medieval dynasties, the Satavahanas restricted land grants exclusively to secular military commanders as hereditary fiefs in lieu of cash salaries.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Satavahana epigraphs (1st–2nd centuries CE) mark the genesis of Indian feudal-style fiscal and administrative immunities (pariharas), whereby the state surrendered both revenue collection and police/administrative jurisdiction (apavesya, arathasavinayika) over lands gifted to religious beneficiaries.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. While the Naneghat inscription of the 1st century BCE mentions the grant of villages as sacrificial fees (dakshina) to priests, the 2nd century CE inscriptions of Gautamiputra Satakarni and Vasishthiputra Pulumavi at Nasik and Karle provide the earliest explicit epigraphic charters recording perpetual, tax-free grants of agricultural fields and villages to Buddhist monks and Brahmanas.

Statement 2 is correct. Satavahana inscriptions specify fiscal and administrative immunities ('pariharas') accompanying donated lands. These included 'apavesya' (not to be entered by royal soldiers and district police), 'alonakhadaka' (exempt from being dug for salt, a royal monopoly), and 'arathasavinayika' (free from the administrative interference of district officials), effectively creating autonomous pockets within the kingdom.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Satavahana land grants were exclusively religious in nature, made to Buddhist sanghas (especially Mahasanghika and Bhadrayaniya sects at Karle and Nasik) and Brahmanas for acquiring spiritual merit. There is no epigraphic evidence under the Satavahanas of secular land grants or hereditary military fiefdoms given to officials in lieu of cash salaries, as the post-Mauryan economy remained highly monetized with abundant lead, potin, copper, and silver coinage.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 21; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the administrative structure and official terminology of the Satavahana Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Continuing Mauryan administrative conventions, the Satavahanas divided their core territory into districts called 'Ahara', which were placed under officials designated as 'Amatyas' and 'Mahamatras'.
2. The official designated as 'Gaulmika' was a purely civilian judicial magistrate stationed exclusively at imperial capital cities to adjudicate commercial disputes among urban guilds.
3. The terms 'Kataka' and 'Skandhavara' occurring frequently in Satavahana inscriptions denote autonomous maritime customs boards that regulated foreign shipping along the Konkan coast.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Satavahana administration blended Mauryan civilian terminology (Ahara, Amatyas, Mahamatras) with pronounced military oversight in the countryside (the Gaulmika heading a rural military platoon) and fortified military camp-capitals (Kataka and Skandhavara).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In their directly administered territories, the Satavahanas preserved key administrative institutions of the Mauryan era. Districts were known as 'Ahara' (such as Govardhana-ahara around Nasik and Mamala-ahara around Karle), and their governors and high functionaries were styled 'Amatyas' and 'Mahamatras'.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In the Satavahana polity, rural administration was entrusted to the 'Gaulmika', who was the commander of a military regiment or platoon called a 'gulma' (traditionally comprising 9 chariots, 9 elephants, 27 horses, and 45 foot-soldiers). Far from being an urban civilian judge, the Gaulmika was stationed in the countryside to maintain peace, enforce royal authority over village populations, and assist in revenue collection.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The epigraphic terms 'Kataka' and 'Skandhavara' refer to military camps and fortified settlements that served as mobile or permanent administrative centres whenever the king was stationed there (for instance, Gautamiputra Satakarni issued his earliest Nasik land grant directly from his victorious military camp, 'Vaijayanti-senakadhavara'). They reflect the coercive military character of the Satavahana state rather than maritime customs bodies.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 21 (The Age of the Satavahanas)

stem: With reference to the economic and cultural history of the Satavahana dynasty, consider the following statements:
items: 1. They extensively minted lead and potin coins for local commerce, while also issuing double-masted ship-motif coins and bilingual silver portrait coins.
2. King Hala compiled the Prakrit lyrical anthology Gathasaptasati, while Gunadhya composed the Brihatkatha in the Paisachi dialect during this period.
3. In keeping with their orthodox Brahmanical revival and Ashvamedha sacrifices, the Satavahanas replaced Prakrit with classical Sanskrit as the official language across all their royal inscriptions.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Satavahanas combined orthodox Vedic ritual legitimacy with vernacular Prakrit patronage and diverse base-metal and maritime coinage. Despite claiming Brahmanical status, their official epigraphic language remained Prakrit rather than Sanskrit.

exp.why: The Satavahanas predominantly issued coins in lead, potin (an alloy of copper, tin, and lead), and copper for regional monetization. Rulers such as Vashishthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni also issued lead/copper coins bearing double-masted ships on the Coromandel coast, testifying to thriving maritime trade, as well as silver portrait coins carrying bilingual legends in Prakrit and a Dravidian Prakrit/Tamil-Brahmi idiom.

The seventeenth Satavahana ruler, Hala, compiled the Gathasaptasati (Sattasai), an anthology of 700 erotic and pastoral verses in Maharashtri Prakrit. Gunadhya, traditionally associated with the Satavahana court, composed the original Brihatkatha in the Paisachi dialect.

Although the Satavahana rulers claimed to be Ekabrahmana and performed Vedic sacrifices like the Ashvamedha and Rajasuya, they did not replace Prakrit with Sanskrit in their epigraphy. All Satavahana royal inscriptions (such as the Nanaghat and Nasik cave inscriptions) were composed in Prakrit and written in the Brahmi script; it was the Western Kshatrapa ruler Rudradaman I who inaugurated chaste Sanskrit royal epigraphy at Junagarh (150 CE).

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20 (The Satavahana Phase); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8.

stem: With reference to the Hathigumpha inscription of King Kharavela at Udayagiri in Odisha, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Composed in Prakrit and incised in the Brahmi script, it provides a chronological year-by-year account of the first thirteen regnal years of Kharavela.
2. It records Kharavela's military campaign against Magadha and his recovery of the Kalinga Jina image that had earlier been taken away by a Nanda ruler.
3. It mentions the extension of an ancient canal into his capital that had originally been excavated three centuries earlier by King Nanda.
4. It describes Kharavela as an orthodox patron of the Ajivika sect who expelled Jain ascetics from the Udayagiri and Khandagiri hills.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela (Mahameghavahana/Chedi dynasty) is a unique secular-chronological Prakrit praśasti recording thirteen regnal years of military campaigns, hydraulic works, and devout Jain patronage in Kalinga.

exp.why: Unlike most ancient Indian inscriptions that only mention a single regnal date, the seventeen-line Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri (near Bhubaneswar), written in Prakrit language and Brahmi script, chronicles Kharavela's career sequentially from his boyhood through his first thirteen regnal years.

In his twelfth regnal year, Kharavela marched against Magadha, humbled its ruler Bahasatimita (Brihaspatimitra), and brought back the revered image of the Kalinga Jina (Rishabhanatha/Mahavira tradition) which had been carried away from Kalinga by Nandaraja (typically identified with Mahapadma Nanda).

In his fifth regnal year, Kharavela extended an aqueduct/canal from the Tansulia road right up to his capital Kalinganagari, explicitly noting that the canal had been excavated three hundred years (ti-vasa-sata) earlier by King Nanda.

Kharavela was an ardent follower and patron of Jainism, not an opponent of Jain ascetics. The Hathigumpha inscription begins with a salutation to the Arhats and Siddhas (early Jain Namokar formula), records the excavation of rock-cut residential caves (lenas) at Udayagiri-Khandagiri for Jain monks, and notes that he respected all religious sects (sava-pasanda-pujako).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; Epigraphia Indica Vol. XX (Hathigumpha Inscription of Kharavela).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Ikshvaku dynasty of Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda) in the Krishna-Guntur region:
items: Statement-I: While the ruling Ikshvaku monarchs performed Vedic sacrifices such as the Ashvamedha and patronized Brahmanical temples, the royal women of the same household were the principal patrons of Buddhist mahachaityas and monasteries.

Statement-II: Following the decline of the Satavahanas, the Ikshvaku monarchs imposed a state ban on Indo-Roman maritime trade and prohibited mercantile guilds in the Krishna delta from making endowments to non-Vedic sects.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri practiced a bifurcated, gendered pattern of religious patronage: kings performed Vedic rituals to assert Kshatriya sovereignty, while queens and princesses endowed Buddhist monastic establishments to integrate the prosperous mercantile and artisanal networks of the Krishna delta.

exp.why: Inscriptions from Nagarjunakonda (ancient Vijayapuri) reveal a striking gendered division of royal patronage under the Ikshvakus (3rd–4th centuries CE). Founder Vashishthiputra Chamtamula performed the Ashvamedha, Agnishtoma, and Vajapeya sacrifices, and later kings built temples to Karttikeya and Shiva. Simultaneously, royal women such as Chamtamula's sister Chamtisiri and queens Rudradharabhattarika and Bhattideva generously funded the construction of the Mahachaitya and viharas for various Buddhist schools.

Far from banning maritime trade or guild endowments, the Ikshvaku state actively fostered long-distance Indo-Roman and Southeast Asian commerce (evidenced by Roman gold coins and an amphitheatre/stadium complex at Nagarjunakonda). The bifurcated patronage model allowed the dynasty to claim orthodox Vedic legitimacy while accommodating the wealthy Buddhist merchant guilds (nigamas) and artisanal corporations of the Krishna-Guntur region.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8 (The Ikshvakus); NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I.

stem: Consider the following landmark events in the political and epigraphic history of Post-Mauryan India:
items: 1. Overthrow of the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha by Pushyamitra Sunga
2. Erection of the Besnagar (Vidisha) Garuda Pillar by the Greek ambassador Heliodorus
3. Commencement of the Saka Era associated with the accession of Kanishka I
4. Issuance of the Junagarh (Girnar) Rock Inscription by the Western Kshatrapa ruler Rudradaman I
prompt: What is the correct chronological order of the above events, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: Sequencing Post-Mauryan history requires distinguishing the early Sunga-Indo-Greek interactions of the 2nd century BCE from the Kushana accession (78 CE) and the later Western Kshatrapa epigraphs dated in the Saka Era (150 CE).

exp.why: Pushyamitra Sunga, the commander-in-chief of the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha, overthrew the Mauryan dynasty and founded the Sunga dynasty around c. 185 BCE.

Heliodorus, the ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas of Taxila to the court of the later Sunga ruler Bhagabhadra at Vidisha (Besnagar), erected the Garuda Pillar in honour of Vasudeva around c. 113 BCE (late 2nd century BCE).

The Saka Era commenced in 78 CE, traditionally marking the accession of the Kushana emperor Kanishka I (and subsequently adopted by the Western Saka Kshatrapas for dating their coins and inscriptions).

The Junagarh (Girnar) Rock Inscription of the Kardamaka Saka Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman I is explicitly dated in the year 72 of the Saka Era, which corresponds to 78 + 72 = 150 CE. Hence, the correct chronological sequence is 1-2-3-4.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 19; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8.

stem: Consider the following pairs of Post-Mauryan inscriptions and their primary historical disclosures:
items: 1. Ayodhya Inscription of Dhanadeva : Performance of two Ashvamedha sacrifices by Pushyamitra Sunga
2. Nasik Cave Inscription of Ushavadata : Permanent monetary endowments invested in weaver guilds to support Buddhist monks
3. Rabatak Inscription : Reign of the Indo-Parthian ruler Gondophernes in northwestern India
4. Takht-i-Bahi Inscription : Early genealogy of the Kushana dynasty recorded in the Bactrian language
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Post-Mauryan inscriptions across Sanskrit, Prakrit, Kharoshthi, and Bactrian scripts provide primary evidence for Sunga Vedic rituals, Saka-Satavahana guild banking, Indo-Parthian rule, and Kushana imperial genealogy.

exp.why: The Ayodhya stone inscription of Dhanadeva (a local ruler of Kosala claiming descent from Pushyamitra Sunga) records that Senapati Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedha (dvir-ashvamedha-yajin) sacrifices.

The Nasik (Pandavleni) Cave Inscription of Ushavadata, son-in-law of the Western Kshatrapa ruler Nahapana, records his charities to Brahmanas as well as a permanent endowment (akshayanivi) of 3,000 kahapanas invested with two weaver guilds (govardhana shrenis) to pay for the robes and upkeep of Buddhist monks out of the interest.

The Rabatak Inscription (discovered in Afghanistan), written in the Bactrian language using the Greek script, belongs to Kanishka I—not Gondophernes. It provides the definitive early genealogy of the Kushana rulers (Kujula Kadphises, Vima Taktu, Vima Kadphises, and Kanishka I) and lists cities across northern India up to Pataliputra and Champa under Kanishka's sway.

The Takht-i-Bahi Inscription (near Mardan in present-day Pakistan), written in Kharoshthi script, belongs to the Indo-Parthian (Pahlava) ruler Gondophernes (dated in year 103 of the Vikrama/Azes era, c. 45–46 CE), not the Kushana genealogy.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I.

stem: With reference to the material, military, and cultural impact of Central Asian and Hellenistic contacts during the Post-Mauryan period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Sakas and Kushanas popularized stitched attire such as trousers, tunics, and long heavy coats alongside leather boots and improved cavalry gear including saddles and reins.
2. The Kushanas were the first to introduce iron-tipped ploughshares and the technique of wet-paddy transplantation into the middle Gangetic plains.

3. While Indo-Greek contact influenced Indian sculptural idioms, Indian astrology and astronomy remained completely insulated from Hellenistic concepts such as the Horashastra until the medieval period.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Central Asian and Indo-Greek contacts revolutionized Indian equestrian warfare, tailored clothing, burnt-brick urban construction, and horoscopic astrology (Horashastra), whereas iron-plough agriculture and wet-paddy transplantation were indigenous pre-Mauryan developments of the Gangetic valley.

exp.why: Being equestrian nomads from Central Asia, the Sakas and Kushanas introduced superior cavalry equipment—including reins, saddles, toe-stirrups of rope, and helmets—along with tailored, stitched garments such as trousers, tunics, turbans, and heavy long coats (vividly depicted in the headless statue of Kanishka at Mathura) and heavy leather boots.

Iron-tipped ploughshares and the intensive technique of wet-paddy transplantation were not introduced by the Kushanas; they had already revolutionized agriculture in the middle Gangetic plains during the sixth to fifth centuries BCE (the age of the Buddha and the Mahajanapadas), laying the agrarian foundation for the rise of Magadha.

Indian astronomy and astrology were deeply influenced by Hellenistic ideas during the Post-Mauryan and Gupta eras. The Sanskrit word Horashastra (horoscopic astrology) was directly derived from the Greek term horoskopos, and later texts like the Yavanajataka and Varahamihira's Romaka Siddhanta and Paulisa Siddhanta explicitly acknowledged Greek astronomical traditions.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 19 (Central Asian Contacts and Their Results).

stem: With reference to the Tamil literary tradition of the Three Sangams (Muchchangam), consider the following statements:
items: 1. According to traditional Tamil accounts, all three Sangams flourished under the royal patronage of the Pandya rulers across three successive capitals—Thenmadurai, Kapadapuram, and Madurai.
2. While no literary work of the First Sangam has survived, the Eight Anthologies (Ettuthokai) are traditionally regarded as the sole surviving texts of the Second Sangam held at Kapadapuram.
3. The earliest systematic textual account of the legend of the Three Sangams appears in the early medieval commentary on the grammatical treatise Iraiyanar Agapporul.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Muchchangam tradition recorded in the commentary on Iraiyanar Agapporul attributes all three Tamil academies to Pandya patronage at Thenmadurai, Kapadapuram, and Madurai. While no work survived from the First Sangam and only the Tolkappiyam survived from the Second Sangam, the extant anthologies (Ettuthokai and Pattupattu) are attributed to the Third Sangam at Madurai.

exp.why: According to the traditional Tamil account of the Three Sangams (Muchchangam), all three academies were patronized by the Pandya kings. The First Sangam (Talai Sangam) was held at Thenmadurai (South Madurai, submerged by the sea), the Second Sangam (Idai Sangam) at Kapadapuram (Alavai, also submerged by the sea), and the Third Sangam (Kadai Sangam) at present-day Madurai (Uttara Madurai).

According to the Muchchangam tradition, while all works of the First Sangam (such as Agattiyam, Paripadal, and Mudunarai) perished, the sole surviving work of the Second Sangam at Kapadapuram is the grammatical treatise Tolkappiyam. The Eight Anthologies (Ettuthokai) and the Ten Idylls (Pattupattu) belong to the Third Sangam held at Madurai.

Although the word 'Sangam' in the sense of an academy of poets was popularized by early medieval Shaiva saint-poets like Appar and Tirugnanasambandar, the earliest detailed and systematic narrative of the three successive Sangams, their duration, members, and royal patrons appears in Nakkirar's commentary (c. 8th century CE) on the Iraiyanar Agapporul.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; Tamil Nadu SCERT Class XI History, Ch. 5

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ancient Tamil treatise Tolkappiyam:
items: Statement-I: Unlike later Sanskrit and Tamil treatises on poetics, the Tolkappiyam confines its scope to orthography, phonology, and syntax, providing little insight into the ecological classification or social conventions of early Tamil society.

Statement-II: In addition to Ezhuthu (orthography and phonology) and Sol (morphology and syntax), the Tolkappiyam incorporates a third book called Porul Adhikaram, which codifies the thematic conventions of Akam (love) and Puram (war and public life) poetry across the five ecological zones.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Tolkappiyam is uniquely structured into three books—Ezhuthu, Sol, and Porul—making it far more than a linguistic grammar. Through the Porul Adhikaram, it codifies human ecology (Aintinai), social customs, emotional aesthetics (Akam), and martial ethics (Puram), serving as a foundational source for early Tamil social history.

exp.why: Statement-I reverses the actual scope of the Tolkappiyam. Far from confining itself to phonology and syntax, the Tolkappiyam is an indispensable primary source for reconstructing the human ecology, flora and fauna, subsistence patterns, marriage customs, and martial ethics of early Tamilakam.

Authored by Tolkappiyar, the Tolkappiyam is divided into three major sections (Adhikarams) of nine chapters (Iyals) each: Ezhuthu Adhikaram (orthography and phonology), Sol Adhikaram (etymology, morphology, and syntax), and Porul Adhikaram (subject matter of poetry). The Porul Adhikaram systematically lays down the poetics of Akam and Puram along with the five-fold physiographic division (Aintinai).

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20; Upinder Singh, Ch. 8; Kamil Zvelebil, The Smile of Murugan

stem: With reference to the classification of the ancient Tamil literary corpus, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Patinenmelkanakku (Eighteen Greater Texts) represents the earliest stratum of Sangam poetry and comprises the Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies) and the Pattupattu (Ten Idylls).

2. Unlike the predominantly heroic and love lyrics of the Patinenmelkanakku, the Patinenkilkanakku (Eighteen Minor Texts) consists largely of post-Sangam didactic and ethical treatises influenced by Jain and Buddhist moral philosophy.
3. The Purananuru and Pattinappalai belong to the Patinenkilkanakku corpus and are composed in the short venpa metre to impart moral maxims on asceticism and statecraft.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Early Tamil literature is stratified into the Patinenmelkanakku (Eighteen Greater Texts: Ettuthokai and Pattupattu, c. 300 BCE–300 CE) which celebrate secular Akam love and Puram heroism, and the Patinenkilkanakku (Eighteen Minor Texts, c. 300–600 CE) which are predominantly didactic works composed in the venpa metre.

exp.why: The Patinenmelkanakku ('Eighteen Greater Texts') constitutes the core Sangam corpus (c. 300 BCE–300 CE) and is subdivided into two collections: the Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies, such as Natrinai, Kuruntokai, Ainkurunuru, Patirruppattu, Akananuru, and Purananuru) and the Pattupattu (Ten Idylls/Long Poems, such as Tirumurugarruppadai, Maduraikkanji, and Pattinappalai).

The Patinenkilkanakku ('Eighteen Minor Texts') was compiled mainly during the post-Sangam or Kalabhra period (c. 300–600 CE). Except for a few Akam/Puram narrative works like Kalavazhi Narpatu and Tinaimalai Nurraimpatu, eleven of the eighteen texts—most notably Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural and the Jain anthology Naladiyar—are didactic and ethical treatises reflecting strong Jain and Buddhist influence.

Purananuru (an anthology of 400 heroic Puram poems belonging to the Ettuthokai) and Pattinappalai (a long poem by Uruttirankannanar celebrating the Chola port of Puhar and King Karikala, belonging to the Pattupattu) are part of the Patinenmelkanakku, not the didactic Patinenkilkanakku.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-I

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the poetic conventions of Akam and Puram in Sangam literature:
items: Statement-I: Under strict Sangam poetic convention as codified in the Tolkappiyam, pure Akam (interior/love) poems prohibit identifying the romantic protagonists or dramatis personae by specific personal or royal names, portraying the lovers solely as universal, anonymous archetypes.

Statement-II: Several prominent Puram (exterior/public) poems in the Sangam anthologies were composed by female poets, such as Avvaiyar and Kakkaipadiniyar, celebrating the martial valor, munificence, and ethical governance of historical Tamil monarchs and velir chieftains.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Sangam poetics draws a sharp aesthetic boundary between Akam (interior emotional life) and Puram (exterior public and heroic life). In pure Akam poetry, identifying the romantic protagonists by personal or royal names is prohibited so that inner emotions remain universal, whereas Puram poems explicitly praise named historical kings and chieftains and include compositions by both male and female bards.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. According to the Tolkappiyam (Porul Adhikaram, Akattinaiyiyal, Sutra 57: 'Makkal nutaliya akanaittinum cutti oruvar peyar kolap peraar'), in pure Akam poetry, none of the romantic protagonists or dramatis personae—the hero (Talaivan), heroine (Talaivi), or confidante (Thozhi)—may be identified by a specific personal or royal name; they must remain anonymous archetypes representing universal human emotion (even though historical rulers or battles may occasionally appear in background landscape similes).

Statement-II is also correct. Sangam literature features over thirty women poets—including Avvaiyar (famous for her Puram poems on the Velir chieftain Athiyaman Neduman Anji), Kakkaipadiniyar Naccellaiyar, and Ponmudiyar—who composed powerful Puram verses on war, diplomacy, and royal generosity. However, the participation of female poets in Puram poetry does not explain the aesthetic rule of protagonist anonymity in Akam poetics.

ref: A.K. Ramanujan, Poems of Love and War; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: In the context of the five-fold ecological division (Aintinai) of Tamilakam described in Sangam literature, consider the following table:
items: 1. Kurinji : Montane hills; hunting and honey collection : Murugan (Seyon)
2. Mullai : Riverine plains; wet-rice plough agriculture : Vendan (Indra)
3. Marudam : Pastoral forest tracts; cattle rearing and shifting cultivation : Mayon
4. Neydal : Littoral coastal tracts; fishing and salt manufacturing : Varunan
prompt: In which of the rows given above is the information correctly matched?
core: The Sangam Aintinai concept links five physiographic eco-zones (Kurinji, Mullai, Marudam, Neydal, and Palai) with specific modes of subsistence, social groups, poetic moods (Uripporul), and presiding deities (Karupporul).

exp.why: Row 1 is correctly matched. Kurinji denotes the hilly/montane eco-zone inhabited by hill tribes (Kuravar/Vedar) engaged in hunting, gathering tubers, and collecting wild honey, with Murugan (Seyon, the Red God) as its presiding deity and clandestine union of lovers (Punardal) as its poetic mood.

Row 2 is incorrectly matched. Mullai refers to the pastoral forest and grassland tracts characterized by cattle rearing, dairy production, and shifting millet cultivation (Idaiyar/Ayar communities), presided over by Mayon (Vishnu/Krishna), with patient waiting (Iruttal) as its poetic mood.

Row 3 is incorrectly matched. Marudam refers to the fertile riverine and wetland agricultural plains where plough cultivators (Uzhavar/Vellalar) practiced wet-rice and sugarcane cultivation, presided over by Vendan (Indra, the god of rain and thunder), with lovers' sulking/infidelity (Udal) as its poetic mood.

Row 4 is correctly matched. Neydal denotes the coastal/littoral zone inhabited by fishing and salt-making communities (Paratavar/Umanar), presided over by Varunan (the sea god), with anxious pining for the separated partner (Irangal) as its poetic mood. (The fifth eco-zone, Palai, represents arid wasteland associated with highway robbery/cattle raids and the war goddess Korravai).

ref: Tamil Nadu SCERT Class XI History, Ch. 5; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the political centres and royal regalia of the Muvendar (Three Crowned Kings) during the Sangam Age, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Cheras ruled from their inland capital at Vanji (Karur), controlled the western maritime emporia of Muziris and Tondi, and adopted the bow-and-arrow as their royal emblem alongside the palmyra flower as their dynastic garland.

2. The early Cholas governed from their inland capital at Uraiyur, developed Puhar (Kaveripattinam) as their chief port and alternative royal seat, and bore the tiger emblem along with the atti (fig/bauhinia) floral garland.

3. The Pandyas ruled from their inland capital at Madurai, controlled the pearl-fishery port of Korkai at the mouth of the Tamraparni river, and used the twin carp (fish) as their royal insignia along with the margosa (neem) flower as their dynastic garland.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Each of the Muvendar (Cheras, Cholas, and Pandyas) maintained dual geopolitical anchors—a fertile inland capital and a strategic maritime emporium—and asserted royal legitimacy through distinct animal emblems on their banners and coins alongside specific dynastic floral garlands (Tarisu/Malai).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Cheras controlled central and northern Kerala and the Kongu region of Tamil Nadu from their inland capital at Vanji (identified with Karur). Their principal western seaports were Muziris (Muchiri) and Tondi. Their royal emblem was the bow and arrow (Vil), and their dynastic floral garland was the palmyra flower (Panampoon).

Statement 2 is correct. The Chola heartland (Cholamandalam) lay in the Kaveri delta. Their inland capital was Uraiyur (renowned for fine cotton textiles), while Puhar (Kaveripattinam), founded by Karikala at the mouth of the Kaveri, served as their premier port and coastal capital. Their royal emblem was the jumping tiger (Puli), and their dynastic garland was the atti flower (Bauhinia racemosa).

Statement 3 is correct. The Pandyas ruled the southern Tamil country from their inland capital at Madurai on the banks of the Vaigai river, while Korkai at the mouth of the Tamraparni (Porunai) river served as their chief port famous for pearl fisheries and chank diving. Their royal emblem was the carp/twin fish (Kayal), and their dynastic garland was the margosa/neem flower (Vembu).

ref: Tamil Nadu SCERT Class XI History, Ch. 5; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20

stem: Consider the following ancient ports of South India mentioned in Sangam literature and Graeco-Roman periplus accounts:
items: 1. Korkai
2. Muziris (Muchiri)
3. Poduke (Arikamedu)
4. Puhar (Kaveripattinam)
prompt: If an ancient maritime merchant sailed southward from the Malabar Coast, rounded Cape Comorin (Kumari), and then sailed northward along the Coromandel Coast, in which sequential order would he encounter these ports?
core: Early historic Indo-Roman and coastal cabotage trade connected the western littoral (Malabar) with the eastern littoral (Coromandel) around Cape Comorin, linking river-mouth emporia controlled by the Cheras, Pandyas, and Cholas.

exp.why: Korkai was the premier early Pandya port and pearl-fishery hub located at the mouth of the Tamiraparani river in the Gulf of Mannar (modern Thoothukudi district). After rounding Cape Comorin from the west coast, Korkai is the first major port encountered on the southeastern littoral.

Muziris (Muchiri, identified with Pattanam near Kodungallur in Kerala) was the principal Chera port at the mouth of the Periyar river on the Malabar (western) coast, making it the starting point of the voyage.

Poduke (identified with Arikamedu near modern Puducherry, at the mouth of the Ariyankuppam river) lies further north up the Coromandel coast beyond the Kaveri delta, making it the last of the four ports encountered.

Puhar (Kaveripattinam) was the chief Chola port located at the mouth of the Kaveri river (modern Mayiladuthurai district), situated north of Korkai and south of Poduke (Arikamedu). Hence, the correct coastal sequence is Muziris (2) -> Korkai (1) -> Puhar (4) -> Poduke (3).

ref: RS Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 20 (The Dawn of History in the Deep South); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the Chera polity and literary traditions of the Sangam Age, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Among the eight anthologies of the Ettuthokai, Pathitrupathu is the only text devoted exclusively to the genealogy and military exploits of the Chera monarchs.
2. According to early Tamil literary tradition, the Chera ruler Senguttuvan led a northern expedition to procure stone from the Himalayas for consecrating the image of Kannagi (Pattini cult).
3. Senguttuvan is credited with constructing the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) across the Periyar river to expand wetland paddy cultivation in the Chera heartland.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Chera political history is uniquely preserved in the Pathitrupathu anthology and the epic Silappadikaram, which celebrate rulers like Nedunjeral Adan and Senguttuvan, whereas major Kaveri delta hydraulic works belong to the Chola tradition under Karikala.

exp.why: Pathitrupathu ('Ten Tens') is the fourth anthology of the Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies) and is the only Sangam anthology dedicated exclusively to a single dynasty, providing panegyric decades on generations of Chera kings (of which the middle eight decades survive).

As narrated in the Vanchikandam of Silappadikaram (composed by his brother Ilango Adigal), the Chera monarch Senguttuvan (Red Chera) undertook a northern campaign to bring a sacred stone from the Himalayas, bathed it in the Ganga, and instituted the Pattini (Kannagi) cult at his capital Vanchi, an ceremony attended by King Gajabahu of Sri Lanka.

The construction of the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) and extensive flood embankments across the Kaveri river is attributed to the early Chola monarch Karikala, not to the Chera ruler Senguttuvan on the Periyar river.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 7 (The Age of the Sangam); NCERT Class XI Themes in Indian History

stem: With reference to the early Chola monarch Karikala and the Sangam literary corpus, consider the following statements:
items: 1. At the Battle of Venni, Karikala defeated a formidable confederacy comprising the Chera and Pandya monarchs alongside eleven Velir chieftains.
2. The Pattinappalai, composed by Mangudi Maruthanar in the Pattuppattu anthology, vividly describes the bustling maritime trade of Kaveripattinam during the reign of Pandya Nedunjeliyan.
3. According to Sangam traditions, Karikala promoted agrarian expansion in the Kaveri delta by clearing forested tracts and constructing flood embankments along the river.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Karikala Chola established Chola hegemony in the Kaveri delta through his military victory at Venni, state-backed reclamation of forest land for wet-rice cultivation, and patronage of maritime commerce at Puhar (Kaveripattinam).

exp.why: Sangam poems in the Purananuru and Agam anthologies recount that at the decisive Battle of Venni (modern Kovilvenni near Thanjavur), Karikala defeated a coalition of the Chera king Peruncheralathan (who committed ritual starvation by facing north, Vadakkiruttal, after receiving a wound on his back), the Pandya ruler, and eleven Velir chieftains.

Pattinappalai (one of the Ten Idylls in Pattuppattu) was composed by Kadiyalur Uruttirankannanar in praise of Karikala Chola and the Chola port city of Kaveripattinam (Puhar). Mangudi Maruthanar was the author of Maduraikanchi, which celebrates the Pandya ruler Nedunjeliyan and his capital Madurai.

Pattinappalai explicitly praises Karikala for converting forests into habitable agricultural lands (kadu-kondu-nadu-akki), excavating irrigation tanks (kulam-tottu-valam-perukki), and building embankments along the Kaveri river.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 7

stem: Ascending the throne at a young age, this celebrated Sangam monarch repulsed an invasion by a hostile coalition of the other two crowned monarchs (Vendar) and five Velir chieftains at the decisive Battle of Talaiyalanganam. He subsequently consolidated control over the pearl-fishing coast of Korkai and the territory of Milalai-kurram. His reign and the vibrant day and night markets (Nalangadi and Allangadi) of his capital are immortalized in the longest poem of the Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls).
prompt: Which of the following Sangam rulers is described in the passage above?
core: Talaiyalanganathu Seruvendra Nedunjeliyan was the most prominent early Pandya monarch of the Sangam era, celebrated in Mangudi Maruthanar's Maduraikanchi for his victory at Talaiyalanganam and the urban prosperity of Madurai.

exp.why: Option C is correct because the Pandya king Nedunjeliyan (renowned by the epithet 'Talaiyalanganathu Seruvendra Nedunjeliyan') defeated the combined forces of the Chera (Yanaikatchai Mantaran Cheral Irumporai), the Chola, and five Velir chieftains (Titiyan, Elini, Erumaiyuran, Irungovenman, and Porunan) at Talaiyalanganam. Mangudi Maruthanar dedicated Maduraikanchi—the longest of the ten poems in the Pattuppattu (782 lines)—to him, providing a vivid depiction of Madurai's day market (Nalangadi) and night market (Allangadi). Option A (Karikala Chola) is associated with the Battle of Venni and Pattinappalai. Option B (Cheran Senguttuvan) is celebrated in the fifth decade of Pathitrupathu and Silappadikaram. Option D (Koperuncholan) was a Chola ruler famous for his friendship with the poet Pisirantaiyar and dying by ritual fasting (Vadakkiruttal).

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 7; Champakalakshmi, Trade, Ideology and Urbanization: South India 300 BC to AD 1300

stem: With reference to the political economy of the Velir chieftains during the Sangam Age, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Velir were salaried provincial governors appointed and transferred directly by the Muvendar (Cheras, Cholas, and Pandyas) to administer upland forest districts on a centralized bureaucratic model.

2. Control over strategic highland passes, forest produce, and iron-ore zones enabled prominent Velir chieftains to participate in prestige redistribution and patronize Sangam bards on a scale rivalling the crowned monarchs.
3. The Muvendar frequently forged matrimonial alliances with leading Velir lineages to secure resource frontiers and military support against rival kingdoms.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sangam polity was structured around two primary tiers of authority: the Muvendar ruling riverine agricultural plains (Marutham) and coastal ports (Neithal), and autonomous Velir clan chieftains controlling hilly (Kurinji) and pastoral-forest (Mullai) resource zones.

exp.why: The Velir were NOT salaried, appointed, or transferable bureaucrats under a centralized administrative hierarchy of the Muvendar. Instead, they were autonomous clan-based chieftains (such as the Kadaiyezhu Vallalgal or Seven Great Patrons: Pari of Parambu hill, Adiyaman of Tagadur, Ay of Podiyil hill, Kari of Mullur, Ori of Kolli hills, Pehan, and Nalli) who ruled independent chiefdoms in the upland and forest regions.

Because the Velir controlled critical non-agrarian eco-zones (Kurinji and Mullai) rich in pepper, sandalwood, ivory, cattle, semi-precious stones, and iron ore, besides strategic ghat passes connecting the west and east coasts, they accumulated substantial wealth and gained fame in Purananuru and Sirupanarruppadai as extraordinarily generous patrons (Vallal) of poets and bards.

To secure transit corridors, highland resources, and military manpower, the crowned kings (Muvendar) regularly entered into marital alliances with prominent Velir families (and conversely waged war against defiant Velir chiefs like Pari to annex their territories).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; Rajan Gurukkal, Social Formations of Early South India

stem: With reference to the nature of kingship and administrative institutions in the Sangam Age, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the North Indian Dharmashastra ideal grounded primarily in Kshatriya varna legitimacy, Sangam kingship (Vendan) derived its primary authority from heroic martial valour (Maram) and munificent redistribution of war booty and agrarian surplus (Kodai).

2. The Aimperunkuzhu (Group of Five) and Enperayam (Group of Eight) mentioned in early Tamil texts functioned as elected legislative chambers vested with constitutional veto power over royal taxation.
3. At the village level, the Manram (or Podiyil) served as a communal gathering space beneath a sacred tree where local disputes were adjudicated and community festivities were conducted.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sangam kingship was rooted in heroic chiefdom norms (martial prowess and gift-giving) assisted by courtly advisory bodies (Aimperunkuzhu and Enperayam) and autonomous village assemblies (Manram/Podiyil), rather than formal constitutional legislatures.

exp.why: In the Puram heroic tradition of the Sangam corpus, royal legitimacy rested not on Brahmanical Kshatriya birth-status or elaborate Vedic consecrations alone (though some Muvendar kings occasionally patronized Vedic sacrifices), but fundamentally on battlefield heroism (Maram), protection of subjects, and generous redistribution (Kodai) of plunder and food to warriors, bards (Panar), and kinsmen.

In late Sangam and post-Sangam texts like Maduraikanchi and Silappadikaram, the Aimperunkuzhu (Council of Five: ministers, priests, army commanders, envoys, and spies) and the Enperayam (Assembly of Eight: administrative scribes, treasury officials, palace guards, leading city elders, and military captains) were royal advisory and executive entourages assisting the king in courtly governance, not elected parliamentary chambers with a constitutional veto over taxation.

The Manram or Podiyil was the traditional focal point of village life—an open communal platform, typically under an ancient tree—where village elders met to settle local disputes, transact community affairs, and host bardic performances and rituals.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 7; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the fiscal structure and political economy of the Sangam Age, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The Muvendar kingdoms maintained a uniform, centrally assessed land-revenue bureaucracy across all five eco-zones (Tinais) surveyed in units of Maa and Veli, rendering maritime customs tolls (Ulgu) and war booty negligible to royal finances.

Statement-II: Marked ecological diversity across the five Tinais restricted intensive plough agriculture largely to the Marutham river valleys, limiting uniform centralized agrarian surplus extraction across all Tamil territories.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Sangam polities operated a hybrid fiscal system combining wet-rice agrarian taxation (Karai/Vari) in the Marutham nuclear river valleys with commercial tolls (Ulgu/Sungam) at thriving ports and predatory cattle/booty raids that funded royal gift-redistribution (Kodai).

exp.why: While land measurement units like Maa and Veli and tax terms like Irai, Karai, and Vari existed in the fertile riverine tracts, the Muvendar did not possess a uniform centralized bureaucracy capable of assessing land revenue across all five Tinais. Instead, maritime customs duties and highway tolls (Ulgu or Sungam, vividly described at Puhar in Pattinappalai) alongside tribute and war booty formed critical pillars of royal revenue for redistribution (Kodaikkadam).

Of the five eco-zones (Kurinji, Mullai, Marutham, Neithal, and Palai), only the Marutham alluvial plains supported regular, surplus-generating wet-rice cultivation through plough agriculture. This ecological unevenness prevented uniform agrarian taxation across hill, pastoral, coastal, and arid zones, explaining why Sangam rulers relied heavily on trade tolls and raids alongside Marutham grain levies.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; R. Champakalakshmi, Trade, Ideology and Urbanization

stem: With reference to the social and occupational groups mentioned in Sangam literature, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the fertile Marutham river plains, the Vellalar constituted the landowning agrarian group, while Uzhavar and Kadaisiyar denoted ploughmen and agricultural labourers respectively.
2. The Paradavar and Umanar were inland pastoralist communities of the Mullai eco-zone who subsisted primarily on cattle rearing and dairy exchange.
3. The Pulaiyar were hereditary warrior chieftains of the arid Palai tracts who lived by highway plunder, whereas the Eyinar were urban guild artisans specializing in rope-making.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sangam society combined an emerging four-fold classification in the Tolkappiyam (Arasar, Anthanar, Vanigar, Vellalar) with eco-zone (Tinai) occupational groups such as Uzhavar, Kadaisiyar, Paradavar, Umanar, Eyinar, and Pulaiyar.

exp.why: In the Marutham agricultural zone, rich landowners were known as Vellalar (who also held high civil and military offices under the Muvendar), ordinary ploughmen were called Uzhavar, and landless agrarian labourers (often women working in paddy fields) were termed Kadaisiyar or Adimai.

This swaps coastal communities with pastoralists. The Paradavar (Parathavar) were coastal fishermen, pearl-divers, and maritime traders of the Neithal (littoral) zone, while the Umanar were salt manufacturers and salt merchants who travelled inland in bullock-cart caravans. Inland pastoralists of the Mullai zone were known as Ayar or Idaiyar.

This reverses the occupational roles of Pulaiyar and Eyinar. The Eyinar (and Maravar) were hunting and warrior communities of the Kurinji/Palai zones associated with cattle raids and highway plunder, whereas the Pulaiyar were a marginalized artisan group specializing in making rope cots and leather/fibre crafts.

ref: NCERT Class XI (Old) Ancient India by R.S. Sharma, Ch. 17; NCERT Class VI Themes in Indian History

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the status of women and social norms during the Sangam Age:
items: 1. Sangam poetic tradition distinguished between Kalavu, representing pre-marital courtship based on mutual affection, and Karpu, signifying chaste wedded life after formal marriage.
2. Women actively participated in literary and artistic domains, as reflected by poets like Avvaiyar and Nachchellaiyar and professional female performers called Viraliyar.
3. Owing to the high cultural visibility of female poets, widow remarriage was universally encouraged across Sangam society and the practice of widow self-immolation (Tippaydal) was entirely unknown.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
