core: While Sangam Akam poetry celebrated female emotional agency (Kalavu) and over thirty female poets contributed to the anthologies, patriarchal codes of feminine chastity (Karpu) imposed severe asceticism on widows and idealized Sati (Tippaydal) among warrior elites.

exp.why: The Tolkappiyam and Akam anthologies classify love into Kalavu (clandestine pre-marital love between a hero and heroine) and Karpu (post-marital wedded fidelity and domestic life instituted after marriage rituals emerged).

Sangam anthologies preserve verses by dozens of female poets, including Avvaiyar (a confidante of chieftain Athiyaman), Nachchellaiyar, and Kakkaipadiniyar. Royal courts also patronized Viraliyar and Panar—wandering female dancers and bards who performed with lute and percussion instruments.

Despite the literary celebration of love and learned female poets, the condition of widows (Kaimmai) was harsh and austere. Poems in the Purananuru describe widows shaving their heads, discarding ornaments, sleeping on bare stones, and eating plain rice and water-lily seeds, while elite warrior widows frequently practiced Tippaydal (entering the funeral pyre of the deceased husband).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; Tamil Nadu SCERT Class XI History, Ch. 5

stem: Which one of the following statements best reflects the relationship between the South Indian Megalithic culture and the religious and funerary traditions documented in Sangam literature?

opts.A: Sangam texts reflect a complete cultural break from the Megalithic Iron Age, replacing urn burials entirely with Vedic fire-altar cremation across all five Tinais.
opts.B: The erection of memorial hero stones (Nadukal) was a royal prerogative restricted exclusively to crowned Muvendar kings and prohibited any written inscriptions on the stone.
opts.C: Worship of the indigenous deity Murugan (Seyon) had already transitioned into purely Sanskritic Agamic temple liturgy devoid of ecstatic possession dances or animal offerings.
opts.D: Sangam poems and the epic Manimekalai attest to direct cultural continuity with the Megalithic tradition, documenting urn burials (Mudumakkal Thazhi), cremation, and the veneration of inscribed hero stones (Nadukal) erected for fallen warriors.

core: Archaeological and literary evidence demonstrates seamless continuity between the late South Indian Iron Age Megalithic culture and the Sangam period, particularly in pluralistic disposal of the dead (urn burials, cists, cremation) and Nadukal (hero stone) worship.

exp.why: Option D is correct because the Purananuru (Mentioning pot-makers fashioning wide-mouthed burial urns or Thazhi for chieftains) and the epic Manimekalai (Ch. 6, listing cremation, exposure, pit burial, cist chambers, and terracotta urns) confirm the coexistence of Megalithic burial customs during the Sangam era. Furthermore, the ritual erection and worship of Nadukal or Virakkal (memorial stones inscribed with a fallen warrior's name and exploits, corroborated by 3rd-century BCE Tamil-Brahmi inscribed hero stones at Pulimankombai) directly grew out of Megalithic commemorative lithic traditions. Option A is false because urn burials continued widely alongside cremation. Option B is false because the Tolkappiyam explicitly details the stages of erecting a Nadukal and inscribing the fallen soldier's or cattle-defender's name and martial feat on it. Option C is false because Murugan worship was centred on indigenous ecstatic dances called Veriyattu performed by the spear-holding priest (Velan) with goat sacrifices and millet-blood offerings.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; K. Rajan, Early Historic Archaeology of Tamil Nadu

stem: With reference to the Indo-Roman trade network in ancient Tamilakam, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: In peninsular India, the heaviest concentration of early Roman Imperial gold and silver coin hoards—particularly from the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius—has been recovered from the inland Coimbatore–Karur (Kongu) belt rather than coastal port sites.

Statement-II: The Coimbatore–Karur corridor commanded the strategic Palghat Gap connecting the Malabar port of Muziris to the eastern coast, while housing major sources of beryl and quartz gems highly prized in the Roman Empire.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The spatial clustering of early Roman Imperial aurei and denarii in the Kongu region (Coimbatore-Erode-Karur) reflects the geopolitical importance of the Palghat Gap overland transit artery and the local Padiyur/Kodumanal beryl and semi-precious gem industry.

exp.why: Archaeological finds of Roman coins in South India show a striking concentration of Julio-Claudian hoards (especially Augustus and Tiberius, 1st century BCE to 1st century CE) in the inland Kongu region around Coimbatore, Pollachi, Tiruppur, and Karur, functioning as high-value bullion in luxury exchange.

Statement-II directly explains Statement-I: Roman merchants landing at Muziris (Muchiri) on the Kerala coast used the Palghat Gap through Coimbatore and the Chera capital Karur (Vanchi) to reach the Coromandel ports (eliminating the hazardous circumnavigation of Sri Lanka) and to procure green-blue aquamarine beryl mined at Padiyur and processed into beads at Kodumanal, alongside black pepper from the Western Ghats.

ref: Romila Thapar, Early India, Ch. 8; R. Champakalakshmi, Trade, Ideology and Urbanization: South India 300 BC to AD 1300

stem: With reference to major archaeological sites associated with the Sangam and Early Historic period in South India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Keeladi, situated on the banks of the Noyyal river in the Kongu region, was an upland megalithic lapidary and crucible-steel site devoid of burnt-brick structural remains.

2. Kodumanal, located in the lower Vaigai river basin, served as the chief coastal emporium of the Pandyas where Mediterranean amphorae and Italian Arretine ware were first excavated by Mortimer Wheeler.
3. Pattanam in the Periyar river delta has been archaeologically identified with the inland Chola capital of Uraiyur, characterized by the complete absence of West Asian or Roman ceramic assemblages.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Recent excavations at Keeladi (Vaigai basin), Kodumanal (Noyyal basin), and Pattanam (Periyar basin/Muziris), alongside classic excavations at Arikamedu, provide the material scaffolding for Early Historic urbanization, literacy, and maritime trade in Tamilakam.

exp.why: This swaps the location and features of Keeladi with Kodumanal. Keeladi is located on the banks of the Vaigai river (Sivaganga district, near Madurai) in the Pandya heartland and is renowned for its urban burnt-brick structures, terracotta ring wells, dyeing vats, weaving spindle whorls, and over a thousand Tamil-Brahmi inscribed potsherds dating back to the 6th century BCE.

Kodumanal (identified with Kodumanam of the Patirruppattu) is an inland industrial and trade settlement on the north bank of the Noyyal river (a tributary of the Kaveri in Erode district), famous for semi-precious quartz/beryl bead-making and iron/crucible-steel furnaces. By contrast, Mortimer Wheeler famously excavated Mediterranean amphorae and Italian Arretine ware at the coastal port of Arikamedu (Poduke) near Puducherry.

Pattanam in the Periyar river delta (Ernakulam district, Kerala) is identified by archaeologists with the celebrated Chera port of Muziris (Muchiri), yielding abundant Roman amphora shards, Terra Sigillata, West Asian Turquoise Glazed Pottery, torpedo jars, and a brick wharf with a wooden dugout canoe.

ref: Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology Reports on Keeladi & Kodumanal; NCERT Class XI Themes in Indian History

stem: With reference to the presence and role of the 'Yavanas' in the Sangam Age, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Sangam anthologies such as the Akananuru describe Yavana merchant vessels arriving at the Chera port of Muziris with gold and wine and returning with cargoes of black pepper.
2. Yavana artisans and metalworkers were noted in Tamil literary traditions for crafting distinctive ornamental oil lamps and luxury artifacts for royal residences.

3. Under the royal decrees of the Muvendar, Yavanas were restricted to designated coastal emporia and were prohibited from entering inland capitals like Madurai or serving in the military apparatus of Tamil rulers.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sangam literature depicts the Yavanas (Greco-Roman and West Asian foreigners) not only as maritime traders exchanging gold and wine for pepper at ports like Muziris and Puhar, but also as skilled craftsmen and stern palace/fortress guards employed by Tamil monarchs in inland capitals like Madurai.

exp.why: Poem 149 of the Akananuru (by Erukkattur Tayankannanar) famously describes the thriving Chera port of Muchiri (Muziris) on the Periyar river, where the 'beautifully built ships of the Yavanas came with gold and returned with pepper' (later termed Yavanapriya in Sanskrit texts), alongside references in Purananuru to sweet, cool wine brought in Yavana vessels.

Sangam poems such as Nedunalvadai and Perumpanarruppadai explicitly praise artistic lamps wrought by the Yavanas—such as lamps shaped like a maiden holding a bowl of oil (Pavai Vilakku) or swan-shaped lamps—adorning royal palaces and elite mansions.

Yavanas were neither restricted to the coast nor barred from military service. Texts such as Mullaippattu, Nedunalvadai, and Silappadikaram vividly describe tall, stern-looking Yavana soldiers clad in leather tunics and wielding swords who served as royal bodyguards at the king's pavilion and guarded the fortress gates of inland Madurai.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; Akananuru 149 & Mullaippattu

stem: In the history of ancient Indian philosophical and didactic literature, Tiruvalluvar's Tirukkural is uniquely celebrated as 'Muppal' (The Three-fold Path). Which one of the following best explains the structural and philosophical basis of this designation?

opts.A: It synthesizes the ritualistic doctrines of the three orthodox Vedic fires with the monastic codes of the Digambara Jaina and Theravada Buddhist orders.
opts.B: It organizes human life into the three worldly spheres of Aram (righteousness), Porul (polity and wealth), and Inbam (love), while omitting a separate book on Vidu (ultimate liberation) on the premise that ethical living within the world naturally leads to spiritual fulfillment.
opts.C: It prescribes a mandatory three-stage ascetic progression wherein householders must renounce family and statecraft to attain liberation through solitary meditation.
opts.D: It was composed jointly by three court poets representing the Chera, Chola, and Pandya kingdoms to codify a uniform criminal law across Tamilakam.

core: Tirukkural is called Muppal because it divides its 133 chapters (1,330 couplets) into three books—Aram (Virtue), Porul (Polity/Wealth), and Inbam or Kamam (Love)—deliberately omitting a fourth book on Vidu (Moksha) because spiritual liberation is treated as the natural fruit of practicing ethics in worldly life.

exp.why: Option B is correct: Unlike the four-fold Sanskrit Purushartha schema (Dharma, Artha, Kama, Moksha), Tiruvalluvar structured the Tirukkural into three sections (Muppal): Arattuppal (38 chapters on moral and householder/ascetic virtue), Porutpal (70 chapters on statecraft, economy, and social conduct), and Kamattuppal/Inbattuppal (25 chapters on human love). Classical commentators like Parimelalagar note that Vidu (Moksha) cannot be defined through didactic rules alone and automatically follows from the proper observance of the first three aims. Option A is incorrect because Tirukkural is famously non-sectarian and avoids Vedic fire-ritualism. Option C is incorrect (Trap T2) because Tirukkural strongly affirms the dignity of the householder (Illaram) rather than mandating universal ascetic renunciation. Option D is incorrect as it is the work of a single author, Tiruvalluvar.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 7; NCERT Class XI Ancient India

stem: With reference to the Tamil epic Silappadikaram, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The narrative of the epic is set entirely within the Pandya capital of Madurai and concludes immediately with Kannagi's burning of the city.

2. Although composed by the Jaina prince-ascetic Ilango Adigal, the epic exhibits a pluralistic religious ethos by weaving Jaina moral philosophy together with invocations of Vedic deities, Tirumal, Murugan, and Korravai.
3. The text serves as a major technical source on ancient Tamil musicology, lute (yazh) tuning, and classical dance choreography.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Silappadikaram ('The Tale of an Anklet') by Ilango Adigal integrates the geography and polity of all three Tamil kingdoms through its three cantos (Puharkkandam, Maduraikkandam, and Vanjikkandam), combining a Jaina ethical core with pluralistic religious traditions and detailed treatises on Tamil performing arts.

exp.why: Silappadikaram is not confined to Madurai, nor does it end with the burning of Madurai. It is structured into three books spanning all three Sangam kingdoms: Puharkkandam (set in the Chola port of Kaveripattinam/Puhar), Maduraikkandam (set in the Pandya capital of Madurai), and Vanjikkandam (set in the Chera capital of Vanji, where Chera king Senguttuvan leads a northern expedition to the Himalayas to fetch a stone for consecrating the temple of Goddess Pattini/Kannagi).

While Ilango Adigal was a Jaina ascetic and gives prominence to the Jaina nun Kavundi Adigal and the doctrine of karma, the epic seamlessly portrays the worship of Tirumal (Vishnu) by cowherds (Aychiyarkuravai), Murugan by hill tribes (Kunrakkuravai), Korravai by hunters (Vettuvavari), and Vedic sacrifices.

Particularly in the Arangetrukadai (the canto describing the courtesan Madhavi's debut dance performance) and Kanalvari, Silappadikaram provides exhaustive technical details on ancient Tamil musical modes (pann), types of yazh (lutes), percussion instruments, stage dimensions, and 11 classical dance forms.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8; R. Parthasarathy, The Cilappatikaram

stem: With reference to the Five Great Epics (Aimperumkappiyangal) of the Tamil literary tradition, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Manimekalai : Composed by Chithalai Chathanar (Sattanar) — Buddhist tradition
2. Jivaka Chintamani : Composed by Tiruttakkadevar — Buddhist tradition
3. Kundalakesi : Composed by Nagakuthanar — Jaina tradition
4. Valayapathi : Extant in fragments — Jaina tradition
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Of the Five Great Tamil Epics (Aimperumkappiyangal), three belong to the Jaina tradition (Silappadikaram, Jivaka Chintamani, and Valayapathi) and two belong to the Buddhist tradition (Manimekalai and Kundalakesi).

exp.why: Manimekalai was composed by the Madurai grain-merchant poet Chithalai Chathanar (Sattanar) as a Buddhist sequel to Silappadikaram, narrating the spiritual journey of Kovalan and Madhavi's daughter Manimekalai into a Buddhist bhikshuni.

Jivaka Chintamani (also known as Mananul, the Book of Marriages) was composed by the Chola prince-turned-ascetic Tiruttakkadevar in the 10th century CE, but it belongs to the Jaina tradition, not the Buddhist tradition. It narrates the life of prince Jivaka who masters the arts of war and wedlock before renouncing the world to attain Jaina liberation.

Kundalakesi, attributed to Nagakuthanar, is a Buddhist polemical epic (not Jaina) about a merchant's daughter who becomes a skilled Buddhist debater expounding Buddhist logic against Jaina and Vedic doctrines. (A Jaina counter-epic, Nilakesi, was later composed among the Five Minor Epics to refute Kundalakesi.)

Valayapathi is a Jaina Tamil epic that survives only in 72 fragmentary stanzas cited in later commentaries (such as the 14th-century commentary on Yapparungalam), expounding Jaina ascetic ethics such as non-violence, chastity, and renunciation.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 14; Kamil Zvelebil, Tamil Literature

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the post-Sangam literary works Manimekalai and Naladiyar:
items: 1. Sattanar's Manimekalai elevates the eradication of hunger (pasi-pini) to the supreme ethical duty through the motif of the Amudhasurabhi and contains systematic chapters on Buddhist epistemology taught by Aravana Adigal.
2. Naladiyar, included in the Pathinenkilkanakku (Eighteen Lesser Texts), was composed as a single-author philosophical treatise by a Buddhist monk at Kaveripattinam.
3. Unlike Silappadikaram, Manimekalai avoids any discussion of non-Buddhist schools such as Ajivika, Lokayata, or Sankhya, restricting its narrative solely to monastic rituals.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Sattanar's Manimekalai is a Buddhist epic that pairs compassionate social service (feeding the hungry via the Amudhasurabhi bowl) with rigorous inter-religious philosophical debate, Naladiyar is a Jaina anthology of 400 quatrains composed by 400 Jaina ascetics.

exp.why: In Manimekalai, the heroine receives the miraculous inexhaustible begging bowl (Amudhasurabhi, originally belonging to Aputra) at Manipallavam and uses it to feed the hungry, prisons, and the destitute, proclaiming that those who relieve the disease of hunger (pasi-pini) are true givers of life. The final cantos expound Buddhist logic (Pramana) and Pratityasamutpada under the aged Buddhist master Aravana Adigal at Kanchipuram.

Naladiyar (also called Naladi Nanuru or Velalar Veda) is neither a single-author text nor a Buddhist work. According to Tamil tradition and internal themes, it is an anthology of 400 four-line venba verses composed by 400 Jaina monks who were patronized in the Pandya country, later compiled by Padumanar into three sections mirroring the Tirukkural.

Far from avoiding non-Buddhist systems, Canto 27 of Manimekalai (Samaya-kanakkar tam tiram ketta kadai) specifically sends Manimekalai in the guise of a male ascetic to Vanji, where she systematically hears and critiques the tenets of ten rival philosophical schools—including Pramana-vada, Saiva, Brahma-vada, Vaishnava, Veda-vada, Ajivika, Nirgrantha (Jaina), Sankhya, Vaisheshika, and Bhuta-vada (Lokayata)—before embracing Aravana Adigal's Buddhist exposition.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8 & 9; Kamil Zvelebil, Companion Studies to the History of Tamil Literature

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Kalabhra period (circa 3rd to 6th century CE) in the history of South India:
items: Statement-I: The Kalabhra rulers imposed a blanket prohibition on literary composition in Tamil and Pali, resulting in a complete absence of didactic and monastic literature across Tamilakam until the revival of the Pandyas under Kadungon.

Statement-II: Later Pallava and Pandya copper-plate charters such as the Velvikudi grant characterize the Kalabhras as 'evil kings' (Kali-arasan) primarily because the Kalabhras patronized heterodox Jaina and Buddhist orders and disrupted early Brahmadeya land grants.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The characterization of the Kalabhra interregnum as a 'Dark Age' stems from the ideological hostility of later Pallava and Pandya copper-plate charters resenting the revocation of Brahmadeya grants and Kalabhra patronage of Jaina and Buddhist monasteries, whereas in reality the period witnessed remarkable flourishing of Tamil didactic literature and Pali Buddhist scholarship.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect: The Kalabhra period was one of intense literary and monastic vitality in both Tamil and Pali/Prakrit. During this era, the Jaina monk Vajranandi founded the Dravida Sangha at Madurai (c. 470 CE), most of the didactic Pathinenkilkanakku Tamil texts and the twin epics were composed, and the celebrated Buddhist scholar Buddhadatta composed his Pali manuals (such as Abhidhammavatara and Vinayavinicchaya) at Kaveripattinam and Uragapura under the patronage of the Kalabhra king Accutavikkanta (Achyuta Vikranta).

Statement-II is correct: The 8th-century Velvikudi copper-plate grant of Pandya king Parantaka Nedunjadaiyan (as well as Pallava charters like the Kasakudi plates) describes the Kalabhras as 'Kali-arasan' (evil rulers) who uprooted the established kings (Adhirajas) and confiscated existing Brahmadeya (tax-free land) grants—specifically recording how the village of Velvikudi, originally granted to a Brahmana by the Sangam Pandya king Palyagasalai Mudukudumi Peruvaludi, was resumed under the Kalabhras before being restored centuries later.

ref: Noboru Karashima (ed.), A Concise History of South India, Ch. 2; Upinder Singh, Ch. 9 (Velvikudi Plates)

stem: With reference to the political rise of the early Gupta dynasty and its coinage, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Sri Gupta, the founder of the dynasty, was the first ruler to assume the imperial title of 'Maharajadhiraja' and inaugurate the Gupta Era in 319–320 CE.
2. The matrimonial alliance between Chandragupta I and the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi played a decisive role in consolidating Gupta authority over Magadha and adjoining regions.
3. The 'King-and-Queen' type gold Dinaras issued by Chandragupta I depict both the monarch and Queen Kumaradevi on the obverse alongside the legend 'Lichchhavayah' on the reverse.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The transition of the Guptas from subordinate chiefs to an imperial power is reflected in the shift of royal titles from 'Maharaja' (held by Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha) to 'Maharajadhiraja' under Chandragupta I, who inaugurated the Gupta Era in 319–320 CE and commemorated his pivotal Lichchhavi alliance on gold Dinaras.

exp.why: In the genealogical records of the Guptas (such as the Prayag Prashasti and Bhitari Pillar Inscription), the first two rulers—Sri Gupta and his son Ghatotkacha—are referred to simply as 'Maharaja', a title typically borne by feudatory or subordinate rulers during the post-Kushana period. It was Chandragupta I (c. 319–335 CE) who first assumed the sovereign imperial title 'Maharajadhiraja' (King of Great Kings) and initiated the Gupta Samvat (Era) in 319–320 CE.

Chandragupta I strengthened his nascent kingdom by marrying Kumaradevi, a princess of the ancient and prestigious Lichchhavi clan (who controlled parts of Vaishali/north Bihar and Nepal). This alliance brought both political legitimacy among oligarchic ganasangha traditions and strategic territorial consolidation across the middle Gangetic basin.

The earliest indisputable Gupta gold coins (Dinaras) are the Chandragupta-Kumaradevi ('King-and-Queen') type. The obverse depicts Chandragupta I standing and offering a ring or bridal bracelet to Queen Kumaradevi with both their names inscribed in Brahmi, while the reverse features a goddess seated on a lion with the plural legend 'Lichchhavayah' (the Lichchhavis), acknowledging the shared political prestige of the alliance.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 23

stem: With reference to the Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription) and the geopolitical strategy of Samudragupta, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Composed in classical Sanskrit as a 'Champu Kavya' by Harisena, the inscription is engraved on an Ashokan pillar and outlines distinct imperial policies tailored to the geographical proximity of conquered territories.

2. Under the policy of 'Grahanamokshanugraha', Samudragupta reinstated the defeated rulers of Aryavarta as autonomous tributary states, whereas he directly annexed the twelve kingdoms of Dakshinapatha into the imperial provinces under 'Prasabhoddharana'.

3. The inscription records that the Atavika (forest) kingdoms were reduced to servitude, while frontier kingdoms such as Samatata, Davaka, Kamarupa, Nepala, and Kartripura paid tribute and performed obeisance.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Samudragupta's Prayag Prashasti illustrates a pragmatic concentric ring model of empire: direct annexation ('Prasabhoddharana') in the contiguous Gangetic plains of Aryavarta, contrasted with capture, liberation, and tributary reinstatement ('Grahanamokshanugraha') in distant Dakshinapatha where direct communication and control from Pataliputra were logistically unviable.

exp.why: The Prayag Prashasti was composed by Harisena—who held the offices of Sandhivigrahika (minister for peace and war), Kumaramatya, and Mahadandanayaka—in the Champu style (combining verse and prose) in refined classical Sanskrit. Engraved on the Ashokan sandstone pillar at Kaushambi/Prayag, it classifies Samudragupta's campaigns according to the geopolitical zone and corresponding administrative policy.

This statement reverses the policies applied to Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha. Against the nine rulers of Aryavarta (the Gangetic heartland), Samudragupta pursued the policy of 'Prasabhoddharana' (violent uprooting and complete annexation into the direct provincial administration of the empire). Conversely, against the twelve rulers of Dakshinapatha (the eastern Deccan and South India, including Kanchi and Vengi), he followed 'Grahanamokshanugraha'—capturing the kings, liberating them ('moksha'), and reinstating them ('anugraha') as tributary subordinates.

Line 21 of the Prayag Prashasti states that Samudragupta reduced all the kings of the forest regions ('Sarva-atavika-rajasya', covering parts of central India/Bundelkhand-Baghelkhand) to the status of servants ('paricharika-krita'). Line 22 further lists five frontier monarchies ('Pratyanta-nripatis')—Samatata (south-east Bengal), Davaka (Nowgong, Assam), Kamarupa (upper Assam), Nepala, and Kartripura (Kumaon-Garhwal)—along with nine republican tribes (Malavas, Arjunayanas, Yaudheyas, Madrakas, Abhiras, etc.) who gratified his imperious commands by paying all kinds of taxes ('sarva-kara-dana') and performing obeisance ('pranama-agamana').

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. III (J.F. Fleet)

stem: With reference to the historical reconstruction of the 'Ramagupta' episode in Gupta dynastic history, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Literary accounts in fragments of Vishakhadatta's Sanskrit drama 'Devichandraguptam' and Banabhatta's 'Harshacharita' narrate how Chandragupta II assassinated a Shaka ruler after his elder brother Ramagupta agreed to surrender Queen Dhruvadevi.

2. Rashtrakuta epigraphic records, including the Sanjan copper plates of Amoghavarsha I, independently allude to this dynastic episode while contrasting the conduct of the Gupta king with Rashtrakuta munificence.

3. While Ramagupta figures prominently in post-Gupta literary traditions and Deccan charters, his historicity remains uncorroborated by any fourth-century copper coinage or Jaina image inscriptions in Central India.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Once dismissed as purely legendary because Ramagupta was omitted from official royal Gupta genealogies (which trace descent rather than collateral succession), the historicity of Ramagupta between Samudragupta and Chandragupta II has been firmly established by the discovery of his Lion/Garuda copper coins and the Durjanpur Jaina Tirthankara inscriptions in eastern Malwa.

exp.why: Surviving extracts of Vishakhadatta's 'Devichandraguptam' (preserved in Bhoja's 'Shringaraprakasha' and Ramachandra and Gunachandra's 'Natyadarpana'), corroborated by Banabhatta's seventh-century 'Harshacharita' and Rajashekhara's 'Kavyamimamsa', describe how Ramagupta was besieged by a Shaka king and agreed to surrender his queen Dhruvadevi (Dhruvasvamini). Prince Chandragupta II entered the Shaka camp disguised as the queen, slew the Shaka ruler, and subsequently overthrew Ramagupta and married Dhruvadevi.

Several Rashtrakuta copper-plate charters—most notably the Sanjan plates of Amoghavarsha I (871 CE) as well as the Cambay and Sangli plates of Govinda IV—explicitly refer to a prince of the Gupta lineage ('Kaliyuga-visesha-sahasa') who killed his own brother, seized his kingdom and queen, and plays on the contrast between that disgraced Gupta ruler and the virtuous Rashtrakuta emperors.

Ramagupta's historicity is directly corroborated by both numismatic and epigraphic discoveries in eastern Malwa (Central India). Numerous copper coins bearing the name 'Ramagupta' in early Gupta Brahmi characters—featuring Lion and Garuda motifs—have been recovered from the Eran-Vidisha (Besnagar) region. Decisive epigraphic proof came in 1969 with the discovery of three Jaina Tirthankara (Chandraprabha and Pushpadanta) image inscriptions at Durjanpur near Vidisha, which explicitly record that the images were commissioned by 'Maharajadhiraja Sri Ramagupta'.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; S.R. Goyal, A History of the Imperial Guptas

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the reign of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya):
items: Statement-I: Chandragupta II's matrimonial alliance with the Vakataka dynasty, through the marriage of his daughter Prabhavatigupta to Rudrasena II and her subsequent regency in the central Deccan, was strategically pivotal in enabling his military campaign that overthrew the Western Kshatrapa ruler Rudrasimha III and secured Gupta access to western sea ports like Bharuch (Barygaza).

Statement-II: Following the annexation of western Malwa and Saurashtra (Kathiawar), Chandragupta II became the first Gupta monarch to issue silver coins (Rupakas), which were closely modelled on the weight standard and obverse royal bust of the defeated Western Kshatrapa coinage while replacing their reverse symbol with the Gupta Garuda.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Chandragupta II neutralized the strategic flank of the central Deccan not by military annexation of the Vakatakas, but through a diplomatic marriage alliance with Rudrasena II and Prabhavatigupta's twenty-year regency; following the resulting conquest of the Western Kshatrapas, he introduced silver Rupakas modelled on Kshatrapa currency to maintain monetary continuity in western India.

exp.why: The Vakataka kingdom of Vidarbha occupied a commanding geographical position in the central Deccan that could help or hinder any northern army marching against the Shaka Western Kshatrapas of Malwa and Gujarat. By marrying his daughter Prabhavatigupta (born of Kuberanaga) to the Vakataka king Rudrasena II—and especially during Prabhavatigupta's two-decade regency for her minor sons Divakarasena and Damodarasena after Rudrasena II's premature death—Chandragupta II secured his southern flank. This enabled his protracted campaign in eastern Malwa (attested by the Udayagiri inscriptions of Virasena and the Sanchi inscription of Amrakardava) that culminated in the defeat of Rudrasimha III and brought the lucrative western maritime trade of Bharuch, Sopara, and Cambay into the Gupta orbit.

Statement-II is also factually correct: prior to Chandragupta II's western campaign, the Guptas primarily issued gold Dinaras and some copper coins, whereas western India had for centuries used the silver Drammas/Karshapanas of the Western Kshatrapas. To avoid disrupting regional trade in newly annexed Malwa and Saurashtra, Chandragupta II issued the first Gupta silver coins ('Rupakas') on the exact Kshatrapa weight standard (~30–33 grains), retaining the ruler's profile bust on the obverse while substituting the Kshatrapa three-arched hill (chaitya) on the reverse with the Vaishnava Garuda emblem. However, Statement-II describes a post-conquest monetary policy and therefore does not explain the geopolitical role of the Vakataka alliance in Statement-I.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 23; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the Mehrauli Iron Pillar Inscription and ancient Indian metallurgy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Sanskrit inscription on the pillar eulogizes a ruler named 'Chandra' for defeating a confederacy of enemies in the Vanga country and crossing the seven mouths of the river Sindhu to vanquish the Vahlikas.
2. The inscription records that the pillar was originally erected on a hill called 'Vishnupada' as a lofty standard ('Dhvaja') in honour of Lord Vishnu.

3. Metallurgical investigations have established that the pillar's exceptional resistance to atmospheric rust is due to the intentional alloying of high-carbon steel with chromium and nickel during smelting, rather than the presence of phosphorus in wrought iron.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Mehrauli Iron Pillar stands as a twin testament to Gupta imperial reach—recording 'Chandra's' victories from Vanga (Bengal) to Vahlika (Balkh/Bactria beyond the Indus)—and to ancient Indian forge-welded wrought iron metallurgy, where high phosphorus content (~0.25%) catalyzes a self-healing passive protective layer of crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate.

exp.why: Composed in three-stanza Shardulavikridita metre in classical Sanskrit and paleographically dated to the fourth–fifth century CE, the Mehrauli Pillar Inscription praises a king named 'Chandra' (almost universally identified with Chandragupta II Vikramaditya). Verse 1 specifically states that he shattered a coalition of enemies united against him in the Vanga (Bengal) countries and defeated the Vahlikas (Bactria/Oxus basin or northwestern frontier) in battle after crossing the seven mouths ('sapta-mukha') of the river Sindhu (Indus).

Verse 3 of the inscription states that the king—having fixed his mind with devotion upon Vishnu—erected this lofty standard ('dhvaja') of the divine Lord Vishnu on the hill known as 'Vishnupada' (often identified with the Udayagiri hills in Vidisha, from where the pillar was later relocated to Delhi/Mehrauli during the Tomara/early medieval period).

The Mehrauli Iron Pillar is NOT made of stainless steel (chromium-nickel alloyed steel). Instead, it was fabricated by forge-welding lumps of wrought iron containing very low carbon (~0.15%), negligible sulphur and manganese, and a remarkably high phosphorus content (averaging ~0.25%) because ancient Indian smelters used wood charcoal without adding limestone flux (which otherwise removes phosphorus into slag). As demonstrated by R. Balasubramaniam's metallurgical studies, this high phosphorus content at the metal-scale interface catalyzes the formation of a dense, adherent passive film of 'misawite' (delta-FeOOH) and crystalline iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate (FePO4.H3PO4.4H2O), which blocks moisture and oxygen penetration.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; R. Balasubramaniam, Story of the Delhi Iron Pillar

stem: With reference to the reigns of the later Imperial Gupta monarchs Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Kumaragupta I, who assumed the title 'Mahendraditya' and performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice as attested by his gold coinage, is identified with 'Shakraditya', the royal founder of the Nalanda Mahavihara.

2. The Junagadh Rock Inscription of Skandagupta provides the primary epigraphic account of his military campaigns against both the Pushyamitras and the invading Hunas in the Gangetic heartland, during which he spent a night sleeping on the bare earth.

3. According to the Bhitari Pillar Inscription, when the embankment of the Sudarshana Lake in Saurashtra burst due to excessive rains during Skandagupta's reign, it was reconstructed by his provincial governor Pushyagupta and the Yavana official Tushaspha.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Kumaragupta I's long reign (c. 415–455 CE) saw the foundation of Nalanda Mahavihara and diverse numismatic issues, its closing years and the reign of Skandagupta witnessed severe military crises against the Pushyamitras and the Hunas (recorded in the Bhitari Pillar Inscription) alongside major hydraulic restoration of the Sudarshana Lake by Parnadatta and Chakrapalita (recorded in the Junagadh Rock Inscription).

exp.why: Kumaragupta I (c. 415–455 CE) adopted the titles 'Mahendraditya' and 'Vyaghra-balaparakrama', issued the largest variety of Gupta coins (including Karttikeya/Peacock-type and Ashvamedha-type gold coins), and is identified with 'Shakraditya'—whom the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) credits with founding the earliest monastery at Nalanda Mahavihara (since both 'Shakra' and 'Mahendra' are synonymous epithets of Lord Indra).

This statement swaps the contents of the Bhitari Pillar Inscription and the Junagadh Rock Inscription. It is the Bhitari Pillar Inscription (located in Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh)—not the Junagadh Rock Inscription—that vividly describes Skandagupta's fierce struggle to restore the fallen fortunes of his dynasty against the Pushyamitras (during which he spent a night sleeping on the bare ground) and his earth-shaking victory when he joined in close combat with the invading Hunas.

This statement contains a double attribution swap. First, the bursting and reconstruction of the Sudarshana Lake embankment during Skandagupta's reign (in Gupta Era 136–137, i.e., 455–456 CE) is recorded in the Junagadh (Girnar) Rock Inscription in Gujarat, not the Bhitari Pillar Inscription. Second, under Skandagupta, the lake was repaired by his newly appointed provincial governor ('Goptri') of Surashtra, Parnadatta, and Parnadatta's son Chakrapalita (the city magistrate of Girinagara), who also built a temple of Lord Vishnu (Chakrabhrit) on the embankment. Pushyagupta the Vaishya and the Yavana Tushaspha belonged to the Mauryan era under Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka respectively (as recorded in Rudradaman's earlier inscription on the same rock).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. III

stem: With reference to the Huna invasions and the political fragmentation of northern India during the fifth and sixth centuries CE, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Gupta emperor Skandagupta permanently eradicated Huna power in the Indian subcontinent by decisively defeating the Huna ruler Mihirakula, as recorded in the Bhitari pillar inscription.
2. The Eran Boar Inscription, dated to the first regnal year of Toramana, provides epigraphic evidence of Huna political penetration deep into the Malwa region of central India.

3. The Huna occupation of the north-western frontiers and the Oxus basin disrupted overland Indo-Central Asian commercial arteries, contributing to the decline of long-distance trade and urban centres in northern India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Skandagupta successfully repulsed the earliest wave of Huna incursions in the mid-fifth century CE, a second and more devastating wave led by Toramana and his son Mihirakula penetrated as far as Malwa and Gwalior in the early sixth century CE before being defeated by Yashodharman of Malwa and the later Gupta ruler Narasimhagupta Baladitya. These invasions severely disrupted overland Central Asian trade routes and accelerated the fiscal and political fragmentation of the Gupta Empire.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect due to a chronological conflation. Skandagupta (c. 455–467 CE) repulsed the first wave of Huna invaders (referred to in the Bhitari pillar and Junagadh rock inscriptions), but this did not permanently eradicate Huna power. Decades later, at the turn of the sixth century CE, a second wave led by Toramana and subsequently his son Mihirakula overran large parts of north-western and central India. Mihirakula was eventually defeated around c. 528–532 CE by King Yashodharman of Malwa (recorded in the Mandasor Pillar Inscription) and the later Gupta ruler Narasimhagupta Baladitya, not by Skandagupta.

Statement 2 is correct. The Eran Stone Boar (Varaha) Inscription in Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, engraved by Dhanyavishnu (brother of the deceased feudatory Maharaja Matrivishnu), explicitly acknowledges the suzerainty of Maharajadhiraja Toramana in his first regnal year. Whereas the earlier Eran Pillar Inscription of 484 CE had acknowledged the Gupta emperor Budhagupta, the Boar Inscription demonstrates that eastern Malwa had passed under Huna control shortly thereafter.

Statement 3 is correct. Huna dominance over Bactria, Gandhara, Punjab, and Kashmir severed the safe overland commercial corridors linking the Gangetic plains with the Silk Route across Central Asia and the Mediterranean world. This disruption of long-distance bullion-generating trade aggravated the paucity of high-purity gold and silver coinage in post-Skandagupta northern India and hastened urban decay.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 23.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the structural evolution of state administration in ancient India:
items: Statement-I: In contrast to the Mauryan Empire, the Gupta administrative structure was significantly more decentralized and witnessed the hereditary transmission and combination of multiple high offices in a single individual.

Statement-II: The Gupta state maintained a much larger cash-salaried bureaucracy than the Mauryas in order to enforce direct royal monopolies over mining, metallurgy, salt production, and artisanal guilds across the provinces.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike the highly centralized Mauryan state where a vast cash-salaried bureaucracy regulated economic production directly, the Gupta Empire operated as a decentralized, multi-tiered polity relying on tributary Samantas, autonomous corporate guilds, and revenue-bearing land grants. Weakening central oversight was further reflected in the hereditary character of posts and the concentration of multiple portfolios in a single official.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Gupta administration was far less centralized than the Mauryan polity. Outside the core provinces (Bhuktis), vast territories were governed by tributary feudatories (Samantas), and royal grants of land (Agraharas and secular grants) transferred fiscal and administrative powers to donees. Furthermore, high offices became hereditary and were frequently combined in one person; for instance, the Prayaga Prashasti records that Harisena simultaneously held the offices of Kumaramatya, Sandhivigrahika (minister for peace and war), and Mahadandanayaka (chief judicial/military officer), and was the son of Mahadandanayaka Dhruvabhuti.

Statement-II is incorrect. The Gupta Empire did not maintain a larger cash-salaried bureaucracy or stricter state monopolies than the Mauryas; in fact, the exact opposite was true. Whereas the Mauryan state (as reflected in Kautilya's Arthashastra) employed numerous superintendents (Adhyakshas) paid in cash (panas) to regulate mines, forests, salt, and manufacturing, the Gupta state lacked such an elaborate economic bureaucracy. Many Gupta officials were remunerated through land revenue assignments, and artisanal and merchant guilds (Shrenis) operated with wide autonomy.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 23; Romila Thapar, Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300, Ch. 9.

stem: With reference to provincial and district governance in the Gupta Empire as reconstructed from the Damodarpur Copper-Plate Inscriptions of Bengal, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Adhishthana-adhikarana at the district level consisted of four royal military commanders dispatched directly from Pataliputra to assess and collect emergency war taxes.
2. The Uparika governing a province (Bhukti) was appointed directly by the Gupta Emperor, whereas the Vishayapati heading a district (Vishaya) was ordinarily appointed by the Uparika.

3. Even when a private individual sought to purchase uncultivated state land by paying gold coins (dinaras) to create a religious endowment, the transaction required the formal participation of the district council and verification by the record-keepers (Pustapalas).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Damodarpur Copper-Plate Inscriptions from Pundravardhana Bhukti reveal a participatory model of district administration in which the Vishayapati governed alongside a corporate advisory council (Adhishthana-adhikarana) representing leading urban bankers, caravan merchants, artisans, and scribes. Even alienations of state-owned wasteland (khila-kshetra) for religious endowments required formal application, inspection by record-keepers (Pustapalas), and the consent of this non-official district board.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Adhishthana-adhikarana (office/council of the district headquarters, such as Kotivarsha Vishaya) did not consist of royal military commanders. Instead, it was a corporate consultative body comprising four prominent non-official/civic representatives of the district's economic and scribal elite: the Nagarasreshthin (chief banker or president of the city guild), the Sarthavaha (leader of the merchant caravans), the Prathamakulika (chief artisan or head of the craft guilds), and the Prathamakayastha (chief scribe).

Statement 2 is correct. The Damodarpur plates from Pundravardhana Bhukti explicitly record the chain of appointment: the provincial governor (Uparika, later styled Uparika-Maharaja) is described as tat-pada-parigrihita (favoured/appointed directly by the feet of the Paramadaivata Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja, i.e., the Gupta Emperor), while the district head (Kumaramatya or Ayuktaka acting as Vishayapati) is described as appointed by the Uparika (tan-niyukta).

Statement 3 is correct. In the Gupta land-sale grants (kraya-shasana) of northern Bengal, private individuals who wished to purchase uncultivated, revenue-free state wasteland (aprahata or khila-kshetra) at the customary rate of two or three dinaras per kulyavapa to donate to Brahmanas or temples could not buy it unilaterally from the king. They had to petition the district authorities, and the land was alienated only after the Pustapalas (record-keepers) verified that the plot was genuinely uncultivated and that its sale would cause no fiscal loss to the state.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization, Vol. I.

stem: In the context of the agrarian and local administrative structure of the Gupta and post-Gupta periods in eastern India, copper-plate inscriptions such as those from Dhanaidaha, Kalaikuri, and Paharpur frequently refer to the Ashtakuladhikarana, the Gramika, and the Mahattaras. Which one of the following best describes their primary institutional role?

opts.A: They constituted rural and sub-district consultative bodies of leading householders, village headmen, and elders who were notified of land purchase applications, inspected plots, and demarcated boundaries during land grants.
opts.B: They served as mobile imperial judicial tribunals presided over by royal Kumaramatyas to adjudicate capital offences and treason across provincial capitals.
opts.C: They functioned as hereditary military garrisons (Gulmas) stationed along forest frontiers to suppress tribal uprisings and enforce state monopolies over elephant forests.
opts.D: They were syndicates of urban revenue farmers who bid at royal auctions at Pataliputra for the right to collect commercial tolls (Shulka) along the Gangetic waterways.

core: Beneath the district (Vishaya) and sub-district (Vithi) levels, Gupta rural administration relied heavily on local community institutions—most notably the Ashtakuladhikarana (a board representing eight leading families or householders), the Gramika (village headman), and the Mahattaras (village elders and dominant landholders). These rural bodies played an indispensable legal and administrative role in receiving land-sale petitions, verifying local tenure, and physically demarcating the boundaries of granted plots.

exp.why: Option A is correct. In the Gupta inscriptions of Bengal (such as the Dhanaidaha plate of Kumaragupta I's reign), where no full-fledged urban district council is mentioned or where rural sub-divisions (Vithi) are addressed, applications for purchasing and donating state wasteland were addressed to the Ashtakuladhikarana (an administrative board representing eight leading rural families/kulas), the Gramika (village headman), the Mahattaras (village elders/notables), and the Kutumbins (peasant householders). They participated in verifying the status of the land, Measuring the plot by standard reeds (nala), and marking its four boundaries with charcoal and chaff. Options B, C, and D are incorrect as these terms denote grassroots agrarian community institutions rather than imperial criminal courts, military garrisons (Gulmas), or urban tax-farming syndicates.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; B.D. Chattopadhyaya, Aspects of Rural Settlements and Rural Society in Early Medieval India.

stem: With reference to the fiscal and revenue terminology recorded in Gupta and contemporary epigraphs, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Udranga : Periodic supplies of fruits, firewood, and flowers that villagers were obliged to furnish to the king and royal officials
2. Bhoga : Regular principal land tax levied by the state specifically on permanent peasant tenants
3. Halivakara : Religious cess paid by Agrahara-holding Brahmanas for the upkeep of Vedic sacrificial altars
4. Hiranya : King's share of certain agricultural or fiscal dues payable in cash or metallic currency rather than in kind
prompt: Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
core: Gupta land grants enumerate a complex array of agrarian taxes and royal dues that were transferred to donees, including Bhaga (the king's customary share of produce), Bhoga (periodic perquisites of fruits, firewood, and flowers), Udranga and Uparikara (taxes on permanent and temporary tenants respectively), Halivakara (a plough tax on cultivators), and Hiranya (dues collected in cash/gold). Understanding these exact fiscal distinctions is essential for analysing the economic privileges of Agrahara grants.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched because the definitions of Udranga and Bhoga have been interchanged. Udranga was a regular fiscal land tax levied by the state on permanent peasant tenants (or a fixed tax on agricultural land, often paired with Uparikara, a tax on temporary tenants or an extra cess).

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Bhoga referred to the periodic supplies of fruits, firewood, flowers, milk, and curds that villagers were customarily required to furnish to the king or touring royal officers, whereas the king's regular share of the agricultural grain produce (ordinarily one-sixth) was termed Bhaga.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Halivakara (or Haladanda) was an agricultural tax levied on every ploughshare owned by peasant cultivators, not a religious cess paid by Brahmanas. In fact, Agrahara-holding Brahmanas were exempted from paying taxes (akara-dayi).

Pair 4 is correctly matched. In ancient Indian fiscal charters (where grants are described as sa-bhaga-bhoga-kara-hiranya-adi), Hiranya literally means 'gold' and technically denoted the king's right to certain taxes or dues payable in cash/metallic coin rather than in grain (dhanya).

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 23; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9.

stem: With reference to social obligations and the evolution of the judicial system during the Gupta and Vakataka periods, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Vishti (forced or unpaid labour) was recognized as a regular source of royal entitlement that could be transferred directly to religious beneficiaries along with land grants.

2. The Dharmashastra treatises of this era, such as the Smritis of Narada, Brihaspati, and Katyayana, articulated for the first time a clear institutional and procedural demarcation between civil law and criminal law.

3. Under the Gupta legal framework, royal courts presided over by the Mahadandanayaka exercised exclusive original jurisdiction over all commercial and kinship disputes, thereby abolishing the judicial authority of merchant guilds (Shrenis) and family councils (Kulas).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Gupta-Vakataka age witnessed two major legal developments: first, the institutionalization of forced labour (Vishti) as a transferable seigneurial right granted to land donees; and second, the sophisticated codification of civil and criminal procedure in the Smritis of Narada, Brihaspati, and Katyayana. Crucially, however, this legal systematization coexisted with deep judicial decentralization, wherein family councils (Kulas) and merchant/artisan guilds (Shrenis) retained legally recognized original jurisdiction over their members.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Whereas in the Mauryan period Vishti was primarily exacted by the state for public works and military logistics, during the Gupta and Vakataka periods it became a regular, wide-ranging fiscal and seigneurial privilege. Inscriptions from central and western India frequently grant villages to Brahmanas 'along with the right to forced labour as it arises' (sa-utpadyamana-vishti or sarva-vishti-parihara-parihrita), empowering the donees to compel local peasants and artisans to perform unpaid labour on their estates.

Statement 2 is correct. Compiled between the fourth and sixth centuries CE, the Narada, Brihaspati, and Katyayana Smritis represent the zenith of classical Hindu jurisprudence (Vyavahara). Brihaspati, in particular, explicitly classified the eighteen titles of law (ashtadasha-vyavaharapada) into two distinct branches: fourteen titles arising out of wealth/property and contract (Dhanamula, corresponding to civil law) and four titles arising out of injury/violence (Himsamula/Sahasa, corresponding to criminal law).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Far from abolishing non-royal tribunals, the Gupta legal system explicitly recognized and reinforced the autonomous judicial authority of corporate and community bodies. Both the Narada Smriti and the Brihaspati Smriti lay down a clear hierarchy of recognized courts—Kula (family or clan councils), Shreni (guilds of artisans or merchants), and Gana/Puga (local assemblies)—whose customs and judgments held full legal validity. Appeals lay sequentially from Kula to Shreni, from Shreni to Gana, and only ultimately to the royal court.

ref: R.S. Sharma, Indian Feudalism, Ch. 1; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the nature and regional variations of royal land grants during the Gupta and Vakataka periods:
items: Statement-I: Several royal copper-plate charters (Agraharas) issued in Central India and the Deccan during the fourth to sixth centuries CE transferred not only fiscal revenues and rights over underground treasures (nidhi and upanidhi) to the donees, but also administrative immunities prohibiting the entry of regular and irregular royal troops (chatas and bhatas).

Statement-II: In the Pundravardhana bhukti (North Bengal) of the Imperial Gupta heartland, copper-plate charters typically recorded the state-authorized purchase of uncultivated fallow land (khila) by private individuals at fixed prices for making religious endowments, rather than the direct royal alienation of settled revenue-paying villages.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Gupta-era land grants exhibited sharp regional variations between the core Gangetic/Bengal provinces and peripheral or Vakataka territories. While Central Indian and Vakataka charters conferred extensive fiscal and police immunities (pariharas), North Bengal copper plates record regulated state sales of uncultivated fallow land through local district councils without relinquishing imperial administrative control.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Epigraphic records, particularly of the Vakatakas (such as the Poona plates of Prabhavatigupta and Chammak plates of Pravarasena II) and the Parivrajakas/Uchchhakalpas in Central India, explicitly list comprehensive immunities (pariharas). Donees were granted fiscal taxes, rights to hidden treasures and deposits (nidhi and upanidhi), and administrative autonomy barring the entry of royal policemen and soldiers (achata-bhata-praveshya), though Vakataka charters still retained the king's right to revoke grants if Brahmanas committed treason.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. The Damodarpur, Paharpur, and Baigram copper plates from Pundravardhana bhukti (North Bengal) reveal a highly bureaucratized mechanism where prospective donors applied to the district office (Adhishthanadhikarana) and record-keepers (Pustapalas) to purchase uncultivated, revenue-free fallow land (khila/aprahata) at fixed rates of two to three dinaras per kulyavapa under perpetual endowment tenure (akshayanivi or apradadharma). Rather than explaining why Central Indian grants conferred military immunities, Statement-II highlights a contrasting regional pattern showing strong royal and bureaucratic oversight in the core Imperial Gupta provinces.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; R.S. Sharma, Indian Feudalism

stem: With reference to the agrarian classification of land and metrology recorded in the Amarakosha and Gupta-era copper-plate inscriptions, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Aprahata : Uncultivated forest or virgin land that had not yet been brought under the plough
2. Kshetra : Barren alkaline wasteland permanently exempted from all royal revenue assessment
3. Kulyavapa : Mandatory emergency irrigation cess levied on peasants utilizing state embankments
4. Vastu : Habitable land designated for homesteads and residential settlements
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Gupta epigraphs and Amarasimha's lexicon Amarakosha classify land precisely according to its agrarian utility—distinguishing cultivated fields (Kshetra), fallow tracts (Khila), virgin forest land (Aprahata), homestead plots (Vastu), and pastures (Gapata Sarah)—while measuring land area by the volume of seed required to sow it (Kulyavapa, Dronavapa, Adhavapa).

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. In the Amarakosha and Bengal copper plates, Aprahata specifically denotes virgin, untilled woodland or wild tract that has never been ploughed, whereas Khila refers to land that has been left fallow or uncultivated for some time.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Kshetra refers to fertile, actively cultivated or cultivable agricultural fields capable of producing crops. Barren or sterile saline land was termed Ushara or Vandhya in the Amarakosha.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Kulyavapa (along with smaller denominations such as Dronavapa and Adhavapa) was not an irrigation tax; it was a standard unit of land area measurement denoting the extent of land that could be sown (vapa) with one kulya (a large winnowing basket measure equivalent to eight dronas) of seed grain. Linear measurements of land were concurrently carried out using calibrated reed rods called Nala (such as the ashtaka-navaka-nala).

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Vastu (or Vastubhumi) denoted habitable residential land used for constructing houses and village settlements, often granted alongside agricultural fields (Kshetra) and fallow tracts (Khila) in composite land charters.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part I

stem: In the context of the economic and technological history of the Gupta period as reflected in literary texts such as the Amarakosha and contemporary epigraphs, which one of the following statements best describes the significance of the terms 'Ghatiyantra', 'Devamatrika', and 'Nadimatrika'?

opts.A: They were specialized bronze coin-minting dies and assaying touchstones used by royal mint-masters to standardize gold Dinaras and silver Rupakas.
opts.B: They referred to celestial navigation instruments and monsoon wind charts employed by Indian merchant mariners sailing across the Bay of Bengal.
opts.C: They denoted the three tiers of hereditary temple trustees authorized to audit tax-free Devadana endowments in peninsular India.
opts.D: They pertained to agrarian hydrology, representing a mechanical pot-garland device for lifting water from wells and the classification of agricultural tracts based on their reliance on rainfall or riverine irrigation.

core: Agrarian expansion during the Gupta age was supported by hydraulic classification and water-lifting devices: the Amarakosha distinguishes rain-fed tracts (Devamatrika) from river-irrigated tracts (Nadimatrika), while the Ghatiyantra (or Araghatta) facilitated deep-well irrigation through a continuous chain of earthen pots.

exp.why: Option D is correct. In Gupta and post-Gupta sources, Ghatiyantra (also referred to as Araghatta) denoted an irrigation mechanism consisting of a garland of clay pots (ghata) attached to a revolving wheel to lift water from deep wells. Furthermore, the Amarakosha classifies agricultural regions based on water dependability into Devamatrika (land nourished solely by rainfall/monsoon clouds) and Nadimatrika (land nourished perennially by rivers and inundation canals), alongside man-made embankment reservoirs termed Setu or Bandha (famously exemplified by Skandagupta's repair of the Sudarshana Lake embankment documented in the Junagadh inscription). Options A, B, and C are fabricated distractors unrelated to ancient Indian hydraulic terminology.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9; Ranabir Chakravarti, Exploring Early India

stem: With reference to the corporate functioning of craft and merchant guilds (Shrenis) during the Gupta period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Guilds operated as autonomous corporate bodies that enforced their own customary laws (Shreni-dharma), issued independent clay seals, and acted as fiduciary banks receiving permanent endowments (Akshayanivi) to fund religious charities out of accrued interest.

2. To prevent commercial conflicts of interest, heads of merchant and artisan guilds—such as the Nagara-shreshthin, Sarthavaha, and Prathama-kulika—were barred from participating in the district administrative councils (Vishayadhikarana) of the Gupta Empire.

3. As recorded in the Mandasor stone inscription, a guild of silk-weavers that migrated from Lata to Dashapura maintained its collective corporate solidarity to finance a Sun temple even after several members diversified into non-artisanal callings such as archery, astrology, and religious discourse.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Dharmashastra texts (Narada and Brihaspati Smritis) and Gupta inscriptions demonstrate the high judicial-financial autonomy of guilds (Shrenis), the formal inclusion of guild leaders in district administrative councils (Vishayadhikarana), and remarkable spatial and occupational mobility among guild members as recorded in the Mandasor inscription.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Narada and Brihaspati Smritis explicitly require the king to respect and uphold the internal regulations and judicial decisions of guilds (Shreni-dharma). Numerous terracotta seals issued by joint guilds of bankers, traders, and artisans (Shreshthi-sarthavaha-kulika-nigama) have been excavated at Vaishali (Basarh) and Bhita. Furthermore, the Indor Copper Plate inscription of Skandagupta (465–466 CE) records a Brahmana depositing a permanent monetary endowment (Akshayanivi) with a guild of oil-men (Tailika-shreni), who undertook to supply two palas of oil daily for a Sun temple lamp out of the interest accrued without touching the principal.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Far from being excluded, guild leaders were integral members of local and district administration under the Imperial Guptas. As documented in the Damodarpur copper-plate inscriptions, the district governor (Vishayapati) administered the district with the direct assistance and participation of the district council (Adhishthanadhikarana or Vishayadhikarana), which comprised the Nagara-shreshthin (chief banker/president of the city guild), the Sarthavaha (leader of the merchant caravans), the Prathama-kulika (chief of the artisan guilds), and the Prathama-kayastha (chief scribe).

Statement 3 is correct. The Mandasor (Dashapura) stone inscription composed by Vatsabhatti in 473 CE records that a guild of silk-weavers (Pattavayashreni) migrated from the Lata region (southern Gujarat) to Dashapura (western Malwa). After settling in Dashapura, while many continued silk-weaving, others adopted diverse professions including archery and martial arts, astronomy/astrology (jyotisha), storytelling, and religious discourse. Despite this occupational diversification, they retained their corporate guild identity and collectively financed the construction of a magnificent Sun temple in 436 CE and its repair in 473 CE.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch. 2 & 3; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the monetary system and numismatic history of the Imperial Guptas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the early Gupta emperors struck gold coins (Dinaras) adhering to the Kushana weight standard of approximately 120 to 124 grains, Skandagupta introduced a heavier indigenous Suvarna standard of 144 grains (80 rattis).

2. Following the annexation of western India by Chandragupta II, the Guptas initiated a regular silver coinage (Rupakas) modeled directly on the weight standard and obverse-reverse fabric of the defeated Western Kshatrapas.

3. In sharp contrast to the prolific copper coinage of the preceding Kushana and Satavahana eras, Imperial Gupta copper issues were relatively scarce, and daily retail transactions increasingly relied on cowrie shells (Kapardakas) and localized exchange.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Gupta numismatics is characterized by a dual paradox: exquisite high-value gold Dinaras (which shifted from the Kushana weight standard to the indigenous 144-grain Suvarna standard under Skandagupta alongside progressive gold debasement) coexisted with a marked paucity of small-denomination copper coins and widespread reliance on cowrie shells for petty retail trade.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. From Chandragupta I to Kumaragupta I, Gupta gold coins—referred to in inscriptions as Dinaras—followed the late Kushana weight standard of roughly 120–124 grains (about 7.8 to 8 grams), even as the artistic motifs were thoroughly Indianized. During the reign of Skandagupta, alongside some lighter issues, the state transitioned to the traditional Indian Suvarna weight standard mentioned in the Manusmriti, weighing 80 rattis or 144 grains (approximately 9.2 to 9.3 grams), though late Gupta issues after Skandagupta witnessed increasing metallic debasement.

Statement 2 is correct. The Guptas had no regular silver coinage until Chandragupta II conquered Malwa and Gujarat from the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas). To avoid disrupting the monetized commercial economy of western India accustomed to Kshatrapa silver drachms, Chandragupta II issued silver Rupakas (~30–33 grains) retaining the ruler's bust on the obverse and replacing the Kshatrapa three-arched hill motif on the reverse with the Vaishnava Garuda emblem.

Statement 3 is correct. Unlike the Kushanas, Satavahanas, and post-Mauryan tribal republics who minted vast quantities of copper and lead coins used in everyday urban-rural markets, Imperial Gupta copper coins are comparatively scarce (mostly restricted to Chandragupta II and Ramagupta/Kumaragupta I). As corroborated by Fa-Hien's eyewitness account and later epigraphs, gold and silver coins were used for large transactions (land purchases, wholesale trade, and royal donations), whereas everyday retail purchases in local markets were conducted primarily with cowrie shells (Kapardakas) and barter.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 23; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the observations of the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Fa-Hien (Faxian) in his travelogue Fo-Kwo-Ki regarding socio-legal conditions in Madhyadesha during the Gupta period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. He observed that the criminal administration was remarkably mild, dispensing with routine capital punishment and corporal torture in favor of pecuniary fines, with amputation of the right hand reserved only for repeated rebellion.

2. He noted that respectable householders in the Gangetic plains abstained from onions, garlic, intoxicants, and meat, while the Chandalas were segregated outside town boundaries and required to strike a piece of wood upon entering settlements.

3. Absorbed primarily in collecting authentic Vinaya Pitaka manuscripts and visiting Buddhist sacred sites, Fa-Hien did not record even the name of the reigning Gupta Emperor Chandragupta II in his entire account.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Fa-Hien's travelogue (Fo-Kwo-Ki, 399–414 CE) provides a vital religious and social portrait of Gupta-era Madhyadesha—highlighting lenient penal administration, absence of household poll registration, widespread vegetarianism among higher castes, and severe untouchability practiced against Chandalas—while omitting political details including the name of Emperor Chandragupta II.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Contrasting Madhyadesha with the harsh legal codes of contemporary China and the earlier Mauryan state, Fa-Hien noted that the king governed without routine decapitation or corporal punishments. Criminals were simply fined in proportion to the gravity of their offense, and only those guilty of repeated treasonous rebellion had their right hands amputated. He also observed that citizens were not subjected to compulsory household registration or movement passes.

Statement 2 is correct. Fa-Hien recorded that throughout the Middle Kingdom (Madhyadesha), respectable people did not kill living creatures, drink intoxicating liquor, or eat onions and garlic, and towns lacked butcher shops and distilleries. The sole exception was the marginalized group of Chandalas, who lived segregated outside village and city walls, engaged in hunting and fishing, and were forced to strike a piece of wood when entering a town so that upper-caste people could avoid both physical contact and sight pollution.

Statement 3 is correct. Unlike Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) in the seventh century who recorded extensive personal audiences and political details about Harshavardhana, Fa-Hien's mission was strictly monastic—specifically to remedy the incomplete state of the Vinaya Pitaka (rules of monastic discipline) in China. Consequently, despite spending six years inside the Gupta Empire during its zenith under Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, Fa-Hien never once mentioned the emperor's name in Fo-Kwo-Ki.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 23; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the social history and legal literature of the Gupta period, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The Dharmashastra texts compiled during the Gupta age completely stripped women of all proprietary claims, abolishing their right to hold or inherit Stridhana.

Statement-II: The Gupta era witnessed a marked tightening of patriarchal norms among the upper varnas, manifested in the lowering of the marriageable age of girls and the earliest dated epigraphic evidence of Sati in the Eran pillar inscription (510 CE).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Social transformation in the Gupta era exhibited a complex duality regarding the status of women: while upper-caste patriarchal subordination intensified (early marriage, enforced widow celibacy, and the first epigraphic Sati at Eran in 510 CE), contemporary Smritis such as Yajnavalkya, Narada, Brihaspati, and Katyayana simultaneously expanded the scope of Stridhana and recognized the widow as the primary heir to a sonless husband's estate.

exp.why: Statement-I makes an invalid sweeping generalization. Far from abolishing Stridhana, Gupta-era jurists significantly broadened its definition and legal protection. The Katyayana Smriti elaborately defined Saudayika Stridhana (gifts received by a woman from affectionate kindred before or after marriage) and granted women independent authority to sell, mortgage, or dispose of even immovable property within it. Moreover, Yajnavalkya, Brihaspati, and Narada elevated the widow to the first position among heirs to the property of a male dying without male issue, primarily to prevent family property from escheating to the royal treasury or passing to distant agnates in an increasingly agrarian, land-owning society.

Statement-II is historically accurate. As agrarian expansion and Brahmadeya land grants integrated tribal communities into the Jati hierarchy and transformed occupational groups like the Kayasthas (scribes) into endogamous castes, anxiety over maintaining ritual purity and control over landed patrimony intensified among the upper varnas. Consequently, late Smritis advocated pre-puberty marriage for girls, restricted widow remarriage among Dvija castes, and glorified extreme marital devotion, culminating in the earliest known epigraphic record of Sati in the Eran posthumous stone pillar inscription of Bhanugupta (510 CE), which records the self-immolation of the wife of general Goparaja after he fell in battle against the Hunas.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 24 (Life in the Gupta Age); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the literary works of Kalidasa and the conventions of Classical Sanskrit dramaturgy during the Gupta period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Classical Sanskrit plays of the Gupta period, including those of Kalidasa, strictly avoided tragic endings in adherence to aesthetic conventions aimed at restoring cosmic and moral harmony.
2. In Kalidasa's plays, royal queens and noble heroines converse in Paninian Classical Sanskrit to distinguish their courtly status from commoners, who speak Prakrit.
3. Both Raghuvamsham and Meghadutam were composed by Kalidasa as multi-act court dramas (Natakas) featuring the Vidushaka as a comic confidant of the protagonist.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Classical Sanskrit dramaturgy under the Guptas operated on strict aesthetic and sociolinguistic conventions derived from the Natyashastra: plays never ended in tragedy (always culminating in union or moral restoration), and characters were linguistically stratified by both gender and status, with kings and learned Brahmanas speaking Sanskrit while nearly all women (including queens) and the Brahmana Vidushaka spoke Prakrit.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under the aesthetic principles of Bharata's Natyashastra, the primary goal of a Sanskrit play (Rupaka) is the realization of Rasa culminating in auspiciousness and harmony (Bharata-vakya). Even when plays depict intense sorrow, separation, or curse—such as Dushyanta's rejection of Shakuntala in Abhijnanashakuntalam—death of the hero or permanent tragedy on stage is forbidden, and the narrative resolves in reconciliation.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Classical Sanskrit drama followed a rigid sociolinguistic convention of code-switching (Bhasha-vidhana): Classical Sanskrit was spoken by the king (Nayaka), ministers, sages, and learned Brahmanas, whereas Prakrit (predominantly Shauraseni Prakrit for prose dialogue and Maharashtri Prakrit for lyrical verses) was assigned to almost all female characters—including royal queens and courtly heroines like Shakuntala—as well as children, lower-status characters, and even the king's Brahmana jester (Vidushaka).

Statement 3 is incorrect because it confuses poetic genres (Kavya) with dramatic works (Nataka/Trotaka). Raghuvamsham (along with Kumarasambhavam) is a Mahakavya (court epic poem), while Meghadutam (along with Ritusamharam) is a Khandakavya (specifically a Sandesha-kavya or messenger lyric poem). Kalidasa's three dramatic works are Abhijnanashakuntalam, Vikramorvashiyam, and Malavikagnimitram.

ref: NCERT Class XI (Old) Ancient India by R.S. Sharma, Ch. 22; A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the secular Sanskrit plays Mrichchhakatika and Mudrarakshasa composed during the Gupta and post-Gupta cultural milieu, consider the following statements:
