According to Chinese Tang dynasty annals (such as the Cefu Yuangui and Jiu Tangshu), in 720 CE the Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha (referred to in Chinese sources as Che-li Na-lo-seng-kia) sent diplomatic missions to the Tang Emperor Xuanzong, offering war elephants and military cooperation against the expanding Arabs (Tazi) and Tibetans (Tufan). The Tang Emperor reciprocated by conferring the honorary title 'Army which Cherishes Virtue' (Huai-te-chun) on the Pallava king's forces.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The famous Buddhist Vihara for Chinese maritime merchants and pilgrims (later known as the 'China Pagoda') was constructed not at Bharukachha under the Maitrakas of Vallabhi, but at the Coromandel port of Nagapattinam on the eastern coast under the authorization of the Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) in coordination with the Tang Emperor.

Statement 3 is correct. When the Tang diplomatic mission led by Wang Hiuen-tse arrived in northern India around 647–648 CE shortly after Harshavardhana's death, the local usurper Arunasva (Aluonashun, ruler of Tirabhukti) attacked and plundered the Chinese entourage. Wang Hiuen-tse escaped to the Himalayas, mobilized a joint military force provided by the Tibetan monarch Songtsen Gampo and the Nepalese Lichchhavi ruler Narendradeva, defeated Arunasva in Tirabhukti, and took him captive to the Tang capital Chang'an.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 7; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: Consider the following pairs of Post-Gupta epigraphs and their primary historical significance:
items: 1. Poona Copper Plate Inscription : Issued by Vakataka Queen-Regent Prabhavatigupta tracing her imperial Gupta genealogy
2. Mandasor Pillar Inscription : Records Pushyabhuti Emperor Harshavardhana's decisive victory over the Huna ruler Mihirakula
3. Aphsad Stone Inscription : Records the dynastic genealogy of the Maukhari rulers of Kannauj up to Grahavarman
4. Kuram Copper Plate Inscription : Records the military victory of Pallava ruler Parameshvaravarman I over the Chalukya king Vikramaditya I
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Post-Gupta epigraphy provides critical dynastic synchronisms: the Poona plates link the Vakatakas and Guptas, the Mandasor pillar records Aulikara king Yashodharman's victory over the Hunas, the Aphsad inscription details the Later Guptas under Adityasena, and the Kuram plates chronicle Pallava-Chalukya warfare.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. The Poona Copper Plate Inscription was issued by Prabhavatigupta, daughter of the Gupta Emperor Chandragupta II and Kuberanaga, while she served as Queen-Regent of the Vakataka kingdom for her minor son Divakarasena. Unusually for a queen after marriage, she prominently traces her paternal Gupta lineage and bears her father's Bhagavata religious leanings.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The Mandasor Stone Pillar Inscription (c. 532 CE), composed by Vasula, belongs to the Aulikara ruler Yashodharman of Malwa, not Harshavardhana of Kannauj. It celebrates Yashodharman's pan-northern military victories and specifically records that he forced the fierce Huna king Mihirakula—whose head had previously bowed only to Lord Sthanu (Shiva)—to bow down before his feet.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. The Aphsad Stone Inscription (in Nawada district, Bihar) was issued by the Later Gupta ruler Adityasena (late 7th century CE) and records the genealogy and campaigns of the Later Guptas of Magadha and Malwa—including their protracted rivalries with the Maukharis and Mahasenagupta's victory over the Kamarupa king Susthitavarman on the banks of the Lauhitya (Brahmaputra). Maukhari genealogy is primarily recorded in the Haraha and Asirgarh inscriptions.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. The Kuram Copper Plate Inscription of the Imperial Pallava ruler Parameshvaravarman I gives a vivid graphic description of the Battle of Peruvalanallur, in which Parameshvaravarman I routed the invading army of the Badami Chalukya king Vikramaditya I, forcing him to flee the battlefield.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9 & 10; D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions

stem: Consider the following major political and cultural milestones across ancient and early medieval India:
items: 1. Regency of Queen Prabhavatigupta in the Vakataka kingdom of the Deccan
2. Defeat of the Huna ruler Mihirakula by the Aulikara king Yashodharman of Malwa
3. Sack of the Chalukya capital Vatapi by the Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman I
4. Capture of Kanchipuram by the Chalukya ruler Vikramaditya II and his royal donation to the Kailasanatha temple
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above milestones, starting from the earliest?
core: Cross-regional chronological anchoring from the 5th to the 8th century CE moves from the Gupta-Vakataka alliance under Prabhavatigupta (c. 390–410 CE) and the defeat of the Hunas by Yashodharman (c. 528–532 CE) to the protracted Pallava-Chalukya conflict spanning the sack of Vatapi (642 CE) and the capture of Kanchipuram (c. 740 CE).

exp.why: Event 1 occurred earliest (c. 390–410 CE, late 4th to early 5th century CE). Following the premature death of Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II, his widow Prabhavatigupta (daughter of Gupta Emperor Chandragupta II) ruled as Queen-Regent for about twenty years, cementing the Gupta-Vakataka strategic alliance during Chandragupta II's campaign against the Western Kshatrapas.

Event 2 occurred second (c. 528–532 CE, early 6th century CE). The Aulikara ruler Yashodharman of Malwa (along with the Gupta ruler Narasimhagupta Baladitya) broke the power of the Alchon Huna ruler Mihirakula in northern and central India, as recorded in the Mandasor Pillar Inscription of c. 532 CE.

Event 3 occurred third (642 CE, mid-7th century CE). Avenging Pulakeshin II's earlier invasion of the Pallava kingdom, the Pallava monarch Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla), aided by his general Paranjoti (Siruthondar) and the exiled Sinhalese prince Manavamma, stormed the Chalukya capital Vatapi (Badami) in 642 CE, slew Pulakeshin II, and assumed the title 'Vatapikonda'.

Event 4 occurred fourth (c. 733–740 CE, mid-8th century CE). Nearly a century after the sack of Vatapi, the Badami Chalukya ruler Vikramaditya II defeated the Pallava king Nandivarman II Pallavamalla and entered Kanchipuram. Instead of plundering the city, Vikramaditya II returned the treasures of the Rajasimheshvara (Kailasanatha) temple—which had been built earlier in the early 8th century by Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha—and had a Kannada inscription engraved on its pillar recording his benevolence.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9 & 10; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 7 & 8

stem: In the transition from the Classical to the Early Medieval period in North India, the political centre of gravity shifted decisively from Pataliputra in Magadha to Kannauj (Mahodaya), triggering the prolonged Tripartite Struggle among the Palas, Pratiharas, and Rashtrakutas. Which of the following best explains the geopolitical and economic rationale behind this shift?

opts.A: Located on an elevated bluff in the fertile Ganga-Yamuna Doab, Kannauj commanded both rich agrarian surplus in an era of expanding land grants and the strategic riverine-overland corridors linking Uttarapatha with the eastern and western plains.
opts.B: Kannauj possessed the richest iron-ore deposits and dense elephant forests in North India, which had previously been exhausted in the Chotanagpur plateau of southern Bihar.
opts.C: Following the decline of Roman trade, Kannauj emerged as the sole customs clearinghouse with direct estuarine access to both the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea maritime networks.
opts.D: The city served as the exclusive canonical seat for performing Vedic Ashvamedha sacrifices, without which early medieval regional dynasties could not legally collect land revenue (bhaga).

core: In the early medieval economy marked by agrarian expansion and feudal land grants, Kannauj eclipsed Pataliputra because its fortified position in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab allowed control over fertile agricultural tracts as well as key riverine and overland trade arteries.

exp.why: Option A is correct: Kannauj (ancient Kanyakubja or Mahodaya), elevated to imperial prominence under the Maukharis and Harshavardhana, sat on a defensible bluff along the Ganga in the heart of the fertile Ganga-Yamuna Doab. In the early medieval period, when agrarian revenue and control over fertile river plains became the primary basis of state power alongside control of the Uttarapatha trade routes connecting the western coast and north-western frontier to Bengal, mastery over Kannauj symbolized paramountcy over North India. Option B is incorrect (Trap T3) because iron-ore deposits and dense elephant forests were the classic geo-economic advantages of Magadha (Pataliputra) and the adjacent Chotanagpur plateau, not Kannauj. Option C is incorrect because Kannauj was an inland continental city in the mid-Gangetic plain, not a coastal estuarine port. Option D is incorrect as no canonical Dharmashastra rule restricted Vedic sacrifices or taxation legitimacy to Kannauj.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the rise of the Pala Empire and its role in the Tripartite Struggle, consider the following statements:
items: 1. According to the Khalimpur copper plate inscription, Gopala was chosen as king by the regional notables (prakritis) of Bengal to terminate a prolonged period of political anarchy known as 'Matsyanyaya'.
2. During the Tripartite Struggle, Devapala deposed the reigning Ayudha ruler Indraraja and convened a grand imperial assembly at Kannauj to install his nominee Chakrayudha on the throne.

3. Despite periodic military setbacks in the western Gangetic plains against the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, the early Pala monarchs successfully consolidated their rule over both Gauda (Bengal) and Magadha (Bihar).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Gopala founded the Pala dynasty around 750 CE after being selected by regional notables to end 'Matsyanyaya' (the law of the fish), while his son Dharmapala intervened in Kannauj politics by deposing Indraraja (Indrayudha) and installing Chakrayudha.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: Verse 4 of the Khalimpur copper plate inscription of Dharmapala records that following the anarchy in Bengal after Shashanka and Yasovarman's invasions, the regional notables or chieftains (prakritis) made Gopala take the hand of Fortune to put an end to 'Matsyanyaya' (a state of lawlessness where the big fish swallow the small fish).

Statement 2 is incorrect (Trap T1 - Ruler Swap): It was Dharmapala (c. 770–810 CE), and not his son Devapala, who defeated Indraraja (Indrayudha) of Kannauj and held a grand imperial durbar at Kannauj attended by vassal rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara, and Kira to install his protege Chakrayudha on the throne.

Statement 3 is correct: Throughout the 8th and 9th centuries, even when the Pratiharas (under Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II, and Mihira Bhoja) and the Rashtrakutas (under Dhruva and Govinda III) checked Pala ambitions in Kannauj, the core Pala dominion across Bengal (Gauda/Vanga) and Bihar (Magadha) remained firmly integrated under Pala administration.

ref: R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, Ch. 29; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the patronage of Buddhist monastic institutions and maritime diplomacy under the Pala rulers, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Gopala, the founder of the Pala dynasty, is credited in Tibetan Buddhist traditions with establishing the monastic university at Odantapuri in Bihar.
2. Dharmapala founded both the Vikramashila Mahavihara in Bihar and the monumental Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur featuring a terraced cruciform stupa layout.
3. At the request of the Shailendra monarch Balaputradeva of Suvarnadvipa, Dharmapala issued a copper plate charter granting five villages for the upkeep of a monastery at Nalanda.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Pala monarchs were the last great royal patrons of Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism in India, founding Odantapuri, Vikramashila, and Somapura Mahaviharas, while Devapala maintained diplomatic ties with the Shailendra dynasty of Southeast Asia.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: Tibetan chronicles (such as those of Buston and Taranatha) record that Gopala founded the great monastery at Odantapuri (near modern Bihar Sharif in Nalanda district), which later served as an architectural model for the Samye monastery in Tibet.

Statement 2 is correct: Dharmapala (who bore the title Paramasaugata) established the Vikramashila Mahavihara (at Antichak in Bhagalpur district, Bihar) and the vast Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur (now in Bangladesh), renowned for its massive central cruciform shrine and terracotta plaques.

Statement 3 is incorrect (Trap T1 - Ruler Swap): The Nalanda copper plate inscription records that it was Devapala (c. 810–850 CE), not Dharmapala, who granted five villages in the Rajagriha and Gaya vishayas for the maintenance of the monastery built at Nalanda at the request of Maharaja Balaputradeva, the Shailendra ruler of Suvarnadvipa (Sumatra/Java).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10; NCERT Class XI Cultural Traditions

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the foundation of the Rashtrakuta Empire and early medieval political ideology:
items: Statement-I: After overthrowing the suzerainty of the Chalukyas of Badami, the Rashtrakuta ruler Dantidurga performed the Hiranyagarbha (golden womb) mahadana ceremony at Ujjayini, where according to the Sanjan copper plates the Gurjara ruler and other kings served as doorkeepers (pratiharas).

Statement-II: In early medieval Indian polity, the Hiranyagarbha ritual could be performed only by monarchs of uncontested Vedic Kshatriya lineage to renounce all future territorial conquests and retire into monastic asceticism.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Dantidurga performed the Hiranyagarbha mahadana at Ujjayini around the mid-8th century CE to claim imperial sovereignty over Malwa; ideologically, the ritual provided sacred rebirth as a Kshatriya ruler and integrated rival chiefs into a subordinate ritual hierarchy.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct: Dantidurga (c. 735–756 CE), initially a feudatory of the Badami Chalukyas, asserted independence and campaigned in Central India. Verse 9 of the Sanjan copper plate inscription of Amoghavarsha I explicitly states that Dantidurga performed the Hiranyagarbha mahadana at Ujjayini, in which kings such as the Gurjara lord acted as pratiharas (doorkeepers), a symbolic double entendre asserting Rashtrakuta supremacy over the Gurjara-Pratiharas.

Statement-II is incorrect (Trap T3 - Conceptual Inversion): Far from being restricted to hereditary Kshatriyas renouncing power, the Hiranyagarbha ('golden womb') ritual in early medieval India was performed with the assistance of Brahmanas specifically by newly ascendant rulers (often of obscure, tribal, or non-Kshatriya feudatory origins) to undergo a symbolic 'rebirth' from a golden vessel as a legitimate Kshatriya sovereign and to establish imperial paramountcy.

ref: NCERT Our Pasts-II (Class VII), Ch. 2; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the literary and scientific patronage at the court of the Rashtrakuta monarch Amoghavarsha I (Nripatunga), consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Kavirajamarga : Earliest extant Kannada treatise on poetics and rhetoric associated with Amoghavarsha I and Srivijaya
2. Prashnottara Ratnamalika : Sanskrit ethical-didactic treatise composed by Amoghavarsha I
3. Ganitasarasangraha : Encyclopaedic Jain hagiographical purana authored by Jinasena
4. Adipurana : Treatise on arithmetic, algebra, and geometry authored by Mahaviracharya
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Amoghavarsha I (c. 814–878 CE) presided over a major literary efflorescence in both Kannada and Sanskrit, patronizing the mathematician Mahaviracharya, the Jain acharya Jinasena, the grammarian Shakatayana, and the court poet Srivijaya.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched: Kavirajamarga ('The Royal Path for Poets'), co-authored or inspired by Amoghavarsha I and executed by his court poet Srivijaya, is the earliest available work on rhetoric, poetics, and grammar in the Kannada language.

Pair 2 is correctly matched: Prashnottara Ratnamalika ('Gem-Garland of Questions and Answers') is a famous Sanskrit didactic and ethical treatise written by Amoghavarsha I himself, later translated into Tibetan.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched (Trap T1 - Author/Text Swap): Ganitasarasangraha is a landmark 9th-century Sanskrit treatise on mathematics (covering arithmetic, algebra, fractions, and geometry) authored by the Jain mathematician Mahaviracharya during the reign of Amoghavarsha I.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched (Trap T1 - Author/Text Swap): Adipurana is a celebrated Sanskrit Jain text narrating the life of the first Tirthankara Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), composed by Jinasena (preceptor of Amoghavarsha I) and completed by his disciple Gunabhadra.

ref: A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the rock-cut architecture under the Rashtrakutas at Ellora, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Commissioned by the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I, the Kailasanatha Temple (Cave 16) was carved out of a single basalt cliff using a top-down vertical excavation method rather than traditional horizontal tunnelling.

2. Architecturally, the Kailasanatha Temple synthesizes a Southern (Dravida) vimana profile with a pillared mandapa, a freestanding Nandi shrine, and dynamic sculptural panels such as Ravana shaking Mount Kailash.

3. Because the early Rashtrakuta monarchs were ardent Shaivites, royal and feudatory patronage at Ellora during the Rashtrakuta period was restricted to Brahmanical caves and excluded Digambara Jain excavations.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Kailasanatha Temple (Cave 16, Ellora) built under Krishna I is a supreme achievement of top-down monolithic rock-cut Dravida architecture, while later Rashtrakuta patronage at Ellora also produced exquisite Digambara Jain caves such as the Indra Sabha.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The Kailasanatha Temple (Cave 16) at Ellora, commissioned by Krishna I (c. 756–773 CE), was excavated vertically from the top of the basalt cliff downwards by cutting three deep trenches into the hillside and sculpting the freestanding temple complex from a single colossal monolith.

Statement 2 is correct: Modeled partly after the Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal, the Kailasanatha Temple follows a Dravida architectural layout comprising an entrance gopura, a Nandi mandapa, a main pillared sabhamandapa, and a multi-storeyed pyramidal vimana, adorned with monumental high-relief sculptures like Ravana attempting to lift Mount Kailash.

Statement 3 is incorrect (Trap T7 - False Sectarian Exclusion): Rashtrakuta patronage was notably multi-sectarian. During the 9th and 10th centuries, under rulers with strong Jain leanings such as Amoghavarsha I, Krishna II, and Indra III, the famous group of Digambara Jain caves at the northern end of Ellora (Caves 30–34, including the Chhota Kailasa, Indra Sabha, and Jagannatha Sabha) were excavated.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4 & 6; Susan Huntington, The Art of Ancient India

stem: With reference to the rise and consolidation of the Imperial Gurjara-Pratiharas during the early medieval period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. According to the Gwalior Prasasti, Mihira Bhoja was the first Gurjara-Pratihara ruler to repulse the early eighth-century Arab forces led by Junaid, the Governor of Sindh.

2. Nagabhata II overthrew Dharmapala's protégé Chakrayudha at Kannauj and shifted the imperial capital of the Pratiharas to the Gangetic Doab, though he suffered a military reverse against the Rashtrakuta monarch Govinda III.
3. A devout worshipper of Vishnu, Mihira Bhoja assumed the title of 'Adivaraha' and issued silver drachm coinage bearing the boar-incarnation motif.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Imperial Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty rose to prominence in the mid-eighth century when Nagabhata I repulsed the Arab armies of Sindh, and subsequently consolidated control over Kannauj under Nagabhata II and Mihira Bhoja ('Adivaraha') despite recurring Rashtrakuta interventions.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. According to the Gwalior (Sagartal) Prasasti of Mihira Bhoja, it was Nagabhata I (who ruled in the second quarter of the 8th century, c. 730–760 CE)—not the 9th-century monarch Mihira Bhoja (c. 836–885 CE)—who crushed the large armies of the 'Mlechchha' king, identified with Junaid, the Umayyad Arab Governor of Sindh, halting Arab expansion eastward beyond Rajasthan and Gujarat.

Statement 2 is correct. Reviving Pratihara fortunes after Vatsaraja's defeat by Dhruva, Nagabhata II (c. 800–833 CE) marched into the Gangetic valley, deposed Dharmapala's nominee Chakrayudha, defeated Dharmapala near Munger, and made Kannauj the imperial capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas. However, his expansion was checked by a northern campaign of the Rashtrakuta king Govinda III.

Statement 3 is correct. Mihira Bhoja (Bhoja I), the greatest ruler of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, was a devotee of Vishnu and adopted the title 'Adivaraha' (the Primeval Boar incarnation of Vishnu, symbolizing the rescue of the earth). This title and the anthropomorphic boar motif appear prominently on his base-silver 'Adivaraha' drachm coins.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire in the early tenth century:
items: Statement-I: Although the Gurjara-Pratihara court witnessed a vibrant literary flowering under Mahendrapala I and Mahipala I—marked by the Sanskrit and Prakrit works of the court poet Rajashekhara—the empire's political prestige and control over its western territories suffered a severe blow in the second decade of the tenth century.

Statement-II: Around 915–918 CE, the Rashtrakuta monarch Indra III marched across the Yamuna, thoroughly devastated the imperial city of Kannauj during Mahipala I's reign, and enabled the Rashtrakutas to wrest control of Gujarat from the Pratiharas.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While the reigns of Mahendrapala I and Mahipala I represented the literary zenith of the Kannauj court under the dramatist Rajashekhara, the devastating raid on Kannauj by the Rashtrakuta king Indra III (c. 915–918 CE) shattered Pratihara military invincibility and detached Gujarat from their empire.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Mahendrapala I (c. 885–910 CE) and his son Mahipala I (c. 912–944 CE) patronized the celebrated Sanskrit poet, dramatist, and critic Rajashekhara, who composed 'Karpuramanjari' (in Sauraseni Prakrit), 'Balaramayana', 'Balabharata', 'Viddhasalabhanjika', and the poetic treatise 'Kavyamimamsa'. Despite this cultural peak, the Pratihara empire suffered a sudden strategic and territorial setback in the 910s CE.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Between 915 and 918 CE, the Rashtrakuta king Indra III (grandson of Krishna II) launched a lightning campaign via Ujjain, crossed the Yamuna, and sacked the Pratihara capital of Kannauj, forcing Mahipala I to flee temporarily. As recorded by Al-Masudi, the Pratiharas simultaneously lost Gujarat and access to the sea to the Rashtrakutas, severely eroding their imperial prestige.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2; R.S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past

stem: With reference to the observations of the ninth- and tenth-century West Asian Arab chroniclers Sulaiman and Al-Masudi regarding the Indian powers of the Tripartite Struggle, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Arab accounts used the title 'Balhara' of Mankir to denote the Pala monarchs of Bengal, praising them for allowing Muslim merchants to build mosques and be governed by their own Qazis.

2. The kingdom of 'Ruhmi' was identified with the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj, who were described as possessing the finest cavalry in India while remaining the most implacable enemy of Arab rule in Sindh.

3. According to Sulaiman, the rulers of 'Juzr' relied primarily on a massive force of fifty thousand war elephants and were renowned for weaving cotton textiles so delicate that a garment could pass through a signet ring.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Arab chroniclers Sulaiman and Al-Masudi designated the Rashtrakutas as 'Balhara' (Vallabharaja of Manyakheta), the Gurjara-Pratiharas as 'Juzr' (famed for cavalry and hostility to the Arabs of Sindh), and the Palas as 'Ruhmi' (famed for huge elephant forces and ultra-fine cotton muslin).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The title 'Balhara' (an Arabic corruption of the Sanskrit royal epithet 'Vallabharaja') of Mankir ('Manyakheta') referred to the Rashtrakuta monarchs of the Deccan, not the Pala rulers of Bengal. Both Sulaiman and Al-Masudi ranked the Balhara (Rashtrakutas) as the greatest and friendliest of Indian kings towards Arab traders, permitting Muslim settlers in coastal and urban centres to build Jami mosques and administer their personal laws under their own Qazis.

Statement 2 is incorrect. It was the kingdom of 'Juzr' or 'Al-Juzr' (an Arabic rendering of 'Gurjara'), not 'Ruhmi', that denoted the Gurjara-Pratihara empire. Sulaiman and Al-Masudi noted that the king of Juzr possessed great riches, maintained four huge armies with the finest cavalry in India, kept his realm safer from robbers than any other country, and was the fiercest adversary of the Arab rulers of Sindh.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The description of fielding an army with up to 50,000 elephants, employing 10,000 to 15,000 washermen in the military camp, and producing cotton fabrics so extraordinarily fine and delicate that a whole robe could pass through a signet ring was recorded by Sulaiman for the kingdom of 'Ruhmi' (or 'Dharma', referring to Dharmapala and the Pala empire of Bengal and Bihar), not 'Juzr'.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India

stem: With reference to the administrative organization of the directly administered territories in Early Medieval India (c. 750–1000 CE), which one of the following statements accurately distinguishes the territorial hierarchy of the Rashtrakuta Empire from that of the Pala and Pratihara Empires?

opts.A: While the Palas and Pratiharas divided their provinces (Rashtras) into districts called Bhuktis, the Rashtrakutas organized their largest provinces as Vishayas and subdivided them into Mandalas.
opts.B: In both the North Indian and Deccan empires, the Bhukti uniformly served as the largest provincial unit governed by an Uparika, whereas the Rashtra denoted a small cluster of revenue-free Brahmana villages.
opts.C: The Rashtrakutas abolished the intermediate district-level tier of Vishaya and administered villages directly through central military governors called Pattalas, unlike the three-tier system of the Palas.
opts.D: While the Bhukti constituted the largest provincial division above the Mandala or Vishaya in the Pala and Pratihara empires, the Rashtrakuta empire was divided into provinces called Rashtras, below which lay the Vishaya and the still smaller subdivision of Bhukti.

core: Continuing Gupta administrative nomenclature, the Pala and Pratihara empires used 'Bhukti' for a province (headed by an Uparika) and 'Mandala/Vishaya' for a district (headed by a Vishayapati), whereas the Rashtrakuta empire inverted the position of 'Bhukti', organizing provinces as 'Rashtras' (under Rashtrapatis), districts as 'Vishayas', and smaller taluk-like sub-units of 50 to 70 villages as 'Bhuktis' (under Bhogapatis).

exp.why: Option (D) is correct. In the directly administered territories of the Pala and Gurjara-Pratihara empires in North and Eastern India, the administrative hierarchy followed the classical Gupta pattern: the largest provincial unit was the 'Bhukti' (placed under a governor called 'Uparika'), which was subdivided into districts called 'Mandalas' or 'Vishayas' (under a 'Vishayapati'), and further into smaller clusters of villages called 'Pattalas' (in the Pratihara realm). Conversely, in the Rashtrakuta empire in the Deccan, the largest provincial unit was termed a 'Rashtra' (headed by a 'Rashtrapati'), which was divided into districts called 'Vishayas' (numbering 1,000 to 4,000 villages under a 'Vishayapati'), and further subdivided into a smaller unit called 'Bhukti' (comprising 50 to 70 villages under a 'Bhogapati'). Options (A), (B), and (C) are incorrect because they misplace the relative hierarchy of Rashtra, Bhukti, Vishaya, and Pattala.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2 (Political Ideas and Organization)

stem: With reference to provincial and local governance in the Rashtrakuta Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike contemporary North Indian polities where women rarely held formal territorial offices, royal princesses and noblewomen in the Rashtrakuta realm occasionally exercised direct administrative charge over provinces and districts.

2. To curb the growth of landed intermediaries in the Deccan, the Rashtrakuta monarchs paid village headmen and regional revenue officials through regular cash salaries from the central treasury rather than rent-free land assignments.

3. The rise of hereditary regional revenue officers in the Deccan, known as Desa-gramakutas or Nad-gavundas, progressively eroded the power of traditional village committees and prefigured the later Deshmukhs and Deshpandes.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Rashtrakuta polity in the Deccan was distinguished by the occasional appointment of royal women to high territorial governorships and the rise of hereditary regional revenue chiefs (Nad-gavundas/Desa-gramakutas) remunerated through rent-free land grants.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Epigraphic records from the Deccan show that royal ladies and noblewomen in the Rashtrakuta (and later Chalukya) domains did not remain behind the veil and actively participated in public administration. For instance, Revakanimmadi, the daughter of the Rashtrakuta emperor Amoghavarsha I and wife of the Western Ganga prince Ereganga, directly administered the important Edathore Vishaya (district) for several years.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Far from paying local and regional officials in regular cash salaries, the Rashtrakuta state—like the contemporary Pala and Pratihara states—remunerated almost all its officials, including village headmen and district/regional officers, through grants of rent-free land and perquisites in kind. This practice blurred the distinction between state officials and hereditary feudal chiefs.

Statement 3 is correct. A major structural transformation in early medieval Deccan polity was the rise of hereditary revenue officers known as 'Nad-gavundas' or 'Desa-gramakutas'. Rewarded with rent-free lands, these families monopolized regional revenue collection, overshadowed both the older village headmen (grama-mahattaras) and village committees, and evolved into the powerful 'Deshmukhs' and 'Deshpandes' of later medieval Maharashtra.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2; A.S. Altekar, The Rashtrakutas and Their Times

stem: Consider the following pairs of early medieval inscriptions and their primary historical contents:
items: 1. Khalimpur Copper Plate : Records the election of Gopala to end matsya-nyaya and Dharmapala's installation of Chakrayudha on the throne of Kannauj
2. Gwalior (Sagartal) Prasasti : Issued by Amoghavarsha I, detailing the northern campaigns of Dhruva Dharavarsha and Govinda III in the Gangetic Doab
3. Sanjan Copper Plates : Issued by Mihira Bhoja, tracing the genealogy of the Imperial Gurjara-Pratiharas and their victories over the Arabs of Sindh
4. Badal Pillar Inscription : Composed during the reign of Narayanapala, eulogizing the hereditary Brahmanical ministerial family of Garga and Guravamisra that advised successive Pala monarchs
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Epigraphic reconstruction of the Tripartite Struggle relies on Dharmapala's Khalimpur Copper Plate and Narayanapala's Badal Pillar Inscription for Pala history, Mihira Bhoja's Gwalior Prasasti for Gurjara-Pratihara genealogy, and Amoghavarsha I's Sanjan Copper Plates for Rashtrakuta imperial campaigns.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Issued in the 32nd regnal year of the Pala emperor Dharmapala, the Khalimpur Copper Plate Inscription records how the 'prakriti' (notables/people) elected his father Gopala to put an end to the state of 'matsya-nyaya' (anarchy where the big fish swallow the small), and describes Dharmapala's grand imperial assembly at Kannauj where he installed Chakrayudha with the assent of the rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara, and Kira.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The Gwalior (Sagartal) Prasasti belongs to the Gurjara-Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja (not Amoghavarsha I). Written in Sanskrit verse, it is the principal source for the genealogy and military achievements of the Imperial Pratiharas from Nagabhata I (who defeated the Arab Mlechchhas), Vatsaraja, and Nagabhata II down to Mihira Bhoja.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. The Sanjan Copper Plates (dated 871 CE) were issued by the Rashtrakuta emperor Amoghavarsha I (not Mihira Bhoja). They provide a detailed account of Rashtrakuta dynastic history, including the northern expeditions of Dhruva Dharavarsha and Govinda III against the Pratiharas and Palas, as well as Amoghavarsha I's own pious act of offering his left-hand finger to Goddess Mahalakshmi to avert a public calamity.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Engraved on the Garuda pillar erected by Guravamisra at Badal (Dinajpur) during the reign of the Pala ruler Narayanapala, the Badal Pillar Inscription traces how five generations of a learned Brahmanical family—from Garga (minister to Dharmapala) and Darbhapani (minister to Devapala) down to Kedaramisra and Guravamisra—served as hereditary chief ministers and diplomatic advisors to the Pala emperors.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the agrarian and political structure of early medieval India (c. 750–1200 CE), consider the following statements:
items: 1. In copper-plate land grants, the stipulation 'sa-danda-dasa-aparadha' denoted the sovereign's retention of judicial jurisdiction over ten major offences within a gifted village to protect the peasantry from exploitation by donees.

2. The widespread practice of religious and secular land assignments coupled with sub-infeudation produced a graded hierarchy of landed intermediaries bearing titles such as Mahasamanta, Ranaka, and Thakkura.

3. The Kaivarta rebellion in eleventh-century Varendra against the Pala monarch Mahipala II, led by the chieftain Divya, is chronicled in Sandhyakara Nandi's Sanskrit double-entendre kavya, the Ramacharita.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Early medieval Indian polity was marked by the parcellization of sovereignty through land grants carrying fiscal and judicial immunities (pariharas) such as sa-danda-dasa-aparadha, creating a stratified hierarchy of samanta feudatories and occasionally provoking agrarian uprisings like the Kaivarta revolt in Pala Bengal.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. In early medieval copper-plate charters (prashastis and tamrashasanas), the fiscal-judicial phrase 'sa-danda-dasa-aparadha' (literally, 'with the right to fines from ten offences') did not signify the king's retention of judicial power. On the contrary, it transferred the state's administrative and judicial right to try and collect fines from ten categories of minor/village-level offences directly to the donee (Brahmanas, temples, monasteries, or secular vassals), illustrating the decentralization of state authority.

Statement 2 is correct. As central rulers and major feudatories granted land revenues and administrative immunities to subordinates—who in turn made further grants (sub-infeudation)—a complex, graded pyramid of landed intermediaries emerged across Northern and Eastern India, reflected in epigraphic titles such as Mahasamantadhipati, Mahasamanta, Samanta, Ranaka, Rauta, and Thakkura.

Statement 3 is correct. During the reign of the Pala ruler Mahipala II (late 11th century), the Kaivartas (an agrarian and fishing community turned landed militia in North Bengal/Varendra) rose in a major rebellion under Divya (Divvoka), who killed Mahipala II and seized Varendra. Its eventual recovery by Mahipala's younger brother Ramapala (with the help of samanta chiefs) is the subject of Sandhyakara Nandi's Ramacharita, a unique Sanskrit shlesha-kavya that simultaneously narrates the story of Lord Rama and King Ramapala.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10; R.S. Sharma, Indian Feudalism

stem: Consider the following major political milestones of the early medieval period:
items: 1. Installation of Chakrayudha on the throne of Kannauj by the Pala emperor Dharmapala
2. Overthrow of the Badami Chalukya ruler Kirtivarman II by Dantidurga
3. Defeat of the Chola forces by the Rashtrakuta monarch Krishna III at the Battle of Takkolam
4. Accession of the Gurjara-Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja
prompt: Which of the following is the correct chronological sequence of the above events, starting from the earliest?
core: Tracing the macro-chronology of the Tripartite Struggle (c. 750–975 CE) links the rise of the Rashtrakutas in the mid-8th century to Dharmapala's northern hegemony around 800 CE, the Pratihara apogee under Mihira Bhoja in the mid-9th century, and Krishna III's southern campaigns in the mid-10th century.

exp.why: Event 1 occurred in the late 8th century (c. 780s–790s CE). Following the withdrawal of the Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva to the Deccan, the Pala ruler Dharmapala (r. c. 770–810 CE) deposed Indrayudha and installed his protégé Chakrayudha on the throne of Kannauj before an assembly of northern rulers.

Event 2 is the earliest milestone, occurring in the mid-8th century (c. 753 CE). Dantidurga, originally a feudatory of the Chalukyas of Badami, performed the Hiranyagarbha mahadana at Ujjayini and overthrew the last Badami Chalukya sovereign Kirtivarman II to establish the Rashtrakuta Empire.

Event 3 is the latest milestone, occurring in the mid-10th century (949 CE). The last great Rashtrakuta emperor Krishna III (r. 939–967 CE) invaded Tondaimandalam and decisively defeated the Chola army of Parantaka I (killing Crown Prince Rajaditya) at the Battle of Takkolam.

Event 4 occurred in the early-to-mid 9th century (c. 836 CE). Mihira Bhoja (r. c. 836–885 CE), the grandson of Nagabhata II (who had earlier ousted Chakrayudha), ascended the Pratihara throne and consolidated Kannauj as the imperial capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas. Hence, the correct chronological sequence is 2 - 1 - 4 - 3.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2; Upinder Singh, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the artistic and cultural legacy of the Pala Empire in Eastern India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. According to the Tibetan chronicler Taranatha, the Eastern Indian school of bronze casting and stone sculpture was pioneered by the master artists Dhiman and his son Bitpalo during the reigns of Dharmapala and Devapala.

2. Because the Pala monarchs were devout patrons of Vajrayana Buddhism, the black basalt (Kashti pathar) sculptural workshops of Bihar and Bengal produced Buddhist deities exclusively and avoided Brahmanical Vaishnava or Shaiva iconography.

3. While portable bronze icons from Nalanda and Kurkihar influenced the Buddhist art of Southeast Asia under the Shailendras, the Vikramashila acharya Atisha Dipankara Srijnana played a pivotal role in the eleventh-century revival of Buddhism in Tibet.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Pala art combined late Gupta aesthetics with distinctive regional features—refined lost-wax (cire perdue) octo-alloy (ashtadhatu) bronzes and finely polished black basalt stelae—serving both Mahayana-Vajrayana Buddhist and Brahmanical patrons while radiating cultural influence to Tibet and Maritime Southeast Asia.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The 16th–17th century Tibetan Buddhist historian Taranatha specifically recorded that during the reigns of Dharmapala and Devapala, two master artists of Varendra—Dhiman and his son Bitpalo—founded the Eastern school of bronze casting, stone sculpture, and manuscript painting.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Although the Pala kings were Paramasaugatas (devout Buddhists), they generously endowed Brahmanical temples and orthodox Brahmanas. Consequently, the Pala-era sculptural workshops utilizing Rajmahal black basalt (Kashti pathar) and octo-alloy bronze produced an immense volume of Brahmanical images—most notably four-armed standing Vishnu (Trivikrama/Vasudeva), Surya, Uma-Maheshvara, and Mahishasuramardini—crafted in the exact same pointed-stele (prabhavali) aesthetic as Buddhist icons.

Statement 3 is correct. Portable cire-perdue bronzes from Nalanda and Kurkihar traveled along maritime trade routes to Java and Sumatra, visibly shaping the Indo-Javanese bronze and stone idiom under the Shailendra dynasty. Later, during the reign of Nayapala (11th century), the renowned Vikramashila scholar Atisha Dipankara Srijnana traveled to Tibet at the invitation of the ruler of Guge, initiating the Sarma ('New Translation') phase and founding the Kadampa tradition of Tibetan Buddhism.

ref: Susan L. Huntington, The 'Pala-Sena' Schools of Sculpture; NCERT Class XI Introduction to Indian Art

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the socio-political transformation of Northern and Western India between the tenth and twelfth centuries:
items: Statement-I: From the late tenth century onwards, courtly panegyrics and kavyas such as Padmagupta's Navasahasankacharita and later bardic chronicles increasingly traced the ancestry of ruling clans like the Paramaras, Pratiharas, Chahamanas, and Chalukyas (Solankis) either to a sacrificial fire-pit (Agnikula) at Mount Abu or to prestigious Solar and Lunar lineages.

Statement-II: The proliferation of such origin myths reflected the historical process of 'Rajputization', wherein diverse newly ascendant warrior clans, former feudatories, and assimilated indigenous or pastoral groups who acquired territorial sovereignty through military enterprise and land grants sought Brahmanical ritual legitimation within the orthodox Kshatriya varna.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: As explained by historian B.D. Chattopadhyaya, the emergence of the Rajputs in early medieval India was not a sudden biological descent from ancient epic warriors, but an integrative socio-political process ('Rajputization') in which heterogeneous ruling lineages consolidated territorial power and used Brahmanical genealogies (Suryavamshi, Chandravamshi, Agnikula) for Kshatriya legitimation.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The earliest literary appearance of the Agnikula myth occurs in Padmagupta's late-10th/early-11th century Sanskrit court epic Navasahasankacharita (patronized by the Paramara king Sindhuraja), which narrates how sage Vashishtha created the progenitor of the Paramaras from a sacrificial fire-pit at Mount Abu to recover his wish-granting cow from Vishvamitra. Later recensions of Chand Bardai's Prithviraj Raso expanded this myth to encompass all four Agnikula clans: Pratiharas, Paramaras, Chalukyas (Solankis), and Chahamanas (Chauhans), alongside widespread claims to Suryavamshi and Chandravamshi descent in royal inscriptions.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains the historical cause behind Statement-I. Modern epigraphic research demonstrates that the Rajput clans of early medieval Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Central India emerged from heterogeneous backgrounds—including former Pratihara samantas, local agrarian-pastoral chiefs (such as Gurjaras), and indigenous tribes (such as Medas and Hunas)—who achieved upward social mobility through agrarian expansion, fort-building, inter-clan marriage networks, and royal land grants, subsequently commissioning court poets and Brahmanas to craft prestigious Kshatriya genealogies.

ref: B.D. Chattopadhyaya, The Making of Early Medieval India; Upinder Singh, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to monetary circulation and maritime trade during the era of the Palas, Pratiharas, and Rashtrakutas (c. 750–1000 CE), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Throughout the period of the Tripartite Struggle, metallic currency completely disappeared across both Northern India and the Deccan, reducing all inter-regional exchange to village-level barter and cowrie shells.

2. Under the Rashtrakutas, western coastal ports such as Sanjan (Samyana), Chaul (Chemuliya), and Thane actively engaged in Indian Ocean commerce with Arab merchants, particularly for the import of warhorses.

3. Following the gradual silting and decline of the ancient port of Tamralipti in the eighth century, maritime trade and continuous silver coinage in Bengal shifted eastward toward the Samatata-Harikela littoral.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Nuanced numismatic and epigraphic historiography (John S. Deyell, Ranabir Chakravarti) refutes the older notion of a total early medieval monetary collapse, showing sustained circulation of billon Drammas and Gadhaiya coins in North/West India, high-purity silver coinage in Harikela (SE Bengal), and vibrant Arab maritime trade along the Rashtrakuta Konkan coast.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. While high-purity gold coins became scarce in the immediate post-Gupta centuries, metallic currency never completely disappeared during 750–1000 CE. Epigraphic records (such as the Siyadoni and Ahar inscriptions) and coin hoards confirm the wide circulation of silver and billon (silver-copper alloy) 'Dramma' coins—including the famous Adivaraha Drammas issued by the Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja and Vigrahapala Drammas in eastern India—alongside Indo-Sasanian style 'Gadhaiya' coins in Gujarat and Rajasthan.

Statement 2 is correct. Rashtrakuta copper plates (such as the Chinchani charters from Sanjan/Samyana) and Arab accounts by Sulaiman and Al-Masudi attest that Konkan ports like Sanjan, Chaul, and Thane were thriving hubs of Indian Ocean trade. The Rashtrakutas appointed Arab muslim governors (Tajika governors like Madhumati/Muhammad at Sanjan) and imported large numbers of Arabian and Persian Gulf warhorses.

Statement 3 is correct. As the ancient Rupnarayan-delta port of Tamralipti (Tamluk) declined after the 8th century due to deltaic silting, the center of gravity of Bengal's overseas trade with Southeast Asia shifted eastward across the Meghna delta to the Samatata-Harikela coast (Noakhali-Comilla-Chittagong region), which remarkably maintained an uninterrupted issue of high-purity silver coins from the 7th to the 13th centuries.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10; Ranabir Chakravarti, Exploring Early India

stem: With reference to the terminal decline of the three participants of the Tripartite Struggle and the rise of their successor states, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the late tenth century, the imperial Rashtrakuta house of Manyakheta was directly overthrown and succeeded in the northern Deccan by the Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra.
2. In Bengal, the Pala dynasty was finally supplanted in the twelfth century by the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga, who established their capital at Nadia.

3. The fragmentation of the Gurjara-Pratihara empire in Northern and Central India facilitated the rise of its former feudatories, such as the Chandelas of Jejakabhukti and the Paramaras of Malwa, as sovereign powers, while Kannauj eventually passed under the rule of the Gahadavalas.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: All three empires of the Tripartite Struggle ultimately succumbed to the structural dynamics of samanta feudalism: the Rashtrakutas were overthrown in 973 CE by their feudatory Tailapa II of the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, the Palas were supplanted by the Karnata-origin Sena dynasty under Vijayasena, and the Pratihara realm splintered into successor Rajput kingdoms.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Weakened by the sacking of Manyakheta by the Paramara king Siyaka II in 972 CE, the last Rashtrakuta ruler Karka II was overthrown in 973 CE not by the Hoysalas, but by his Tardavadi feudatory Tailapa II (Taila II), who restored Chalukya rule by founding the Western (Later) Chalukya dynasty of Kalyani. The Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra rose much later in southern Karnataka, initially as feudatories of the Kalyani Chalukyas.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In the mid-twelfth century, the weakened Pala dynasty in Bengal was overthrown and succeeded not by the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga, but by Vijayasena of the Sena dynasty—a Brahma-Kshatriya lineage originally hailing from the Karnata region of the Deccan (as recorded in the Deopara Prashasti) who had earlier entered Pala service as samantas in Radha (West Bengal).

Statement 3 is correct. Following the devastating raids of the Rashtrakuta kings Indra III and Krishna III on Kannauj in the 10th century, the Gurjara-Pratihara empire disintegrated as its former feudatories—including the Chandelas of Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand), the Paramaras of Malwa, the Chahamanas of Shakambhari, and the Chalukyas of Gujarat—declared independence. Following the Ghaznavid raids in the early 11th century, Kannauj itself came under the sovereign rule of the Gahadavala dynasty founded by Chandradeva.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 2 & 3; Upinder Singh, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the political rise and consolidation of the Imperial Cholas in early medieval South India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Vijayalaya established the sovereign independence of the Chola dynasty by overthrowing Rashtrakuta suzerainty and capturing Kanchipuram.
2. Aditya I ended Pallava supremacy in Tondaimandalam by defeating the last Pallava ruler Aparajita.
3. The early territorial expansion of the Cholas suffered a major military setback when Parantaka I's forces were defeated by the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna III at the Battle of Takkolam.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Imperial Cholas rose from being Pallava feudatories under Vijayalaya—who captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars—to full sovereign status under Aditya I, who defeated his Pallava overlord Aparajita. Although Parantaka I conquered Madurai from the Pandyas, his northern frontier collapsed temporarily in 949 CE when Rashtrakuta king Krishna III defeated the Chola army at Takkolam.

exp.why: Vijayalaya (c. 850 CE) did not overthrow the Rashtrakutas or establish full sovereign independence at Kanchipuram. He began his career as a feudatory of the Pallavas of Kanchi and established a foothold in the Kaveri delta by capturing Tanjore (Thanjavur) from the Muttaraiyar chieftains, who were allied with the Pandyas.

Vijayalaya's son and successor, Aditya I (c. 871–907 CE), initially fought alongside the Pallavas at the Battle of Sri Purambiyam against the Pandyas, but subsequently turned against his Pallava overlord Aparajita around 893 CE, defeated him in battle, and annexed Tondaimandalam (the Kanchipuram region) into the sovereign Chola kingdom.

Under Parantaka I (907–955 CE), the Cholas captured Madurai from the Pandyas, earning him the title 'Maduraikonda'. However, in 949 CE at the Battle of Takkolam, the Rashtrakuta monarch Krishna III, aided by his Western Ganga feudatory Butuga II, inflicted a crushing defeat on the Chola forces, killing Crown Prince Rajaditya and occupying Tondaimandalam for nearly three decades.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 9; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the geo-strategic and maritime consolidation achieved under Rajaraja I (985–1014 CE), consider the following statements:
items: 1. He annexed the entire island of Sri Lanka, including the southern hill kingdom of Rohana, and captured the royal insignia of the Sinhala monarch Mahinda V.
2. He abolished the Eastern Chalukya monarchy and directly annexed the kingdom of Vengi as a centrally governed Chola Mandalam.
3. His naval conquest of the Maldives was the earliest military campaign of his reign, preceding his expedition against the Chera navy at Kandalur Salai.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Rajaraja I systematically secured control over the Indian Ocean littoral and peninsular trade routes through sequential campaigns: first destroying the Chera fleet at Kandalur Salai, conquering northern Sri Lanka (while southern Rohana remained unsubdued until Rajendra I), converting Vengi into a dynastic protectorate, and concluding his reign with the naval conquest of the Maldives.

exp.why: Rajaraja I conquered only the northern half of Sri Lanka (Ilamandalam / Mummudicholamandalam), sacking Anuradhapura and establishing Polonnaruwa (renamed Jananathamangalam) as the Chola provincial capital. The Sinhala king Mahinda V fled to the rugged southern province of Rohana. It was Rajaraja's son, Rajendra I, who invaded Rohana around 1017 CE, captured Mahinda V along with the Sinhala crown and royal insignia, and completed the annexation of the island.

Rajaraja I did not extinguish the Eastern Chalukya line or annex Vengi as a direct Chola Mandalam. Instead, to secure a buffer and northern alliance against the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, he intervened in Vengi's succession crisis, restored the Eastern Chalukya princes Saktivarman I and Vimaladitya to the throne as Chola allies, and cemented a dynastic union by marrying his daughter Kundavai to Vimaladitya.

The destruction of the Chera fleet at Kandalur Salai (celebrated in his epigraphic epithet 'Kandalur Salai Kalam-arutta' around 988 CE) was the very first major military campaign of Rajaraja I's reign. Conversely, the naval conquest of the 'twelve thousand ancient islands of the sea' (Munneer Palantivu Pannirayiram, identified with the Maldives) was the final military exploit at the close of his reign around 1013–1014 CE.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas, Ch. 8; Noboru Karashima, A Concise History of South India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the northern expedition of the Chola emperor Rajendra I:
items: Statement-I: Following the defeat of the Pala ruler Mahipala I, Rajendra I permanently annexed the Gangetic delta and organized it into a new provincial Mandalam administered by Chola viceroys.

Statement-II: To commemorate the northern march to the Ganges, Rajendra I founded the capital city of Gangaikondacholapuram and excavated the vast Cholagangam tank as a 'liquid pillar of victory' (Ganga-jalamaya-jayastambha).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Rajendra I's northern expedition (c. 1022–1023 CE) through Kalinga, Odda, Dandabhukti, and Vangala to the Ganges was a politico-ritual demonstration of imperial chakravartin prestige rather than a campaign for permanent territorial annexation in North India. The sacred Ganges water brought back by the vanquished northern rulers was poured into the newly excavated Cholagangam tank at Gangaikondacholapuram.

exp.why: As recorded in the Tiruvalangadu copper plates, Rajendra I's general marched north through Kalinga, Kosala, Dandabhukti, and Uttara-Rada, defeating the Pala ruler Mahipala I on the banks of the Ganges. However, the Cholas never permanently annexed Bengal or the Gangetic delta into a provincial Mandalam; the campaign was a rapid military raid designed to emulate Samudragupta's digvijaya and bring back sacred Ganges water.

Assuming the title 'Gangaikondachola' (The Chola who took the Ganga), Rajendra I shifted the royal capital from Thanjavur to the newly built city of Gangaikondacholapuram. There he constructed a monumental Shiva temple and excavated the vast Cholagangam irrigation reservoir, into which the sacred pots of Ganges water were poured as a 'Ganga-jalamaya-jayastambha' (liquid pillar of victory).

ref: Tiruvalangadu Copper Plates; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the maritime relations between the Imperial Cholas and the Sailendra Empire of Srivijaya (Southeast Asia):
items: Statement-I: In 1025 CE, Rajendra I dispatched a major overseas naval expedition across the Bay of Bengal against the Sailendra kingdom of Srivijaya, raiding thirteen strategic port-cities including Kadaram and Palembang along the Strait of Malacca.

Statement-II: The Chola naval offensive against Srivijaya was driven by militant Shaivite hostility toward the Mahayana Buddhist establishments patronized by the Sailendra monarchs on the Coromandel coast.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Rajendra I's unprecedented 1025 CE naval raid on Srivijaya (Kadaram) was motivated by commercial geopolitics—specifically Srivijaya's interference with Chola merchant guilds and direct maritime trade to Song China across the Malacca Strait—and not by religious conflict. Earlier, both Rajaraja I and Rajendra I had generously endowed the Buddhist Chudamani Vihara built by the Sailendra ruler at Nagapattinam.

exp.why: Rajendra I's Tanjore inscription (c. 1030–1031 CE) documents his grand naval expedition of 1025 CE against Sangrama Vijayottungavarman, the Sailendra ruler of Srivijaya (Kadaram). The Chola armada simultaneously raided key entrepots controlling the Strait of Malacca and the Malay Peninsula, including Palembang (Srivijaya), Kadaram (Kedah), Pannai, Malaiyur, and Tambralinga.

The campaign had nothing to do with religious intolerance against Buddhism. As attested by the Anaimangalam (Larger Leiden) copper plates, Rajaraja I had granted the revenues of Anaimangalam village to support the Chudamani Vihara—a Buddhist monastery constructed at the Chola port of Nagapattinam by the Sailendra king Mara Vijayottungavarman—and Rajendra I himself ratified this endowment. The 1025 CE conflict arose because Srivijaya sought to monopolize the Malacca Strait chokepoint and obstruct Tamil merchant guilds (such as the Ayyavole and Manigramam) from trading directly with Song China.

ref: Hermann Kulke, K. Kesavapany & Vijay Sakhuja (eds.), Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa: Reflections on the Chola Naval Expeditions to Southeast Asia

stem: Consider the following territorial units in the administrative structure of the Chola Empire:
items: 1. Valanadu
2. Mandalam
3. Ur (Grama)
4. Nadu
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct descending sequence (from the largest territorial unit to the smallest) in the Chola administrative hierarchy?
core: The Chola Empire was spatially organized into a four-tier hierarchy descending from Mandalam (province) to Valanadu (commissioner's division above the Nadu), Nadu (agrarian district), and Ur or Grama (the primary village unit). Rajaraja I systematically interposed the Valanadu tier above the historical Nadus to integrate local Nattar assemblies into the imperial revenue framework.

exp.why: Valanadu (ranked second from top) was a large intermediate administrative division below the Mandalam and above the Nadu. Reorganized extensively under Rajaraja I (often bounded by rivers and named after royal titles), each Valanadu grouped several Nadus together to curb the autonomous power of local Nattar elites.

Mandalam (ranked first/largest) was the highest provincial unit of the Chola Empire (roughly 8 to 9 in number, such as Cholamandalam, Jayankondacholamandalam, and Rajarajapandimandalam), often corresponding to conquered former kingdoms and governed by royal princes or senior viceroys.

Ur or Grama (ranked fourth/smallest) constituted the foundational village settlement at the base of the territorial hierarchy beneath the Nadu (whereas exceptionally large and autonomous Brahmadeya settlements were constituted as separate revenue units styled Taniyur).

Nadu (ranked third from top, below Valanadu and above individual Ur/village settlements) was the fundamental ecological and agrarian district administered by the corporate assembly of dominant landholders known as the Nattar.

ref: Y. Subbarayalu, Political Geography of the Chola Country; Noboru Karashima, South Indian History and Society

stem: With reference to the central bureaucracy and royal chancery mechanics of the Imperial Cholas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The terms Perundanam and Sirudanam in Chola inscriptions denoted major and minor agrarian taxes levied respectively on irrigated wet lands and rain-fed dry lands.
2. The Udankuttam comprised a body of senior executive officers in immediate attendance upon the king who coordinated communication between the monarch and various administrative departments.

3. Oral decrees issued by the Chola monarch (Tiruvaykkelvi) were recorded by a specialized chancery official styled Tirumandira Olai and scrutinized by the Tirumandira Olai Nayagam before entering the state registers.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Chola state developed a sophisticated bureaucratic apparatus divided into higher (Perundanam) and lower (Sirudanam) cadres of officials, remunerated primarily through revenue assignments (jivitam). Royal oral orders (Tiruvaykkelvi) underwent a rigorous multi-stage documentary verification through the Tirumandira Olai, Tirumandira Olai Nayagam, and the Udankuttam before being engraved on copper plates or temple walls.

exp.why: Perundanam and Sirudanam were not agrarian land taxes. In Chola epigraphy, they denoted the higher (senior) and lower (junior) cadres or ranks of royal officials in the Chola civil-cum-military bureaucracy, often distinguished by honorific titles such as Muvendavelan or Brahmadirajan.

The Udankuttam ('the assembly in immediate attendance') was a body of senior executive officials constantly attending upon the Chola monarch at court, advising on policy implementation and transmitting royal directives to the respective revenue and provincial departments (Puravuvari).

As detailed in Chola copper-plate charters (such as the Leiden and Tiruvalangadu grants), an oral royal command (Tiruvaykkelvi) was first committed to palm-leaf writing by a personal royal scribe called the Tirumandira Olai, then verified and counter-signed by a panel of senior chancery supervisors called the Tirumandira Olai Nayagam, before being forwarded to the revenue registry (Puravuvari-tinaikkalam) for execution.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas, Ch. 17; Burton Stein, Peasant State and Society in Medieval South India

stem: With reference to the administrative structure and agrarian integration under the Imperial Cholas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To establish a centralized bureaucracy, the Chola monarchs dissolved the traditional Nattar assemblies of the Nadu units and replaced local landholding elites with cash-salaried civil servants transferable across the empire.
2. A Taniyur was a large, prosperous Brahmadeya settlement that was demarcated as an independent revenue and administrative unit outside the jurisdiction of the surrounding Nadu.
3. Courtly titles such as Muvendavelan and Araiyan were conferred exclusively upon princes of the royal bloodline serving as provincial viceroys over newly conquered Mandalams.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Chola statecraft did not abolish local corporate bodies like the Nattar; instead, it integrated dominant Velala landholders into the state apparatus through prestigious titles (Muvendavelan, Araiyan) while counterbalancing their local power by creating royal Brahmadeyas and autonomous Taniyurs.

exp.why: The Imperial Cholas did not dissolve the Nattar (the corporate assembly of dominant Velala landholders of a Nadu) or replace them with a modern cash-salaried transferable bureaucracy. Instead, the Chola state co-opted local agrarian elites into royal service for revenue assessment and administration, remunerating officials primarily through revenue assignments (Jivita) rather than cash salaries.

As certain Brahmadeya settlements expanded demographically and economically through temple urbanization and agrarian growth, the Chola state elevated them to the status of a Taniyur ('separate village'), functioning as a distinct administrative and fiscal unit independent of the Nadu within which it was geographically situated.

Titles such as Muvendavelan (a velan or peasant serving three kings) and Araiyan (chief) were not restricted to royal princes; they were prestigious honorary titles bestowed by Chola kings upon wealthy Velala landowners as markers of status to integrate them into high civil and military offices.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10; NCERT Class VII Our Pasts-II, Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the corporate local assemblies in the Chola Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Ur functioned as the general assembly of tax-paying peasant proprietors in Vellanvagai villages, the Sabha operated as the assembly of Brahmin landholders in Brahmadeya settlements.
2. Under Chola constitutional practice, an Ur and a Sabha were mutually exclusive bodies and did not coexist within the same village settlement.
3. Unlike the Ur and the Sabha, the Nagaram was a purely commercial guild of itinerant merchants that was barred from owning or administering agricultural land.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Chola local self-government operated through three primary territorial assemblies—the Ur (peasant villages), the Sabha (Brahmin villages), and the Nagaram (marketing centers)—which frequently interacted, coexisted in mixed settlements, and held corporate agrarian rights.

exp.why: The Ur was the assembly of non-Brahmin tax-paying landholders (Urar) in ordinary peasant villages (Vellanvagai), whereas the Sabha (or Mahasabha) was the assembly of Brahmin landholders (Perumakkal) in rent-free or tax-concessional Brahmadeya/Agrahara villages.

Epigraphic records from the Chola period confirm that an Ur and a Sabha could and did coexist within the same large village settlement—particularly when a part of an existing peasant village was granted as a Brahmadeya—and the two assemblies jointly deliberated on irrigation management, boundary disputes, and village security.

The Nagaram was a territorial corporate assembly of resident merchants and artisans in market towns (distinct from supra-regional itinerant guilds like the Ayyavole-500 or Manigramam). Chola inscriptions show that Nagarams owned corporate agricultural land, managed temple endowments, and assessed local tolls and land taxes within their jurisdiction.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas, Ch. 18; Upinder Singh, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the Uttaramerur Inscriptions of the Chola ruler Parantaka I, which laid down the rules for membership in the executive committees (Variyams) of the Sabha, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A candidate seeking nomination was required to be between 35 and 70 years of age, possess a house built on his own legally owned site, and hold a prescribed minimum extent of tax-paying land.

2. Any person who had served on a committee during the preceding three years, or who had failed to submit his accounts at the end of his tenure along with his close relatives, was disqualified from contesting.
3. To ensure occupational representation in village governance, one-third of the seats in the Samvatsara-variyam were reserved for resident artisans and landless agricultural tenants.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Uttaramerur inscriptions (919 CE and 921 CE) of Parantaka I codify strict property, educational, age, and ethical qualifications for Variyam membership, enforcing anti-monopolization through a three-year cooling-off period and strict financial accountability while restricting membership to propertied elites.

exp.why: The Uttaramerur inscriptions stipulate that a candidate for the Variyam committees must be aged between 35 and 70 years, own a house built on his own tax-paying site, and own at least a quarter veli of tax-paying land (reduced to one-eighth veli if the candidate was proficient in one Veda and one of the four Bhashyas).

To prevent oligarchic capture of the committees, anyone who had served on a Variyam in the preceding three years was barred. Furthermore, those who had failed to submit financial accounts of their tenure—as well as their specified patrilineal and matrilineal relatives—were strictly disqualified.

There was no reservation of seats for artisans or landless tenants in the Variyam committees. The Sabha of a Brahmadeya was an assembly of landholding Brahmins, and the mandatory land-ownership and Vedic scholarship requirements excluded landless labourers and village artisans from committee membership.

ref: NCERT Class VII Our Pasts-II, Ch. 2; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: Which one of the following statements accurately describes the Kudavolai system practiced in the Brahmadeya villages under the Imperial Cholas?

opts.A: It was a system of universal adult suffrage in which all adult residents of a village cast palm-leaf ballots into an earthen pot to elect the village headman by simple majority.
opts.B: It was a rotational revenue-farming auction in which the right to collect water cess on behalf of the Eri-variyam was awarded to the highest bidder from the Nadu.
opts.C: It was a secret-ballot judicial trial conducted by the Nyayattar committee to ostracize members of the Sabha found guilty of misappropriating temple endowments.
opts.D: It was a method of selection by lot in which palm-leaf tickets bearing the names of pre-qualified candidates from each village ward (Kudumbu) were placed in a pot and drawn to constitute the executive Variyam committees.

core: The Kudavolai ('pot-ticket') system under the Cholas was not a modern majoritarian election based on universal franchise, but a structured sortition (selection by lot) from a pool of pre-qualified candidates nominated from the 30 wards (Kudumbus) of the village.

exp.why: Option D is correct: Under the Kudavolai system recorded in the Uttaramerur inscriptions, the village was divided into 30 wards (Kudumbus). Eligible residents of each ward wrote the names of qualified candidates on palm-leaf tickets (Olai), tied them in a bundle per ward, and placed them into an earthen pot (Kudam). In the full assembly of the Mahasabha, a young boy unaware of local politics drew one ticket per ward to select members for executive committees such as the Samvatsara-variyam (Annual Committee), Totta-variyam (Garden Committee), and Eri-variyam (Tank Committee). Option A is incorrect because it involved sortition from pre-qualified elites rather than majority voting by universal adult suffrage. Options B and C are fabricated descriptions.

ref: NCERT Class VII Our Pasts-II, Ch. 2; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas, Ch. 18

stem: With reference to the fiscal, judicial, and proprietary powers of the village Sabha under the Imperial Cholas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Sabha exercised corporate ownership over the uncultivated common lands and wastelands of the village and possessed the authority to reclaim or alienate them for public and religious purposes.

2. If an individual landholder defaulted on the payment of land revenue beyond the stipulated grace period, the Sabha had the authority to confiscate and sell the defaulter's land by public auction to recover the arrears without requiring a decree from the royal court.
3. The Pon-variyam committee of the Sabha exercised the sovereign prerogative to mint gold coins in the name of the village deity to finance inter-regional maritime trade.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Because the Chola village Sabha was collectively responsible for remitting the lump-sum revenue demand of the state, it enjoyed extensive fiscal and proprietary autonomy, including corporate ownership of village wasteland and statutory authority to auction the lands of tax defaulters.

exp.why: The Sabha held corporate proprietorship over village common lands, pastures, tanks, and uncultivated wastelands. It could bring wastelands under the plough, grant tax-free lands (Irayili) to temples after receiving a lump-sum capital deposit (Iraikaval), and sell or gift communal lands for public works.

Chola inscriptions explicitly confirm that since the Sabha was collectively liable to the royal treasury for the village's total revenue assessment, it held the independent statutory power to confiscate and publicly auction the lands of defaulting landholders if revenue arrears remained unpaid beyond the prescribed period, without needing a separate royal court decree.

While the Pon-variyam (Gold Committee) of the Sabha was responsible for testing and certifying the fineness and weight of gold used in temple endowments, local transactions, and tax payments, the sovereign right to mint royal coinage (such as Kasu and Madai) rested with the imperial state and licensed royal mints, not village assemblies.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas, Ch. 18 & 20; Upinder Singh, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the classification of land tenures recorded in Chola inscriptions, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Vellanvagai : Land of non-Brahmin peasant proprietors
2. Shalabhoga : Land donated to Jain institutions
3. Pallichchhandam : Land granted for the maintenance of a school
4. Tirunamattukkani : Land gifted to temples
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Chola epigraphs categorize land grants according to the nature of the recipient institution or proprietor: Vellanvagai (peasant land), Brahmadeya (Brahmin land), Shalabhoga (school maintenance), Devadana/Tirunamattukkani (temple land), and Pallichchhandam (Jain/Buddhist institutional land).

exp.why: Vellanvagai refers to the ordinary tax-paying land of non-Brahmin peasant proprietors (Vellalar), which constituted the majority of agricultural villages in the Chola heartland.
Shalabhoga refers to land granted for the maintenance of a school (Shala) or educational institution, not land donated to Jain institutions.
Pallichchhandam refers to land donated to Jain or Buddhist religious institutions (Palli), whereas land for a school was termed Shalabhoga.
Tirunamattukkani (also known as Devadana) refers to revenue-free or concessional land gifted to Hindu temples for their upkeep and ritual expenses.

ref: NCERT Class VII Our Pasts-II, Ch. 2 (Kings and Kingdoms)

stem: With reference to the agrarian revenue administration and fiscal terminology of the Imperial Cholas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Comprehensive cadastral land measurement and soil classification surveys were executed under Rajaraja I and Kulottunga I, earning the monarchs the epigraphic title 'Ulagalandan'.

2. Chola revenue charters maintained a conceptual distinction between 'Kadamai', which denoted the principal land tax payable to the state, and 'Kudimai', which signified the tenancy obligations owed by cultivators to landholders.

3. In Chola fiscal records, 'Vetti' referred to a specialized cash customs duty levied on overseas maritime merchants, whereas 'Puravu' denoted voluntary charitable gifts made by peasants to village temples.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Imperial Chola fiscal state relied on periodic scientific cadastral surveys (under Rajaraja I in 1001 CE and Kulottunga I in 1086 CE) that standardized measurement rods to assess land revenue (Kadamai/Irai/Puravu) separately from local tenancy obligations (Kudimai) and compulsory communal labor (Vetti).

exp.why: Rajaraja I (around 1001 CE) and Kulottunga I (around 1086 CE) carried out extensive land surveys using standardized measuring rods (such as the Ulagalandan-kol) to grade land fertility and assess productivity, earning the title 'Ulagalandan' (One who measured the world/earth).

As analyzed by epigraphists like Noboru Karashima and Y. Subbarayalu, Chola inscriptions systematically distinguish between 'Kadamai' (or Irai/Puravu), the major land revenue owed to the king/state, and 'Kudimai', the local dues and tenancy obligations borne by the occupant-cultivators (Kudi).
