core: Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur exemplified Deccani cultural syncretism through the Kitab-i-Nauras and Nauraspur, Malik Ambar revolutionized Ahmadnagar's fiscal and military administration through the Kathi settlement and Bargigiri guerrilla warfare, while Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda built the Charminar and compiled the first Dakhani Urdu Diwan.

exp.why: Ibrahim Adil Shah II (1580–1627) of the Adil Shahi dynasty of Bijapur was venerated as 'Abla Baba' (Friend of the Poor) and 'Jagadguru Badshah' for his broad-minded patronage of Hindu and Muslim scholars, musicians, and saints alike. He composed the Kitab-i-Nauras in Dakhani, a collection of 59 songs (geets) and 17 couplets (dohas) designed to be sung in specific Indian ragas, beginning with praises of Saraswati, the Hindu goddess of learning and music.

Malik Ambar (1548–1626), the Abyssinian (Habshi) Peshwa of the Nizam Shahi kingdom of Ahmadnagar, adapted Todar Mal's Zabti principles to Deccan conditions. He abolished exploitative tax-farming (Ijara), had arable land measured using a standard measuring rod (Kathi), fixed state demand at two-fifths of the produce in cash or kind, recognized hereditary peasant proprietary rights (Mirasdars), and organized Maratha light cavalry into Bargigiri guerrilla units against the Mughals.

It was Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (1580–1612) of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda—not Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur—who holds the distinction of being the first Sahib-e-Diwan poet in Dakhani Urdu (Kulliyat-e-Quli Qutb Shah) and who founded the city of Hyderabad and constructed the Charminar in 1591 to commemorate the end of a devastating plague epidemic.

ref: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals Part Two; Richard M. Eaton, Sufis of Bijapur & A Social History of the Deccan

stem: Having spent seven years as an exiled guest at the Vijayanagara court before ascending his ancestral throne in 1550, this Deccan Sultan developed a deep affinity for Sanskrit and Telugu literature. Celebrated affectionately as 'Malkibharama' in vernacular ballads, he patronized eminent Telugu poets such as Addanki Gangadhara Kavi and Kandukuri Rudrakavi, while developing the Kollur diamond mines and the port of Masulipatnam into premier engines of maritime trade. He also commissioned the historic Hussain Sagar lake and the Purana Pul bridge.
prompt: Which of the following rulers of the Deccan Sultanates is described in the passage above?

opts.A: Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur
opts.B: Taj-ud-Din Firuz Shah of the Bahmani Sultanate
opts.D: Burhan Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar

core: Ibrahim Qutb Shah (r. 1550–1580) of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda integrated local Telugu literary and agrarian elites into his Sultanate's administration, earning the vernacular sobriquet 'Malkibharama' (Malik Ibrahim).

exp.why: Option (C) is correct: Ibrahim Qutb Shah (r. 1550–1580), the fourth ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda, lived in exile for seven years at Vijayanagara under the protection of Aliya Rama Raya before taking the throne. Fluent in Telugu, he was hailed as 'Malkibharama' by Telugu litterateurs; Addanki Gangadhara Kavi dedicated the Telugu kavya 'Tapatisamvaranopakhyanamu' to him, and he granted an agrahara to Kandukuri Rudrakavi. He also built the Purana Pul across the Musi river and commissioned Hussain Sagar (supervised by his son-in-law Hussain Shah Wali), before his son Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah later founded the new capital of Hyderabad (Bagnagar) in 1591 and composed the earliest secular Kulliyat in Dakhani Urdu. Option (A) is incorrect because Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur was known as 'Jagadguru Badshah' and 'Abala Baba' and authored the 'Kitab-i-Nauras' in Dakhani. Option (B) is incorrect because Firuz Shah Bahmani ruled from Gulbarga and built Firuzabad on the Bhima river. Option (D) is incorrect because Burhan Nizam Shah I ruled Ahmadnagar and patronized Shah Tahir.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 11; Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II

stem: With reference to the evolution of state tutelary sovereignty and sectarian patronage across the four dynasties of the Vijayanagara Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The early Sangama rulers were predominantly Shaivites who revered Kalamukha ascetics such as Kriyasakti Pandita as their royal preceptors and adopted Lord Virupaksha of Hampi as the empire's tutelary deity.

2. When the Tuluva monarchs led by Krishnadevaraya embraced Vaishnavism as their personal faith, they abolished the Sangama convention of signing official royal decrees in the name of the Shaiva deity 'Sri Virupaksha'.
3. Alongside the Sri Vaishnava tradition, Krishnadevaraya extended prominent royal patronage to the Madhva (Dvaita) philosophical school led by Saint Vyasatirtha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While personal royal devotion in Vijayanagara shifted from Shaivism (under the Sangamas) toward Vaishnavism (under the Saluvas, Tuluvas, and Aravidus), the Tuluva monarchs preserved constitutional and sacral continuity by retaining 'Sri Virupaksha' as the official royal sign-manual on state charters.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The founders of the Sangama dynasty (Harihara I and Bukka I) were ardent Shaivites. Alongside the Advaita scholars Vidyaranya and Sayana of Sringeri, inscriptions heavily attest to the role of Kalamukha Shaiva ascetics Bearing the title 'Kriyasakti Pandita' (such as Kasivilasa Kriyasakti) as the 'Rajaguru' (royal preceptor) of the early Sangama kings, who placed their realm under the tutelary sovereignty of Pampapati (Sri Virupaksha) at Hampi.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Although the Saluva and Tuluva monarchs (including Krishnadevaraya and Achyutaraya) were devout Vaishnavas who deeply venerated Lord Venkateshwara of Tirupati and Lord Vitthala of Hampi, they did NOT abolish the Shaiva royal sign-manual. To preserve the institutional and sacral legitimacy of the Vijayanagara throne, Tuluva emperors continued to conclude and authenticate their official copper-plate charters and decrees in Kannada script with the traditional sign-manual 'Sri Virupaksha' (it was only much later under the Aravidu ruler Venkata II at Chandragiri/Vellore that 'Sri Venkatesha' replaced 'Sri Virupaksha' as the royal signature).

Statement 3 is correct: Although Krishnadevaraya authored the Sri Vaishnava (Visishtadvaita) epic 'Amuktamalyada', his religious patronage was pluralistic. He held the great Madhva (Dvaita) logician and philosopher-saint Vyasatirtha (Vyasaraya) in the highest esteem as his spiritual preceptor, granting him numerous villages and supreme ritual honours at both Hampi and Tirumala-Tirupati.

ref: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 14 & 16; Burton Stein, Vijayanagara (New Cambridge History of India); NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II

stem: Consider the following statements regarding agrarian expansion and hydraulic management in the Vijayanagara Empire:
items: Statement-I: To mobilize private capital for rural hydraulic infrastructure across the dry uplands of the peninsula, the Vijayanagara state institutionalized the Dasavanda and Kattu-Kodage tenures, under which individuals constructing or repairing irrigation tanks received a hereditary, tax-free share of the land irrigated by those reservoirs.

Statement-II: Major temples in the Vijayanagara Empire functioned as agrarian development institutions by re-investing cash endowments donated by royal elites and Nayakas into the excavation of irrigation channels in temple villages.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Vijayanagara's dry-zone agrarian expansion relied on two distinct decentralized mechanisms: state-sanctioned private entrepreneur tenures (Dasavanda and Kattu-Kodage) for tank building, and institutional reinvestment of monetary endowments by major temples into Devadana village irrigation works.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct: Because the core Rayalaseema and Karnataka plateau zones of the Vijayanagara Empire were semi-arid and depended on seasonal rain-fed streams rather than perennial deltas, the state encouraged decentralized private investment in tank and canal construction. Under the 'Dasavanda' tenure (prevalent in the Telugu and Tamil regions) and the 'Kattu-Kodage' tenure (prevalent in Karnataka), a private individual or local chief who built a new tank or restored a breached reservoir at his own expense was rewarded with a hereditary, tax-exempt fraction (often one-tenth to one-fourth) of the newly irrigated wetland.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I: Epigraphic records from major shrines such as the Tirumala-Tirupati Devasthanam demonstrate that temples acted as rural development banks. When kings, Nayakas, or merchants made cash endowments (Poliyuttu) to fund perpetual food offerings (prasada), the temple treasuries invested that capital into digging tanks and feeder channels (kaluvai) inside temple-owned (Devadana/Tiruvidaiyattam) villages, using the resulting surge in grain revenues to finance ritual services. While both statements are true, Statement-II describes institutional temple banking in Devadana lands, which is a parallel mechanism and not the cause of the Dasavanda/Kattu-Kodage tenures granted to private tank builders in Statement-I.

ref: Noboru Karashima, A Concise History of South India; Burton Stein, Peasant State and Society in Medieval South India; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: With reference to the judicial administration and policing mechanisms in the Vijayanagara Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Parasara-Madhaviya, an authoritative commentary on the Parasara Smriti composed by Madhavacharya, incorporated a dedicated treatise on Vyavahara (jurisprudence) that guided judicial administration in the empire.

2. Under the Kavalgar policing system, hereditary watchmen (Arasu-kavalkars and Talaiyaris) enjoyed immunity from financial liability if highway robberies or thefts occurred within their jurisdictions.

3. Dispute resolution in the provinces was not monopolized by royal courts, as village assemblies, temple boards, and artisan-merchant guilds exercised recognized judicial authority over customary civil disputes.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Vijayanagara combined Sanskritic dharmashastric jurisprudence (codified in Madhavacharya's Parasara-Madhaviya) and decentralized corporate adjudication with a strictly accountable rural policing network (Kavalgars/Talaiyaris) who were financially liable to compensate theft victims if stolen goods went unrecovered.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The original 'Parasara Smriti' (considered in classical tradition as the Dharmashastra best suited for the Kali Yuga) dealt only with Achara (conduct) and Prayaschitta (penance), lacking a section on Vyavahara (law and jurisprudence). Madhavacharya (Vidyaranya), advisor to the early Sangama kings, composed the monumental commentary 'Parasara-Madhaviya' in which he appended an original, comprehensive section on Vyavahara to serve as the legal manual for Vijayanagara's courts.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Far from enjoying financial immunity, the Kavalgars (both the higher-tier 'Arasu-kavalkars' or Palaiyakkarars guarding forest passes and highways, and the village-level 'Talaiyaris') operated under strict fiduciary liability. In return for enjoying tax-free 'Umbali' land grants and collecting watch-fees ('Padikaval' or 'Kaval-kanikkai') from peasants and travelling merchants, they were legally bound to prevent crime. As corroborated by foreign travellers like Abdur Razzaq and epigraphic records, if a robbery occurred in their jurisdiction and they failed to apprehend the thieves and recover the stolen property, the Kavalgars were compelled to compensate the victim's loss out of their own estates.

Statement 3 is correct: While the king presided over the highest royal court (Sabha or Dharmasana) at the capital through the Pradvivaka (Chief Justice), everyday civil, caste, and commercial disputes across the countryside were adjudicated decentrally by village assemblies, caste councils (Jati-kuta / Samayacharas), temple authorities, and corporate merchant-artisan guilds (such as the Five Panchalas) according to local customary law (Deshachara).

ref: T.V. Mahalingam, Administration and Social Life under Vijayanagar; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 14

stem: With reference to the maritime trade networks and major seaports of the Vijayanagara Empire and the Bahmani Sultanate during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Dabhol and Chaul on the northern Konkan coast functioned as the principal western seaports under the direct sovereign control of the Vijayanagara emperors throughout the fifteenth century.
2. Bhatkal was the premier Coromandel port on the eastern seaboard of the Vijayanagara Empire, serving as the main embarkation point for printed cotton textiles exported to Malacca and Pegu.

3. Following the Portuguese capture of Goa in 1510, Krishnadevaraya imposed an imperial maritime trade embargo against Portuguese merchants and diverted Vijayanagara's cavalry horse imports exclusively to the Red Sea port of Aden.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Geopolitics in peninsular India hinged on control of distinct maritime corridors: Dabhol and Chaul were the premier Konkan ports of the Bahmani Sultanate; Bhatkal, Honavar, and Mangalore were Vijayanagara's Kanara (western) ports for Persian Gulf horse imports and iron/sugar exports; and Pulicat was Vijayanagara's Coromandel (eastern) gateway to Southeast Asia.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect: Dabhol (Mustafabad) and Chaul on the northern Konkan (Maharashtra) coast were the premier maritime ports of the Bahmani Sultanate (and subsequently the Bijapur and Ahmadnagar Sultanates), NOT under the Vijayanagara Empire. Vijayanagara's western maritime outlet lay further south along the Kanara (Karnataka) coast through ports such as Honavar, Bhatkal, Barkur, and Mangalore, supplemented by commercial ties with Calicut on the Malabar coast.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Bhatkal was located on the western (Kanara) coast facing the Arabian Sea, where it served as Vijayanagara's most prosperous western port exporting iron, hardware, rice, and sugar to Ormuz in exchange for Persian Gulf warhorses and copper. By contrast, Pulicat (Pazhaverkadu)—connected directly by an overland highway to Tirupati, Chandragiri, and Hampi—was Vijayanagara's premier eastern (Coromandel) port exporting South Indian Kalamkari and printed textiles to Malacca, Sumatra, and Pegu (Burma).

Statement 3 is incorrect: After Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Adil Shahi Sultanate of Bijapur in 1510, Krishnadevaraya did NOT impose a trade embargo on the Portuguese. Instead, recognizing that the Portuguese controlled the maritime horse trade from Ormuz, Krishnadevaraya cultivated cordial diplomatic and commercial relations with Portuguese Goa—even utilizing Portuguese arquebusiers during the siege of Raichur (1520)—in order to monopolize the supply of Arabian and Persian warhorses and deny them to the rival Deccan Sultanates.

ref: Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Political Economy of Commerce: Southern India 1500–1650; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 9

stem: In the historiography of the Vijayanagara Empire and its successor Nayaka polities, early colonial reconstructions relied heavily on Persian court chronicles such as Ferishta's Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi and European travellers' narratives compiled by Robert Sewell. However, modern historians reconstruct grass-roots agrarian relations, tank endowments, and chieftain genealogies using a massive archival corpus of vernacular documents known as 'Kaifiyats' (based on village registers called Dandakavile or Kavile), which were systematically collected across South India at the turn of the nineteenth century under the supervision of Colonel Colin Mackenzie.
prompt: What were these 'Kaifiyats' in the context of South Indian historical archives?

opts.A: Bilingual diplomatic treaties concluded between the Aravidu monarchs and the Dutch East India Company factories on the Coromandel coast
opts.B: Canonical Sanskrit manuals compiled by temple Sthanikas prescribing the sculptural iconography of Raya Gopurams and Kalyana Mandapams
opts.C: Local village historical chronicles, land-tenure records, and genealogical accounts maintained by hereditary village accountants (Karanams) across the Deccan and South India
opts.D: Maritime customs ledgers maintained by the Zamorin of Calicut to regulate the toll duties paid by Arab and Chinese merchant fleets

core: The Mackenzie Kaifiyats are vernacular village historical chronicles compiled from the palm-leaf registers (Dandakavile/Kavile) of hereditary village accountants (Karanams/Shanbhogs) by Colonel Colin Mackenzie and his Indian assistants (led by Kavali Venkata Borriah) between 1799 and 1821.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct: Between 1799 and 1821, Colonel Colin Mackenzie (later the first Surveyor General of India), assisted by native scholars such as the Kavali brothers (Kavali Venkata Borriah and Kavali Venkata Lakshmiah), dispatched surveyors across the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema), Mysore, and the Carnatic to collect local histories. These accounts, known as 'Kaifiyats' (from the Arabic-Persian word for a statement or description of particulars), were drafted from traditional palm-leaf village registers ('Dandakavile' or 'Kavile') maintained for generations by hereditary village accountants ('Karanams' in Telugu/Tamil regions and 'Shanbhogs' in Karnataka). They preserve granular grass-roots records of succession from the Kakatiya and Vijayanagara eras, Nayaka and Poligar genealogies, irrigation tank constructions, agrahara and devadana grants, and local taxation—serving as an indispensable bottom-up corrective to court-centric Persian histories like Muhammad Qasim Ferishta's 'Tarikh-i-Firishta' ('Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi', written at the Bijapur court). Options (A), (B), and (D) are fabricated descriptions.

ref: NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 7 (An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara); Nicholas B. Dirks, Castes of Mind; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, Sources of Indian History

stem: With reference to the military innovations and memoir of Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the First Battle of Panipat, Babur synthesized the Ottoman Rumi device of roping together wheeled carts (Araba) for artillery protection with the Uzbek Tulughma flanking maneuver.
2. In his memoir Tuzuk-i-Baburi, Babur expressed high admiration for the extensive network of perennial artificial irrigation canals across the plains of Hindustan.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Babur revolutionized North Indian warfare by integrating Ottoman gunpowder breastworks (Araba) with Central Asian mobile cavalry flanking tactics (Tulughma). In Tuzuk-i-Baburi, he critically observed the absence of artificial running water canals in Hindustan and documented indigenous water-lifting devices like the Persian wheel and leather buckets.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. At the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur deployed the Ottoman Rumi tactic—using a frontline barrier of 700 wheeled carts (Araba) lashed together with rawhide ropes to shield his matchlockmen and artillery (commanded by Ustad Ali Quli and Mustafa)—combined with the Uzbek Tulughma tactic of fast-moving flanking cavalry divisions that encircled Ibrahim Lodi's army from the rear.

Statement 2 is incorrect. In the Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama), Babur explicitly lamented the absence of artificial running water canals in the towns and agricultural tracts of Hindustan, noting that autumn crops grew by rainfall alone while spring crops could grow even without rain. He recorded in detail how Indian peasants irrigated fields from wells using the Persian wheel (Araghatta/Saqiya) with buckets in Lahore and Dipalpur, or leather buckets (Charas) drawn by yoked bullocks over a pulley in Agra, Chandwar, and Bayana.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 12; Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Beveridge Translation)

stem: Which one of the following medieval rulers reorganized his imperial court and society on a cosmological scheme into three functional divisions—Ahl-i-Daulat (soldiers and administrators), Ahl-i-Sa'adat (religious scholars, Sayyids, and jurists), and Ahl-i-Murad (musicians, poets, and artists)—and assigned specific days of the week based on planetary astrology to conduct the affairs of each group?
core: As chronicled by Khwandamir in the Qanun-i-Humayuni, Emperor Humayun articulated an early Mughal cosmological theory of sovereignty that classified courtly elites into three functional groups (Ahl-i-Daulat, Ahl-i-Sa'adat, and Ahl-i-Murad) and aligned royal audiences and wardrobe colors with astral symbolism.

exp.why: Option B is correct. As documented by the Persian historian Khwandamir in the Qanun-i-Humayuni (1534), Nasiruddin Humayun sought to elevate Timurid kingship through astronomical and cosmological symbolism. He categorized the people of the state into three orders: Ahl-i-Daulat (men of the state, comprising royal kinsmen, military commanders, and wazirs), Ahl-i-Sa'adat (men of good fortune/virtue, comprising the Ulama, Qazis, Sayyids, and learned scholars), and Ahl-i-Murad (men of joy and pleasure, comprising musicians, dancers, poets, and artisans). He also instituted the Bisat-i-Nishat (Carpet of Mirth) representing the celestial spheres and wore garments matching the astrological color of the ruling planet of each day of the week while attending to the corresponding class. Options A, C, and D are incorrect because Balban's kingship followed Sasanian court etiquette (Sijda and Paibos), while Akbar and Jahangir later modified court rituals around Sulh-i-Kul and Jharokha Darshan rather than Humayun's specific tripartite Qanun-i-Humayuni classification.

ref: Khwandamir, Qanun-i-Humayuni; Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II (Mughal Empire)

stem: With reference to the provincial and local administrative machinery established by Sher Shah Suri, consider the following statements:
items: 1. At the Sarkar level, the Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran was primarily responsible for administering civil justice and supervising the revenue assessments of the Pargana Amins.
2. The Munsif-i-Munsifan functioned as the chief military commander of the Sarkar, maintaining a standing cavalry contingent to suppress local rebellions.

3. Under the principle of local responsibility, village headmen (Muqaddams) were held statutorily liable to either trace the culprits of highway robberies occurring within their jurisdiction or make good the loss of stolen property.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Sher Shah Suri's Sarkar administration separated executive-military policing (Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran) from revenue supervision and civil adjudication (Munsif-i-Munsifan). At the grassroots level, he enforced strict policing accountability by holding village Muqaddams personally responsible for crimes committed within their territorial limits.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. At the Sarkar (district) level under Sher Shah Suri, the Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran (Chief Shiqdar) was the executive and military officer in charge of maintaining law and order, suppressing rebellions, and supervising the Pargana Shiqdars. It was the Munsif-i-Munsifan (Chief Munsif) who supervised the land revenue assessment of the Pargana Amins (Munsifs) and adjudicated civil and revenue disputes.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Munsif-i-Munsifan was a civil judge and chief revenue supervisor at the Sarkar level, not a military commander. The military contingent at the Sarkar level was commanded by the Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran.

Statement 3 is correct. As chronicled by Abbas Khan Sarwani in Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi, Sher Shah enforced the doctrine of local responsibility for policing. Village headmen (Muqaddams) and local Zamindars were legally bound to protect travelers and merchants passing through their boundaries. If a robbery occurred, the Muqaddam had to produce the offenders or compensate the victim for the stolen goods; if a murder occurred and the killer was not traced, the Muqaddam himself faced capital punishment.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 13 (Sher Shah and the Sur Empire)

stem: With reference to the currency and commercial reforms of Sher Shah Suri, consider the following statements:
items: 1. He discontinued the debased mixed-metal (billon) coinage of the Delhi Sultanate and standardized a pure silver Rupiya weighing 178 grains alongside a copper Dam.
2. To promote free trade across North India, he completely abolished all customs duties, including taxes levied at the imperial frontiers and at the point of final sale.
3. The silver Rupiya introduced by Sher Shah served as the foundational precursor to the Mughal silver coinage that remained the standard monetary unit until the nineteenth century.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sher Shah Suri restored monetary stability by replacing debased billon tankas with a standardized tri-metallic system anchored by the 178-grain silver Rupiya and copper Dam. In trade policy, he eliminated internal transit and ferry tolls while retaining customs levies strictly at the imperial frontier and the final point of sale.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Prior to Sher Shah, the currency of the later Delhi Sultanate relied heavily on debased billon (mixed silver and copper) coins of fluctuating purity. Sher Shah demonetized these debased coins and minted finely executed coins of uniform weight in gold (Mohur), pure silver (Rupiya of 178 grains), and copper (Dam of 380 grains, subdivided into halves, quarters, eighths, and sixteenths).

Statement 2 is incorrect. Sher Shah did not abolish all customs duties. Rather, he abolished the numerous vexatious internal transit duties, octroi, and ferry tolls (Rahdari) levied at every Pargana boundary. He decreed that customs duty on commercial goods could be collected only at two points: first at the frontier of entry into the empire (such as Sakrigali on the Bengal border or the Indus frontier for Central Asian goods), and second at the actual market where the goods were sold.

Statement 3 is correct. Sher Shah's 178-grain silver Rupiya was adopted directly by Akbar and his Mughal successors as the core silver currency of the empire, and later formed the basis of the British East India Company's silver rupee of 180 grains up to 1835 and beyond.

ref: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 13

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the agrarian revenue administration of Sher Shah Suri:
items: Statement-I: Sher Shah Suri's annual measurement-based assessment system (Zabt-i-har-sala) frequently caused administrative delays and economic distress to peasants when local harvest prices diverged from imperial court prices.

Statement-II: Under Sher Shah's system, the state's share fixed in kind through a single imperial crop-yield schedule (Ray') was commuted into cash using prevailing price rates of the central royal camp and required annual approval from the Sultan.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Sher Shah's Ray' schedule standardized crop yields across good, middling, and bad lands, but its annual conversion into cash rates using central court/camp prices created severe rigidities across diverse regional markets—a structural flaw that Akbar later resolved through localized Dastur circles under the Ain-i-Dahsala.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. As noted by Abul Fazl in the Ain-i-Akbari when explaining the need for Akbar's later reforms, the annual fixation of cash revenue rates (Zabt-i-har-sala) inherited from Sher Shah caused substantial hardship to both the peasantry and revenue collectors, especially when local grain prices in distant provinces fell significantly below the prices prevailing near the imperial court or when royal sanction was delayed.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Sher Shah prepared a uniform imperial schedule of crop yields (Ray') by averaging the produce of good, middling, and bad land and fixing one-third as the state's share. However, to collect revenue in cash, this physical grain demand had to be commuted every year at prices fixed by the Sultan based on rates prevailing around the central court/imperial camp rather than localized multi-year regional price averages. Because both productivity and grain prices varied sharply across provinces, applying a single court-approved annual price schedule led to the exact delays and peasant distress described in Statement-I.

ref: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari; Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the evolution of the Mughal land revenue administration under Emperor Akbar, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Karori experiment initiated in 1573, revenue officials (Amils) were appointed across North India to oversee land measurement using bamboo rods joined by iron rings (Tanab) and collect audited data on actual crop yields and local prices.

2. Under the Ain-i-Dahsala promulgated in 1580, the state's revenue demand was expressed in cash rates called Dastur-ul-Amal, which were calculated only after averaging both the actual crop yields and the prevailing local market prices of the preceding ten years for each revenue circle.
3. The Ain-i-Dahsala was a decennial settlement that permanently froze the peasant's total cash tax liability for ten-year blocks without requiring annual measurement of the area actually sown.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Akbar's Ain-i-Dahsala (1580), architected by Raja Todar Mal, replaced annual central price commutations with localized cash revenue rates (Dasturs) derived from a 10-year retrospective average of yields and prices (1570–1580). Crucially, it was not a 10-year permanent freeze on total tax; the standard cash rate per Bigha was applied annually to the land actually cultivated and measured.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In 1573–74, Akbar launched the Karori experiment across the Khalisa (crown) lands of North India, appointing Amils (called Karoris because each was placed in charge of a revenue circle expected to yield one crore Dams, i.e., Rs. 2,50,000). Simultaneously, the old hempen rope (Jarib), which shrank when wet and stretched when dry, was replaced by the Tanab made of bamboo rods joined by iron rings. The Karoris gathered verified data on local prices, productivity, and cultivation from 1570 to 1580.

Statement 2 is correct. In 1580, on the basis of data compiled by Raja Todar Mal and Khwaja Shah Mansur, Akbar instituted the Ain-i-Dahsala. Unlike Sher Shah's uniform central schedule, the empire was divided into distinct assessment circles (Dasturs) with homogeneous productivity and market conditions. Standard cash revenue rates per Bigha for each crop (Dastur-ul-Amal) were fixed only after taking the average of both actual crop yields and local market prices over the preceding ten years (1570–1580).

Statement 3 is incorrect. A common misconception is that 'Dahsala' meant a ten-year decennial settlement like the British settlement of 1790. In reality, Dahsala referred to the ten-year retrospective average (1570–1580) used to calculate the standard cash rate (Dastur) per Bigha for each crop. Under the Zabt system, the peasant's total tax liability was NOT frozen for ten years; rather, the cultivated fields were still measured every harvest season (Paimaish), the standard Dastur rate per Bigha was applied to the area actually sown, and remissions (Nabud, up to 12.5%) were granted for crop failure.

ref: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 14

stem: With reference to the classification of agricultural land and state policy on fallow rehabilitation under Akbar's Zabt (Dahsala) revenue system, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Polaj : Land cultivated annually for every crop in succession and never allowed to lie fallow
2. Parauti : Land that had lain fallow for three to four years and was taxed at progressively increasing concessional rates reaching the full rate in the fifth year
3. Chachar : Land left out of cultivation temporarily for a year or two to recover its strength and taxed at the full Polaj rate as soon as cultivated
4. Banjar : Land remaining uncultivated for five years or more and assessed at highly concessional rates to encourage its reclamation
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: To balance revenue maximization with agrarian expansion, Akbar's Zabt system classified arable land into four categories based on continuity of cultivation (Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, and Banjar). While continuously or recently cultivated lands (Polaj and Parauti) paid the full standard assessment when cropped, longer-term fallow and waste lands (Chachar and Banjar) received graded multi-year fiscal concessions so peasants could absorb the capital cost of land reclamation.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under the Ain-i-Akbari classification, Polaj was the ideal category of land that was annually cultivated for each crop in succession and never allowed to lie fallow, paying the full standard revenue rate (one-third of the average produce).

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched because the descriptions of Parauti and Chachar have been swapped. Parauti was land left out of cultivation temporarily for a short period (1 to 2 years) so that it might recover its fertility; because it required minimal reclamation cost, it paid the full Polaj rate as soon as it was brought back under cultivation.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Chachar was land that had lain fallow for 3 to 4 years due to inundation, exhaustion, or lack of resources. When brought back under the plough, it was taxed at concessional graduated rates—two-fifths in the first year, three-fifths in the second, four-fifths in the third and fourth, and reaching the full Polaj rate only in the fifth year.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Banjar was land that had remained uncultivated for five years or more. To incentivize peasants to clear scrub and reclaim such waste land, the state charged only nominal, progressively graduated shares (such as one or two sers per bigha initially) before bringing it up to full assessment over several harvests.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 13 (Consolidation of the Mughal Empire); Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari

stem: With reference to the modes of land revenue assessment practiced across different provinces of the Mughal Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Kankut system, the revenue demand was fixed through a summary assessment based on previous years' revenue records without any field measurement, whereas Nasaq involved measuring the land by ropes or paces followed by sample crop appraisal before harvest.

2. Within the Ghalla-Bakhshi (Batai) mode of assessment, Lang-batai denoted the division of the standing crop in the fields immediately after sowing, whereas Khet-batai denoted the division of grain on the threshing floor after winnowing.
3. By the end of Akbar's reign, the measurement-based Zabt (Dahsala) system had completely replaced earlier regional methods and was compulsorily enforced across the provinces of Bengal and Sindh.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mughal agrarian administration was pragmatic rather than uniform, co-opting regional methods alongside the imperial Zabt (measurement) system. Kankut combined rough area measurement with standing-crop yield estimation, Nasaq relied on summary assessment from past fiscal records without fresh measurement, and Ghalla-Bakhshi divided the actual harvest through distinct physical stages.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it reverses the definitions of Kankut and Nasaq. In Kankut (or Danabandi; literally 'grain-estimation'), the total area of the field was first measured using jars/ropes or by pacing, after which the per-bigha yield of the standing crop was estimated by mutual inspection and sample cutting. Conversely, Nasaq was not an independent method of crop measurement at all, but a summary valuation or group assessment based on past revenue records and previous assessments without fresh measurement or crop-sharing.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it swaps Khet-batai with Lang-batai/Ras-batai. Under Ghalla-Bakhshi (crop-sharing or Batai), Khet-batai was the division of the standing crop in the field itself by demarcating plots right after sowing or ripening; Lang-batai was the division of the harvested crop stacked into heaps (langs) before threshing; and Ras-batai was the division of the grain heap on the threshing floor after threshing and winnowing.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Zabt (Dahsala) system based on bamboo-jarib measurement was concentrated in the core heartland provinces (Lahore, Multan, Delhi, Agra, Awadh, Allahabad, Malwa, and parts of Gujarat). It was never compulsorily enforced in Bengal—which relied predominantly on Nasaq/Muqtai (fixed summary assessment due to riverine deltaic ecology)—or in Sindh, Kashmir, and parts of Thatta and Kabul, where Ghalla-Bakhshi (crop-sharing) remained the norm.

ref: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1556-1707), Ch. 6; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: With reference to the stratification of the peasantry and village-level revenue administration in Mughal India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Khud-kashta were resident peasants who owned their ploughs and bullocks and held hereditary occupancy rights over the lands they cultivated in their own village.

2. Pahi-kashta were non-resident or migratory cultivators who were frequently offered concessional revenue terms to bring uncultivated or abandoned land under the plough in villages other than their own.

3. Unlike the Qanungo, who served as the hereditary registrar of revenue records at the pargana level, the Patwari functioned as an employee of the village community rather than a salaried servant of the imperial treasury.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mughal village society was internally stratified based on residence, capital ownership (ploughs and bullocks), and tenurial security among Khud-kashta, Pahi-kashta, and Muzarian. At the grassroots administrative interface, the village accountant (Patwari) remained a servant of the village community paid through customary village allowances, whereas the Qanungo operated at the pargana tier as the state-recognized repository of revenue schedules and past assessments.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Khud-kashta (also called Malik-i-zamin or Mirasdar in the Deccan) were resident proprietors/cultivators of the village who cultivated land using their own family labour, ploughs, and bullocks. As long as they paid the state land revenue, their occupancy rights were hereditary and inviolable; they could even lease out spare plots to sharecroppers (Muzarian).

Statement 2 is correct. Pahi-kashta (or Pahis) were non-resident peasants who belonged to one village but contracted to cultivate lands in another village, either temporarily or by migrating with their ploughs. Because the Mughal state and Zamindars constantly sought to expand cultivation into arable waste, Pahi-kashta were routinely attracted with lower, concessional revenue rates compared to resident Khud-kashta.

Statement 3 is correct. A common misconception is to treat the Patwari as an imperial state official paid from the royal exchequer. As Abul Fazl notes in the Ain-i-Akbari, the Patwari was a village accountant maintained and paid by the villagers themselves (through customary perquisites) to record individual peasant holdings and collections, although his bahi (ledger) was inspected by state auditors. In contrast, the Qanungo was the pargana-level hereditary registrar of revenue practices and schedules, remunerated earlier through a 1% commission and under Akbar via a state jagir/allowance.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 8 (Peasants, Zamindars and the State); Satish Chandra, Medieval India

stem: With reference to the nature of Zamindari rights and agrarian perquisites in Mughal India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Zamindari rights over revenue collection and fiscal perquisites were non-transferable service tenures that could not be sold, mortgaged, or partitioned among heirs without a specific imperial Farman from the Emperor.
2. Milkiyat denoted the extensive personal lands of the Zamindars, which they cultivated directly through hired or servile labour for their private use and could sell or mortgage at will.

3. When the state temporarily bypassed a Zamindar to collect land revenue directly from the peasantry, the Zamindar remained entitled to a customary share of the produce known as Malikana, whereas Nankar represented a revenue-free land grant or cash allowance given for active revenue collection service.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike Jagirdari assignments (which were purely transferable, non-hereditary state fiscal assignments), Zamindari in Mughal India possessed a dual character: it was simultaneously a hereditary, alienable, and divisible private proprietary right over fiscal perquisites (Malikana) and personal demesne lands (Milkiyat), as well as an administrative obligation to assist the state in revenue collection in return for Nankar.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. While imperial or subadari confirmation (Sanad) was sought for recognition of succession, Zamindari (particularly primary/intermediary talluqa and biswi shares) was treated in Mughal law and custom as a form of private property (Milk). Hundreds of surviving 17th-century sale deeds (Bai-nama) and mortgage deeds (Girvinama) prove that Zamindari shares were freely inherited, partitioned among heirs, bought, sold, and mortgaged without requiring a personal Farman from the Emperor for every transaction.

Statement 2 is correct. Zamindars held extensive personal lands termed Milkiyat (property) or Sir/Khud-kasht. These lands were cultivated directly for the private subsistence and market profit of the Zamindar, often using hired wage-labourers or low-caste agricultural servants, and the Zamindar enjoyed complete freedom to sell, bequeath, or mortgage them.

Statement 3 is correct. Because the Zamindar's claim over a share of the land's produce was recognized as an antecedent proprietary right, even when the state set aside a Zamindar (making him 'be-dakhil') and collected revenue directly from the ryots, it still had to pay him Malikana (usually 10% in Northern India). When the Zamindar actively performed the state service (khidmat) of collecting and remitting revenue, he received his remuneration either as a deduction from revenue or as revenue-free land called Nankar.

ref: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India, Ch. 5 (The Zamindars); NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the core architecture of the Mansabdari system instituted by Emperor Akbar, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Zat rank determined the personal status of a noble in the imperial administrative hierarchy as well as his personal pay scale, while the Sawar rank indicated the specific number of cavalrymen he was obligated to maintain.

2. Under the three-tier classification introduced within each Zat grade during Akbar's reign, a Mansabdar was placed in the first category when his Sawar rank exceeded his Zat rank, and in the second category when both ranks were equal.

3. A Mansab was neither hereditary nor tied to a permanent territorial fief, and upon the death of a Mansabdar, his accumulated assets were inventoried under the law of escheat (Zabt) to settle his fiscal liabilities (Mutalaba) to the state treasury.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Introduced in its dual-rank form (Zat and Sawar) around 1595–96, Akbar's Mansabdari system integrated the civil and military bureaucracy into a single graded hierarchy. By capping Sawar at or below Zat and enforcing non-hereditary service alongside post-mortem fiscal audits (Mutalaba), the Crown prevented the emergence of autonomous feudal baronies.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The word Zat meant personal: it fixed the Mansabdar's exact standing in the court precedence list and his personal salary (talab-i-khassa), which also covered the maintenance of his personal household transport (elephants, camels, mules, and carts). The Sawar rank was a military obligation fixing the number of horsemen and horses (tabinan) he had to maintain and bring to the muster.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Akbar's regulations, a Mansabdar's Sawar rank could not exceed his Zat rank (except in rare emergency wartime assignments in turbulent frontiers). Within any given Zat rank, Mansabdars were divided into three classes causing slight variations in their personal Zat pay: First Class when the Sawar rank was equal to the Zat rank (e.g., 5000 Zat / 5000 Sawar); Second Class when the Sawar rank was half or more than half of the Zat rank (e.g., 5000 Zat / 3000 Sawar); and Third Class when the Sawar rank was less than half of the Zat rank (e.g., 5000 Zat / 1000 Sawar).

Statement 3 is correct. Mansabs were purely personal appointments held at the pleasure of the Emperor, and Jagirs assigned against them were rotated every 3 to 4 years. Because nobles routinely took cash advances (musaadat) or had unadjusted treasury dues (Mutalaba), the state invoked Zabt (escheat) upon a noble's death to inventory his estate, recover state dues, and often return the surplus or grant fresh lower Mansabs to deserving sons at the Emperor's discretion.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 13; M. Athar Ali, The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb

stem: With reference to the military organization and cavalry regulations of the Mughal Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Dah-bisti rule enforced during Akbar's reign, a standard Mansabdari cavalry contingent was required to maintain twenty horses for every ten troopers to ensure mobility, verified through the Dagh and Chehra procedures supervised by the Mir Bakshi.

2. Unlike the Tabinan, who were regular troopers recruited and commanded directly by individual Mansabdars, the Ahadis were gentlemen-troopers recruited personally into the Emperor's service who stood outside regular Mansabdari contingents and had their own separate Diwan and Bakshi.

3. The Dakhilis constituted a body of supplementary troops recruited and paid on behalf of the state, but placed under the command of Mansabdars rather than serving in the Emperor's personal household establishment.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mughal military efficiency rested on the Mir Bakshi's enforcement of horse-to-trooper ratios (Dah-bisti) and anti-fraud musters (Dagh and Chehra), alongside a three-part differentiation of cavalrymen: Tabinan (Mansabdars' own contingent levies), Ahadis (elite imperial gentlemen-troopers directly under the Crown), and Dakhilis (state-recruited supplementary soldiers attached to Mansabdars).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Recognizing that a single-horse trooper (Yak-aspa) became immobilized if his mount tired or died on campaign, Akbar instituted the Dah-bisti ('ten-twenty') rule whereby every contingent of 10 horsemen had to maintain 20 horses (configured as combinations of three-horsed Seh-aspa, two-horsed Du-aspa, and one-horsed Yak-aspa troopers). The Mir Bakshi enforced this through Chehra (descriptive roll of the soldier) and Dagh (double-branding of the horse—one imperial mark and one noble's mark).

Statement 2 is correct. While Tabinan were regular horsemen recruited, equipped, and commanded by Mansabdars out of their Sawar pay, Ahadis (literally 'single men' or 'gentlemen-troopers') were young men of noble lineage or proven skill who did not hold a Mansab high enough for a contingent, yet were deemed too respectable to serve as ordinary Tabinan under a noble. They served the Emperor directly, had their own separate Diwan and Bakshi under a high courtier, could muster up to five horses, and drew substantially higher salaries than regular troopers.

Statement 3 is correct. Students frequently confuse Ahadis with Dakhilis. Unlike Ahadis (who remained directly in the imperial household service), Dakhilis ('handed-over' or 'supplementary' troops) were foot-soldiers and horsemen recruited and paid by the state at fixed rates, but handed over and attached to the contingents of Mansabdars to supplement their regular forces.

ref: William Irvine, The Army of the Indian Moghuls; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 13

stem: With reference to the evolution of the Mansabdari system during the seventeenth century, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: The introduction of the 'Du-aspa Sih-aspa' category by Emperor Jahangir enabled the Mughal state to double a selected Mansabdar's cavalry contingent obligation and corresponding Sawar allowance without raising his Zat rank.

Statement-II: Under the foundational rules of the Mansabdari system instituted by Akbar, elevating a noble's Zat rank automatically reduced his personal pay scale (Talab-i-Khasa) while diverting the fiscal increment exclusively to the maintenance of infantry (Piadgan).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Jahangir introduced the Du-aspa Sih-aspa (two-three horses) rank to allow selected trusted nobles to maintain double the cavalry troopers without raising their Zat rank. Raising the Zat rank to accommodate a higher Sawar figure would have inflated the noble's personal salary (Talab-i-Khasa) and disrupted court protocol seniority.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Introduced by Jahangir in his tenth regnal year (initially conferred upon Mahabat Khan), the 'Du-aspa Sih-aspa' (literally trooper with two or three horses) provision was a sub-division within the Sawar rank. For the portion of the Sawar rank designated as Du-aspa Sih-aspa, both the Mansabdar's military contingent obligation (cavalrymen and horses) and the state's financial allowance (Talab-i-Tabinan) were doubled relative to the ordinary (Barawurdi) rate, without altering his Zat rank.

Statement-II is incorrect. Under Akbar's regulations, a Mansabdar's ordinary Sawar rank could not exceed his Zat rank (if Sawar equalled Zat, he was placed in the First Class of that Zat). Therefore, if the Emperor wanted a noble of 3,000 Zat / 3,000 Sawar to command 6,000 horsemen under the old rules, he would first have to raise his Zat rank to 6,000. Doing so did not reduce his personal pay; on the contrary, elevating the Zat rank substantially increased the noble's personal salary (Talab-i-Khasa) and elevated his official status in court protocol, imposing a heavy fiscal and political burden on the state.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 15; Athar Ali, The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb

stem: With reference to the administrative reforms introduced by Emperor Shah Jahan in the Mansabdari and Jagirdari systems, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 'Month-Scale' (Mahwar) was introduced primarily to calibrate a Mansabdar's obligations in accordance with the ratio between the officially assessed revenue (Jama) of his Jagir and its actual realized yield (Hasil).
2. A reduction in the monthly scale of a Mansabdar's Jagir brought about a proportionate reduction in the number of cavalrymen and remount horses he was required to maintain.

3. Under the Rule of Proportion for troop muster, a Mansabdar posted within the same province (Suba) where his Jagir was located was required to maintain only one-fifth of his numerical Sawar rank, whereas one posted in another Suba of Hindustan had to maintain one-third.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Shah Jahan introduced the Month-Scale (Mahwar) to bridge the growing gap between Jama (assessed revenue) and Hasil (actual collection), scaling down troop and horse obligations accordingly. Concurrently, his Rule of One-Third/One-Fourth/One-Fifth scaled actual cavalry muster inversely to the distance between a noble's Jagir and his place of posting.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. By the reign of Shah Jahan, the Jama-dami (officially assessed income in dams) of most Jagirs had become artificially inflated compared to the Hasil (actual revenue collected). If a Jagir yielded only half of its assessed Jama, it was classified as a six-monthly (Shash-maha) Jagir; if it yielded one-fourth, it was a three-monthly (Sih-maha) Jagir.

Statement 2 is correct. Because the Mansabdar's actual cash realization from a lower-month Jagir was smaller than his paper salary entitlement, Shah Jahan's Month-Scale proportionately reduced his military maintenance burden, particularly the ratio of Dah-bisti (the required proportion of two-horse and one-horse troopers) and the number of remount horses in his contingent.

Statement 3 is incorrect because it reverses the geographical gradient of Shah Jahan's Rule of Proportion. Under Shah Jahan's edict, a Mansabdar posted within the very same Suba in which his Jagir was situated had to muster one-third (1/3) of his indicated Sawar rank; if posted in another Suba within Hindustan, he had to muster one-fourth (1/4); and only during distant trans-frontier expeditions—such as the Balkh and Badakhshan campaigns—was the requirement reduced to one-fifth (1/5).

ref: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India; Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II

stem: In the fiscal and agrarian administration of the Mughal Empire, the revenue category termed 'Paibaqi' specifically referred to:

opts.A: Imperial crown lands whose collected revenues were deposited permanently into the central royal treasury to meet the Emperor's household and standing army expenses.
opts.B: Revenue-yielding tracts earmarked for assignment as Jagirs to Mansabdars, which remained temporarily unallotted due to transfers or resumptions and were administered by imperial officials in the interim.
opts.C: Hereditary and non-transferable revenue grants conferred upon religious scholars, mystics, and indigent persons as charitable subsistence allowances.
opts.D: Cesses levied over and above the standard Dahsala assessment to compensate provincial governors for the maintenance of local riverine fleets.

core: Mughal imperial territory was fiscally divided into Khalisa-i-Sharifa (crown lands reserved for the central treasury) and land earmarked for Jagir assignments. Paibaqi denoted the pool of Jagir-designated lands lying vacant or unassigned at a given moment, whose revenues were temporarily collected by the Diwan's department pending fresh allotment.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. In Mughal revenue terminology, 'Paibaqi' (literally 'remaining to be assigned') referred to revenue circles earmarked for Jagir assignments that had been resumed from previous Jagirdars (due to transfer, demotion, or death) and were awaiting allotment to new Mansabdars. During this interim period, imperial Amins and Karoris under the Diwan-i-Paibaqi collected the revenue. Option (A) describes 'Khalisa-i-Sharifa' (imperial crown land). Option (C) describes 'Suyurghal' or 'Madad-i-Maash' (charitable grants administered by the Sadr-us-Sudur). Option (D) refers to local Abwabs or Mir Bahri cesses, not Paibaqi.

ref: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India, Ch. 7; Noman Ahmad Siddiqi, Land Revenue Administration under the Mughals

stem: With reference to the typology of revenue assignments (Jagirs) in the Mughal Empire, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Jagir-i-Tankha : Transferable revenue assignment granted to a Mansabdar in lieu of his cash salary
2. Mashrut Jagir : Permanent, hereditary revenue grant conferred under the royal red seal by Jahangir upon deserving nobles in their homeland
3. Watan Jagir : Hereditary and non-transferable assignment held by an autonomous chieftain or Raja over his ancestral dominion upon induction into the Mughal service
4. Altamgha Jagir : Temporary revenue assignment strictly conditional upon holding a specific military or administrative post, such as the command of a strategic fort
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Mughal Jagirdari system differentiated between ordinary transferable salary assignments (Jagir-i-Tankha), post-specific conditional assignments (Mashrut Jagirs), hereditary chieftaincy homelands (Watan Jagirs), and permanent royal-seal grants for favoured nobles (Altamgha Jagirs).

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Jagir-i-Tankha was the standard revenue assignment given to a Mansabdar in lieu of his cash salary entitlement (Talab). To prevent nobles from developing local autonomous roots, Tankha Jagirs were routinely transferred every three to four years.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. A 'Mashrut' (conditional) Jagir was an assignment linked exclusively to a specific office or duty (such as Qiladar of a strategic fort or Faujdar of a turbulent district) and was resumed the moment the official left that post. The description given here actually defines an 'Altamgha Jagir'.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. When autonomous Rajput Rajas and powerful regional Zamindars were absorbed into the Mughal Mansabdari hierarchy, their ancestral principalities were recognized as their 'Watan Jagirs'. Unlike Tankha Jagirs, Watan Jagirs were non-transferable and hereditary, though succession required imperial confirmation (Tika) and payment of Peshkash.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. 'Altamgha' (derived from the Central Asian Turko-Mongol tradition of the royal red/gold seal) was instituted by Jahangir to grant deserving, long-serving nobles permanent and hereditary revenue rights over their birthplace or home locality without being subject to routine transfers. The description in Pair 4 defines a 'Mashrut Jagir'.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India; M. Athar Ali, The Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb

stem: With reference to the agrarian and fiscal crisis of the Mughal Empire during the reign of Aurangzeb, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Following the annexation of the Sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda, Emperor Aurangzeb completely abolished the crown lands (Khalisa-i-Sharifa) in the Deccan and distributed all conquered revenue circles permanently as hereditary Watan Jagirs to the newly inducted Deccani nobility.

Statement-II: During the latter half of Aurangzeb's reign, the large-scale induction of Deccani and Maratha nobles into the Mansabdari ranks, coupled with the reservation of productive revenues for the imperial war chest, precipitated an acute crisis of 'Be-jagiri' (shortage of available Paibaqi lands for assignment).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Contrary to liquidating crown lands after conquering Bijapur and Golconda in 1686-1687, Aurangzeb retained a substantial portion of the most fertile Deccan territories in the imperial Khalisa to directly finance his prolonged military campaigns. Combined with the massive influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles promised high Mansabs, this shrank the Paibaqi pool and triggered an acute crisis of Be-jagiri.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. After the annexations of Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687), Aurangzeb did not abolish the Khalisa-i-Sharifa in the Deccan or convert all conquered lands into hereditary Watan Jagirs. On the contrary, facing sky-rocketing military expenditures in the Deccan theatre, Aurangzeb reserved large and productive tracts of the newly annexed kingdoms within the imperial Khalisa to directly fund his campaign treasury.

Statement-II is correct. To win over nobles from Bijapur, Golconda, and the Maratha polity, Aurangzeb granted Mansabs liberally, causing the number of Mansabdars and their aggregate salary claims to swell dramatically. Because vast revenues were locked into the Khalisa for the war effort and devastation in the Deccan depressed actual collections (Hasil), the pool of assignable Paibaqi land dried up, creating the chronic crisis of 'Be-jagiri' (literally 'absence of Jagirs'), famously lamented in contemporary administrative chronicles as 'one pomegranate among a hundred sick men' (Yak anar wa sad bimar).

ref: Satish Chandra, Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court; J.F. Richards, Mughal Administration in Golconda

stem: With reference to the institutional checks and balances among the central ministries of the Mughal Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Following Akbar's reorganization of the central administrative machinery to curb the monopoly of the Vakil, the Diwan-i-Kul emerged as the chief controller of imperial finances, revenue assessment, and Jagir allotments.

2. The Mir Bakshi served as the permanent ex-officio Commander-in-Chief of all Mughal field armies and disbursed cash salaries directly from an autonomous military treasury without requiring the financial sanction of the Diwan-i-Kul.
3. The Mir Saman (Khan-i-Saman) exercised administrative control over the imperial household establishment, royal stores, and state-run manufacturing workshops (Karkhanas).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mughal central administration operated on strict horizontal checks between the Diwan-i-Kul (finance and treasury) and the Mir Bakshi (military recruitment, branding, and pay certification). While the Mir Bakshi verified troop muster and issued pay certificates, actual disbursement of cash or Jagir assignment required the sanction of the Diwan-i-Kul.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. After the fall of Bairam Khan (who held absolute power as Vakil), Akbar systematically stripped the office of Vakil of its substantive financial and military powers, making it largely ceremonial when filled. Fiscal authority was vested in an independent minister, the Diwan-i-Kul (or Wazir), who oversaw revenue collection, audit, expenditure, and the Tankha/Paibaqi Jagir machinery.

Statement 2 is incorrect on two counts. First, the Mir Bakshi was the head of the military administration (handling Mansab recommendations, Dagh and Chehra verification, and intelligence via Waqia-navis), NOT the permanent ex-officio Commander-in-Chief of field armies; the Emperor himself was the supreme commander and appointed specific princes or senior nobles as Sipahsalar/Mir-i-Lashkar for individual campaigns. Second, the Mir Bakshi did not maintain a separate military treasury; once he verified a Mansabdar's muster and issued a certificate (Sarkhat), the claim had to go to the Diwan-i-Kul for treasury payment or Jagir assignment.

Statement 3 is correct. The Mir Saman (later styled Khan-i-Saman), a high-ranking noble of cabinet stature, was in charge of the Buyutat (imperial household department), overseeing royal stores, state purchases, protocol gifts (Khilat), and the state-run manufacturing workshops (Karkhanas) producing luxury textiles, weaponry, and court goods.

ref: Ibn Hasan, The Central Structure of the Mughal Empire; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 15

stem: With reference to the provincial (Suba) and district (Sarkar) administration of the Mughal Empire after Akbar's institutional reforms, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To prevent the concentration of regional power, the Diwan-i-Suba was appointed directly by the Emperor on the recommendation of the Imperial Diwan and functioned independently of the Subadar.
2. At the Sarkar level, the Amalguzar exercised both military-police command to suppress rebellious Zamindars and the authority to assess and collect land revenue.
3. In major urban centres, the Kotwal was entrusted with maintaining a register of inhabitants, regulating weights and measures, and safeguarding the property of deceased persons leaving no heirs.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mughal territorial administration under Akbar institutionalized horizontal checks and balances at both the Suba and Sarkar levels by separating executive-military command (Subadar and Faujdar) from fiscal administration (Diwan-i-Suba and Amalguzar).

exp.why: In 1579–80, Akbar reorganized the empire into Subas and established administrative dyarchy. The provincial Diwan (Diwan-i-Suba) ceased to be an assistant to the governor (Subadar/Sipahsalar); instead, he was appointed directly by the Emperor on the advice of the Imperial Diwan (Diwan-i-Ala) to act as a fiscal check on the Subadar.

At the Sarkar (district) level, executive-military functions and revenue administration were strictly bifurcated. The Faujdar was the executive and military head responsible for maintaining law and order, safeguarding highways, and using armed force against rebellious Zamindars, whereas the Amalguzar (or Amil) was solely the chief revenue officer responsible for assessment and collection of land revenue.

As detailed in Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari, the Kotwal combined municipal, magisterial, and police duties in large towns. He appointed Mir-i-Mohallas to keep registers of houses and newcomers, supervised market weights and prices, prevented illicit distillation, and inventoried heirless estates (Bait-ul-Mal).

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 13; Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari (Regulations for the Subadar, Faujdar, Amalguzar, and Kotwal)

stem: With reference to the revenue-free charitable and religious grants known as Madad-i-Maash (or Suyurghal) in the Mughal Empire, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Akbar, Madad-i-Maash grants normally consisted of half cultivated land and half cultivable waste in order to encourage the expansion of agriculture.
2. A Madad-i-Maash grantee acquired only the right to collect the state's share of revenue and could not dispossess the resident Khud-kashta peasants of their occupancy rights.
3. To overcome the acute shortage of assignable lands during his Deccan campaigns, Aurangzeb issued a Farman in 1690 abolishing the hereditary succession of Madad-i-Maash grants.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Mughal Madad-i-Maash (Suyurghal/Aima) grants transferred only the state's fiscal claim over land revenue without altering peasant proprietary rights, and evolved from revocable royal loans under Akbar into fully hereditary holdings under Aurangzeb's Farman of 1690.

exp.why: To prevent grantees from monopolizing prime revenue-yielding lands and to bring virgin tracts under the plough, Akbar laid down the rule that Suyurghal or Madad-i-Maash grants (administered by the Sadr-us-Sudur) should consist of 50% already cultivated land and 50% cultivable waste (banjar).

A Madad-i-Maash grant was strictly an alienation of the state's right to collect land revenue (mal-i-wajib) in favour of scholars, mystics, or destitute nobles. It did not confer Zamindari or proprietary title over the soil where resident Khud-kashta peasants held hereditary occupancy rights.

Far from abolishing heritability, Aurangzeb's famous Farman of 1690 made Madad-i-Maash grants completely hereditary. Although theoretically classified as a loan (Ariyat), the 1690 decree permitted the grant to pass automatically to the grantee's heirs upon death without curtailment, consolidating a rural gentry class loyal to the regime.

ref: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1556–1707), Ch. 8 (Revenue Grants); Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ideological and legal foundations of sovereignty under Emperor Akbar:
items: Statement-I: The Mahzar of 1579 recognized Akbar as the Imam-i-Adil (Just Ruler), empowering him to choose one among conflicting interpretations of the Mujtahids (Islamic jurists) if it served the welfare of the state.
Statement-II: Through the Mahzar of 1579, Akbar formally repudiated Islamic jurisprudence and proclaimed himself a Prophet with authority to override the injunctions of the Quran.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Drafted by Shaikh Mubarak in 1579, the Mahzar operated within the framework of Islamic jurisprudence to subordinate the orthodox Ulama at the Mughal court by vesting ultimate interpretive arbitration in the Emperor as Sultan-i-Adil.

exp.why: Signed by the leading theologians of the empire in September 1579, the Mahzar declared that the rank of a Sultan-i-Adil (Just Ruler) was higher in the eyes of God than that of a Mujtahid (interpreter of law). Therefore, whenever the Mujtahids differed on a legal question, Akbar could select any one interpretation for the convenience of mankind and the stability of the state.

Calling the Mahzar an 'Infallibility Decree' (a mistranslation popularized by Vincent Smith) is misleading. Akbar neither claimed prophethood nor repudiated the Quran; the Mahzar explicitly stipulated that any new royal ordinance could not contravene an explicit injunction (Nass) of the Quran.

ref: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals (Part II), Ch. 8; S.A.A. Rizvi, Religious and Intellectual History of the Muslims in Akbar's Reign

stem: Consider the following administrative, fiscal, and ideological measures undertaken during the reign of Emperor Akbar:
items: 1. Establishment of the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri
2. First abolition of Jizya throughout the Mughal dominions
3. Promulgation of the Ain-i-Dahsala system of revenue settlement
4. Introduction of the Dagh regulation and the Karori experiment
prompt: What is the correct chronological order of the above measures, starting from the earliest?
core: Akbar's early conciliatory tax abolitions (1563–64) preceded his administrative centralization through the Dagh and Karori reforms (1573–74), which in turn provided the empirical ten-year price and yield data required to promulgate the Ain-i-Dahsala in 1580.

exp.why: Akbar ordered the construction of the Ibadat Khana (Hall of Prayer) at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 (initially open to Sunni theologians, and later opened to scholars of all religions including Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, and Christians in 1578).

Following the abolition of the pilgrim tax in 1563, Akbar abolished the poll tax on non-Muslims (Jizya) for the first time across the Mughal Empire in 1564 to integrate non-Muslim subjects and Rajput chieftains into an inclusive imperial polity.

The Ain-i-Dahsala (ten-year settlement devised by Raja Todar Mal and Khwaja Shah Mansur) was promulgated in the 24th regnal year (1580 CE), using local productivity and price data compiled between 1570 and 1580.

In 1573–74 (18th–19th regnal year), following the conquest of Gujarat, Akbar introduced the compulsory branding of horses (Dagh) and appointed Amils/Karoris across Northern India to collect facts on actual yields and local prices—Making the correct chronological sequence 2 (1564) -> 4 (1573–74) -> 1 (1575) -> 3 (1580).

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 13; Irfan Habib, Akbar and His India

stem: With reference to the military and fort administration of Chhatrapati Shivaji, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Every major fort was placed under the joint charge of three officers of equal rank—the Havaldar, the Sabnis, and the Karkhanis—who were deliberately selected from three different castes to prevent collusion.
2. Shivaji discouraged the grant of hereditary military Jagirs (Mokasa or Saranjam) and paid his regular standing troops either in cash or by assignments on the district treasury.
3. In the Maratha cavalry organization, the Bargirs were irregular troopers who provided their own horses and weapons, whereas the Silahdars formed the permanent state-equipped royal cavalry (Paga).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Shivaji's military architecture rested on non-feudal cash payments, state-equipped Paga cavalry (Bargirs), and a three-tier caste-balanced collegium in hill forts so that no single commander could betray a fort to an enemy.

exp.why: Forts (Gad/Killa) were the backbone of Shivaji's defence. To prevent any single officer from surrendering a fort through bribery or treason, Shivaji instituted a system of triple control: the Havaldar (in charge of the garrison and keys, always a Maratha), the Sabnis (in charge of accounts and muster rolls, always a Brahmin), and the Karkhanis (in charge of commissariat and stores, always a Chandraseniya Kayastha Prabhu).

As recorded in Sabhasad Bakhar, Shivaji strictly avoided granting hereditary land assignments (Saranjam/Mokasa) to military commanders lest they become autonomous feudal warlords like the old Deshmukhs. Regular soldiers were paid in cash or via non-hereditary treasury orders (Varat).

The definitions are swapped. In Shivaji's cavalry, the Bargirs were the regular household troopers of the state-maintained Paga whose horses and arms were supplied entirely by the royal stable, whereas the Silahdars were auxiliary troopers who furnished their own horses and equipment for campaigns.

ref: Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times; Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600–1818 (New Cambridge History of India)

stem: With reference to the Ashtapradhan council of ministers under Chhatrapati Shivaji, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Amatya (Mazumdar) : Finance Minister and Chief Accountant of the Kingdom
2. Sachiv (Surnavis) : Intelligence, royal household affairs, and court chronicles
3. Mantri (Waqia-navis) : Royal correspondence and revision of state drafts and charters
4. Sumant (Dabir) : Foreign affairs, treaties, and reception of ambassadors
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Shivaji's Ashtapradhan assigned distinct departmental responsibilities to eight ministers directly accountable to the Chhatrapati, with the Amatya heading finance, the Sachiv supervising royal correspondence, the Mantri managing intelligence and court chronicles, and the Sumant handling foreign diplomacy.

exp.why: The Amatya (formerly styled Mazumdar) was the Finance Minister responsible for checking all public accounts of income and expenditure of the kingdom and countersigning district revenue statements.

The Sachiv (also known as Surnavis or Chitnis) was the Superintendent of Royal Correspondence, responsible for ensuring that all royal letters, charters, and Pargana accounts were drafted in the proper official style and language.

The Mantri (also known as Waqia-navis) was the Chronicler and Interior Minister responsible for compiling a daily record of the king's doings and court proceedings, supervising royal household security, and managing intelligence.

The Sumant (also known as Dabir) served as the Foreign Minister, advising the Chhatrapati on relations with foreign states, war and peace, receiving foreign envoys, and keeping track of intelligence from outside kingdoms.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 18; Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times

stem: With reference to the administrative structure of the Ashtapradhan under Chhatrapati Shivaji, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Among the eight ministers of Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, only the Panditrao and the Nyayadhish were exempted from leading military campaigns.
2. The Ashtapradhan functioned as a cabinet with collective responsibility whose members held hereditary offices remunerated through permanent Mokasa land grants.
3. The Amatya was responsible for checking and countersigning all public accounts of the kingdom, whereas the Mantri maintained the records of the king's daily court proceedings.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Chhatrapati Shivaji, the Ashtapradhan was a purely advisory council of non-hereditary, salaried ministers directly and individually accountable to the sovereign, whereas six of the eight ministers (all except the ecclesiastical Panditrao and judicial Nyayadhish) were required to command military expeditions. The transformation of Maratha ministerial posts into hereditary offices backed by autonomous Saranjam or Mokasa land assignments occurred only later in the eighteenth century under the Peshwas.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Given the constant military exigencies of the infant Maratha state (Swarajya), six out of the eight ministers in Shivaji's Ashtapradhan—including the Peshwa (Mukhya Pradhan), Amatya, Sachiv, Mantri, Sumant, and Senapati (Sar-i-Naubat)—were required to perform military duties and lead campaigns whenever called upon. Only the Panditrao (in charge of ecclesiastical and charitable affairs) and the Nyayadhish (chief justice) were exempted from military command.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Shivaji's Ashtapradhan did not function as a modern cabinet with collective responsibility; each minister was individually responsible to the Chhatrapati, who was not bound by their advice. Furthermore, Shivaji strictly prohibited hereditary succession to ministerial offices and paid his ministers in cash from the state treasury rather than granting permanent hereditary jagirs (Mokasa/Saranjam)—a practice that only became entrenched later during the Peshwa era.

Statement 3 is correct. In the Ashtapradhan, the Amatya (formerly styled Majumdar) was the finance minister responsible for auditing and countersigning the public accounts of the realm as well as district revenue statements.
