The Mantri (also called Wakins or Waqia-Navis) acted as the court chronicler and intelligence minister who recorded the king's daily proceedings, household affairs, and royal audiences.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 19; Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818

stem: With reference to the land revenue reforms introduced by Chhatrapati Shivaji in Swarajya, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Modeled on Malik Ambar's revenue system in the Nizam Shahi sultanate, Shivaji replaced rope measurement with a standardized measuring rod called Kathi to classify and assess cultivable land.

2. Under the revenue settlement supervised by Annaji Datto, the state established direct assessment with the peasant proprietors through salaried Karkuns and provided Tagai loans for agricultural recovery.
3. Shivaji completely abolished the offices of the hereditary village Patils and pargana Deshmukhs by confiscating all their Watan and Mirasdari lands across Swarajya.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Shivaji's land revenue system built upon Malik Ambar's Ryotwari-style settlement by introducing a standardized measuring rod (Shivashahi Kathi) and deploying salaried Karkuns to assess cultivators directly. Rather than physically liquidating the hereditary Watandars (Deshmukhs, Deshpandes, and Patils), Shivaji broke their autonomous military power and forced them to receive their fixed customary perquisites through state revenue officials.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Recognizing that hemp ropes shrank when wet and stretched when dry, Shivaji adopted Malik Ambar's scientific measurement reforms and introduced a standardized measuring rod called the Kathi (specifically the Shivashahi Kathi, measuring 5 cubits and 5 fists). Twenty square Kathis constituted one Bigha, and 120 Bighas formed one Chavar.

Statement 2 is correct. In 1679, Annaji Datto completed a comprehensive revenue survey and settlement under which state-appointed salaried officials (Karkuns) under Tarfdars and Subadars assessed the peasantry directly ( fixing state demand initially at 30% and later at 40% after abolishing miscellaneous cesses). Shivaji also instructed officials to advance interest-free or low-interest Tagai (Taccavi) loans to distressed peasants to purchase cattle and seed.

Statement 3 is incorrect. While Shivaji deeply distrusted the autonomous power of the hereditary Deshmukhs, Deshpandes, and Patils (Watandars/Mirasdars), he did not completely abolish their offices or confiscate all Mirasdari and Watan lands across Swarajya. Instead, he demolished their unauthorized private strongholds (garhis), prohibited them from collecting arbitrary exactions directly from the peasantry, and ensured that their fixed customary dues (Haqq/Rusum) were paid to them strictly through state Karkuns.

ref: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals, Part II; A.R. Kulkarni, Maharashtra in the Age of Shivaji

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Maratha fiscal levies of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi:
items: Statement-I: Under Chhatrapati Shahu and the Peshwas, while the bulk of the Chauth collection was distributed as Mokasa among Maratha military commanders (Sardars) for maintaining troops, the proceeds of Sardeshmukhi were reserved exclusively as the Chhatrapati's personal royal prerogative.

Statement-II: Unlike Chauth, which originated as a military protection levy of one-fourth of the revenue assessment extracted from external territories through the armed expeditions of Maratha chiefs, Sardeshmukhi was an additional ten percent levy claimed by the Maratha monarch by virtue of his legal status as the hereditary head Deshmukh (Sardeshmukh) of the country.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Chauth (25% of revenue) and Sardeshmukhi (an additional 10%) rested on fundamentally different legal and political foundations in Maratha statecraft. Because Chauth was enforced by the military expeditions of Maratha Sardars against external (Mughlai) territories, three-fourths of its proceeds (Mokasa) were assigned to those Sardars to maintain their contingents, whereas Sardeshmukhi belonged to the Chhatrapati's personal treasury by virtue of his hereditary legal claim as the supreme Deshmukh.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In the fiscal settlement institutionalized by Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath under Chhatrapati Shahu, the Chauth (25% levy) was partitioned between the ruler (Rajbabti, 25% of Chauth), discretionary royal grants (Sahotra 6% and Nadgaunda 3%), and the Maratha Sardars (Mokasa, 66% of Chauth) who maintained troops and collected the dues. By contrast, the proceeds of Sardeshmukhi were treated as the Chhatrapati's personal royal right (though later partitioned internally within the royal establishment).

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Chauth originated as a military tribute or protection tax paid by territories outside Swarajya (Mughlai lands) to escape Maratha raids, which required sharing its proceeds (Mokasa) with the Maratha military commanders who enforced collection in the field. Conversely, Sardeshmukhi (10%) was claimed by Shivaji and his successors on the legal fiction that the Maratha sovereign was the hereditary Sardeshmukh (head Deshmukh) responsible for protecting the interests of the lower Watandars and subjects, justifying its retention as a crown prerogative.

ref: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 19

stem: In the context of the eighteenth-century Maratha fiscal system reorganized under Chhatrapati Shahu and Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath, which one of the following best describes the term 'Mokasa'?

opts.A: The sixty-six percent share of the Chauth collection, remaining after the deduction of Babti, Sahotra, and Nadgaunda, which was assigned to Maratha military commanders for maintaining troops.
opts.B: Hereditary peasant proprietorship land in the core Swarajya villages whose holders paid a fixed land tax and could not be evicted so long as they cultivated the soil.
opts.C: Tenancy-at-will agricultural land cultivated by temporary migrant peasants who held no hereditary rights in the village community.
opts.D: Tax-free religious endowment land granted permanently to temples, mathas, and learned Brahmanas under the seal of the Panditrao.

core: Under Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath's complex fiscal partitioning of the Chauth of the Deccan, only 25% (Babti) went directly to the Chhatrapati, 6% (Sahotra) to the Pant Sachiv, and 3% (Nadgaunda) at the King's pleasure, while the remaining 66%—termed Mokasa—was granted to Maratha Sardars to finance their cavalry contingents. This decentralized allocation provided the fiscal autonomy that propelled the rise of the Maratha Confederacy.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct. After securing the imperial grants of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi in 1719, Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath devised an intricate mechanism for dividing Chauth collections: (1) Babti or Rajbabti (25% of Chauth reserved for the Chhatrapati), (2) Sahotra (6% reserved for the Pant Sachiv), (3) Nadgaunda (3% awarded at the Chhatrapati's discretion), and (4) Mokasa (the remaining 66% of the Chauth), which was distributed as military assignments (Saranjam/Mokasa) to Maratha Sardars for maintaining troops and collecting the levy. Option (B) describes 'Miras' (held by Mirasdars), Option (C) describes 'Upari' tenures, and Option (D) describes 'Inam' or 'Devasthan/Dharmadaya' grants.

ref: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 2; Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818

stem: With reference to the Mughal-Maratha Treaty of 1719 and its institutional impact on the Maratha polity, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The treaty was concluded directly between Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath and the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb to terminate the twenty-seven-year Deccan War.

2. Under the imperial farmans of 1719, the Mughal Emperor transferred the direct administrative Subadari of the provinces of Gujarat and Malwa to Chhatrapati Shahu without any tribute or military service obligation.
3. Following the 1719 agreement, Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath abolished the Saranjami system and mandated that all Chauth collections from the Deccan be collected solely by salaried state Karkuns.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The landmark Mughal-Maratha Treaty of 1719—termed by Richard Temple as the 'Magna Carta of the Maratha Dominion'—was negotiated by Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath with the Sayyid brother Hussain Ali Khan and ratified by Emperor Muhammad Shah. It recognized Shahu's rule over Shivaji's Swarajya and the right to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi across the six Mughal Subas of the Deccan in exchange for an annual Peshkash and a contingent of 15,000 Maratha horsemen, while catalysing the decentralized Saranjami Confederacy.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Emperor Aurangzeb had already died in 1707. The Treaty of 1719 was negotiated by Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath with Sayyid Hussain Ali Khan (the Mughal Viceroy of the Deccan and one of the Kingmaker Sayyid Brothers) during the last days of Emperor Farrukhsiyar and was formally ratified through imperial farmans issued by Emperor Rafi-ud-Darajat / Muhammad Shah in 1719.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The 1719 farmans recognized Shahu's sovereignty over Shivaji's core homeland (Swarajya) and granted the Marathas the right to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi from the six Mughal Subas of the Deccan (Khandesh, Berar, Aurangabad, Bidar, Golconda/Hyderabad, and Bijapur)—not the direct administrative Subadari of Gujarat and Malwa, which were contested later in the 1720s and 1730s under Peshwa Baji Rao I. Moreover, in return for the Deccan grants, Shahu agreed to maintain a contingent of 15,000 horsemen for the Emperor's service and pay an annual tribute (Peshkash) of ten lakh rupees.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Far from abolishing the Saranjami system, Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath institutionalized it after 1719 by partitioning the Chauth of the Deccan into autonomous spheres of collection assigned to powerful Maratha Sardars as Saranjam/Mokasa. Because individual Sardars collected their own shares directly in distant provinces, this arrangement laid the structural foundation of the semi-autonomous Maratha Confederacy (Gaekwads, Holkars, Scindias, and Bhonsles).

ref: Satish Chandra, Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court 1707-1740; Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following fiscal and military administrative developments in medieval India:
items: 1. Introduction of the dual Zat and Sawar ranks in the Mughal Mansabdari system
2. Introduction of the standardized silver Rupiya and crop-wise Ray' revenue schedules by Sher Shah Suri
3. Coronation of Chhatrapati Shivaji at Raigad and formalization of the Ashtapradhan council
4. Introduction of the Month-Scale (Mahwar) in Mughal Jagir assignments to bridge the gap between Jama and Hasil
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above developments, starting from the earliest?
core: Tracking the institutional evolution of medieval fiscal-military states requires linking administrative mechanisms to their specific reigns: Sher Shah Suri's tri-metallic currency and Ray' crop schedules (1540–1545) laid the groundwork for Akbar's Dahsala (1580) and dual Zat-Sawar Mansabdari ranks (1595–1596), which were subsequently modified by Shah Jahan's Month-Scale (Mahwar, c. 1630s–1640s) before Shivaji's royal coronation at Raigad (1674).

exp.why: Item 1 occurred in 1595–1596 (40th regnal year of Emperor Akbar), when Akbar bifurcated the Mansab rank into 'Zat' (indicating personal status and pay scale) and 'Sawar' (fixing the actual number of cavalrymen the Mansabdar had to maintain).

Item 2 occurred between 1540 and 1545 during the reign of Sher Shah Suri, who minted the standardized 178-grain silver Rupiya and compiled the Ray' (schedule of average crop yields per bigha for good, middling, and low-grade land), which later served as the baseline for Akbar's early Zabti experiments.

Item 3 occurred in June 1674, when Shivaji was formally crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad fort, initiated the Rajyabhisheka Shaka era, and formalized the Sanskrit nomenclature and protocols of his eight-member Ashtapradhan council.

Item 4 occurred during the reign of Emperor Shah Jahan (1628–1658), who introduced the Month-Scale (Mahwar, such as Shash-maha or Sih-maha jagirs) to proportionally scale down a Mansabdar's cavalry and Dagh obligations when the actual revenue realization (Hasil) of his assigned Jagir fell substantially below its official assessed valuation (Jama). Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 2 (1540–1545) -> 1 (1595–1596) -> 4 (c. 1630s–1640s) -> 3 (1674).

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 14, 15, 17 & 19

stem: With reference to the early Tamil Bhakti movement led by the Alvars and Nayanars between the sixth and tenth centuries CE, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Alvars and Nayanars forged an ideological alliance with the heterodox Buddhist and Jaina sects in Tamilakam to oppose royal land grants to Brahmanical temples.
2. Women saint-poets such as Andal and Karaikkal Ammaiyar challenged conventional patriarchal household roles and had their compositions canonized within their respective sectarian traditions.
3. The Chola rulers institutionalized the Tamil Bhakti movement by patronizing the ritual singing of Shaiva hymns in royal temples and consecrating metal images of the saint-poets.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the early Tamil Bhakti movement drew saints from diverse social strata including women and non-Brahmanas, it actively competed against Buddhism and Jainism for royal patronage rather than allying with them. The imperial Cholas subsequently integrated these popular vernacular hymn traditions into grand temple rituals to consolidate royal legitimacy.

exp.why: Far from allying with Buddhism and Jainism, a major recurring theme in the hymns of both the Vaishnava Alvars and Shaiva Nayanars (such as Appar and Sambandar) is fierce ideological opposition to the Shramana sects, competing directly with them for the patronage of the Pallava, Pandya, and Chola monarchs.

Andal (the only woman among the twelve Alvars, who envisioned herself as the beloved of Vishnu in Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumozhi) and Karaikkal Ammaiyar (one of the three women among the sixty-three Nayanars, who adopted extreme asceticism) bypassed traditional domestic expectations, and their poems were preserved within the canonical anthologies.

Chola monarchs such as Parantaka I and Rajaraja I gave institutional stability to the Bhakti movement by making endowments for the recitation of Tevaram hymns in temples and installing bronze and stone icons of saints like Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar for ritual worship.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Theme 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the canonical devotional literature of early medieval South India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Nalayira Divya Prabandham, frequently revered as the Tamil Veda, is a tenth-century anthology of Shaiva Nayanar hymns compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi.
2. The Tevaram comprises the devotional songs of the earliest Vaishnava Alvars—Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar—arranged by Nathamuni on the basis of musical modes.
3. Both the Tiruvacakam composed by Manikkavasagar and the Periyapuranam composed by Sekkizhar belong to the canonical Vaishnava Alvar literature of Tamilakam.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Tamil Bhakti literary canon is bifurcated into two distinct sectarian anthologies compiled during the tenth to twelfth centuries: the Vaishnava Nalayira Divya Prabandham (compiled by Nathamuni) and the twelve-volume Shaiva Tirumurai (largely compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi and completed by Sekkizhar).

exp.why: The Nalayira Divya Prabandham ('Four Thousand Sacred Compositions') is the canonical anthology of the twelve Vaishnava Alvars and was compiled by the Sri Vaishnava acharya Nathamuni in the tenth century, whereas Nambi Andar Nambi compiled the Shaiva Tirumurai.

The Tevaram consists of the first seven volumes of the Shaiva Tirumurai containing the poems of the three prominent Shaiva Nayanar saints—Tirunavukkarasar (Appar), Tirujnanasambandar, and Sundarar—compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi, not Vaishnava Alvar songs compiled by Nathamuni.

Both works belong to the Shaiva Tirumurai canon rather than Vaishnava Alvar literature: Manikkavasagar's ecstatic lyrics of love for Shiva (Tiruvacakam) constitute the eighth Tirumurai, while Sekkizhar's twelfth-century hagiography of the sixty-three Nayanars (Periyapuranam) forms the twelfth and final Tirumurai.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Theme 6; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, Ch. 14

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the philosophical foundations of Vedantic Bhakti in medieval India:
items: Statement-I: Unlike Ramanujacharya, who treated devotion to a personal deity (Saguna Bhakti) merely as a lower-order preparatory stage to be transcended through pure non-dual knowledge, Adi Shankaracharya established loving self-surrender (Prapatti) to a qualified Brahman as the ultimate metaphysical path to liberation.

Statement-II: In Ramanujacharya's Vishishtadvaita philosophy, individual conscious souls (Chit) and insentient matter (Achit) are not illusory projections of Maya, but are eternally real attributes that constitute the body of a personal Supreme Lord.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Adi Shankaracharya's Advaita Vedanta posited an attribute-less Nirguna Brahman as the sole ultimate reality (Paramarthika Satya), relegating personal devotion to a lower empirical plane (Vyavaharika Satya). Conversely, Ramanujacharya's Vishishtadvaita provided a rigorous philosophical justification for Saguna Bhakti by affirming the real, eternal relationship between a personal God, individual souls, and the material cosmos.

exp.why: Statement-I reverses the philosophical positions of the two thinkers. Adi Shankaracharya's Advaita Vedanta held that ultimate liberation comes only through Jnana (knowledge of the absolute identity of Atman and Nirguna Brahman), treating Saguna Bhakti as a preparatory step within empirical reality. It was Ramanujacharya who elevated Saguna Bhakti and Prapatti (unconditional self-surrender) to a personal Vishnu-Narayana as the highest path to salvation.

Statement-II accurately states the core doctrine of Ramanujacharya's Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism). Rejecting Shankara's Illusionism (Mayavada), Ramanuja argued that Brahman is an organic unity in which conscious souls (Chit) and non-conscious matter (Achit) exist as real, eternal modes (Prakara) or the body (Sharira) of the Supreme Lord (Ishvara).

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 16; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part-II

stem: Consider the following pairs of medieval Vedantic Acharyas, their philosophical schools, and their core metaphysical doctrines:
items: 1. Madhvacharya : Dvaita (Tattvavada) — Doctrine of Panchabheda affirming five eternal and absolute ontological distinctions among God (Ishvara), individual souls (Jiva), and insentient matter (Jada).
2. Nimbarkacharya : Shuddhadvaita — Doctrine of pure non-dualism untouched by Maya, advocating Pushtimarg (the path of nourishing divine grace) centered on child Krishna.
3. Vallabhacharya : Dvaitadvaita (Svabhavika Bhedabheda) — Doctrine that individual souls and matter are simultaneously distinct and non-distinct from Brahman, akin to waves and the ocean.
4. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu : Achintya Bheda Abheda — Doctrine of inconceivable, simultaneous oneness and difference between the Supreme Lord and His manifold energies (Shakti).
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Subsequent to Ramanuja, Vaishnava Vedanta diversified into distinct ontological systems trying to reconcile the transcendence of Brahman with the reality of the world and devotion. Mastering the exact mapping between Madhvacharya (Dvaita), Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita), Vallabhacharya (Shuddhadvaita), and Chaitanya (Achintya Bheda Abheda) is critical for distinguishing medieval philosophical lineages.

exp.why: Madhvacharya (13th century, Karnataka) propounded Dvaita or Tattvavada, asserting that Vishnu is the only independent reality (Svatantra) while souls and matter are dependent realities (Paratantra), separated by five eternal distinctions (Panchabheda).

Nimbarkacharya propounded Dvaitadvaita (Svabhavika Bhedabheda) and popularized the worship of Radha-Krishna in the Sanakadi Sampradaya. Shuddhadvaita and Pushtimarg were propounded by Vallabhacharya, not Nimbarkacharya.

Vallabhacharya (late 15th–early 16th century) founded the Rudra Sampradaya/Pushtimarg based on Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism), holding that the universe is a real manifestation of Brahman's Sat and Chit aspects without any intervention of Maya. Dvaitadvaita belongs to Nimbarkacharya.

The Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition inspired by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (and systematized by Jiva Goswami) is grounded in Achintya Bheda Abheda—holding that the creation and souls are simultaneously one with and different from Lord Krishna in a manner beyond human logical comprehension.

ref: Nitin Singhania, Indian Art and Culture, Ch. on Bhakti & Sufi Movements; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: With reference to the twelfth-century Virashaiva (Lingayat) movement in Karnataka, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Led by Basavanna along with fellow Sharanas such as Allama Prabhu and Akka Mahadevi, the movement established the Anubhava Mantapa as an egalitarian forum for spiritual deliberation expressed through Kannada Vachanas.

2. In their radical rejection of temple-centric idol worship, the Virashaivas prohibited the wearing or veneration of any physical emblem of Shiva and restricted spiritual practice strictly to unmanifest meditation.

3. Challenging Dharmashastric notions of ritual pollution and karma, the Virashaivas rejected the theory of rebirth and practiced only the ceremonial burial of their dead rather than funerary cremation.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Virashaiva movement under Basavanna mounted one of the most structured socio-religious critiques of caste hierarchy, priestly mediation, and static temple worship (Sthavaralinga) in medieval India. Instead of abolishing symbols altogether, it democratized sacrality by making every devotee's body a moving temple (Jangama) bearing a personal Ishtalinga.

exp.why: Basavanna (initially a minister in the court of the Kalachuri ruler Bijjala II at Kalyani), along with mystics like Allama Prabhu and Akka Mahadevi, convened the Anubhava Mantapa ('Hall of Spiritual Experience') and composed pithy, accessible free-verse lyrics in Kannada known as Vachanas.

While Virashaivas opposed static idol worship in rich temples (Sthavaralinga) and Brahmanical priestly mediation, they did not prohibit physical emblems of Shiva. On the contrary, the defining practice of the sect (from which the term 'Lingayat' derives) is that every initiate—irrespective of gender or caste birth—wears a personal Ishtalinga in a small silver or wooden casket suspended around the neck or over the left shoulder.

The Virashaivas rejected the Brahmanical doctrine of transmigration/rebirth (believing that on death a true devotee unites directly with Shiva and does not return to this world), repudiated the five-fold pollution norms (Pancha Sutakas) of the Dharmashastras, encouraged post-puberty marriage and widow remarriage, and replaced funerary cremation exclusively with ceremonial burial.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Theme 6 (The Virashaiva Tradition in Karnataka)

stem: With reference to the Bhakti tradition in Maharashtra between the thirteenth and seventeenth centuries, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Varkari panth centered on emotional, egalitarian devotion to Lord Vitthala of Pandharpur through annual collective pilgrimages, the Dharkari tradition emphasized devotion to Lord Rama alongside active socio-political regeneration.

2. Sant Dnyaneshwar composed the Dasbodh as a practical treatise on spiritual and worldly conduct, whereas Samarth Ramdas authored the Bhavartha Dipika as a pioneering Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita.
3. Sant Eknath enriched vernacular Marathi literature through allegorical devotional drama-poems known as Bharuds, while Sant Tukaram popularized devotional lyric poetry in the Abhanga metre.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Maharashtra Dharma evolved along two complementary streams: the mystical, anti-caste Varkari tradition (spanning Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Janabai, Eknath, and Tukaram) centered on Vitthala at Pandharpur, and the activist Dharkari tradition led by Samarth Ramdas centered on Rama and Maharashtra Dharma.

exp.why: The Varkari sect ('pilgrim-devotees' who undertake the annual Vari to Pandharpur) focused on loving, non-ritualistic devotion to Vithoba/Vitthala, cutting across caste and gender boundaries. In contrast, the Dharkari stream associated with Samarth Ramdas worshipped Lord Rama and Hanuman, stressing physical strength, social organization, and harmonization of worldly duty (Prapancha) with spiritual upliftment (Paramartha).

The authorship of the two classics is swapped. Sant Dnyaneshwar (13th century) authored the Bhavartha Dipika (popularly called the Dnyaneshwari), a monumental Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, as well as the Amritanubhav. Samarth Ramdas (17th century) authored the Dasbodh and Manache Shlok.

Sant Eknath (16th century) translated the eleventh book of the Bhagavata Purana into Marathi and popularized Bharuds—witty, allegorical poems using everyday personas and situations to convey spiritual truths to the masses. Sant Tukaram (17th century) brought the Marathi Abhanga poetic tradition to its zenith through deeply personal and socially critical verses.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 16; State Board History of Medieval Maharashtra

stem: Consider the following prominent religious philosophers and mystic saints of medieval India:
items: 1. Basavanna
2. Ramanujacharya
3. Vallabhacharya
4. Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of their historical periods, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: The Bhakti and Sufi traditions evolved in distinct chronological waves across the subcontinent: early southern Acharyas like Ramanujacharya (11th-early 12th century) preceded the mid-12th-century Virashaiva movement of Basavanna, followed by the 13th-14th century Chishti Sufi climax under Nizamuddin Auliya, and finally the late 15th-early 16th century northern Vaishnava revival led by Vallabhacharya.

exp.why: Basavanna (c. 1105-1167 CE) flourished in the mid-twelfth century in Karnataka as a minister in the court of the Kalachuri ruler Bijjala II (r. 1157-1167 CE), spearheading the egalitarian Virashaiva (Lingayat) movement through Vachana literature in Kannada.

Ramanujacharya (traditionally 1017-1137 CE; active primarily in the eleventh and early twelfth centuries in Tamil Nadu) was the earliest among the four figures. He expounded the philosophy of Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism) and bridged the popular Alvar devotional tradition with Vedantic theology prior to the rise of the Virashaivas.

Vallabhacharya (1479-1531 CE) belonged to the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. A contemporary of Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara and Sikandar Lodi, he propounded Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism) and founded the Krishna-centric Pushtimarg sect in the Braj region.

Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya (1238-1325 CE), also known as Mahbub-i-Ilahi, was the most celebrated Chishti saint of the Delhi Sultanate during the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, witnessing the reigns of seven Sultans from Ghiyasuddin Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions), Timeline p. 167

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the interaction between indigenous yogic traditions and Sufism in medieval India:
items: Statement-I: In medieval India, the Nathpanthi Siddhas and Jogis engaged in extensive ideological and practical exchanges with both the Nirguna Sant poets and the Chishti and Shattari Sufi silsilahs.

Statement-II: The Chishti and Shattari Sufis strictly prohibited Hatha Yogic breathing exercises (Pas-i-Anfas) inside their khanqahs and barred the translation of Sanskrit yogic treatises like the Amritakunda into Persian and Arabic.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Medieval Indian Sufism, particularly within the Chishti and Shattari orders, actively absorbed Hatha Yogic practices of the Nathpanthi Jogis, incorporating breath-control techniques (Pas-i-Anfas) and translating Sanskrit yogic manuals like the Amritakunda into Persian and Arabic as Hauz-ul-Hayat.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Followers of Gorakhnath (Nathpanthi Jogis) frequently visited Chishti khanqahs (such as those of Shaikh Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar and Nizamuddin Auliya). Their terminology of interiorized mysticism, chakras, and breath regulation deeply influenced both Nirguna Sants like Kabir and Indian Sufi orders, especially the Chishtis and Shattaris.

Statement-II is incorrect because it reverses the historical reality. Far from prohibiting yogic exercises, Chishti and Shattari Sufis adopted Hatha Yogic breath control (Pranayama) as Pas-i-Anfas ('guarding of the breath') to aid in zikr (remembrance of God) and muraqaba (meditation). Furthermore, the Sanskrit Hatha Yoga text Amritakunda ('Pool of Nectar') was translated into Arabic and Persian under the title Hauz-ul-Hayat ('Cistern of the Water of Life'), and Shattari master Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus wrote Bahr-ul-Hayat incorporating yogic postures.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6; Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: With reference to the Nirguna Bhakti tradition of Sant Kabir and its textual legacy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The compositions attributed to Kabir were preserved across distinct regional and sectarian compilations, including the Bijak by the Kabirpanth in Varanasi, the Kabir Granthavali in Rajasthan, and the Adi Granth Sahib in Punjab.
2. Kabir composed his Ulatbansi ('upside-down sayings') in classical Paninian Sanskrit to refute orthodox Brahmanical scholars on their own scriptural terms.
3. Drawing from diverse mystical streams, Kabir's poetry conceptualizes the Ultimate Reality simultaneously as Allah, Ram, Alakh (the Unseen), and Shabda (mystic sound).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Kabir's Nirguna verses survive in three major regional recensions (Bijak in the eastern Hindi belt, Kabir Granthavali in Rajasthan, and the Adi Granth in Punjab) and employ vernacular Sant Bhasha (including paradoxical Ulatbansi) rather than Sanskrit to articulate a non-sectarian, monotheistic Ultimate Reality.

exp.why: Verses ascribed to Kabir were compiled long after his death in three distinct overlapping geographical and sectarian traditions: the Bijak is preserved by the Kabirpanth in Varanasi and elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar; the Kabir Granthavali is associated with the Dadupanth in Rajasthan; and many of his oldest authenticated compositions are preserved in the Adi Granth Sahib compiled in Punjab.

Ulatbansi ('upside-down' or paradoxical poems, such as 'a lotus blooms without water' or 'fire rages in the ocean') were NOT composed in classical Paninian Sanskrit. They were composed in vernacular Sant Bhasha (Sadhukkari) drawing on Nathpanthi enigmatic idioms to signify the difficult, counter-intuitive experience of realizing the formless Ultimate Reality. Kabir explicitly rejected the elitism of Sanskrit, comparing Sanskrit to stagnant well-water (kup jal) and the spoken vernacular (Bhasha) to flowing river water (bahata nir).

Kabir synthesized vocabulary from multiple traditions to transcend sectarian boundaries: he used Islamic terms like Allah, Khuda, Hazrat, and Pir; Vedantic/Vaishnava terms like Ram, Hari, and Brahman; and Nathpanthi yogic concepts like Alakh (the Unseen), Nirakar (the Formless), Shabda (Sound), and Shunya (Emptiness) to point toward a single, indivisible Ultimate Reality.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 (pp. 161-162)

stem: With reference to the religious philosophy and social institutions established by Guru Nanak in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: He compiled his own hymns along with the compositions of Baba Farid, Ravidas, and Kabir into the authoritative scripture known as the Adi Granth Sahib.
opts.B: He advocated complete monastic renunciation of family life and the adoption of Hatha Yogic austerity as the sole path to spiritual liberation.
opts.C: He instituted the martial brotherhood of the Khalsa Panth and mandated the five emblems (Panj Kakar) to resist state persecution.
opts.D: He conceptualized the Supreme Reality as formless (Nirankar) and genderless, advocating congregational worship (Sangat) and caste-free community dining (Langar) within an ethical householder life.

core: Guru Nanak's Nirguna Bhakti rejected both orthodox ritualism and ascetic renunciation (Udas/Hatha Yoga), institutionalizing collective remembrance of the Formless Divine (Nam-Simran) through egalitarian congregational worship (Sangat) and community kitchens (Langar/Pangat) while living as a householder.

exp.why: Option D is correct because Guru Nanak (1469-1539 CE) preached a strict form of Nirguna Bhakti in which the Supreme Being (Ik Onkar / Nirankar / Akal Purakh) is without form, gender, or incarnations (rejecting the theory of Avatara). He organized his followers into a community implementing collective worship (Sangat) and free community dining across caste lines (Langar/Pangat), while insisting on an ethical householder life (Grihastha) based on Nam, Dan, Isnan and honest labour (Kirat Karo). Option A is incorrect because it was the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, who compiled the Adi Granth Sahib in 1604 CE. Option B is incorrect because Guru Nanak explicitly critiqued the Nathpanthi Siddhas and Jogis for abandoning social responsibilities in favour of forest asceticism. Option C is incorrect because the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa Panth in 1699 CE.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 (pp. 163-164)

stem: With reference to the Saguna Bhakti saints and vernacular devotional literature of North India during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Goswami Tulsidas composed all his devotional works, including both the Ramcharitmanas and the Vinaya Patrika, exclusively in the Awadhi dialect.
2. Surdas was initiated into the Gaudiya Vaishnava sect by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and composed the Sursagar primarily in the Maithili language.
3. Mirabai recognized Raidas, a mystic from the leather-working caste, as her spiritual preceptor and did not establish an institutionalized monastic sect or matha around herself.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: North Indian Saguna Bhakti enriched distinct vernaculars across sectarian lines: Tulsidas wrote in both Awadhi (Ramcharitmanas) and Brajbhasha (Vinaya Patrika, Kavitavali), Surdas belonged to Vallabhacharya's Pushtimarg Ashtachhap circle writing in Brajbhasha, and Mirabai defied caste norms by accepting Raidas as her guru without founding a formal sect.

exp.why: While Tulsidas composed his magnum opus Ramcharitmanas (along with Janaki Mangal and Parvati Mangal) in the Awadhi dialect, he did NOT write exclusively in Awadhi. He was equally a master of Brajbhasha, in which he composed major devotional classics including the Vinaya Patrika, Kavitavali, and Gitavali.

Surdas was NOT a disciple of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu or a Maithili poet. He was initiated by Vallabhacharya into the Pushtimarg (Shuddhadvaita) sect, served as the foremost among the Ashtachhap (eight liturgical poets of Shrinathji compiled by Vitthalnath), and composed his works (Sursagar, Sur Saravali, Sahitya Lahari) in Brajbhasha. (It was Vidyapati who famously composed Vaishnava padavalis in Maithili).

Mirabai (fifteenth-sixteenth century), a Rajput princess of Merta married into the Sisodia clan of Mewar, defied patriarchal and caste conventions by acknowledging Raidas (Ravidas), a Nirguna saint from the untouchable leather-working caste, as her guru. Unlike Kabir, Nanak, or Vallabha, she did not attract a formal institutionalized sect or monastic order (matha), yet her bhajans in Rajasthani and Braj remained a vibrant oral tradition across Rajasthan and Gujarat.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 (pp. 164-165); Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Vaishnava Bhakti movement in Eastern India during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the Gaudiya Vaishnavism of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in Bengal, Srimanta Sankardeva's Ekasarana Dharma in Assam prohibited the worship of multiple deities and even excluded the female consort Radha alongside Krishna in its devotional liturgy.

Statement-II: Srimanta Sankardeva emphasized Dasya bhava (servitude to the one supreme Lord) and centered community worship inside Namghars and Satras around the recitation of the sacred scripture (Bhagavata Purana) placed on the Guru Asana rather than consecrated dual-idol rituals.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Srimanta Sankardeva's Ekasarana Nama Dharma in Assam differed structurally from Bengal's Gaudiya Vaishnavism by adopting Dasya bhava (servant's devotion to a single Lord, Krishna) over Madhurya bhava (Radha-Krishna conjugal mysticism) and enshrining the sacred text (Bhagavata/Kirtan Ghosha) in Namghars rather than worshipping Radha-Krishna idol pairs.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. While Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's Gaudiya Vaishnavism in Bengal placed the dual worship of Radha and Krishna (Madhurya bhava or bridal mysticism) at the heart of devotion, Srimanta Sankardeva's Ekasarana Nama Dharma ('Shelter-in-One Religion') in Assam demanded exclusive devotion to a single supreme deity (Krishna/Narayana), strictly forbade blood sacrifices and the worship of other gods/goddesses, and did not include Radha as a worshipful consort alongside Krishna.

Statement-II is correct and explains Statement-I. Sankardeva's theology was grounded in Dasya bhava (the attitude of a devoted servant to the sole Master) and prioritized Sravana and Kirtana (listening to and chanting the glories of Lord Krishna) over elaborate Brahmanical idol-consecration ceremonies. Consequently, in the Satras (monasteries) and Namghars (community prayer halls), a sacred manuscript of the Bhagavata Purana or Kirtan Ghosha is venerated on the pedestal (Guru Asana/Thapana) instead of consecrated stone or metallic Radha-Krishna idol pairs.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch. 6 (p. 165); NCERT Class VII Our Pasts-II

stem: With reference to the medieval mystic traditions of Kashmir, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Lal Ded (Lalleshwari), a fourteenth-century Shaivite yogini, composed mystical verses known as Vakhs in the vernacular Kashmiri language that rejected ritualistic orthodoxy and caste distinctions.
2. Shaikh Nuruddin Wali (Nund Rishi), whose poetic compositions are called Shruks, was deeply influenced by Lal Ded and advocated non-violence, vegetarianism, and ecological harmony.
3. The Rishi Silsilah was an orthodox Central Asian Sufi order introduced into Kashmir by scholars accompanying Timur to replace the vernacular Kashmiri literary tradition with Persian.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Kashmir's Rishi Silsilah, founded by Shaikh Nuruddin Wali (Nund Rishi), was an indigenous syncretic Sufi order shaped by the vernacular Vakhs of the Shaivite mystic Lal Ded. Unlike immigrant Central Asian orders, the Rishis championed the Kashmiri vernacular, strict vegetarianism, tree plantation, and non-violence.

exp.why: Lal Ded (Lalleshwari, c. 1320–1392) was a Kashmiri Trika Shaivite mystic who composed four-line devotional and philosophical verses called Vakhs in colloquial Kashmiri. Her poetry critiqued external temple rituals, idol worship, and caste hierarchies while emphasizing inward realization of Shiva.

Shaikh Nuruddin Wali (popularly revered as Nund Rishi or Alamdar-i-Kashmir) acknowledged Lal Ded as his spiritual forerunner. His Kashmiri quatrains, known as Shruks, blended Islamic mysticism with indigenous ascetic practices, including strict vegetarianism, abstaining from harming living beings, and planting shade-giving trees as an act of worship (highlighted in his famous maxim that food lasts only as long as forests survive).

While Central Asian Kubrawiyya scholars like Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani migrated to Kashmir in the fourteenth century and promoted Persianate Islamic culture, the Rishi Silsilah founded by Nund Rishi was a purely indigenous Kashmiri Sufi order. Far from replacing Kashmiri with Persian, the Rishis elevated vernacular Kashmiri into a primary vehicle of mystical literature.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions); Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: With reference to the metaphysical doctrines and institutional terminology of Sufism in medieval India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Wahdat-ul-Wujud : Doctrine of phenomenological 'Unity of Appearance' propounded by Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi asserting the strict separation between Creator and creation
2. Wahdat-ush-Shuhud : Doctrine of ontological 'Unity of Being' formulated by Ibn al-Arabi holding that God and creation are fundamentally one in essence
3. Futuh : Tax-free revenue-bearing land grants officially conferred by the Sultanate state for the maintenance of a Sufi hospice
4. Wilayat : Spiritual domain or territorial jurisdiction over which a Sufi master (Pir) exercises spiritual authority
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Ibn al-Arabi's monistic Wahdat-ul-Wujud (Unity of Being) facilitated Hindu-Muslim syncretism in India, whereas Naqshbandi reformer Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi countered it with Wahdat-ush-Shuhud (Unity of Appearance). Institutionally, early Chishtis subsisted on Futuh (unasked charity) rather than state Inam grants, while demarcating their spiritual jurisdiction as Wilayat.

exp.why: Pair 1 is reversed with Pair 2. Wahdat-ul-Wujud ('Unity of Being'), formulated by Ibn al-Arabi (1165–1240), is an ontological doctrine holding that Ultimate Reality (Haqq) and creation (Khalq) are one, and that all existence is a manifestation of the Divine essence. This doctrine was widely embraced by Chishti and Qadiri mystics in India.

Pair 2 is reversed with Pair 1. Wahdat-ush-Shuhud ('Unity of Witnessing/Appearance') was articulated by the Naqshbandi scholar Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani) in the early seventeenth century to critique Ibn al-Arabi's monism. It argues that any perceived unity between the Creator and creation is merely subjective and experiential during mystical intoxication, not an objective ontological identity.

Futuh refers to unsolicited, unasked-for charity (in cash or kind) voluntarily offered by visitors and devotees to a Sufi Khanqah, which Chishtis distributed immediately through the open kitchen (langar). Official tax-free land or revenue grants conferred by the state to religious scholars and institutions were termed Inam, Milk, Idrar, or Madad-i-Ma'ash.

In Indo-Muslim Sufi institutional practice, Wilayat (or Walayat) denoted the specific spiritual territory or geographic domain under the protective authority and jurisdiction of a Sufi Pir (Wali) or his appointed Khalifa.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 6; Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, A History of Sufism in India

stem: With reference to the early Chishti Silsilah masters in the Indian subcontinent, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The devotional Punjabi verses (Slokas and Shabads) composed by Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti of Ajmer were later incorporated into the Guru Granth Sahib by Guru Arjan Dev.
2. Unlike Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki and Nizamuddin Auliya who established their principal hospices in Delhi, Baba Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar centered his spiritual activities at Ajodhan in the Punjab.
3. Shaikh Nasiruddin Mahmud, popularly known as 'Chiragh-i-Dehlavi', was the principal spiritual successor (Khalifa) of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The five great early Indian Chishti masters formed an unbroken spiritual lineage from Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer) to Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi), Baba Farid (Ajodhan/Pakpattan), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi), and Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi (Delhi). Among them, it was Baba Farid whose vernacular Punjabi poetry was canonized in the Guru Granth Sahib.

exp.why: It was Shaikh Fariduddin Masud 'Ganj-i-Shakar' (Baba Farid, 1175–1265), the spiritual disciple of Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, whose devotional verses (112 Slokas and 4 Shabads) in local Punjabi/Multani were compiled into the Adi Granth (Guru Granth Sahib) by the fifth Sikh Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, in 1604—not Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti.

While Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (d. 1235) and Nizamuddin Auliya (d. 1325) operated from their Khanqahs in Delhi (Mehrauli and Ghiyaspur respectively), Baba Farid withdrew from the capital's political bustle to establish his Jamat Khana at Ajodhan (modern Pakpattan in Pakistani Punjab) along the Sutlej river.

Shaikh Nasiruddin Mahmud 'Chiragh-i-Dehlavi' (d. 1356) was the foremost Khalifa of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi and the last of the five great early Chishti masters before the silsilah's regional dispersion across the Deccan, Bengal, and Gujarat.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 6 (Table of Major Teachers of the Chishti Silsila)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the relationship between Sufi orders and the state during the Delhi Sultanate period:
items: Statement-I: The Suhrawardi saints of Multan such as Shaikh Bahauddin Zakariya strictly refused state land grants and official court titles, whereas the early Chishti masters of Delhi actively accumulated wealth and accepted high administrative posts under the Sultans.

Statement-II: The Chishti silsilah believed that formal association with royal courts alienated a mystic from spiritual austerity and the common masses, whereas the Suhrawardi silsilah held that possessing wealth and maintaining cordial relations with rulers enabled saints to better serve the poor.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Chishti and Suhrawardi orders held diametrically opposite views on political power and material wealth during the Delhi Sultanate. While early Chishtis practiced voluntary poverty (faqr), subsisted on unasked charity (futuh), and shunned royal courts, Suhrawardi saints like Bahauddin Zakariya accepted state endowments and official titles like Shaikh-ul-Islam.

exp.why: Statement-I reverses the historical positions of the two orders. It was the Suhrawardi saints of Multan and Uch (most notably Shaikh Bahauddin Zakariya) who accepted royal patronage, accumulated substantial wealth, and accepted the official title of Shaikh-ul-Islam from Sultan Iltutmish. Conversely, early Chishti masters like Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid, and Nizamuddin Auliya strictly refused land grants (inam) and declined royal visits or government offices.

Statement-II accurately explains the underlying philosophical divergence: Chishtis viewed state service and guaranteed endowments as spiritually corrupting and a barrier between the mystic and ordinary people, whereas Suhrawardis argued that wealth is a neutral tool (like a remedy) that, when held by a righteous heart free of greed, empowers a mystic to relieve poverty and guide rulers toward justice.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the genres of Indo-Persian Sufi literature produced in medieval India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Fawaid-ul-Fuad is an autobiographical treatise personally penned in Arabic by Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya to codify the legalistic rules of the Chishti hospice.

2. In Sufi literary tradition, the genre of 'Maktubat' refers to biographical dictionaries of deceased saints, whereas 'Tazkiras' refer to collections of personal epistles written by a Sufi master to his disciples.
3. Siyar-ul-Auliya, the earliest known biographical compendium of Chishti saints in India, was authored by Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddis Dehlavi during the reign of Emperor Shah Jahan.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Indo-Persian Sufi textual sources fall into three distinct genres: Malfuzat (recorded conversations of a Pir, pioneered by Amir Hasan Sijzi's Fawaid-ul-Fuad), Maktubat (collections of theological and spiritual letters by a master), and Tazkiras (biographical compendia of saints, beginning in India with Mir Khwurd's Siyar-ul-Auliya).

exp.why: Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya did not personally author any book. Fawaid-ul-Fuad ('Morals for the Heart') is a Persian Malfuzat—a chronological compilation of the oral discourses and conversations of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya recorded between 1308 and 1322 by his prominent disciple and court poet Amir Hasan Sijzi Dehlavi.

The definitions are swapped. Maktubat (literally 'written letters') are collections of epistles written by Sufi masters to their disciples and contemporaries explaining spiritual and social matters (e.g., Maktubat-i-Sadi of Sharafuddin Yahya Maneri and Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani of Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi). Tazkiras (literally 'memorials') are biographical compendia of Sufi saints.

Siyar-ul-Auliya, the earliest Indian Chishti Tazkira, was authored in the fourteenth century (during the reign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq) by Saiyid Muhammad bin Mubarak Kirmani, famously known as Mir Khwurd. Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddis Dehlavi later authored a famous Tazkira titled Akhbar-ul-Akhyar during the reigns of Akbar and Jahangir.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 6 (Source 10: A Church in Khambat & Section on Sufi Texts)

stem: With reference to the Sufi Premakhyan literary tradition in medieval North India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Sufi poets of this tradition composed allegorical romances in the vernacular Awadhi (Hindavi) language using the Persian script, adapting indigenous Indian folk tales into the Persian Masnavi poetic framework.

2. In works such as Qutban's Mrigavati and Manjhan's Madhumalati, the human hero's arduous quest for the beloved serves as a mystical allegory for the soul's progression from Ishq-i-Majazi (earthly love) to Ishq-i-Haqiqi (divine truth).

3. Chronologically, Mulla Daud's Chandayan, composed during the reign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq in the fourteenth century, preceded Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Padmavat, which was completed during the reign of Sher Shah Suri in the sixteenth century.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Between the 14th and 16th centuries, Chishti and Shattari Sufi poets pioneered the Hindavi/Awadhi Premakhyan genre—beginning with Mulla Daud's Chandayan (1379) and culminating in Jayasi's Padmavat (1540)—blending Persian Masnavi conventions with Indian folkloric romances and Nath-yogic imagery to allegorize the ascent from human love (Ishq-i-Majazi) to divine union (Ishq-i-Haqiqi).

exp.why: The Sufi Premakhyans were composed in the vernacular Awadhi/Hindavi dialect using indigenous poetic meters (Doha-Chaupai) and Indian rasa aesthetics, yet they were originally written in the Persian script and structured according to the classical Persian Masnavi convention (including praise of God, the Prophet, the reigning Sultan, and the poet's Pir).

Qutban's Mrigavati (1503, dedicated to Sultan Husain Shah Sharqi) and Mir Sayyid Manjhan Rajgiri's Madhumalati (1545) use the trials of an earthly prince seeking union with an idealized princess to symbolize the Sufi seeker's (Salik) journey through spiritual stations (Maqamat), transforming metaphorical human love (Ishq-i-Majazi) into realization of Divine Beauty (Ishq-i-Haqiqi).

Mulla Daud inaugurated the Hindavi Sufi Premakhyan genre with Chandayan (based on the Lorik-Chanda folk ballad) around 1379 CE during the reign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq (dedicated to his Wazir Khan-i-Jahan Junan Shah). Nearly two centuries later, Malik Muhammad Jayasi completed Padmavat around 1540 CE during the reign of Sher Shah Suri.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part-II, Ch. 6; Muzaffar Alam, The Languages of Political Islam in India

stem: With reference to the ideological and spiritual traditions of the Naqshbandi and Qadiri Sufi Silsilahs during the Mughal period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Naqshbandi Silsilah opposed musical assemblies (Sama), loud vocal recollection of God (Dhikr-i-Jahri), and pilgrimage to the tombs of saints (Ziyarat), advocating instead silent meditation (Dhikr-i-Khafi) and strict adherence to the Sharia.

2. Prince Dara Shikoh was initiated into the Naqshbandi Silsilah under Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi, whereas the Qadiri saint Mian Mir spearheaded the orthodox reaction against Emperor Akbar's policy of Sulh-i-Kul.

3. Dara Shikoh authored the Persian treatise Majma-ul-Bahrain to highlight the philosophical commonalities between Islamic Sufism and Hindu Vedanta, and translated fifty-two Upanishads into Persian as Sirr-i-Akbar.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: During the 17th century, Sufi orders in Mughal India polarized into two broad ideological currents: the reformist, Sharia-centric Naqshbandi Silsilah led by Khwaja Baqi Billah and Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani), and the syncretic, Wujudi-oriented Qadiri Silsilah represented by Mian Mir, Mulla Shah Badakhshi, and Prince Dara Shikoh.

exp.why: Introduced into India during the late reign of Akbar by Khwaja Baqi Billah and expanded by Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi, the Naqshbandi order was the most orthodox of the Sufi silsilahs. It rejected popular practices perceived as un-Islamic innovations (bid'at), such as listening to spiritual music (Sama), loud chanting (Dhikr-i-Jahri), and tomb veneration (Ziyarat), insisting instead on silent recollection of God (Dhikr-i-Khafi) and strict observance of the Sharia.

The Sufi affiliations are swapped. Prince Dara Shikoh and his sister Jahanara Begum were initiated into the liberal Qadiri Silsilah by Mulla Shah Badakhshi, the spiritual successor of Mian Mir of Lahore. Conversely, it was Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi of the Naqshbandi Silsilah who vehemently criticized Akbar's policy of Sulh-i-Kul and replaced Ibn Arabi's pantheistic doctrine of Wahdat-ul-Wujud (Unity of Being) with Wahdat-ush-Shuhud (Unity of Phenomenal Witnessing).

Guided by the Qadiri commitment to Wahdat-ul-Wujud, Dara Shikoh composed Majma-ul-Bahrain ('The Mingling of the Two Oceans') to demonstrate that the highest truths of Sufism and Advaita Vedanta differed only in terminology. With the assistance of Banaras Sanskrit pandits, he also rendered fifty-two Upanishads into Persian under the title Sirr-i-Akbar ('The Greatest Mystery').

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 16 & 17; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6

stem: He was a prolific medieval poet, chronicler, and musician who pioneered the 'Sabaq-i-Hind' (Indian style) of Persian literature and enriched Chishti Sama assemblies by blending Persian and Indian musical modes into Qawwali and Tarana. In his famous masnavi 'Nuh Sipihr' (Nine Skies), he celebrated India's climate, flora, fauna, Sanskrit scholarship, and regional languages (Hindavi), proudly styling himself an 'Indian Turk'. A devoted lifelong disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, he passed away within months of his spiritual master's death and was buried beside his dargah in Delhi. Who among the following historical personalities is described in the passage above?
core: Amir Khusrau (1253–1325 CE), titled Tuti-i-Hind ('Parrot of India'), represents the zenith of Indo-Persian cultural synthesis under the Delhi Sultanate through his creation of the Sabaq-i-Hind literary idiom, his historical masnavis, and his musical contributions to the Chishti Khanqah of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya.

exp.why: Amir Khusrau served across the courts of several Delhi Sultans from Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq while remaining the dearest disciple of the Chishti saint Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya. He developed the distinctive 'Sabaq-i-Hind' (Indian style) of Persian poetry, composed five historical masnavis including Nuh Sipihr (in which he praised India's intellectual achievements, decimal system, chess, Sanskrit, and Hindavi dialects), and introduced the qawl, tarana, and khayal forms into Chishti Sama. Option (A) Amir Hasan Sijzi was a fellow disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya who compiled the malfuzat Fawa'id-ul-Fu'ad; Option (B) Ziauddin Barani authored Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; and Option (D) Malik Muhammad Jayasi was the 16th-century Awadhi Sufi poet who composed Padmavat.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6 (Bhakti-Sufi Traditions); Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India

stem: With reference to the expansion of the Chishti Silsilah in the Deccan and its role in the growth of Dakhani vernacular literature, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Following Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq's transfer of the capital to Daulatabad, Shaikh Burhanuddin Gharib—a disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya—established the Chishti tradition in the Deccan with Khuldabad emerging as its spiritual centre.

2. In the Bijapur and Gulbarga regions, Chishti Sufis composed short folk poems in Dakhani Urdu, such as the Chakki-Nama and Luri-Nama, which were sung by village women while performing household chores like grinding grain and putting children to sleep.

3. Khwaja Banda Nawaz Gesu Daraz settled in Gulbarga under the initial invitation and patronage of Sultan Tajuddin Firuz Shah Bahmani, though later ideological differences led the Sultan's brother, Ahmad Shah I Wali, to shift royal patronage toward the saint.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The migration of Chishti mystics from Delhi to the Deccan during the 14th century catalyzed the rise of Dakhani Urdu as a literary vehicle and indigenized Sufi theology through vernacular women's folk songs (Chakki-Nama, Charkha-Nama) in the Bahmani and Adil Shahi realms.

exp.why: When Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq ordered the relocation of Delhi's elite and mystics to Daulatabad (Deogiri) in 1327–28, Shaikh Burhanuddin Gharib, a senior khalifa (spiritual successor) of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya, migrated south and planted the roots of the Chishti Silsilah in the Deccan. His tomb at Khuldabad became one of the foremost pilgrimage sites of southern India.

As documented by historians like Richard Eaton and featured in NCERT Themes in Indian History, Chishti Sufis of the Bijapur region during the 17th and 18th centuries composed accessible verses in Dakhani (an early form of Urdu) modeled on indigenous Marathi and Kannada folk songs. These included the Chakki-Nama (sung while grinding grain at the hand-mill), Charkha-Nama (sung while spinning thread), and Luri-Nama (lullabies), using everyday domestic tasks as metaphors for dhikr (remembrance of God) and the spiritual bond with the Pir.

Syed Muhammad Husaini, renowned as Khwaja Banda Nawaz Gesu Daraz (a disciple of Shaikh Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi), moved from Delhi to Gulbarga around 1400 CE in the wake of Timur's invasion. Sultan Tajuddin Firuz Shah Bahmani initially welcomed him warmly and granted him villages near the royal fort, but tensions soon arose between the rationalist Sultan and the orthodox scholasticism of Gesu Daraz. Consequently, the saint threw his spiritual support behind the Sultan's brother, Ahmad Shah I Wali, who later succeeded to the throne and moved the Bahmani capital to Bidar.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6 (Charkha-nama & Luri-nama Source Boxes); Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 9

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the classification and practices of Sufi traditions in medieval India:
items: 1. While the Ba-shara orders organized community life around institutionalized hospices (khanqahs) and adhered to Islamic canonical law, the Be-shara mystics—such as the Qalandars and Madaris—eschewed institutional discipline and opted for radical mendicancy.

2. The Shattari Silsilah, popularized in sixteenth-century India by Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior, translated and adapted Hatha Yoga techniques and Sanskrit cosmological concepts into Persian mystical manuals such as the Bahr-ul-Hayat.

3. Modeling themselves on the early Chishti tradition of political aloofness, the Shattari saints strictly prohibited their followers from accepting land grants, titles, or patronage from the Mughal emperors.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sufi traditions in India spanned a wide institutional and doctrinal spectrum: from antinomian wandering Be-shara ascetics (Qalandars, Madaris) who defied Khanqah norms, to Ba-shara orders like the Shattaris who combined Sharia observance with Hatha Yoga synthesis and close royal ties with the Mughals.

exp.why: Medieval chroniclers classified Sufi mystics into Ba-shara (those who followed the Sharia, maintained structured khanqahs, and transmitted spiritual authority through an established silsilah) and Be-shara (those not bound by formal Sharia stipulations). The Be-shara mystics—including the Qalandars, Madaris, Malamatis, and Haidaris—rejected fixed khanqah life, shaved their heads and facial hair, practiced celibacy and wandering mendicancy, and deliberately invited social blame to conquer ego.

Introduced into India by Shah Abdullah Shattari and brought to prominence by Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior (d. 1562), the Shattari Silsilah sought a rapid, direct path ('shattar' meaning rapid) to divine realization. Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus studied Sanskrit yogic traditions for years in the hills of Chunar and translated the yogic text Amritakunda into Persian as Bahr-ul-Hayat ('Ocean of Life'), besides authoring Jawahir-i-Khamsa, which combined Sufi meditative practices with yogic breath control (pranayama) and astral cosmology.

Far from practicing political aloofness, the Shattari saints believed that spiritual perfection could be attained amidst worldly affluence and political engagement, much like the Suhrawardi order. Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus and his elder brother Shaikh Bahlul (Shaikh Phul) maintained exceedingly close personal and political relations with the Mughal Emperors Babur and Humayun; later, Akbar granted Shaikh Muhammad Ghaus a generous madad-i-ma'ash (revenue-free grant), and the legendary musician Mian Tansen was closely associated with his hospice in Gwalior.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6; Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, A History of Sufism in India, Vol. II

stem: With reference to the philosophical concepts and literary contributions of Bhakti saints from marginalized, artisan, and regional backgrounds, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Sant Ravidas : Propounded the 'Nipakh' (non-sectarian) path and founded the Brahma Sampradaya in Rajasthan
2. Dadu Dayal : Envisioned 'Begumpura', a casteless and tax-free utopian city free from sorrow and anxiety
3. Chokhamela and Soyarabai : Composed Marathi Varkari abhangas interrogating Brahmanical notions of ritual purity and untouchability
4. Lal Ded (Lalleshwari) : Composed mystical Kashmiri verses known as 'Vakhs' blending Trika Shaivite non-dualism with Sufi spirituality
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Subaltern and regional Bhakti sants articulated powerful critiques of social hierarchy through distinct idioms: Sant Ravidas envisioned the casteless city of Begumpura, Dadu Dayal preached the non-sectarian Nipakh path in Rajasthan, Chokhamela and Soyarabai challenged untouchability in Maharashtra, and Lal Ded forged a syncretic Kashmiri idiom in her Vakhs.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched because the concept of 'Nipakh' (a non-sectarian path transcending Hindu and Muslim orthodoxy) and the founding of the Brahma (or Parabrahma) Sampradaya—later known as the Dadu Panth in Rajasthan—belong to the sixteenth-century cotton-carder saint Dadu Dayal (1544–1603), not Sant Ravidas.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched because the famous hymn envisioning 'Begumpura' ('the city without sorrow'—an egalitarian utopia free from caste discrimination, capitation taxes, and fear of oppression) was composed by the fifteenth-century cobbler saint Sant Ravidas (Raidas) of Banaras, whose verses are preserved in the Adi Granth.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Chokhamela and his wife Soyarabai were fourteenth-century Varkari saints from the marginalized Mahar community in Maharashtra. In their poignant Marathi abhangas addressed to Lord Vitthala of Pandharpur, they openly questioned the theological basis of ritual pollution (sutak), arguing that since all human bodies share the same biological birth and divine spark, caste untouchability is morally hollow.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Lal Ded (Lalleshwari), a fourteenth-century Kashmiri mystic poet, composed four-line vernacular verses known as Vakhs ('speech'). Her poetry fused the non-dualistic philosophy of Kashmiri Trika Shaivism with the incoming Rishi-Sufi sensibilities of Shaikh Nuruddin Wali (Nund Rishi), rejecting idol worship, priestly ritualism, and caste distinctions.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6; Upinder Singh & Satish Chandra, Medieval India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the social base of the Nirguna Bhakti and Sufi movements in medieval India:
items: Statement-I: Between the thirteenth and seventeenth centuries, urban artisans, weavers, leatherworkers, and mercantile communities such as the Khatris gravitated in large numbers toward the monotheistic Nirguna Bhakti movement and Sufi silsilahs.

Statement-II: While the expansion of towns and monetized commerce under the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire enhanced the economic vitality of craft producers and traders, orthodox Brahmanical Dharmashastras continued to assign them a low or degraded ritual status within the four-fold Varna hierarchy, prompting them to embrace egalitarian devotional traditions that rejected caste discrimination and priestly ritualism.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The structural mismatch between the rising economic prominence of urban artisans and traders during the Sultanate-Mughal urban revolution and their depressed ritual status in orthodox Brahmanical texts served as the primary sociological driver behind the popularity of Nirguna Bhakti (Kabir, Ravidas, Nanak, Dadu) and Sufism.

exp.why: Statement-I is historically accurate. The leadership and mass following of the monotheistic Nirguna Sant tradition and the Sikh movement drew heavily from urban and semi-urban craft and trading groups: Kabir was a Julaha (weaver), Ravidas a Chamar (leatherworker), Sena a barber, Sadhana a butcher, Namdev a calico-printer/tailor, Dadu Dayal a Pinjara (cotton-carder), and Guru Nanak and his early urban followers belonged largely to the mercantile Khatri and cultivator Jatt communities.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains the causal mechanism behind Statement-I. The introduction of new technologies (such as the spinning wheel, treadle loom, and Persian wheel), expanding overland and maritime trade, and growing urbanization between the 13th and 17th centuries improved the economic standing and self-awareness of artisans, weavers, and merchants. However, because orthodox Smriti literature continued to relegate artisans to the low Shudra or Antyaja strata and viewed sea-faring or urban trade with ritual suspicion, these groups eagerly embraced Nirguna Bhakti and Sufi teachings, which affirmed direct personal access to a formless God, the dignity of manual labour (such as Guru Nanak's Kirat Karo), and the complete rejection of caste hierarchy and Vedic priesthood.

ref: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, Ch. 9 (Social Background of the Bhakti Movement); NCERT Themes in Indian History Part II, Theme 6

stem: With reference to the Mauryan rock-cut caves at the Barabar and Nagarjuni hills in Bihar, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Lomas Rishi cave bears a royal inscription of Emperor Ashoka recording its dedication to Buddhist monks during the twelfth year of his reign.
2. The entrance facade of the Lomas Rishi cave replicates contemporary wooden structural architecture in stone, featuring a chaitya arch and a relief frieze of elephants worshipping stupas.
3. Both the Barabar hill caves excavated under Ashoka and the Nagarjuni hill caves excavated under his grandson Dasharatha feature interiors finished with a mirror-like polish.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Barabar and Nagarjuni caves represent the earliest surviving rock-cut architecture in India, patronized by Emperor Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha for the Ajivika sect rather than Buddhist monks. Architecturally, they are characterized by petrified wooden skeuomorphism on the Lomas Rishi facade and distinctive Mauryan mirror-like interior polish.

exp.why: The Lomas Rishi cave does not carry any inscription of Emperor Ashoka (its doorway arch actually bears a much later Sanskrit inscription of the Maukhari ruler Anantavarman). Furthermore, the caves excavated by Ashoka at Barabar (such as the Sudama/Nigoha-kubha and Karna Chaupar caves) and by his grandson Dasharatha at Nagarjuni (Gopi, Vadathika, and Vapiyaka caves) were dedicated to ascetics of the Ajivika sect founded by Makkhali Gosala, not to Buddhist monks.

The Lomas Rishi cave is the earliest example of rock-cut wooden skeuomorphism in India. Its entrance faithfully translates free-standing timber construction into stone, featuring inward-leaning jambs, a gabled ogee (chaitya) arch, carved rafters, and a semicircular lunette frieze showing two rows of elephants approaching stupas amidst latticework.

A hallmark of imperial Mauryan stone craftsmanship is the mirror-like burnishing of hard granite surfaces. This polish is preserved inside both the Barabar caves (excavated under Ashoka) and the neighbouring Nagarjuni hill caves (excavated and inscribed by his grandson Dasharatha upon his accession).

ref: NCERT Class XI Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 2; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the structural anatomy and cosmological symbolism of a Buddhist Stupa, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 'Harmika' refers to the cylindrical drum or circular terrace that supports the hemispherical dome and serves as an elevated path for ritual circumambulation (pradakshina).
2. The 'Medhi' is a square railing structure positioned at the apex of the hemispherical dome, symbolizing the sacred enclosure of the cosmic mountain and the abode of the gods.
3. Rising from the center of the top enclosure is the 'Yashti', which represents the cosmic axis (axis mundi) and is surmounted by the 'Chhatra' symbolizing the Three Jewels (Triratna) of Buddhism.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A Buddhist stupa is a three-dimensional cosmological mandala in which each structural tier carries specific metaphysical meaning. The cylindrical terrace (Medhi) supports the dome of heaven (Anda), while the square railing at the summit (Harmika) marks the celestial sanctuary pierced by the cosmic axis (Yashti) and crowned by the triple umbrella (Chhatra).

exp.why: This description belongs to the 'Medhi', not the 'Harmika'. The Medhi is the raised cylindrical drum or circular terrace upon which the hemispherical dome (Anda) rests, often approached by a double stairway (Sopana) to serve as an upper circumambulatory pathway (Pradakshinapatha).

This description belongs to the 'Harmika', not the 'Medhi'. The Harmika is the small square balcony-like railing atop the flattened summit of the Anda. Cosmologically, it represents the sacred enclosure of the Bodhi tree or the heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods (Trayastrimsa) atop Mount Meru.

The 'Yashti' is the central mast or shaft rising through the Harmika, functioning as the cosmic pillar (axis mundi) linking earth and heaven. It supports the 'Chhatra' (or Chhatravali), a triple-tiered parasol symbolizing supremacy and the Triratna: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 3; Susan Huntington, The Art of Ancient India

stem: With reference to the comparative artistic features of the Bharhut Stupa and Sanchi Stupa-I, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the narrative reliefs of both Bharhut and Sanchi Stupa-I, the anthropomorphic form of the Buddha is absent and his presence is indicated through aniconic symbols such as footprints, an empty throne, or a stupa.

2. Compared to the shallow and linear low-relief carvings of Bharhut, the sculptural panels on the Toranas of Sanchi Stupa-I exhibit deeper carving, greater three-dimensional plasticity, and more naturalistic movement.
3. Both Bharhut Stupa and Sanchi Stupa-I systematically inscribed Prakrit epigraphic labels directly alongside every narrative panel to identify the specific Jataka tales and Yaksha figures depicted.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While both Bharhut (Shunga period, c. 2nd century BCE) and Sanchi Stupa-I (Satavahana period gateways, c. 1st century BCE–1st century CE) belong to the early aniconic tradition of Buddhist narrative art, Sanchi marks a major stylistic advance in spatial depth and naturalism, and dispenses with the incised didactic captioning that characterizes Bharhut.

exp.why: Both the Bharhut railings and the four Toranas of Sanchi Stupa-I belong to the early pre-iconic phase of Buddhist art. In their narrative panels depicting events from Gautama Buddha's life and Jataka stories, the Master is never shown in human form; instead, artists employed indexical signs such as the Bodhi tree (Enlightenment), the Wheel of Law (First Sermon), footprints (Buddhapada), an empty throne, or a stupa (Mahaparinirvana).

Bharhut sculptures are characterized by archaic, flat, two-dimensional planes where figures are compressed between the surface and background with stiff postures. By contrast, the sculptors of the Sanchi Stupa-I gateways (including ivory carvers from Vidisha) achieved high relief, subtle modelling of volumes, overlapping figures, and fluid narrative continuity.

Incised Prakrit epigraphic labels in Brahmi script identifying specific Jataka stories (e.g., 'Miga Jataka', 'Mahakapi Jataka', 'Jetavana Anadhapediko deti') and individual Yakshas/Devatas (e.g., 'Kupiro Yakho', 'Chulakoka Devata') are a unique hallmark of the Bharhut Stupa. At Sanchi Stupa-I, although hundreds of votive donor inscriptions (dana-lekha) exist on the railings and gateways, descriptive narrative labels identifying the Jataka scenes are absent.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 3; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the regional evolution of Stupa architecture in ancient India:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the Great Stupa at Sanchi, the Mahachaitya at Amaravati and the stupas of Nagarjunakonda in the Krishna valley featured rectangular projections (Ayaka-platforms) at the four cardinal points of the drum, each surmounted by five free-standing 'Ayaka' pillars.

Statement-II: Because the Vengi school under the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus adhered to the early Theravada aniconic canon throughout its history, the Palnad limestone casing slabs of the Amaravati stupa avoided anthropomorphic images of the Buddha and relied on colossal arched Torana gateways identical to Sanchi.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
