core: The Andhra/Vengi school of stupa architecture (Amaravati, Bhattiprolu, Jaggayyapeta, Nagarjunakonda) developed a distinct structural idiom from Central India: it introduced cardinal Ayaka platforms with five pillars, encased the brick dome and drum in intricately carved greenish-white Palnad limestone slabs, omitted Sanchi-style arched Toranas, and transitioned from aniconic symbols to dynamic anthropomorphic Buddha imagery.

exp.why: A defining architectural feature of the Andhra stupas (Mahachaitya at Amaravati and stupas at Nagarjunakonda, Ghantasala, and Jaggayyapeta) is the presence of rectangular offsets or projections (Ayaka-platforms) extending from the Medhi (drum) at the four cardinal directions. Each platform supported five tall, free-standing octagonal pillars (Ayaka-stambhas), symbolizing the five great miraculous events in the Buddha's life: Birth, Great Renunciation, Enlightenment, First Sermon, and Mahaparinirvana.

Statement-II is incorrect on two counts. First, while early Amaravati reliefs (2nd–1st century BCE) were aniconic, during its mature Satavahana and Ikshvaku phases (2nd–3rd centuries CE), the Vengi school profusely carved anthropomorphic figures of the Buddha alongside symbolic representations on its greenish-white Palnad limestone casing slabs (kancuka). Second, Andhra stupas did not possess colossal multi-architrave Torana gateways like Sanchi; instead, their gateways were simple openings in the Vedika flanked by lions on the coping stones, as the primary sculptural surface had shifted directly onto the limestone slabs encasing the drum and dome.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 3 & 4; Harle, The Art and Architecture of the Indian Subcontinent

stem: With reference to the early rock-cut caves of the Western Deccan (2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Chaitya hall at Bhaja features vertical pillars resting on stepped water-jar (ghata) bases and surmounted by bell capitals carrying kneeling elephants and Mithuna couples, whereas the Karla Chaitya is supported by plain, unornamented octagonal pillars that slope noticeably inward.

2. The famous early narrative relief panels depicting Surya driving a four-horse chariot over a demon of darkness and Indra riding his elephant Airavata are carved at the entrance of the Great Chaitya at Karla.

3. Cave 3 (the Gautamiputra cave) at the Nasik (Pandavleni) rock-cut complex is an apsidal Chaitya hall containing a colossal rock-cut seated image of the Buddha in Dharmachakrapravartana mudra excavated during the reign of Rudradaman I.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Western Deccan rock-cut caves trace a clear chronological evolution from wooden imitation to structural maturity: early caves like Bhaja (2nd century BCE) display inward-sloping plain octagonal pillars and famous Surya/Indra reliefs in its Vihara verandah, whereas later caves like the Karla Chaitya (1st century CE) and Nasik Vihara Cave 3 (2nd century CE) feature vertical ghata-base pillars with animal/Mithuna capitals.

exp.why: This statement swaps the architectural features of the Bhaja and Karla Chaityas. The Bhaja Chaitya (Cave 12, c. 2nd century BCE) is one of the earliest rock-cut halls in the Western Ghats; its 27 plain, unornamented octagonal shafts rake inward to mimic wooden posts countering the outward thrust of a timber roof. Conversely, the Great Chaitya at Karla (c. 1st century CE) marks the zenith of Hinayana rock-cut architecture, featuring vertical pillars resting on stepped water-jar (ghata-pallava) bases with octagonal shafts, bell-shaped capitals, and sculpted groups of kneeling elephants and riding Mithuna couples.

The celebrated narrative relief sculptures depicting Surya in his four-horse chariot accompanied by female attendants and Indra astride Airavata uprooting trees are carved on the verandah walls of Vihara Cave 19 at Bhaja (c. 2nd century BCE), not at the Karla Chaitya.

Cave 3 at Nasik (Pandavleni) is a quadrangular monastic Vihara (not an apsidal Chaitya hall) excavated under Satavahana patronage and dedicated by Queen Mother Gautami Balasri during the 19th regnal year of her grandson Vasishthiputra Pulumavi (recording the exploits of Gautamiputra Satakarni). Furthermore, belonging to the aniconic Theravada phase, its rear wall features a low-relief stupa flanked by female worshippers, rather than a colossal anthropomorphic image of the Buddha.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 4; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the architectural transformation of Buddhist rock-cut caves in Western India between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE:
items: Statement-I: During the later Vakataka phase at Ajanta (5th century CE), the excavation of separate apsidal Chaitya-grihas declined sharply, and the quadrangular monastic Vihara evolved into a composite liturgical-cum-residential structure housing a pillared mandapa and a sanctum (garbhagriha) cut into the center of the rear wall.

Statement-II: The ascendancy of Mahayana devotionalism shifted monastic liturgy from the collective circumambulation of an aniconic stupa in a dedicated apsidal hall to the direct iconographic veneration of a colossal anthropomorphic image of the Buddha enshrined within the monastery itself.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In the early Hinayana phase of rock-cut architecture, the worship hall (apsidal Chaitya) and residential quarters (astylar quadrangular Vihara) were strictly segregated. Under Vakataka patronage in the 5th century CE, Mahayana image-worship led to the insertion of a central Buddha shrine into the rear wall of the Vihara, merging the sanctuary and monastery into a single architectural unit.

exp.why: In the early phase at Ajanta (2nd–1st century BCE), Caves 9 and 10 were excavated as apsidal Chaitya-grihas, while Caves 12, 13, and 15A were purely residential astylar Viharas without any interior shrine. During the Vakataka phase under Harishena (late 5th century CE), only two apsidal Chaityas (Caves 19 and 26) were excavated, whereas nearly twenty caves (such as Caves 1, 2, 4, 16, and 17) were designed as colonnaded quadrangular Viharas with an antechamber (antarala) and a central sanctum (garbhagriha) carved into the rear wall.

Statement-II provides the liturgical reason for the architectural shift described in Statement-I. Earlier Theravada/Hinayana practice centered on ritual pradakshina around a rock-cut stupa, which structurally necessitated an apsidal hall with side aisles. As Mahayana Bhakti practices popularized darshana and puja before a colossal seated Buddha image (usually in Dharmachakrapravartana mudra), monks integrated the image-shrine directly into the back wall of the residential Vihara, rendering separate apsidal Chaitya halls largely redundant.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 4; Walter Spink, Ajanta: History and Development

stem: With reference to the patronage, chronology, and spatial iconography of the Ajanta Caves, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The second and most prolific phase of excavation across all twenty-nine caves was personally commissioned by the Vakataka monarch Harishena after his initiation into the Mahayana Buddhist monastic order.

2. While Caves 9 and 10 are apsidal Chaitya-grihas from the earlier Satavahana phase featuring aniconic stupa worship, Caves 19 and 26 represent later Vakataka-era Chaitya-grihas where an anthropomorphic image of the Buddha is carved directly onto the front of the central stupa.
3. Cave 26 houses both the colossal rock-cut sculpture of the reclining Buddha attaining Mahaparinirvana and the sculpted relief panel depicting the temptation of the Buddha by Mara (Mara Vijaya).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Ajanta evolved across two distinct chronological phases: an early Satavahana/Hinayana phase (2nd century BCE to 1st century CE) and a later Vakataka/Mahayana phase (late 5th century CE). During the Vakataka phase under King Harishena of the Vatsagulma branch, individual caves were commissioned by multiple courtly and monastic patrons rather than solely by the king.

exp.why: First, not all 29 caves belong to the Vakataka phase; Caves 9, 10, 12, 13, and 15A belong to the earlier Satavahana (pre-Mahayana/Hinayana) phase. Second, the Vakataka monarch Harishena (Vatsagulma branch) was not a Buddhist monk; the Vakataka rulers were predominantly followers of the Brahmanical/Shaiva faith who fostered religious pluralism. Specific caves in the second phase were patronized individually by Harishena's minister Varahadeva (Cave 16), the local feudatory ruler Upendragupta (Caves 17–20), and the Buddhist monk Buddhabhadra (Cave 26).

Caves 9 and 10 are early apsidal Chaitya-grihas (2nd–1st century BCE) featuring plain, aniconic rock-cut stupas at the apse end. In contrast, Caves 19 and 26 are 5th-century CE Mahayana Chaitya-grihas where the central votive stupa is elaborately elongated and has a prominent high-relief anthropomorphic figure of the Buddha sculpted into a niche on its front facade.

While Cave 1 is renowned for its painted mural of Mara Vijaya alongside the Bodhisattva Padmapani and Vajrapani murals, Cave 26 contains the famous sculpted stone relief of Mara Vijaya as well as the colossal rock-cut sculpture of the reclining Buddha in Mahaparinirvana along its right aisle wall.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4 (Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture); Upinder Singh: A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the technical process of ancient Indian mural paintings at the Ajanta and Bagh caves:
items: Statement-I: In the strict technical classification of painting methods, the ancient murals of the Ajanta and Bagh caves are categorized primarily as tempera or fresco-secco works rather than true buon fresco.

Statement-II: While most pigments used by the Ajanta painters—such as red and yellow ochres, terre verte (glauconite), and kaolin—were obtained locally from the Deccan trap formations, the brilliant blue pigment was derived from imported lapis lazuli.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Ajanta and Bagh murals were executed using the tempera/fresco-secco technique: pigments mixed with water-soluble organic binders (animal glue or vegetable gums) were painted over a dried lime-wash layer laid atop a mud-husk plaster base, unlike true Italian buon fresco where pigments are applied directly onto wet lime mortar without organic binders.

exp.why: In true buon fresco, water-suspended pigments are applied directly to freshly laid, wet lime plaster so that the pigment chemically binds into the surface through calcium carbonate crystallization as the mortar dries. At Ajanta and Bagh, artisans prepared the rough basalt or sandstone wall with a base coat of ferruginous mud mixed with cow dung, rice husks, and vegetable fibres, covered it with a thin coat of fine lime wash, and painted on the dried (or re-moistened) surface using pigments mixed with organic binders such as animal glue or vegetable gum—making the technique tempera/fresco-secco.

The mineral palette at Ajanta relied heavily on locally weathered volcanic minerals of the Deccan trap, including red and yellow ochre (iron oxides), green earth/terre verte (glauconite), white kaolin/lime, and organic lampblack. The notable exception was ultramarine blue, which was absent in the earliest phase and obtained in the Vakataka phase from imported lapis lazuli sourced via trade networks from Badakhshan (Afghanistan/Persia). However, the geographical origin of the pigments does not explain why the painting process is classified as tempera/fresco-secco rather than buon fresco.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4 & Ch. 5; Archaeological Survey of India Technical Notes on Ajanta Murals

stem: With reference to the multi-sectarian rock-cut cave complex at Ellora (Verul), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the predominantly single-storeyed viharas of earlier Western Deccan Buddhist sites, the Buddhist group at Ellora includes grand triple-storeyed monastic excavations such as Cave 11 (Do Thal) and Cave 12 (Tin Thal).

2. Cave 10 (Vishvakarma Cave) is the sole dedicated Chaitya-griha among the Buddhist caves at Ellora and features a rock-cut vaulted roof carved with stone ribs that imitate timber rafters, fronted by a projecting balcony facade.

3. While the Jain caves at the northern extremity of the cliff (such as the two-storeyed Indra Sabha, Cave 32) belong to the Digambara sect and were excavated last during the ninth and tenth centuries, the excavation of several early Brahmanical caves chronologically overlapped with the Buddhist phase during the seventh and eighth centuries.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Ellora's 34 caves (Buddhist Caves 1–12 in the south, Brahmanical Caves 13–29 in the centre, and Digambara Jain Caves 30–34 in the north) reflect architectural innovation and sectarian coexistence. Rather than being excavated in three strictly isolated centuries, the Buddhist and early Brahmanical phases overlapped between the 6th and 8th centuries CE.

exp.why: A hallmark of the Buddhist group at Ellora (Caves 1–12) is the expansion of monastic architecture into monumental multi-storeyed halls. Both Cave 11 (historically misnamed 'Do Thal' because its ground floor remained buried under debris until modern clearance) and Cave 12 ('Tin Thal') are full triple-storeyed rock-cut monasteries containing pillared halls and shrines.

Cave 10, popularly known as the Vishvakarma or 'Carpenter's Cave', is the only apsidal Chaitya hall among the 12 Buddhist caves at Ellora. Its barrel-vaulted stone ceiling is sculpted with curved ribs mimicking wooden beams, its exterior replaces the traditional monolithic horseshoe window with a pillared balcony/chandrasala, and its central stupa bears a colossal seated Buddha in pralambapadasana (European posture) flanked by attendants.

Caves 30–34 at the northern end belong to the Digambara Jain tradition (including Cave 32, Indra Sabha, and Cave 33, Jagannatha Sabha) and represent the final phase of activity at Ellora during the 9th–10th centuries CE under later Rashtrakuta and Yadava patronage. However, archaeological and stylistic evidence confirms that the Buddhist caves (c. 600–730 CE) and the earlier Brahmanical caves (such as Ravan ki Khai and Rameshvara, begun in the 6th–7th centuries CE) experienced substantial chronological overlap.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4 & Ch. 6; Susan Huntington: The Art of Ancient India

stem: With reference to the Kailashnath Temple (Cave 16) at Ellora, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It was constructed by quarrying dressed basalt blocks from the Charanandri hills and interlocking them without mortar in the curvilinear Nagara architectural style.
2. Its primary excavation in the eighth century CE was patronized by the Rashtrakuta monarch Krishna I.

3. Architecturally, the complex integrates a two-storeyed entrance gateway (Gopuram), a detached Nandi Mandapa linked to the main pillared hall via a rock-cut bridge, and a monumental three-dimensional relief of Ravana attempting to lift Mount Kailasha (Ravananugraha) carved beneath the main structure.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Cave 16 (Kailashnath) at Ellora is the world's largest single monolithic rock-cut temple, carved vertically top-down out of the living basalt cliff under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (r. 756–773 CE). It exemplifies the Dravida/Karnata-Dravida architectural idiom closely related to the Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal.

exp.why: The Kailashnath temple is neither a structural masonry temple built of quarried blocks nor Nagara in style. Instead, architects excavated three massive U-shaped trenches vertically downward from the top of the sloping basalt cliff of the Charanandri hills, sculpting the entire multi-storeyed temple out of a single living rock mass (monolith) from the finial downward. Stylistically, it follows the Dravida (specifically Karnata-Dravida) temple architecture with a tiered pyramidal Vimana crowned by an octagonal cupola-like shikhara.

Epigraphic evidence, notably the Baroda copper-plate inscription of Karka II, credits the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I (8th century CE) with commissioning this extraordinary rock-cut Shaiva monument named Krishneshvara/Kailasanatha.

Laid out like a complete free-standing Dravida temple complex within an open rock-cut courtyard, Cave 16 features a double-storeyed entrance Gopuram, freestanding monolithic dhvajastambhas and elephants, a central Nandi Mandapa connected to the main Gudhamandapa by a solid rock-cut bridge, five subsidiary peripheral shrines around the ambulatory, and a deeply undercut basement panel depicting Ravananugraha (Ravana shaking Mount Kailasha while Shiva calmly presses it down with his toe).

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (Temple Architecture and Sculpture); Harle, J.C.: The Art and Architecture of the Indian Subcontinent

stem: Consider the following architectural and iconographic description of an ancient Indian rock-cut monument: 'Its main excavation is designed on a grand cruciform mandala plan featuring a distinctive double-axis layout. While the east-west axis leads to a free-standing square sanctum (garbhagriha) pierced by four doorways and guarded by towering dvarapalas, the north-south axis from the main northern entrance culminates in a deep southern recess housing a colossal three-headed bust representing the Aghora, Tatpurusha, and Vamadeva aspects of the deity, flanked by monumental relief panels of Ardhanarishvara and Gangadhara.' Which one of the following rock-cut complexes and sectarian traditions is described in the passage above?

opts.A: Cave 1 at Badami, representing the Pancharatra Vaishnava doctrine of cosmic emanations (Vyuhas)
opts.B: Cave 29 (Dhumar Lena) at Ellora, representing the Tantric synthesis of Shaktism and Vajrayana Buddhism
opts.C: Cave 1 at Elephanta (Gharapuri), representing the Pashupata Shaiva theology centered on the Maheshmurti (Sadashiva)
opts.D: Cave 6 at Udayagiri (Vidisha), representing the early Gupta synthesis of Saura and Shakta iconography

core: The Great Cave (Cave 1) at Elephanta (ancient Gharapuri island off Mumbai, mid-6th century CE) is organized around a unique double-axis cruciform plan that balances ritual circumambulation of the four-doorway Linga shrine along the east-west axis with the visual epiphany of the 18-foot Maheshmurti (Sadashiva) along the north-south axis.

exp.why: Option C is correct because Cave 1 at Elephanta (Gharapuri), dated to the mid-6th century CE (associated with Kalachuri/Konkan Maurya patronage and Pashupata Shaivism), is renowned for its dual-axis layout. Entering from the north, the devotee's gaze leads straight down the north-south axis to the southern wall housing the colossal three-faced Maheshmurti/Sadashiva (where the serene central face is Tatpurusha/Mahadeva, the fierce left face holding serpents is Aghora/Bhairava, the gentle right face holding a lotus is Vamadeva/Uma, and the fourth and fifth aspects, Sadyojata and Ishana, are implied at the back and top). This central bust is directly flanked by the panels of Shiva as Ardhanarishvara and Gangadhara, while the perpendicular east-west axis focuses on the sarvatobhadra (four-doorway) Linga sanctum. Option A is incorrect because Badami Cave 1 is Shaivite (famous for the 18-armed Nataraja) and lacks a cruciform four-door Linga shrine or Maheshmurti. Option B is incorrect because although Cave 29 (Dhumar Lena) at Ellora shares a cruciform Linga-shrine layout inspired by Elephanta, it is a purely Shaiva cave without the colossal Maheshmurti triad or Buddhist-Shakta affiliation. Option D is incorrect because Udayagiri (Vidisha) caves are compact single-axis early 5th-century Gupta shrines.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4 & Ch. 6; Stella Kramrisch: The Presence of Siva

stem: With reference to the rock-cut architecture of the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves in Odisha, excavated primarily during the reign of King Kharavela of the Mahameghavahana (Cheti) dynasty, which one of the following statements accurately describes their structural and functional character?

opts.A: They are centered around deep apsidal Chaitya-grihas containing monolithic votive stupas at the rear, modeled directly on the contemporary Hinayana caves of Bhaja and Karle in the Western Ghats.
opts.B: They completely lack apsidal congregational Chaitya halls and instead consist of single- and double-storeyed residential monastic cells (lena/gumpha) featuring low doorways, pillared verandahs, and sloping rear floors serving as stone pillows for Jain ascetics.
opts.C: They were originally excavated as Ajivika retreats with mirror-like interior Mauryan polish and were later converted into Mahayana Buddhist shrines bearing narrative friezes of the Jataka tales.
opts.D: They represent free-standing monolithic rathas carved top-down from granite boulders to enshrine colossal Tirthankara images in the Kayotsarga posture during the first century BCE.

core: The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves (1st century BCE, near Bhubaneswar) represent the eastern Indian Jain rock-cut tradition patronized by King Kharavela and his royal family. Unlike the Western Deccan Buddhist caves, this complex contains no apsidal Chaitya-grihas; it comprises cellular monastic dormitories (gumphas) tailored to the austere practices of Jain monks.

exp.why: Option B is correct because the rock-cut excavations at Udayagiri and Khandagiri (attested in Kharavela's 17-line Prakrit Hathigumpha inscription in Udayagiri Cave 14) were designed specifically as rain-retreat residences (lena/gumpha) for Jain ascetics. Unlike the Buddhist complexes of the Western Deccan (Option A), they are entirely devoid of apsidal congregational Chaitya halls or rock-cut stupas. Instead, caves such as Rani Gumpha (a grand double-storeyed monastery with an open three-sided courtyard and narrative sculptural friezes), Ganesh Gumpha, and Ananta Gumpha feature rows of small cells entered through very low doorways (forcing monks to bow upon entering) and interiors whose floors slope upward toward the rear wall to act as built-in stone head-rests/pillows without bedding. Option C confuses them with the Mauryan Barabar/Nagarjuni caves in Bihar, which have mirror-like polish and were gifted to the Ajivikas. Option D confuses sandstone rock-cut cells with later monolithic granite rathas (such as Mamallapuram) and later medieval Somavamshi-era Tirthankara relief additions found in some Khandagiri caves.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4; Upinder Singh: A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the regional rock-cut cave architecture of ancient and early medieval India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Bojjannakonda and Lingalakonda hillocks at Sankaram in Andhra Pradesh are renowned for numerous monolithic rock-cut votive stupas carved directly out of the living rock.
2. The Khambhalida caves in Gujarat are excavated out of limestone rock and feature a chaitya hall flanked by large relief sculptures of the Bodhisattvas Padmapani and Vajrapani.
3. The Sittanavasal rock-cut cave in Tamil Nadu, known as Arivar Koil, was excavated as a Bhagavata Vaishnava shrine housing a colossal reclining statue of Anantasayana Vishnu.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Regional rock-cut complexes across peninsular and western India reflect diverse geological substrates and sectarian patronage, ranging from monolithic rock-cut votive stupa clusters in coastal Andhra and Buddhist limestone chaityas in Saurashtra to Jain murals and beds in Tamil Nadu.

exp.why: At Sankaram (near Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh), the twin hillocks of Bojjannakonda and Lingalakonda contain a remarkable concentration of monolithic rock-cut stupas, rock-cut caves, and brick structural remains spanning the Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana phases of Buddhism.

The Khambhalida Buddhist caves in Rajkot district of Gujarat (4th-5th century CE) are carved out of porous limestone rock. The central chaitya cave is famous for its facade flanked by large, expressive relief sculptures of the Bodhisattvas Padmapani (Avalokiteshvara) and Vajrapani under shelter trees.

Sittanavasal (Arivar Koil, 'Temple of the Arhats') in Pudukkottai district of Tamil Nadu is a celebrated Jain rock-cut monastery and temple (with early Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions on stone beds and later Pandya-era frescoes of the Samavasarana lotus pond), not a Vaishnava shrine. The colossal reclining Anantasayana Vishnu carved from a single granite block is a hallmark of the Undavalli rock-cut caves in Andhra Pradesh.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8 & 9

stem: With reference to the Gandhara School of Art, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Throughout its history, the school utilized spotted red sandstone and depicted the Buddha with a completely shaven head and foldless, transparent wet drapery.
2. Drawing upon Greco-Roman (Hellenistic) sculptural traditions, it emphasized anatomical realism, muscular contours, and wavy hair gathered into a topknot (ushnisha).
3. In its later phase between the fourth and fifth centuries CE, lime plaster (stucco) and terracotta increasingly replaced stone as the primary medium for sculpting images.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Flourishing in the north-western borderlands under Kushana patronage, the Gandhara school synthesized Buddhist iconography with Greco-Roman sculptural forms, using grey-blue phyllite/schist in its early phase and malleable lime-stucco in its later phase.

exp.why: Spotted red sandstone from Sikri quarries was the hallmark of the Mathura school, whereas foldless, transparent wet-look drapery was characteristic of the Gupta-era Sarnath school. Early Gandhara sculptors carved grey-blue schist (and greenish phyllite) and draped the Buddha in a heavy, thick sanghati resembling a Roman toga with deep, rhythmic folds.

Gandhara art applied Hellenistic and provincial Roman formal techniques to Buddhist subjects, modelling the Buddha with youthful Apollo-like facial features, pronounced muscular anatomy beneath heavy drapery, and wavy locks of hair gathered into a prominent cranial protuberance (ushnisha).

During the later Gandhara (or Indo-Afghan) phase from the 3rd to 5th centuries CE (seen at sites like Hadda, Taxila's Jaulian monastery, and Bamiyan), sculptors shifted from hard grey schist to lime-stucco (plaster) and clay over armatures, which allowed faster modelling and greater emotional expressiveness.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4; Susan Huntington, The Art of Ancient India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Mathura School of Art:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the Gandhara school which remained overwhelmingly devoted to Buddhist themes, the Mathura school under the Kushanas simultaneously produced early anthropomorphic icons of Buddhist, Jain, and Brahmanical figures alongside dynastic royal portraits, all sharing a unified plastic vocabulary of monumental volume and inner vitality (prana).

Statement-II: Rather than borrowing from foreign Hellenistic models, the master guild workshops of Mathura evolved their sculptural idiom directly from a pre-existing indigenous repertoire of folk Yaksha and Naga prototypes carved in local spotted red sandstone, adapting this shared stylistic template across diverse religious and royal commissions.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Mathura school was an indigenous, multi-religious artistic powerhouse whose artisanal guilds adapted the pre-existing Yaksha volumetric aesthetic—characterized by broad shoulders, open eyes, and inner breath (prana)—simultaneously to Buddhist Bodhisattvas, Jain Tirthankaras, Brahmanical deities, and Kushana royal portraits.

exp.why: Mathura was a major commercial and religious crossroads under the Kushanas. Its workshops simultaneously produced early seated and standing Buddhas (such as the Katra mound image), Jain ayagapattas (votive tablets) and sarvatobhadrika (four-fold Tirthankara) images from Kankali Tila, early icons of Vasudeva-Krishna, Shiva, Surya, and Durga, as well as the secular Devakula gallery of headless Kushana royal portraits (Kanishka and Vima Kadphises) at Mat.

Statement-II directly explains Statement-I: because the Mathura sculptors worked within common guild workshops using Sikri spotted red sandstone and derived their formal language from massive, frontally posed indigenous Yaksha prototypes (like the Parkham Yaksha) infused with prana (vital breath), the very same muscular, monumental plastic style naturally appeared across Buddhist, Jain, and Brahmanical images alike.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4; Ananda Coomaraswamy, The Origin of the Buddha Image

stem: In the context of ancient Indian sculptural traditions, a particular regional school flourished in riverine deltaic workshops under the patronage of the Satavahanas and later the Ikshvakus. Unlike contemporary northern schools that prioritized isolated, static cult icons, this school excelled in crowded, kinetic narrative reliefs carved on greenish-white Palnad limestone. Its compositions are distinguished by attenuated, slender human figures bent in acute 'tribhanga' (triple-flexion) postures, intricately carved circular lotus medallions on stupa railings, and dramatic collective scenes such as the taming of the rampaging elephant Nalagiri. Which one of the following schools of art is described in this passage?
core: The Amaravati (or Vengi) school in the Krishna-Godavari delta represents the zenith of ancient Indian narrative relief sculpture, using greenish-white Palnad limestone to depict dynamic Jataka tales and courtly dramas with slender, three-dimensionally overlapping figures.

exp.why: Option B is correct. The Amaravati (Vengi) school flourished in the lower Krishna valley (at sites such as Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Jaggayyapeta, and Goli) between the 2nd century BCE and 3rd century CE under the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus. It uniquely utilized greenish-white Palnad limestone (often called 'White Marble' due to its crystalline appearance). While Gandhara (D) and Mathura (C) focused heavily on standalone anthropomorphic icons of the Buddha, Amaravati excelled in complex, illusionistic narrative medallions (such as the famous medallion depicting the taming of the mad elephant Nalagiri at Rajagriha), featuring elongated, graceful figures in dramatic 'tribhanga' poses and intense emotional movement. The Sarnath school (A) flourished later under the Guptas in cream Chunar sandstone.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 3 & 4; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India

stem: With reference to the evolution of Buddhist sculpture during the Gupta period, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Kushana-period Mathura Buddha images featured an elaborately carved halo (prabhamandala) filled with dense floral scrolls and an unpleated robe covering both shoulders, Gupta-period Sarnath Buddha images reverted to a plain halo with scalloped margins and a pleated robe covering only the left shoulder.
2. The Sarnath workshop of the Gupta period predominantly utilized fine-grained, cream-coloured Chunar sandstone to carve serene images of the Buddha with downcast eyes and inward meditative poise.

3. The life-size standing copper image of the Buddha discovered at Sultanganj in Bihar exemplifies the high technical mastery of the lost-wax (cire perdue) metal-casting tradition during the Gupta-post-Gupta era.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Gupta Buddhist sculpture at Sarnath and Mathura refined earlier Kushana robustness into a classical idiom marked by cream Chunar sandstone, completely smooth diaphanous ('wet') drapery, downward-looking meditative eyes, and richly foliated halos.

exp.why: The statement reverses the actual chronological evolution between the Kushana and Gupta eras. In Kushana-period Mathura images (e.g., the Katra seated Buddha), the halo (prabhamandala) was largely plain with only a simple scalloped border around the edge, and the striated robe covered only the left shoulder. By contrast, in Gupta-period Sarnath sculptures, the halo grew into a magnificent circular disc richly carved with concentric bands of lotus and floral scrollwork, and the robe (sanghati) became completely foldless and diaphanous, covering both shoulders.

The Sarnath school under the Guptas (5th century CE) used buff/cream-coloured sandstone quarried from Chunar. Its masterwork—the seated Buddha in Dharmachakra Pravartana mudra—exhibits a smooth, slender body, completely transparent wet-look drapery without folds, and half-closed downcast eyes expressing spiritual serenity.

The monumental standing copper Buddha (over 2 metres high and weighing nearly half a ton) excavated at Sultanganj in Bhagalpur district of Bihar was cast using the cire perdue (lost-wax) process over an earthen core, showcasing the same diaphanous clinging robe and serene Abhaya mudra characteristic of the eastern Gupta artistic tradition.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4; Joanna Williams, The Art of Gupta India

stem: With reference to the iconographic mudras (hand gestures) and asanas (postures) in Buddhist art, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Bhumisparsha Mudra specifically symbolizes the Buddha's delivery of his First Sermon at the Deer Park in Sarnath by setting the Wheel of Law in motion.
2. The Dharmachakra Mudra depicts the seated Buddha touching the ground with the fingertips of his right hand to invoke the Earth goddess as witness to his triumph over Mara at Bodh Gaya.
3. The Pralambapadasana refers to the posture seen in several Ajanta and Ellora cave sculptures where the Buddha is seated upright on a high throne with both legs hanging down pendant.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Buddhist iconography encodes specific biographical episodes of Gautama Buddha's life through standardized mudras and asanas: Bhumisparsha signifies the Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, Dharmachakra signifies the First Sermon at Sarnath, and Pralambapadasana represents the majestic 'European' seated posture.

exp.why: Bhumisparsha Mudra ('earth-touching gesture', where the seated Buddha extends his right hand over his right knee to touch the lotus throne with palm inward) represents the moment of Enlightenment (Sambodhi) at Bodh Gaya, when Gautama called upon the Earth goddess Sthavara (Prithvi) to bear witness to his spiritual merit and triumph over the demon Mara—not the First Sermon at Sarnath.

Dharmachakra Pravartana Mudra (where both hands are held in front of the chest with the thumb and index finger of each hand joined to form a wheel) specifically represents the turning of the Wheel of Law during the Buddha's First Sermon at the Deer Park (Mrigadava) in Sarnath, not the triumph over Mara at Bodh Gaya.

Pralambapadasana (also known as Bhadrasana or the 'European posture') depicts the Buddha seated upright on a lion throne (simhasana) with both legs hanging down pendant and feet resting on a lotus footstool, prominently seen in late Vakataka and post-Gupta rock-cut caves at Ajanta (e.g., Cave 26 chaitya arch and Cave 19), Ellora (Cave 10, Vishvakarma cave), and Kanheri.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 4; CCRT Buddhist Iconography Resources

stem: With reference to the iconography of Bodhisattvas and Buddhist deities in Indian art, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Maitreya : Wields a flaming sword of wisdom cleaving ignorance and holds the Prajnaparamita manuscript
2. Manjushri : Holds a ritual water-flask (kundi) of immortality and wears a miniature stupa in his crown
3. Avalokiteshvara (Padmapani) : Holds a lotus stalk in hand and bears an effigy of Dhyani Buddha Amitabha in his crown
4. Hariti : Depicted as a matronly goddess of fertility and protector of children alongside her consort Panchika
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: In Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist iconography, specific Bodhisattvas are identified by distinct cognitive attributes: Maitreya (the future Buddha) holds the nectar flask (kundi) and wears a stupa in his crown, whereas Manjushri (embodiment of transcendent wisdom) holds a flaming sword and the Prajnaparamita scripture.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. Maitreya, the future Buddha currently residing in the Tushita heaven, is iconographically identified by the nectar flask (kundi or kamandalu) held in his left hand and a miniature stupa (chaitya) adorning his crown, not the sword of wisdom.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Manjushri is the Bodhisattva of supreme wisdom (prajna). His signature attributes are a flaming sword (khadga) in his right hand to cleave the clouds of ignorance (avidya) and the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita manuscript held in his left hand or resting on a blue lotus.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Avalokiteshvara in his Padmapani ('Lotus-bearer') form embodies universal compassion (karuna). He is depicted holding a lotus stalk and wearing a miniature effigy of his spiritual progenitor, Dhyani Buddha Amitabha, in his matted crown (jatamukuta).

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Originally an ogress (yakshini) converted by the Buddha, Hariti became revered across Gandhara, Mathura, and Ajanta as the benevolent protector of children and goddess of abundance, frequently sculpted in couple reliefs alongside her yaksha consort Panchika (the general of Kubera).

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 3 & 4; Susan Huntington, The Art of Ancient India

stem: With reference to the architectural features and archaeological discoveries at major Buddhist Stupas across India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Maha Stupa at Kanaganahalli (Sannati) in Karnataka yielded limestone relief slabs containing the only known inscribed portrait sculpture of Emperor Ashoka, identified in Brahmi script as 'Raya Asoko'.

2. Unlike the hemispherical dome surmounted by a square railing at Sanchi, the Gupta-era reconstruction of the Dhamek Stupa at Sarnath takes the form of a solid cylindrical tower built of stone and brick without a crowning harmika.

3. The Kesariya Stupa in Bihar is distinguished by the discovery of an inscribed Western Kshatrapa green schist relic casket and terracotta Dhyani Buddha images inside its core, whereas the Devnimori Stupa in Gujarat features a tall multi-tiered polygonal brick mandala layout.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Regional Buddhist stupas evolved beyond the early hemispherical Sanchi prototype into cylindrical towers (Dhamek at Sarnath), terraced brick mandalas (Kesariya in Bihar), stone-encased Satavahana drum stupas with royal portrait slabs (Kanaganahalli in Karnataka), and Kshatrapa brick stupas containing inscribed relic caskets (Devnimori in Gujarat).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Excavations at the Satavahana-era Maha Stupa at Kanaganahalli (near Sannati on the banks of the Bhima River in Kalaburagi district, Karnataka) unearthed sculpted limestone casing slabs (ayaka pattas), including a unique portrait relief of Emperor Ashoka flanked by his queens, inscribed in Brahmi as 'Raya Asoko'.

Statement 2 is correct. Marking the spot where the Buddha delivered his First Sermon (Dharmachakra Pravartana), the Dhamek Stupa at Sarnath was enlarged during the Gupta period into a massive solid cylindrical tower (about 43.6 metres high) with a lower basement faced in stone carved with intricate floral and geometric arabesques and an upper brickwork drum lacking a separate square harmika.

Statement 3 is incorrect because the archaeological identities of Kesariya and Devnimori have been interchanged. It is the Devnimori Stupa (Sharadpeeth, Aravalli district, Gujarat) that yielded a Western Kshatrapa-era inscribed green schist relic casket (dated to the reign of Rudrasena) along with finely moulded terracotta Buddha statues inside its core. Conversely, the Kesariya Stupa in East Champaran district, Bihar, is famous for its towering terraced brick mandala architecture featuring polygonal cells housing stucco Buddha figures.

ref: ASI Excavations at Kanaganahalli & Kesariya; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India Ch. 7 & 8

stem: With reference to the rock-cut cave temples of Badami and Aihole in Karnataka, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The four numbered rock-cut caves at Badami were excavated by the Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman I to commemorate his conquest of Vatapi and include both Brahmanical shrines and a Buddhist Chaitya hall.

2. Cave 3 at Badami contains a dated inscription of the Early Western Chalukya ruler Mangalesha (578 CE) and features monumental high-relief sculptures of Trivikrama and Mahavishnu seated on the coiled serpent Ananta.
3. The Ravana Phadi cave at Aihole is an early Chalukyan Shaiva rock-cut shrine noted for its dynamic relief panel of a multi-armed Nataraja flanked by the Saptamatrikas.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Carved into red sandstone cliffs during the 6th century CE under the Early Western Chalukyas of Vatapi, the Badami caves (1 Shaiva, 2 Vaishnava, and 1 Jain) and the Ravana Phadi cave at Aihole represent a foundational landmark in Deccan rock-cut iconography.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The four major rock-cut cave temples at Badami (ancient Vatapi) were excavated by the Early Western Chalukyas in the 6th century CE, long before the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I invaded Vatapi in 642 CE. Furthermore, the four numbered caves comprise one Shaiva cave (Cave 1), two Vaishnava caves (Caves 2 and 3), and one Jain cave (Cave 4), with no Buddhist Chaitya hall among the four main caves.

Statement 2 is correct. Cave 3, the largest and most ornately sculpted cave at Badami, bears a Kannada/Sanskrit inscription of the Chalukya prince Mangalesha dated to Saka year 500 (578 CE), executed during the reign of his brother Kirtivarman I. It houses colossal Vaishnava reliefs including Trivikrama, Narasimha, Varaha, Harihara, and Vishnu seated on Ananta (Shesha).

Statement 3 is correct. Dating to the mid-6th century CE, the Ravana Phadi cave at Aihole is one of the earliest Chalukyan rock-cut shrines. Its side chamber features a celebrated relief of a ten-armed dancing Shiva (Nataraja) surrounded by life-size, slender figures of the Saptamatrikas (Seven Divine Mothers), Ganesh, and Kartikeya.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 6; Harle, The Art and Architecture of the Indian Subcontinent

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Pallava rock-cut architecture at Mamallapuram:
items: Statement-I: The monolithic Pancha Rathas at Mamallapuram, carved out of live granite outcrops during the reign of Narasimhavarman I, serve as petrified architectural prototypes replicating diverse contemporary wooden and structural temple forms.

Statement-II: Among the Pancha Rathas, the Draupadi Ratha replicates the apsidal elephant-back (Gajaprishtha) plan of a Buddhist Chaitya hall, whereas the Nakula-Sahadeva Ratha models a simple square thatched hut (kutagara) without a tiered pyramidal superstructure.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While the Pancha Rathas at Mamallapuram act as a stone catalog of early Dravida roof and plan geometries, each monument corresponds to a distinct architectural prototype: Draupadi Ratha models a square thatched hut (kuta), Nakula-Sahadeva Ratha models an apsidal Chaitya (gajaprishtha), Bhima Ratha models a barrel-vaulted oblong hall (sala), and Dharmaraja Ratha models a multi-storeyed pyramidal vimana.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Excavated top-down from single granite boulders during the Mamalla phase under Narasimhavarman I (mid-7th century CE), the Pancha Rathas were never consecrated for active worship (as their interiors and plinths remained partially unfinished) and visually document how early Dravida architects translated perishable timber, thatch, and brick temple archetypes into solid stone.

Statement-II is incorrect because it swaps the architectural forms of the Draupadi and Nakula-Sahadeva Rathas. It is the Draupadi Ratha (dedicated to Durga) that models a simple one-storeyed square hut with a curvilinear thatched roof (kutagara) devoid of tiered talas. Conversely, the Nakula-Sahadeva Ratha replicates the apsidal 'elephant-back' (Gajaprishtha or Vesara/Hastiprishtha) plan derived from Buddhist Chaitya halls.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 6; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India

stem: With reference to the material mediums, techniques, and dynastic traditions of Indian sculpture, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Sultanganj Buddha : Cast in an eight-metal alloy (Ashtadhatu) during the late Sena period
2. Kurkihar and Nalanda Vajrayana icons (such as Trailokyavijaya and Marichi) : Carved predominantly in mottled red Sikri sandstone under Kushana patronage
3. Seated Buddha in Dharmachakra Pravartana Mudra at Sarnath : Carved in buff-colored Chunar sandstone during the Gupta period with an unpleated diaphanous robe
4. Parkham Yaksha from Mathura : Cast in hollow bronze using the lost-wax process during the Satavahana period
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Mastering ancient Indian sculptural schools requires distinguishing their signature materials and eras: early colossal Yakshas in grey/buff sandstone (Mauryan-Shunga), Mathura in spotted red Sikri sandstone (Kushana), Sarnath in cream Chunar sandstone (Gupta), Sultanganj in pure lost-wax copper (Gupta), and Nalanda/Kurkihar in black basalt stelae and Ashtadhatu bronzes (Pala-Sena).

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. The monumental 2.3-metre-high standing Buddha discovered at Sultanganj (Bhagalpur district, Bihar) dates to the Gupta/post-Gupta transition (5th to 7th century CE) and was cast in pure unalloyed copper over an earthen core using the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique. The eight-metal alloy (Ashtadhatu) became characteristic of later Pala-Sena metal casting.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The prolific workshops at Nalanda, Kurkihar, and Odantapuri flourished under the Pala and Sena dynasties (8th to 12th centuries CE), producing intricate Vajrayana deities like Marichi and Trailokyavijaya either in Ashtadhatu bronze or carved in fine-grained black basalt/phyllite stone stelae (kashti pathar) resembling polished metal. Mottled red Sikri sandstone was the medium of the Kushana-era Mathura school.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. The 5th-century CE Seated Buddha in Dharmachakra Pravartana Mudra from Sarnath is the pinnacle of the Gupta sculptural idiom. Carved in cream/buff Chunar sandstone, it features a smooth, transparent (wet-look) sanghati devoid of heavy drapery folds, downcast meditative eyes, an ornate scalloped nimbus (prabhamandala), and a pedestal showing the wheel flanked by deer and the five initial disciples.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. The colossal standing Parkham Yaksha (Manibhadra), discovered near Mathura, is carved out of grey-buff sandstone and dates to the late Mauryan or Shunga period (c. 3rd–2nd century BCE), bearing a Brahmi inscription naming its sculptor Gomitaka, a pupil of Kunika.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 2, 3, 4 & 7; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India

stem: Consider the following landmark rock-cut cave monuments in India:
items: 1. Varaha Cave at Udayagiri, Vidisha
2. Sudama Cave in the Barabar Hills
3. Cave 3 (Vaishnava Cave) at Badami
4. Great Chaitya Hall at Karla
prompt: What is the correct chronological order of the initial excavation of these monuments, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: The evolution of Indian rock-cut architecture progresses chronologically from Mauryan granite polish in Bihar (3rd century BCE), to Satavahana/Kshatrapa apsidal Chaitya halls in the Western Ghats (1st–2nd century CE), to Gupta Brahmanical rock-cut shrines in Malwa (early 5th century CE), and Early Western Chalukya sandstone caves in Karnataka (late 6th century CE).

exp.why: The Varaha Cave (Cave 5) and adjacent dated caves at Udayagiri near Vidisha (Madhya Pradesh) were excavated during the reign of the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II Vikramaditya in the early 5th century CE (bearing an inscription dated to Gupta Era 82, i.e., 401–402 CE), placing it third in the chronological sequence.

The Sudama Cave in the Barabar Hills (Jehanabad district, Bihar) is the earliest surviving dated rock-cut cave in India. Dedicated by Emperor Ashoka in the 12th year of his reign (c. 257 BCE) to the Ajivika sect, its interior displays the famous mirror-like Mauryan polish on hard granite, placing it first in the sequence.

Cave 3 at Badami (Bagalkot district, Karnataka) bears a dated inscription of the Early Western Chalukya prince Mangalesha from Saka Era 500 (578 CE), placing it fourth (latest) in the chronological sequence.

The Great Chaitya Hall at Karla (Pune district, Maharashtra), the largest Hinayana rock-cut Chaitya griha in India featuring original teakwood ribs and patronage inscriptions of the Western Kshatrapa ruler Nahapana's son-in-law Ushavadata and the Satavahanas, dates to the 1st–2nd century CE (c. 120 CE), placing it second in the sequence. Thus, the correct chronological order is 2 - 4 - 1 - 3.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art Ch. 2, 4 & 6; Percy Brown, Indian Architecture (Buddhist and Hindu Periods)

stem: An early sixth-century structural stone temple in central India marks a watershed in the evolution of North Indian temple architecture. Unlike earlier Gupta-era shrines that were built on low platforms with flat roofs, this west-facing temple stands on a high plinth (jagati), features four subsidiary shrines at the corners of the platform creating a Panchayatana layout, and preserves one of the earliest extant examples of a stunted curvilinear tower (rekha-prasada shikhara) alongside grand narrative relief panels of Sheshashayi Vishnu and Gajendramoksha on its sanctum outer walls.
prompt: Which one of the following temples is described in the passage given above?
core: The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (Lalitpur, Uttar Pradesh) represents Stage III of Gupta temple architecture, introducing both the Panchayatana five-shrine layout on a raised jagati and the earliest stone prototype of the curvilinear Nagara Rekha-prasada Shikhara.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because the Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (early 6th century CE) is a rare west-facing Vaishnava stone temple that marks the transition to the classical Nagara style (Stage III of Gupta architecture). It stands on a high plinth (jagati) with four corner subsidiary shrines (Panchayatana style), possesses a stunted curvilinear Rekha-prasada Shikhara, and houses iconic Gupta rathika relief panels of Sheshashayi Vishnu, Nara-Narayana, and Gajendramoksha. Option (A) Temple 17 at Sanchi is a Stage I Gupta shrine with a flat roof and a low platform. Option (B) Parvati Temple at Nachna Kuthara is a Stage II Gupta temple featuring a covered ambulatory passage around the sanctum and a flat-roofed upper storey. Option (C) Bhitargaon is a terraced brick temple with true arches and terracotta panels rather than a stone Panchayatana complex.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (Temple Architecture and Sculpture); Harle, The Art and Architecture of the Indian Subcontinent

stem: With reference to the structural and iconographic differences between the Nagara and Dravida styles of temple architecture, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Nagara style is characterized by a curvilinear tower (Shikhara) that curves inward as it rises over the sanctum, the Dravida style features a stepped pyramidal tower (Vimana) composed of progressively smaller storeys of pavilions.

2. At the entrance to the sanctum (Garbhagriha), Nagara temples characteristically feature fierce guardian figures (Dvarapalas), whereas Dravida temples replace them with images of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna.

3. Unlike Dravida temple complexes which are enclosed within high compound walls (Prakaras) pierced by monumental gateways (Gopurams), classical Nagara temples generally lack elaborate boundary walls and feature multiple towers rising over both the sanctum and the assembly halls.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Nagara and Dravida architectures diverge sharply in superstructure geometry (curvilinear Shikhara with Amalaka vs stepped pyramidal Vimana with octagonal/domical Shikhara), enclosure layouts (open Jagati vs walled Prakaras with Gopurams), and sanctum doorway iconography (auspicious river goddesses vs fierce Dvarapalas).

exp.why: In the Nagara style, the tower over the Garbhagriha (called Shikhara) has a continuous curvilinear profile (Rekha-prasada/Latina) topped by a ribbed disc (Amalaka) and Kalasha. In the Dravida style, the tower over the Garbhagriha (called Vimana) rises like a stepped geometric pyramid of receding horizontal tiers (talas) crowned by a polygonal or octagonal cupola (called Shikhara in the South).

This statement swaps the doorway iconography of the two styles. At the entrance to the North Indian Nagara Garbhagriha, the doorjambs (shakhas) are typically adorned with auspicious motifs such as Mithunas (couples) and the personified river goddesses Ganga (on Makara) and Yamuna (on Kurma). Conversely, in South Indian Dravida temples, the entrance to the Garbhagriha is guarded by fierce, weapon-wielding Dvarapalas (door-guardians) and Bhutas.

Dravida temples are consistently enclosed within concentric compound walls (Prakaras) entered through towering Gopurams, and only the main sanctum carries a true Vimana in early/mid phases. In contrast, classical Nagara temples stand on an open raised stone terrace (Jagati) without high boundary walls, and each preceding hall (Ardhamandapa, Mandapa, Mahamandapa) carries its own ascending superstructure culminating in the main Shikhara.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the classification of Nagara temple superstructures based on their architectural form, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Latina (or Rekha-prasada) is the most common Nagara superstructure over the Garbhagriha, built on a square base with walls that curve inward cleanly to a single point at the top.

2. The Phamsana type of Nagara building rises from a rectangular ground plan into a semi-cylindrical, wagon-vaulted roof inspired by ancient timber Chaitya halls, as exemplified by the Teli ka Mandir at Gwalior.

3. The Valabhi type consists of several horizontal slabs that slope upward in a straight incline to a single point and is typically used to roof the assembly halls (Mandapas) in medieval North Indian temples.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Early Nagara superstructures are classified into three distinct morphological types—Latina (square-based inward-curving tower), Phamsana (broad-based pyramidal roof of straight-sloping horizontal slabs), and Valabhi (rectangular-based barrel/wagon-vaulted roof).

exp.why: The Latina (or Rekha-prasada) is the quintessential early Nagara Shikhara type. It rises from a square base and its walls curve gradually inward toward a single point at the summit, crowned by an Amalaka. In later periods, the simple Latina evolved into the Sekhari and Bhumija composite forms.

This statement describes the Valabhi style, not the Phamsana style. It is the Valabhi subtype that has a rectangular ground plan with a roof rising into a semi-cylindrical, barrel-vaulted (wagon-vaulted) chamber derived from ancient timber and bamboo Chaitya roofs, famously seen in the 8th-century Teli ka Mandir at Gwalior and the Vaital Deul at Bhubaneswar.

This statement describes the Phamsana style, not the Valabhi style. Phamsana buildings are broader and shorter than Latina ones; their roofs are composed of several horizontal slabs that rise gently in a straight pyramidal incline rather than curving inward. In mature Nagara temples, the Phamsana design is characteristically used for the Mandapas (assembly halls), while the Garbhagriha is topped by a taller Latina/Sekhari Shikhara.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (Nagara Sub-types)

stem: With reference to the Odisha (Kalinga) school of Nagara temple architecture, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the Kalinga architectural tradition, the Pidha Deul serves as the tall vertical tower housing the main sanctum (Garbhagriha), whereas the Rekha Deul serves as the tiered pyramidal assembly hall (Jagamohana) in front of it.
2. The Khakhara Deul, which features an elongated barrel-vaulted roof resembling a Dravidian Gopuram, is dedicated exclusively to Vaishnava shrines in Odisha.

3. A defining structural feature of Odisha temples is that their interior sanctum and assembly hall walls are profusely carved with high-relief sculptures, while their exterior facades are left completely plain and supported by internal stone colonnades.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Kalinga (Odisha) school divides temples into Rekha Deul (curvilinear sanctum tower), Pidha Deul (stepped pyramidal Jagamohana), and Khakhara Deul (barrel-vaulted Shakta shrines), characterized by lavishly sculpted exteriors, bare interiors, and pillarless ceilings reinforced with iron girders.

exp.why: The architectural roles of Rekha Deul and Pidha Deul are reversed here. In the Kalinga style, the Rekha Deul is the tall building with a near-vertical sugar-loaf tower that curves sharply inward near the top and houses the main Garbhagriha (sanctum). The Pidha Deul has a square ground plan topped by a stepped pyramidal roof of receding horizontal platforms (pidhas) and serves as the Jagamohana (assembly/prayer hall) in front of the sanctum.

The Khakhara Deul (derived from 'kakharu', meaning pumpkin gourd, and structurally equivalent to the Valabhi wagon-vaulted style) is dedicated almost exclusively to Shakti (feminine/Tantric) deities in Odisha, not Vaishnava deities. Famous examples include the 8th-century Vaital Deul (Baitala Deula) at Bhubaneswar dedicated to Goddess Chamunda and the Varahi Deula at Chaurasi.

In Odisha temples, the exact opposite is true: the exterior walls are lavishly and intricately carved with sculptural relief, whereas the interior walls of the Garbhagriha and Jagamohana are generally left completely bare and unadorned. Furthermore, early and mature Odisha Jagamohanas avoided internal stone pillars, using corbelled masonry reinforced with heavy forged iron beams/girders to support the roof.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (Odisha Temples); Vidya Dehejia, Early Stone Temples of Orissa

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Chandela (Khajuraho) school of Nagara architecture:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the dark, enclosed interiors of the Odisha school of Nagara temples, the interiors of mature Chandela temples at Khajuraho, such as the Kandariya Mahadeva and Lakshmana temples, are unusually well-lit and ventilated.

Statement-II: Major Khajuraho temples are constructed on the Sandhara plan with an internal ambulatory passage (Pradakshinapatha) and feature projecting lateral balconies with open pillared windows (Kakshasana) across the Mandapa, Mahamandapa, and sanctum ambulatory.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Mature Chandela temples at Khajuraho integrate the Ardhamandapa, Mandapa, Mahamandapa, Antarala, and Garbhagriha into a single compact unit on a high Jagati, utilizing the Sandhara layout with projecting balconied windows (ardha-chandra/kakshasana) to flood both the halls and the inner ambulatory with natural light and air.

exp.why: In contrast to Kalinga (Odisha) temples where the Jagamohana and Deul have thick solid walls with minimal openings—leaving the interiors dim and richly carving only the exteriors—mature Chandela temples at Khajuraho (like Lakshmana, Vishvanatha, and Kandariya Mahadeva) are celebrated for their brightly lit, airy interiors that showcase extensive sculptural ornamentation inside the halls and ambulatory as well as on the outside.

Major royal temples at Khajuraho are built on the Sandhara plan (possessing an enclosed internal Pradakshinapatha around the Garbhagriha) creating a double-cross or Latin-cross axial layout. Crucially, the sides of the Mahamandapa and the outer walls of the sanctum ambulatory project outward into open, pillared balconies with sloped seat-backs (Kakshasana). These projecting lateral balconies admit abundant sunlight and cross-ventilation directly into the interior halls and circumambulatory passage, directly explaining Statement-I.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (Central India / Khajuraho)

stem: With reference to the Solanki (Maru-Gurjara) school of temple architecture in Western India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Although North Indian Nagara temples generally lack ritual water tanks, the Solanki school in Gujarat and Rajasthan frequently incorporated elaborate stepped tanks (Kunds) studded with miniature shrines directly in front of the temple complex.

2. The eleventh-century Sun Temple at Modhera is an east-facing brick temple built without an assembly hall (Sabha Mandapa), so that sunlight can fall unobstructed from the outer gateway onto the sanctum wall.

3. A distinctive aesthetic hallmark of the Maru-Gurjara tradition, seen in both the Modhera Sun Temple and the Dilwara Jain Temples at Mount Abu, is the replication of regional wood-carving traditions in stone and marble, particularly in intricate domical ceilings (Vitanas) and ornamental archways (Toranas).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Solanki (Maru-Gurjara) style of Western India is distinguished within the Nagara tradition by its stepped ritual water tanks (like the Surya Kund at Modhera), freestanding ornamental Toranas, detached open-pillared Sabha Mandapas, and filigree-like stone and marble carvings inspired by Gujarati woodworking.

exp.why: While ritual water tanks (Kalyani/Pushkarini) are a standard feature of South Indian Dravida complexes and are usually absent in North Indian Nagara temples, the Solanki (Maru-Gurjara) school in arid Gujarat and western Rajasthan is a major exception. The Sun Temple at Modhera (built under Bhima I in 1026 CE) features the grand hundred-square-metre stepped rectangular tank called Surya Kund, containing 108 miniature shrines carved into its steps.

The Sun Temple at Modhera is built of golden-brown sandstone, not brick. Furthermore, it very prominently possesses a magnificent detached, open-pillared assembly/dancing hall (Sabha Mandapa or Ranga Mandapa) in addition to a closed hall (Gudha Mandapa) attached to the Garbhagriha. All three axial components—the Surya Kund with its Torana, the open Sabha Mandapa, and the Gudha Mandapa/Garbhagriha—are aligned along the east-west axis so that on the equinoxes, the rising sun shines directly through the open pillars of the Sabha Mandapa into the inner sanctum.

Gujarat and western Rajasthan possessed a centuries-old tradition of intricate domestic and religious wood carving. Under Solanki patronage and Jain merchant ministers (such as Vimal Shah and Vastupala-Tejapala at the Dilwara Temples in Mount Abu), sculptors translated this wood-carving aesthetic into sandstone and white Makrana marble, producing translucent corbelled domical ceilings (Vitanas) with suspended lotus pendants (Padmashilas) and cusped flying arches (Toranas).

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (West India / Modhera & Mount Abu)

stem: With reference to the regional variations of temple architecture in eastern and Himalayan India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Siddheshvara Mahadeva Temple, Barakar : Early Pala stone shrine featuring a tall, curving Rekha shikhara crowned by a large amalaka
2. Jor-Bangla Temple, Bishnupur : Twin terracotta structure mimicking the sloping, curved cornices of bamboo-thatched hut roofs
3. Martand Sun Temple, Anantnag : Clustered Nagara Latina shrines with deodar-wood porch canopies typical of the Kumaon hills
4. Jageshwar Temple Complex, Almora : Limestone peristyle cellular courtyard enclosing a central shrine with trefoil-arched niches
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Regional temple architecture adapted classical Nagara grammar to local climate, materials, and cross-cultural influences—producing early curving Pala stone shikharas and later Chala-roofed terracotta shrines in Bengal, cellular peristyle courtyards with trefoil arches in Karkota Kashmir, and clustered stone Latina/Phamsana shrines with wooden canopies in Kumaon-Garhwal.

exp.why: The 9th-century Siddheshvara Mahadeva Temple at Barakar (Burdwan district, West Bengal) exemplifies the early Pala-period Vanga style. Built in stone prior to the late-medieval terracotta Bangla-roof phase, it features a tall, steeply curving shikhara (resembling early Odishan Rekha-deul towers) crowned by a prominent amalaka.

Built in the 17th century under the Malla rulers at Bishnupur (Bankura district, West Bengal), the Jor-Bangla (Keshta Raya) Temple is a classic example of the regional Chala/Bangla terracotta idiom. It joins two sloping 'do-chala' hut-like structures—one serving as a porch and the other as a shrine—surmounted by a small ratna tower, directly translating vernacular bamboo-and-thatch roof geometry into moulded brick.

Pair 3 and Pair 4 are swapped. The 8th-century Martand Sun Temple in Anantnag (Jammu & Kashmir), commissioned by the Karkota ruler Lalitaditya Muktapida, does not follow the Kumaon wooden-canopied Latina layout. Instead, it is built of ashlar limestone on a grand cellular peristyle courtyard plan (84 subsidiary cells surrounding a water-filled courtyard) with distinct trefoil arches, pediments, and Gandhara-Hellenistic fluted columns.

The Jageshwar group of temples in Almora district (Kumaon region, Uttarakhand), patronized by the Katyuri rulers between the 7th and 12th centuries, consists of densely clustered stone Nagara Latina and Phamsana shrines situated in a deodar forest valley, originally fitted with sloping wooden slab roofs/canopies over the mandapa to shed heavy rain and snow—not a Kashmiri peristyle cellular courtyard with trefoil arches.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (Temple Architecture and Sculpture - The Hills & Eastern India)

stem: Consider the following stages in the architectural and technological evolution of Pallava temples in South India:
items: 1. Monolithic free-standing Rathas sculpted top-down from in-situ granite outcrops as seen at the Pancha Rathas in Mamallapuram.
2. Excavated rock-cut cave mandapas supported by heavy square-and-octagonal pillars as seen at Mandagapattu.
3. Free-standing structural masonry temples built with quarried and dressed stone blocks as seen at the Shore Temple in Mamallapuram and the Kailasanatha Temple in Kanchipuram.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the technological evolution of Pallava temple architecture from the earliest to the latest?
core: Pallava architecture provides a textbook lithic transition in early Dravida art: beginning with excavated rock-cut cave mandapas (Mahendravarman I), progressing to free-standing cut-out monoliths or Rathas (Narasimhavarman I Mamalla), and culminating in structural stone-masonry temples (Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha).

exp.why: This represents the second phase under Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla' (c. 630–668 CE). Architects moved from hollowing out cliff faces to sculpting entire external and internal temple forms (the Pancha Rathas) top-down out of living granite whale-back boulders at Mamallapuram.

This represents the earliest phase inaugurated by Mahendravarman I (c. 600–630 CE). In the famous Sanskrit inscription at the Lakshitayatana rock-cut cave temple at Mandagapattu, the king celebrates constructing a shrine for Brahma, Ishvara, and Vishnu without the perishable materials of brick, timber, metal, or mortar—marking the dawn of rock-cut cave mandapas in Tamilakam.

This represents the third and mature structural phase under Narasimhavarman II 'Rajasimha' (c. 700–728 CE) and later Nandivarman II. Abandoning the geological constraints of live rock outcrops, architects quarried sandstone and granite blocks to erect true free-standing structural Dravida temples such as the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram and the Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram. Hence, the chronological sequence is 2 - 1 - 3.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India

stem: With reference to the architectural characteristics of the Great Living Chola Temples of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Imperial Chola temple complexes, the central sanctum superstructure (Vimana) rises dramatically higher than the outer gateway towers (Gopurams).

2. While the Vimana of the Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur rises in a graceful concave curve with recessed contours, the Vimana at Gangaikondacholapuram exhibits a rigid, straight-edged pyramidal profile.
3. The Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram dispenses with the pillared front mandapa and replaces it with an uncarved brick ambulatory hall.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Imperial Chola architecture prioritised the monumental verticality of the sanctum Vimana over the relatively modest gateway Gopurams, while evolving stylistically from the taut, straight-sided geometric pyramid of Rajaraja I's Thanjavur Vimana to the fluid, concave contours of Rajendra I's Gangaikondacholapuram and the ornate chariot-mandapa of Rajaraja II's Darasuram.

exp.why: During the Imperial Chola zenith (11th–12th centuries), the architectural hierarchy centred on the Sri-Vimana directly over the garbhagriha. At Thanjavur, the Vimana soars to roughly 66 metres (216 feet), dwarfing the two-tiered entrance Gopurams (Keralantakan and Rajarajan tiruvasal). Only in the late Chola, Pandya, Vijayanagara, and Nayaka periods did the outer Gopurams eclipse the central Vimana in height.

The architectural profiles of the two temples are reversed in the statement. The Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur (completed c. 1010 CE under Rajaraja I) has a strict, straight-edged, geometric pyramidal profile across its 13 storeys (talas). Conversely, the Brihadishvara Temple at Gangaikondacholapuram (built by Rajendra I, c. 1035 CE), which is slightly shorter with 9 storeys, introduces a softer, graceful concave curve and recessed octagonal contours.

Built in stone by Rajaraja II in the 12th century, the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram is renowned for its elaborately sculpted front pillared hall (Alankara/Raja-gambhira Mandapa), which is designed in the form of a celestial chariot (ratha-mandapa) complete with spoked stone wheels and drawn by galloping horses and elephants—not an uncarved brick hall.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6; UNESCO World Heritage Dossier: Great Living Chola Temples

stem: With reference to the architectural developments under the Vijayanagara and Nayaka dynasties in South India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To maintain an unobstructed visual axis toward the sanctum, Vijayanagara architects dispensed with enclosure walls (Prakaras) and erected temples on open, un-walled Jagati terraces.

2. In Vijayanagara temple complexes, the Amman shrine functioned as an open multi-pillared pavilion for celebrating the annual symbolic wedding of the deity, whereas the Kalyana Mandapa was an enclosed secondary sanctum built to house the chief consort goddess.

3. Unlike Vijayanagara architecture, the subsequent Nayaka architectural tradition at Madurai and Rameswaram discontinued covered Prakara corridors and monolithic Yali pillars in favour of plain, unpillared brick ambulatory halls.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Vijayanagara and Nayaka architecture expanded the Dravida temple from a single shrine into a fortified ritual city enclosed by high concentric Prakara walls pierced by monumental Raya Gopurams, incorporating dedicated Amman shrines for the consort goddess, open pillared Kalyana Mandapas for ritual divine weddings, and vast corridors lined with monolithic Yali and horse pillars.

exp.why: Vijayanagara temple complexes did not abandon enclosure walls; rather, they enclosed the sacred precinct within massive, high-walled concentric stone fortifications (Prakaras) entered through towering gateways known as Raya Gopurams. Open, un-walled Jagati platforms are characteristic of Central Indian Chandela (Khajuraho) and Karnataka Hoysala temples.

The functions of the Amman shrine and the Kalyana Mandapa are swapped. Under Vijayanagara patronage, two major structural additions became standard inside the main courtyard: the Amman shrine, an enclosed subsidiary temple dedicated permanently to the chief goddess/consort of the presiding deity, and the Kalyana Mandapa, an ornate, open multi-pillared pavilion raised on a sculpted plinth where the annual symbolic wedding (Kalyana) of the deity and his consort was publicly celebrated.

Nayaka architecture (16th–18th centuries) at sites like the Meenakshi-Sundareswarar Temple in Madurai and Ramanathaswamy Temple in Rameswaram did not discontinue covered corridors or sculpted piers; rather, it represents the absolute climax of long, covered concentric Prakara corridors (such as the famous pillared corridor at Rameswaram) and thousand-pillared halls supported by monolithic piers carved in high relief with rearing Yalis (mythical lion-griffins), rampant horses, and royal donor portraits.

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6; NCERT Class XII: Themes in Indian History Part II (An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the temple architecture of the Early Western Chalukyas of Badami:
items: Statement-I: At the royal sacred complex of Pattadakal, temples crowned with curvilinear northern Rekha-Nagara superstructures stand alongside temples built in the southern tiered Dravida Vimana style.
Statement-II: The Durga Temple at Aihole incorporates an apsidal ground plan and a pillared circumambulatory verandah adapted from early Buddhist Chaitya halls.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Early Chalukyan architecture in the Malaprabha valley (Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal) served as an experimental laboratory that juxtaposed Nagara and Dravida idioms and adapted apsidal Buddhist Chaitya layouts into Hindu stone temples, ultimately laying the structural foundation for the hybrid Deccani Vesara tradition.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The 8th-century UNESCO World Heritage complex at Pattadakal demonstrates remarkable architectural eclecticism: four major shrines (including the Galaganatha, Papanatha, Jambulinga, and Kashi Vishwanatha temples) carry northern curvilinear Rekha-Nagara shikharas, while six shrines (most notably the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples commissioned by Queens Lokamahadevi and Trailokyamahadevi) follow the southern tiered Dravida Vimana idiom.

Statement-II is also correct. The Durga Temple at Aihole (late 7th–early 8th century) is a unique architectural experiment featuring an apsidal (Gajaprishtha or elephant-backed semicircular) sanctum and a colonnaded outer ambulatory derived from earlier Buddhist Chaitya-griha architecture, surmounted by an early northern-style curvilinear shikhara. However, Statement-II describes an apsidal ground-plan experiment at Aihole and does not explain why both Nagara and Dravida royal temples were simultaneously patronised at Pattadakal (which stemmed from Chalukyan geopolitical and cultural synthesis at the crossroads of northern post-Gupta and southern Pallava realms, especially after Vikramaditya II's Kanchipuram campaigns).

ref: NCERT Class XI: An Introduction to Indian Art, Ch. 6 (The Deccan - Pattadakal & Aihole)

stem: With reference to Hoysala temple architecture in Karnataka, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The adoption of soft, fine-grained chloritic schist (soapstone) in place of sandstone enabled Hoysala artisans to execute deep undercutting in jewellery motifs and mechanically turn bell-shaped pillars on lathes.
2. The Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu, and Somnathpur are monolithic rock-cut structures excavated downward into granite hills without a raised Jagati platform.
