The Bundi school (which blossomed in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries under rulers like Rao Chattar Sal and Rao Bhao Singh) is renowned for its keen observation of nature—featuring overlapping plantain groves, date palms, lotus-filled ponds with cranes and ducks, and a signature sky treatment where red/crimson ribbons interlock with gold and white clouds.

Statement 2 is correct. Because the Rathore rulers of Bikaner (such as Raja Rai Singh, Karan Singh, and Anup Singh) served as high-ranking Mughal mansabdars and recruited master Muslim painters from the Mughal imperial workshop (such as Ali Raza, Ruknuddin, and Hassan Raza of the Usta lineage), the Bikaner school adopted the Mughal documentary practice of recording the artist's name, father's name, and exact Vikram Samvat date on the painting's verso or margin, alongside setting up a Bahi (archival register).

Statement 3 is incorrect. The spontaneous mastery of dramatic tiger and lion hunting expeditions set inside dense, tangled rocky jungles—where the landscape itself becomes the true protagonist—especially under the reign of Raja Umed Singh (r. 1770-1819), is the hallmark of the Kota school (an offshoot of Bundi), not the Marwar (Jodhpur) school. Marwar painting under rulers like Maharaja Man Singh focused heavily on Nath Charita manuscripts, Dhola-Maru romances, and equestrian portraits with tall spiralling turbans.

ref: NCERT Class XII An Introduction to Indian Art Part-II, Ch. 1 (Rajasthani Schools: Bundi, Kota, Bikaner, Marwar)

stem: With reference to the evolution of the Pahari Schools of miniature painting between the 17th and 18th centuries, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: By the mid-18th century, the Pahari miniature tradition transitioned from the fierce, bold primary colours of the early Basohli idiom to the delicate, lyrical naturalism of the Guler and Kangra styles.

Statement-II: The early Basohli school under Kirpal Pal was renowned for the illustration of Bhanudatta's Rasamanjari by the artist Devidasa and the application of iridescent green beetle wing-cases to simulate emeralds in painted jewellery.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While early Basohli painting is defined by fiery primary colours, receding foreheads, and beetle-wing embellishments, the mid-18th-century shift toward Guler-Kangra lyricism was driven by the influx of Mughal-trained naturalism through the family of Pandit Seu (Manaku and Nainsukh) and the patronage of Raja Sansar Chand.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The earliest phase of Pahari painting in the late 17th century at Basohli exhibited vigorous, expressive figures against flat planes of mustard yellow and red. By the 1740s–1780s, this gave way to the softer, atmospheric, and naturalistic Guler idiom, which matured into the lyrical Kangra school under Raja Sansar Chand (1775–1823).

Statement-II is factually correct, as Devidasa completed the famous Rasamanjari series in 1694–1695 under Raja Kirpal Pal of Basohli, utilizing raised white paint for pearls and actual clipped elytra (wing-cases) of iridescent green beetles to mimic emerald jewels. However, Statement-II describes the technical traits of early Basohli art and does not explain WHY the stylistic shift toward Guler-Kangra naturalism occurred; that transition was caused by the migration of artists trained in the imperial Mughal style (notably Pandit Seu and his sons Manaku and Nainsukh) into the western Himalayan hills following the decline of the Delhi court.

ref: NCERT Class XII: An Introduction to Indian Art Part-II, Ch. 3 (The Pahari Schools of Painting); Nitin Singhania Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following milestones in the history of Indian painting:
items: 1. Execution of the Pandya-period Jain murals at Sittanavasal Cave (Arivar Koil)
2. Compilation and illustration of the Nimatnama (Book of Delicacies) at Mandu in Malwa
3. Earliest surviving mural fragments in Caves 9 and 10 at Ajanta
4. Illustration of Buddhist Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita palm-leaf manuscripts under the Pala rulers
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological sequence of the above milestones, from the earliest to the latest?
core: Indian painting evolved sequentially from the early historic Satavahana murals at Ajanta (2nd–1st century BCE) and early medieval Pandya frescoes at Sittanavasal (9th century CE), to eastern Indian Pala palm-leaf manuscripts (11th–12th century CE) and pre-Mughal Sultanate paper manuscripts like the Malwa Nimatnama (c. 1500 CE).

exp.why: Milestone 1 belongs to the 9th century CE. The extant Jain fresco-secco paintings on the ceiling and pillars of the Sittanavasal cave temple (Pudukkottai, Tamil Nadu)—featuring the famous lotus pond (Khatika-bhumi) with Bhavyas—were extensively renovated and painted during the reign of the Pandya king Srimara Srivallabha (c. 815–862 CE).

Milestone 2 dates to the turn of the 16th century (c. 1495–1505 CE). The Nimatnama, a culinary and survival treatise compiled at Mandu, was initiated under Sultan Ghiyas-ud-din Khalji of Malwa and completed under his son Nasir-ud-din Shah, blending indigenous Western Indian conventions with Turkman/Shirazi Persian elements.

Milestone 3 is the earliest (c. 2nd–1st century BCE). Caves 9 and 10 at Ajanta are Hinayana (Theravada) chaitya halls excavated during the Satavahana period; their surviving mural fragments (such as the Chaddanta Jataka and Shyama Jataka) predated the Vakataka phase by nearly six centuries.

Milestone 4 dates to the 11th and 12th centuries CE. Executed at Buddhist monastic centres like Nalanda, Odantapuri, and Vikramashila under Pala kings such as Mahipala and Ramapala, these palm-leaf miniatures represent the eastern Indian precursor to miniature painting before the widespread adoption of paper. Hence, the correct chronological sequence is 3-1-4-2.

ref: NCERT Class XI & XII: An Introduction to Indian Art Parts I & II; CCRT Indian Painting

stem: With reference to traditional narrative cloth and scroll paintings of India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Srikalahasti Kalamkari : Hand-carved wooden block-printing of vegetable dyes inspired by Persian motifs
2. Machilipatnam Kalamkari : Freehand drawing using a pointed bamboo kalam to depict Hindu temple narratives
3. Raghurajpur Pattachitra : Painting of the Jagannath triad on gauze-layered cloth stiffened with tamarind-seed paste and chalk
4. Phad Painting : Horizontal cloth scrolls of folk deities Pabuji and Devnarayan narrated overnight by Bhopa priest-singers
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Andhra Pradesh's two GI-tagged Kalamkari traditions differ fundamentally in technique: Srikalahasti is an entirely freehand temple-cloth art using a bamboo pen (kalam), whereas Machilipatnam (Pedana) uses hand-carved wooden blocks shaped by Deccani-Persian trade.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. Srikalahasti Kalamkari (Chittoor/Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh) flourished around Hindu temples and relies entirely on freehand drawing and dyeing using a sharp pointed bamboo or date-palm stick (kalam) wrapped in wool to regulate the flow of fermented jaggery-and-iron black dye (kasimi) and alum mordants.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Machilipatnam (Pedana) Kalamkari in Krishna district evolved under Golconda Sultanate and Persian trade contacts; it uses intricately hand-carved teakwood blocks to print outlines and mordants, featuring motifs such as the Tree of Life (Mihrab and cypress patterns) rather than freehand temple scroll narratives.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. In the Raghurajpur heritage craft village of Odisha, Chitrakaras prepare the patta by gluing layers of cotton gauze together with a paste boiled from crushed tamarind seeds (niryas kalpa), coating it with soft clay-stone/chalk powder, burnishing it with pebbles, and painting Vaishnavite and Jagannath themes directly with a brush without preliminary charcoal or pencil sketching.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Phad is a monumental horizontal scroll painting tradition practiced by the Joshi clan of Bhilwara and Shahpura in Rajasthan. The scrolls serve as mobile temples carried by nomadic Bhopa priest-singers and Bhopi women, who illuminate specific episodes with an oil lamp while singing the ballads of Pabuji and Devnarayan to the accompaniment of the ravanahatha.

ref: NCERT Class XI: Living Craft Traditions of India; Nitin Singhania Ch. 2 (Folk Paintings)

stem: With reference to the folk and ritual painting traditions of Eastern India and the Himalayas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In traditional Madhubani (Mithila) paintings, artists paint symbolic motifs in the Kohbar Ghar (bridal chamber) and systematically fill every empty background gap with floral, animal, or geometric patterns.
2. Manjusha paintings of the Bhagalpur region are executed predominantly in deep indigo and charcoal-black shades to depict historic Mughal military campaigns in Bihar.
3. Traditional Himalayan Thangka paintings are executed directly on wet lime-plastered monastery cave walls without using cloth or silk backings.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Madhubani art is characterized by Kohbar ritual iconography and complete filling of background space, whereas Bhagalpur's Manjusha art narrates the Bihula-Bishahari snake folklore strictly in pink, green, and yellow, and Thangkas are portable cotton-canvas scroll paintings mounted in silk brocade.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Madhubani (Mithila) painting originated as domestic ritual wall and floor art (Aripan) by women of the Mithila region. Central to it is the Kohbar Ghar (nuptial chamber) painting depicting purain (lotus ring) and bamboo (bans) symbols of fertility, accompanied by a stylistic horror vacui where no background space is left blank, every gap being filled with flowers, leaves, birds, or geometric borders.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Manjusha art (also known as Angika art) of Bhagalpur, Bihar, is a ritual folk tradition centred on the folklore of Bihula's devotion to save her husband Bala Lakhandar and the appeasement of the snake goddess Bishahari. Far from using indigo and charcoal black to depict Mughal battles, authentic Manjusha art uses strictly three vibrant colours—pink, green, and yellow—with swirling snake motifs painted on temple-shaped jute and paper boxes (manjushas).

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Tibetan word 'Thangka' literally means 'something that is rolled up'. Unlike fixed wall murals, Thangkas are portable scroll paintings executed on a primed cotton canvas (treated with kaolin clay/chalk and animal glue) according to strict Buddhist iconometric grids, and framed in sewn silk brocade mountings for ceremonial display and monastic processions.

ref: NCERT Class XII: An Introduction to Indian Art Part-II, Ch. 8 (The Living Art Traditions of India); CCRT Folk Arts

stem: Consider the following pairs of tribal ritual wall-painting traditions of India and their defining characteristics:
items: 1. Warli Painting : Votive murals of ceremonial horses offered to Baba Pithora by the Rathwa community and sanctified by a Badwa shaman
2. Pithora Painting : Square ritual Chowks enclosing the fertility goddess Palaghata, painted using white rice paste by tribal women of the North Sahyadri range
3. Saura Painting : Anthropomorphic stick figures drawn inside a geometric enclosure (Idital) to appease village deities and ancestors in Odisha
4. Sohrai-Khovar Painting : Harvest and marriage murals created in Hazaribagh using natural earth slips and comb-cut sgraffito techniques
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: India's tribal mural traditions are anchored in distinct community rituals: Warli centers on the square Lagnachowk and mother goddess Palaghata in Maharashtra, Pithora centers on ceremonial horses painted by Rathwa/Bhilala Lakharas in Gujarat-MP, Saura features Idital ritual enclosures in Odisha, and Sohrai-Khovar employs earth-slip sgraffito in Jharkhand.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. Votive murals of ceremonial horses painted by specialized male painters (Lakharas) and ritually consecrated through trance by a chief shaman (Badwa) to fulfill vows to Baba Pithora belong to the Pithora painting tradition of the Rathwa, Bhil, and Bhilala communities of eastern Gujarat (Chhota Udaipur) and western Madhya Pradesh.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The square ritual Lagnachowk (of the Devchowk and Pancha-siriya types) housing the armless marriage and fertility goddess Palaghata—surrounded by scenes of the circular Tarpa dance constructed from two triangles joined at the apex using white rice paste on red geru mud walls—is the hallmark of the Warli tribe of Thane/Palghar districts in Maharashtra and the Gujarat border.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. The Lanjia Saura tribe of southern Odisha (Rayagada and Gajapati districts) creates sacred wall icons known as Idital (or Ikons) inside their homes. Painted by ritual specialists (Iditalmars) with white rice paste on red-ochre clay walls, each Idital acts as a house-like rectangular enclosure populated by human stick figures, horses, sun, moon, and the tree of life to honour deities and ward off illness.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Practiced by indigenous women in the Hazaribagh region of Jharkhand, Sohrai paintings celebrate the post-monsoon cattle and harvest festival using coloured earth clays (red, yellow, black, and white kaolin), while Khovar murals decorate bridal chambers using a distinctive sgraffito technique where wet white clay is combed with fingers or bamboo combs to expose an underlying coat of black manganese earth.

ref: NCERT Class XII: An Introduction to Indian Art Part-II, Ch. 8 (The Living Art Traditions of India)

stem: With reference to the transformation of Indian painting during the colonial and early nationalist periods (18th to early 20th century), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Company School at centres like Patna and Murshidabad, Indian miniature painters shifted from opaque gouache on handmade wasli paper to transparent watercolours on imported European paper to document local flora, fauna, and occupational castes.

2. Kalighat Bazaar paintings of 19th-century Calcutta employed rapid, sweeping brushstrokes on inexpensive mill paper, expanding beyond religious icons to satirize westernized urban babus and corrupt priests.

3. While Raja Ravi Varma synthesized European academic oil realism with Indian Puranic themes and popularized them through his oleograph press, Abanindranath Tagore's Bengal School rejected European oil realism in favour of an indigenous wash technique inspired by Ajanta and Japanese brushwork.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Colonial-era Indian art evolved through three distinct trajectories: the documentary watercolour realism of the Company School, the bold subaltern satire of Kalighat bazaar patuas, and the ideological debate between Raja Ravi Varma's European academic oil realism and Abanindranath Tagore's nationalist Bengal School wash technique.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. As Mughal and provincial courts declined, traditional painters migrated to East India Company hubs such as Murshidabad, Patna (Patna Qalam), Lucknow, and Thanjavur. To suit British patrons' tastes for picturesque documentation and natural history, they replaced traditional opaque mineral tempera on burnished wasli with transparent watercolours, muted sepia/grey washes, shaded volume, and linear perspective on watermarked European paper (such as Whatman paper).

Statement 2 is correct. Rural scroll painters (patuas) who settled around the Kalighat temple in 19th-century Calcutta adapted to urban mass demand by painting single sheets of cheap, machine-made mill paper with bold, fluid outlines and tubular shading. Alongside Hindu deities, they produced biting social caricatures of decadent, anglicized Bengali babus, courtesans, and contemporary scandals such as the Tarakeswar affair.

Statement 3 is correct. Raja Ravi Varma of Travancore mastered European academic oil painting, chiaroscuro, and perspective to give human form to Sanskrit literary and Puranic figures, democratizing this imagery across Indian households via his chromolithographic (oleograph) press established in Bombay in 1894. Reacting against what they viewed as Western materialism in Ravi Varma's oil realism, Abanindranath Tagore and E.B. Havell founded the Bengal School, developing a spiritual, misty 'wash' technique that synthesized Ajanta line-work, Mughal miniature sensibility, and Japanese ink-wash methods learned from Okakura Kakuzo and Yokoyama Taikan.

ref: NCERT Class XII: An Introduction to Indian Art Part-II, Ch. 6 (The Modern Indian Art); Nitin Singhania Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the classification of classical Indian philosophical schools (Darshanas):
items: Statement-I: Both classical Samkhya and early Purva Mimamsa are classified within the Astika (orthodox) fold of Indian philosophy despite rejecting the necessity of a personal Creator God (Ishvara) to explain the genesis of the universe.
Statement-II: Both classical Samkhya and Purva Mimamsa accept the doctrine of moral causation (Karma) and the transmigration of the soul (Samsara).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In the Indian philosophical tradition, the boundary between Astika (orthodox) and Nastika (heterodox) schools is strictly epistemological rather than theological: it rests on the acceptance of the Vedas as an infallible source of valid knowledge (Shabda-pramana), not on theism or belief in Karma.

exp.why: Classical Samkhya (Nirishvara Samkhya) explains cosmic evolution exclusively through the interplay of unconscious Prakriti and conscious Purusha without invoking a Creator God. Similarly, Jaimini's Purva Mimamsa treats the universe and the Vedas as eternal and self-existent, rejecting an omnipotent Creator (Ishvara) who dispenses the fruits of rituals. Yet both are premier Astika schools because they uphold the epistemic authority (Pramanya) of the Vedas.

Both Samkhya and Purva Mimamsa affirm the law of Karma and the cycle of rebirth (Samsara). However, this does not explain why they are classified as Astika, because prominent Nastika (heterodox) systems—specifically Buddhism and Jainism—also rigorously uphold Karma and transmigration while rejecting the epistemic authority of the Vedas.

ref: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, Indian Philosophy Vol. II; NCERT Class XI Introduction to Indian Art & Philosophy

stem: With reference to the metaphysical principles of the Samkhya and Yoga schools of Indian philosophy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the Samkhya system, Purusha is conceptualized as the dynamic, active primordial substance composed of the three Gunas (Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas), whereas Prakriti is the passive and immutable witness-consciousness.

2. According to classical Samkhya, liberation (Kaivalya) from suffering occurs only through the attainment of discriminative knowledge (Viveka-jnana) that realizes the absolute ontological distinction between Purusha and Prakriti.

3. While accepting the dualistic metaphysics and twenty-five cosmic principles (Tattvas) of Samkhya, Patanjali's Yoga system introduces Ishvara as a distinct, transcendent Purusha untouched by afflictions (Kleshas) and karmic fructification.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Samkhya and Yoga share an allied metaphysical framework (Samkhya-Yoga) founded on radical dualism between unconscious, dynamic matter (Prakriti) and plural, immutable pure consciousnesses (Purushas), differing primarily on the inclusion of Ishvara and practical meditative discipline.

exp.why: The ontological roles of Purusha and Prakriti are swapped here. In Samkhya metaphysics, Prakriti (Pradhana) is the unmanifest, dynamic, and unconscious primordial materiality constituted by the equilibrium of the three Gunas (Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas). Purusha is pure, immutable, non-agentive consciousness (Sakshi/witness) entirely devoid of the three Gunas (Trigunatita).

Bondage in Samkhya arises from Aviveka (non-discrimination), whereby the immutable Purusha falsely identifies itself with the modifications of Prakriti (specifically Buddhi/intellect). Consequently, emancipation (Kaivalya or Apavarga) is achieved only when true discriminative cognition (Viveka-khyati or Viveka-jnana) dawns, severing this false identification.

Patanjali's Yoga Darshana is frequently termed 'Seishvara Samkhya' (theistic Samkhya). It adopts the 25 Tattvas of Kapila's Samkhya and adds a 26th principle—Ishvara—defined in the Yoga Sutras (1.24) as a special Purusha (Purusha-vishesha) untouched by afflictions (Klesha), actions (Karma), and their maturation (Vipaka), serving as an ideal object of devotion and concentration (Ishvara-pranidhana).

ref: Ishvarakrishna's Samkhyakarika; Patanjali's Yoga Sutras; M. Hiriyanna, Outlines of Indian Philosophy

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ontology and natural philosophy of the Vaisheshika school:
items: Statement-I: According to the Vaisheshika system of Kanada, all nine fundamental substances (Dravyas)—including ether (Akasha), time (Kala), and space (Dik)—are atomic (Paramanurupa) in constitution and undergo periodic aggregation and dissolution.

Statement-II: Vaisheshika realism explains the genesis of every composite physical object in the universe through the combination of eternal, indivisible, and partless atoms (Paramanus) of earth, water, fire, and air.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Vaisheshika pluralistic realism classifies nine fundamental substances (Dravyas), carefully distinguishing between the four composite-forming atomic physical elements (Prithvi, Ap, Tejas, Vayu) and the non-atomic, all-pervasive (Vibhu) continua (Akasha, Kala, Dik, Atman).

exp.why: In Vaisheshika ontology, not all nine substances (Dravyas) are atomic. Only the first four material elements—earth (Prithvi), water (Ap), fire (Tejas), and air (Vayu)—exist as eternal, indivisible atoms (Paramanus) that combine to form composite objects, while mind (Manas) is atomic in dimension (Anu) but does not form composites. By contrast, ether (Akasha), time (Kala), space (Dik), and the self (Atman) are non-atomic, eternal, partless, and all-pervasive (Vibhu).

Kanada's doctrine of Paramanuvada (atomism) holds that the material cosmos is formed when eternal, partless, and qualitatively distinct Paramanus of earth, water, fire, and air combine initially into dyads (Dvyanuka) and subsequently into perceptible triads (Tryanuka/Trasarenu) and larger aggregates, guided by the unseen moral force (Adrishta) of living beings.

ref: Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutra; Chandradhar Sharma, A Critical Survey of Indian Philosophy

stem: With reference to the Purva Mimamsa school founded by Jaimini, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It propounds the epistemological doctrine of Svatah-pramanya, which holds that the validity of all cognition is intrinsic to the conditions that generate the cognition itself and is not dependent on external verification.

2. It postulates the metaphysical principle of 'Apurva' as an imperceptible potency generated by the proper performance of a Vedic ritual that bridges the temporal gap between the transient act and its deferred fruition.

3. Both the Bhatta and Prabhakara sub-schools of Purva Mimamsa maintain that ultimate liberation (Moksha) requires the complete ascetic renunciation of obligatory Vedic rituals (Nitya-karmas) in favour of pure contemplative knowledge (Jnana).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: To defend the self-existent and infallible authority (Apaurusheyatva) of the Vedic injunctions, Purva Mimamsa developed the epistemological theory of intrinsic validity (Svatah-pramanya), the causal doctrine of Apurva, and the lifelong ethical imperative of obligatory ritual action (Nitya-karma).

exp.why: Purva Mimamsa champions Svatah-pramanya-vada (intrinsic validity of knowledge) in direct opposition to the Nyaya doctrine of Paratah-pramanya (extrinsic validity). According to Mimamsakas, every cognition arises with an inherent presumption of truth; external inference is needed only negatively to detect defects (Dosha) or contradiction (Badha). This secures the unassailable authority of Vedic testimony (Shabda).

Because a sacrificial ritual perishes as soon as its performance concludes whereas its promised reward (such as Svarga/heaven) materializes in the distant future, Jaimini and later Mimamsakas formulated the concept of 'Apurva'—an unseen transcendental potency generated in the performer's soul (or in the action) that endures until it produces the merited fruit without needing a supervisory God.

This statement inverts the core orthodoxy of Purva Mimamsa and confuses it with Advaita Vedanta. Both Kumarila Bhatta (Bhatta school) and Prabhakara Mishra (Prabhakara school) strictly oppose the ascetic renunciation (Sannyasa) of obligatory Vedic duties (Nitya and Naimittika karmas). While a seeker of liberation must abstain from desire-prompted (Kamya) and prohibited (Nishiddha) actions to halt new karmic bondage, obligatory rituals must be performed throughout life to avoid the sin of omission (Pratyavaya).

ref: Jaimini's Mimamsa Sutra; Surendranath Dasgupta, A History of Indian Philosophy Vol. I

stem: Consider the following pairs of sub-schools of Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta) and their core metaphysical doctrines regarding Brahman, the individual soul (Jiva), and the universe (Jagat):
items: 1. Advaita (Adi Shankara) : Vivartavada (Apparent, non-real transformation of immutable Brahman into the phenomenal world through Maya)
2. Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja) : Pancha-bheda (Five-fold eternal and absolute ontological distinctions between God, individual souls, and inanimate matter)
3. Dvaita (Madhvacharya) : Prakara-Prakari Bhava (Sentient souls and insentient matter constitute the real internal body and inseparable modes qualifying the one non-dual Brahman)
4. Shuddhadvaita (Vallabhacharya) : Avikrita-Parinamavada (Pure non-dualism wherein Brahman manifests as the real universe without undergoing internal modification or involving the illusion of Maya)
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: The sub-schools of Vedanta diverge over whether the causal emergence of the world from Brahman is an illusory appearance (Vivartavada in Advaita), a real organic qualification of Brahman's body (Prakara-Prakari in Vishishtadvaita), an unmodified pure manifestation (Avikrita-Parinamavada in Shuddhadvaita), or wholly distinct creation under five eternal differences (Pancha-bheda in Dvaita).

exp.why: Adi Shankara's Advaita Vedanta explains the appearance of the pluralistic universe (Jagat) through Vivartavada—the doctrine of apparent or illusory superimposition (Adhyasa), analogous to a rope appearing as a snake, whereby Nirguna Brahman remains wholly unchanged while appearing as the world through the cosmic principle of Maya.

Pancha-bheda (five-fold eternal differences: between Ishvara and Jiva, Ishvara and Jada, Jiva and Jiva, Jiva and Jada, and Jada and Jada) is the foundational doctrine of Madhvacharya's Dvaita (dualistic) Vedanta, not Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita.

Prakara-Prakari Bhava (and Sharira-Shariri Bhava, the body-soul relationship) belongs to Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism), wherein sentient souls (Chit) and insentient matter (Achit) are real attributes (Prakara) forming the cosmic body of Lord Narayana (Prakari). Madhvacharya's Dvaita categorically rejects any non-dual organic unity or body-soul identity between Brahman and the world.

Vallabhacharya's Shuddhadvaita (Pure Non-Dualism) purges Vedanta of Shankara's concept of Maya. Through Avikrita-Parinamavada (unmodified transformation), he argues that the universe and individual souls are real, direct manifestations of Brahman (comparing them to sparks emerging from fire or ornaments shaped from pure gold) in which the attributes of Sat, Chit, and Ananda are selectively concealed (Tirobhava) and revealed (Avirbhava) without tainting Brahman's purity.

ref: Badarayana's Brahmasutra; S.N. Dasgupta, A History of Indian Philosophy Vols. III & IV

stem: With reference to the classical treatises and commentaries of the Six Schools of Indian Philosophy (Shad-Darshana), consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Samkhyakarika of Ishvarakrishna : Samkhya Darshana
2. Padarthadharmasangraha of Prashastapada : Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta) Darshana
3. Nyayabhashya of Vatsyayana : Yoga Darshana
4. Slokavarttika of Kumarila Bhatta : Purva Mimamsa Darshana
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Each classical Darshana evolved through a stratified textual tradition comprising foundational aphorisms (Sutras), primary commentaries (Bhashyas) or systematic compendia (Prakaranas), and critical sub-commentaries (Varttikas).

exp.why: Composed by Ishvarakrishna (circa 4th–5th century CE), the Samkhyakarika is the earliest surviving, authoritative metrical text of the classical Samkhya school, systematically presenting its dualistic metaphysics and theory of causation (Satkaryavada).

Prashastapada's Padarthadharmasangraha (also known as the Prashastapadabhashya, circa 6th century CE) is the foundational systematic compendium of the Vaisheshika school (reorganizing Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutra into an analytical treatise on the categories/Padarthas), not Uttara Mimamsa.

Paksilasvamin Vatsyayana's Nyayabhashya is the earliest extant classical commentary on Gautama's Nyaya Sutras (belonging to the Nyaya Darshana). The primary classical Bhashya on Patanjali's Yoga Sutras is the Vyasa-bhashya (Yogabhashya) attributed to Vyasa.

The Slokavarttika (along with the Tantravarttika and Tuptika) was authored by Kumarila Bhatta (7th century CE) as an extensive critical sub-commentary on Shabara's Bhashya on Jaimini's Purva Mimamsa Sutras, establishing the Bhatta school of Purva Mimamsa.

ref: A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India; M. Hiriyanna, Outlines of Indian Philosophy

stem: With reference to Bharata Muni's Natyashastra and its foundational framework of Indian performing arts, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In synthesising the Natyaveda as the Panchama Veda, Brahma derived the element of Pathya (recitation and spoken text) from the Rigveda and Gita (melody and song) from the Samaveda.

2. In the Vedic synthesis of the Natyashastra, the element of Abhinaya (mimetic gesture and histrionic action) was drawn from the Atharvaveda, whereas Rasa (aesthetic sentiment) was derived from the Yajurveda.

3. Within the fourfold scheme of Chaturvidha Abhinaya, Aharya Abhinaya communicates through external costume, make-up, and stage properties, while Sattvika Abhinaya manifests involuntary psycho-physical states arising from inner emotional identification.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Bharata Muni's Natyashastra conceptualises drama (Natya) as a fifth Veda (Panchama Veda) accessible to all varnas, synthesising Pathya from the Rigveda, Gita from the Samaveda, Abhinaya from the Yajurveda, and Rasa from the Atharvaveda, communicated through four channels of histrionic expression (Chaturvidha Abhinaya).

exp.why: Chapter 1 of the Natyashastra (Natyotpatti) records that Brahma created the Natyaveda by extracting Pathya (recitative text and dialogue) from the Rigveda and Gita (musical melody and chant) from the Samaveda.

This statement interchanges the contributions of the Yajurveda and the Atharvaveda. Because the Yajurveda is the Veda of sacrificial ritual action (Karma-kanda) involving physical postures and gestures of priests, Brahma derived Abhinaya (mimetic gesture and physical enactment) from the Yajurveda, whereas Rasa (aesthetic sentiment and psychological states) was extracted from the Atharvaveda.

Chaturvidha Abhinaya comprises Angika (bodily movement and mudras), Vachika (speech, intonation, and song), Aharya (costume, jewellery, make-up, and stage props), and Sattvika (eight involuntary psycho-physical manifestations such as tears, horripilation, trembling, or pallor born of genuine inner concentration).

ref: Natyashastra of Bharata Muni, Chapter 1 & Chapter 6; NCERT Class XI Introduction to Indian Art

stem: With reference to the classical treatises on Indian performing arts such as Bharata Muni's Natyashastra and Nandikeshvara's Abhinaya Darpana, which one of the following statements accurately distinguishes the triadic categories of Nritta, Nritya, and Natya?

opts.A: Nritta is the interpretative dance form that conveys specific Rasas and Bhavas through facial expressions and Hasta-mudras, whereas Nritya consists exclusively of abstract rhythmic footwork devoid of semantic meaning.
opts.B: Tandava and Lasya are dramatic modes restricted exclusively to Natya and cannot be executed within the rhythmic structure of Nritta or the expressive framework of Nritya.
opts.C: Nritta comprises pure, abstract rhythmic movement based on Tala and Laya without narrative mood, Nritya integrates rhythmic movement with mimetic expression (Abhinaya) to convey semantic meaning and Bhava, and Natya encompasses full dramatic representation combining plot, character impersonation, and speech.
opts.D: Natya relies solely on Angika Abhinaya without Vachika or Sattvika elements, whereas Nritta requires all four branches of Chaturvidha Abhinaya to narrate mythological episodes.

core: Classical Indian dance architecture rests on the triad of Nritta (pure abstract rhythm and geometry of movement devoid of narrative Bhava), Nritya (expressive dance translating poetic lyrics into Bhava and Rasa through Abhinaya and Hasta-mudras), and Natya (complete dramatic theatre integrating word, music, and character representation).

exp.why: Option C is correct because Nandikeshvara's Abhinaya Darpana and Dhananjaya's Dasharupaka explicitly define Nritta as 'Bhaava-vihinam' (devoid of narrative mood or specific semantic meaning), focusing on pure rhythmic patterns (Adavus, Tukdas, Toras) governed by Tala (time-cycle) and Laya (tempo). Nritya ('Rasa-bhava-vyanjakam') blends rhythmic movement with Mukhajabhinaya (facial expressions) and Hasta-mudras (hand gestures) to interpret poetry and evoke Bhava and Rasa. Natya represents the overarching dramatic art involving plot (Itivritta), character impersonation (Anukarana), and spoken/sung dialogue. Option A is incorrect as it swaps Nritta and Nritya. Option B is incorrect because both Tandava (vigorous, cosmic, masculine energy codified via Tandu) and Lasya (graceful, lyrical, feminine energy associated with Parvati) permeate Nritta and Nritya alike. Option D is incorrect because Natya employs all four forms of Abhinaya (including Vachika and Sattvika), whereas Nritta relies primarily on Angika movement and Aharya presentation without narrative Vachika.

ref: Abhinaya Darpana of Nandikeshvara; CCRT Classical Dances of India

stem: Consider the following landmark milestones in the historical evolution of Indian classical musicology:
items: 1. First formal technical definition of the term 'Raga' as a specific melodic structure that colours and delights the mind of listeners, alongside the systematic differentiation between Marga (celestial/canonical) and Desi (regional) music.
2. Formulation of the mathematical scheme of 72 Melakarta (Janaka) parent scales based on systematic permutations of the twelve semitones (Swarasthanas) of the octave.

3. Codification of Gandharva music, the two foundational parent scales (Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama), and the demonstration of 22 microtonal intervals (Shrutis) through the two-Vina (Dhruva and Chala Vina) experiment.

4. Composition of the encyclopaedic seven-chapter Saptadhyayi at the Yadava court of Devagiri, serving as the last major shared textual authority before the clear divergence of the Hindustani and Carnatic systems.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the musicological milestones given above (from earliest to latest)?
core: Indian musicological grammar evolved sequentially from the Grama-Murchhana-Jati system of Bharata's Natyashastra (c. 200 BCE–200 CE), to Matanga's formalisation of Raga and Desi music in the Brihaddeshi (c. 6th–8th century CE), Sarangadeva's encyclopaedic Sangita Ratnakara (13th century CE), and Venkatamakhin's 72 Melakarta matrix in the Chaturdandi Prakashika (17th century CE).

exp.why: Milestone 1 refers to Matanga Muni's Brihaddeshi (c. 6th–8th century CE). While earlier texts like the Natyashastra focused on Jatis (melodic archetypes), Matanga was the first musicologist to define 'Raga' scientifically ('Yo'sau dhvanivisheshastu svaravarnavibhushitah, ranjako janachittanam sa cha raga udahrtah') and to classify regional musical traditions under Desi Sangita.

Milestone 2 refers to Venkatamakhin's Chaturdandi Prakashika (composed c. 1660 CE under Nayaka patronage at Thanjavur), which established the 72 Melakarta (Katapayadi Sankhya was later integrated) mathematical matrix of Sampurna parent scales using Shuddha and Prati Madhyama divisions.

Milestone 3 is the earliest milestone, found in Chapters 28–33 of Bharata Muni's Natyashastra (c. 200 BCE–200 CE). Bharata codified Gandharva/Marga music, detailed the Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama scales, and empirically proved the 22 Shrutis per octave using two identically tuned Vinas (Dhruva Vina kept fixed and Chala Vina progressively shifted by one Pramana Shruti).

Milestone 4 refers to Sarangadeva's Sangita Ratnakara (also called Saptadhyayi for its seven chapters covering Swara, Raga, Prakirnaka, Prabandha, Tala, Vadya, and Nartana), composed in the first half of the 13th century CE under the Yadava ruler Singhana II at Devagiri. Thus, the chronological order is 3 -> 1 -> 4 -> 2.

ref: N.A. Jairazbhoy, The Rags of North Indian Music; P. Sambamoorthy, History of Indian Music

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the structural and aesthetic grammar of Hindustani and Carnatic classical music:
items: Statement-I: Hindustani classical music strongly enforces the Raga-Samay (time-theory) protocol associating Ragas with specific Prahars of the day or night, whereas modern Carnatic concert performance permits Ragas to be rendered without rigid diurnal time restrictions.

Statement-II: Hindustani music organises its Ragas under ten heuristic parent Thaats and anchors melodic progression around diurnal note indicators such as the shift between Shuddha and Tivra Madhyama (the Adhvadarshak Swara) and Sandhiprakash tonalities, whereas Carnatic music prioritises the mathematical completeness of the 72 Melakarta (Janaka-Janya) pitch matrix and Kriti-centred Manodharma improvisation.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Hindustani classical music subordinates scale classification (10 Thaats) to a diurnal psycho-acoustic cycle (Raga-Samay Chakra) governed by the position of the Vadi swara (Purvanga vs Uttaranga) and the Madhyama (Adhvadarshak Swara), whereas Carnatic music organises Ragas through the 72 Melakarta mathematical matrix and Kriti-anchored Manodharma Sangita without strict time-of-day restrictions.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. In the Hindustani classical tradition, each Raga is mapped to one of the eight three-hour Prahars of the day/night cycle or to a specific season (such as Malhar in the monsoon or Basant/Bahar in spring), and performing a morning Raga like Bhairav at night is considered an aesthetic breach. Conversely, while historical treatises mentioned time associations, contemporary Carnatic concert practice allows any Raga to be performed at any hour.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains the structural reason behind Statement-I. As codified by Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande, Hindustani Raga grammar revolves around ten Thaats and a diurnal cycle where the fourth note, Madhyama, acts as the 'Adhvadarshak Swara' (time-guiding note—Shuddha Ma predominating in morning/late-night Ragas and Tivra Ma in evening Ragas), alongside twilight 'Sandhiprakash' Ragas employing Komal Re and Komal Dha. In contrast, Carnatic music focuses on the exhaustive mathematical symmetry of Venkatamakhin's 72 Melakarta (Janaka) and Janya scales and channels extempore improvisation (Manodharma Sangita—comprising Raga Alapana, Neraval, Kalpanaswaram, and Ragam-Tanam-Pallavi) around lyrical Kritis rather than diurnal Prahar constraints.

ref: V.N. Bhatkhande, Hindustani Sangeet Paddhati; P. Sambamoorthy, South Indian Music

stem: With reference to the major vocal genres of Hindustani classical music, consider the following statements comparing Dhrupad and Khayal:
items: 1. A classical Dhrupad performance begins with an elaborate, unmetered, syllable-based Nom-Tom Alap followed sequentially by Jod and Jhala, and its rhythmic cycle is traditionally accompanied on the Pakhawaj.
2. The four classical stylistic lineages known as Vanis or Banis—namely Gauhar, Khandar, Nauhar, and Dagar—historically belong to the Dhrupad tradition.
3. The Gwalior Gharana, regarded as the oldest Gharana of Khayal gayaki, was founded in the mid-nineteenth century by Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh to blend Thumri elements into Dhrupad.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Dhrupad is an austere, meditative vocal form structured around a prolonged Nom-Tom Alap (Alap-Jod-Jhala), a four-part Bandish (Sthayi, Antara, Sanchari, Abhog) accompanied by the Pakhawaj, and classified into four Vanis (Gauhar, Khandar, Nauhar, Dagar), whereas Khayal emphasises ornate melodic improvisation (Bada and Chhota Khayal) with Tabla accompaniment across Gharanas led earliest by Gwalior.

exp.why: Dhrupad places primary emphasis on Raga purity and microtonal precision through an expansive unmetered Alap articulated using abstract sacred syllables derived from the mantra 'Om Anant Hari Narayana' (Nom-Tom), progressing into rhythmic pulse (Jod) and fast climax (Jhala), before the composed Bandish set to Talas like Chautal (12 beats) accompanied on the barrel-shaped Pakhawaj.

During the Mughal and Rajput court eras (traditionally traced to Swami Haridas, Mian Tansen, and Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior), Dhrupad crystallised into four stylistic Vanis/Banis: Gauhar Vani (serene, slow, and alap-centric), Khandar Vani (vigorous and rich in gamaka), Nauhar Vani (characterised by agile leaps or Chhut across octaves), and Dagar Vani (subtle, lyrical meend-oriented rendering).

The Gwalior Gharana—the mother Gharana of Khayal singing—was established by Nathan Peerbaksh and his grandsons Haddu Khan, Hassu Khan, and Natthu Khan under the patronage of the Scindia rulers of Gwalior, not by Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh. Nawab Wajid Ali Shah (pen-name 'Akhtarpiya') was instead the foremost royal patron and composer of the Lucknow Thumri and Kathak traditions.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art; Sangeet Natak Akademi Compendium on Hindustani Music

stem: With reference to classical and semi-classical vocal genres of North Indian (Hindustani) music, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Thumri prioritises lyrical emotion (Bhava) and Bol-banav in lighter ragas such as Khamaj, Kafi, and Bhairavi, Dhamar is an older form strictly anchored to the 14-beat Dhamar Tala whose compositions predominantly depict Krishna's play of Holi in Braj.

2. Tappa originated from the folk melodies of camel riders in the North-West and Punjab region and was refined into a courtly classical vocal form featuring rapid, knotty melodic turns by Mian Ghulam Nabi Shori.

3. Between the two major regional styles of Thumri, the Purbi (Benaras) Ang is characterised by fast, mercurial, Tappa-style intricate Tans, whereas the Punjabi Ang is slow, sober, and dominated by folk-inflected Bol-alapi.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Semi-classical Hindustani genres relax rigid raga rules to foreground emotional expression (Thumri) or virtuosic rhythmic-melodic agility (Tappa), while Dhamar (Hori) preserves the austere Dhrupad idiom within the asymmetrical 14-beat Dhamar Tala.

exp.why: Thumri focuses on Shringara and Bhakti Rasa through 'Bol-banav' (improvising myriad emotional shades on a single poetic phrase in Brajbhasha or Awadhi), freely blending notes in light ragas like Bhairavi, Kafi, Khamaj, Pilu, and Desh. Dhamar (often called Hori-Dhamar) is closely allied to Dhrupad, accompanied on the Pakhawaj in the asymmetrical 14-beat Dhamar Tala (5+2+3+4), with lyrics celebrating the spring festival of Holi associated with Lord Krishna.

Tappa evolved from the Punjabi/Pashto folk songs of camel drivers ('Dapa') and was elevated to a sophisticated court genre in the late 18th century by Mian Ghulam Nabi Shori ('Shori Mian') at the court of Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula of Awadh. It is renowned for rapid, rolling, zig-zag ornamentations (Zamzama and Gitkiri) executed with minimal slow progression.

This statement reverses the stylistic traits of Purbi (Benaras) and Punjabi Thumri. The Purbi (Benaras) Ang is slow-paced, serene, and deeply rooted in Bol-alapi and folk genres of the eastern Gangetic plains (such as Chaiti, Kajri, and Sawani), whereas the Punjabi Ang (popularised by stalwarts like Ustad Bade Ghulam Ali Khan of the Patiala Gharana) is marked by lively tempo, heavy use of Tappa-influenced mercurial Tans, Murkis, and intricate vocal acrobatics.

ref: Peter Manuel, Thumri in Historical and Stylistic Perspectives; CCRT Performing Arts Resource

stem: With reference to the historical evolution, pedagogy, and compositional architecture of Carnatic classical music, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: Purandara Dasa, the eldest among the eighteenth-century Tiruvarur Trinity, composed the famous Telugu Pancharatna Kritis in praise of Lord Rama using the signature mudra 'Shyama Krishna'.
opts.B: Tyagaraja systematized the foundational graded beginner exercises (Sarali Varisai and Janta Varisai) in the Mayamalavagowla raga and standardized the Suladi Sapta Talas for musical pedagogy.
opts.C: In a traditional Carnatic concert, the Ragam-Tanam-Pallavi serves as the opening warm-up composition with pre-composed lyrics across all sections, whereas the Varnam is the late-concert centerpiece reserved exclusively for manodharma (improvisation).
opts.D: Muthuswami Dikshitar, the youngest of the Carnatic Trinity, composed predominantly in Sanskrit in the slow-tempo Vainika style using the signature mudra 'Guruguha' and assimilated several Hindustani ragas into the Carnatic repertoire.

core: Carnatic classical music rests on the 16th-century pedagogical foundation laid by Purandara Dasa (Pitamaha) and the 18th–19th-century compositional zenith of the Tiruvarur Trinity (Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri). Each member of the Trinity possessed a distinct linguistic medium, rhythmic preference, and signature mudra, while the concert format moves structurally from the pre-composed Varnam to the improvisational pinnacle of Ragam-Tanam-Pallavi.

exp.why: Option D is correct: Muthuswami Dikshitar (1775–1835), the youngest of the Tiruvarur Trinity, spent his formative years in Varanasi where he was exposed to Hindustani Dhrupad music. Consequently, he assimilated Hindustani ragas (such as Yamuna Kalyani, Hamir Kalyani, and Brindavana Saranga) into the Carnatic fold, composed predominantly in scholarly Sanskrit rather than Telugu, favoured the contemplative slow-tempo (Chauka Kala) Vainika style suited to the Veena with rich gamakas, and signed his kritis with the mudra 'Guruguha' (referring to Lord Subrahmanya). Option A is incorrect (Trap T6): Purandara Dasa (1484–1564) belonged to the Vijayanagara era and is revered as the 'Sangeeta Pitamaha' (Grandfather of Carnatic Music), not part of the 18th-century Tiruvarur Trinity; the Telugu Pancharatna Kritis in praise of Lord Rama were composed by Tyagaraja, while 'Shyama Krishna' was the mudra of Syama Sastri. Option B is incorrect (Trap T6): It was Purandara Dasa, not Tyagaraja, who codified the beginner pedagogical framework—Sarali Varisai, Janta Varisai, Dhattu Varisai, Alankaras in the Suladi Sapta Talas, and Pillari Geethams—set in the symmetrical Mayamalavagowla raga. Option C is incorrect (Trap T6): The Varnam is performed at the opening of a Carnatic concert as a scholarly warm-up piece uniting sahitya (lyrics) and swara passages, whereas Ragam-Tanam-Pallavi (RTP) is the supreme centerpiece of manodharma (improvisational music) performed in the latter half of a concert.

ref: NCERT Class XI Introduction to Indian Art; CCRT Classical Music of India; Nitin Singhania Art & Culture Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the classical dance forms of Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The sequential concert repertoire (Margam) of modern Bharatanatyam—progressing from Alarippu to Tillana—was standardized in the nineteenth century by the Tanjore Quartet.
2. Kuchipudi was systematized as a Vaishnavite dance-drama tradition by Siddhendra Yogi, who composed 'Bhamakalapam' based on themes from the Bhagavata Purana.

3. Unlike Kuchipudi, which strictly separates the dancer from vocal delivery, a traditional Bharatanatyam solo requires the dancer to personally execute Vachika Abhinaya on stage while balancing on the edges of a brass plate (Tarangam).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While both Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi adhere to the principles of Bharata's Natyashastra and Nandikeshvara's Abhinaya Darpana, they differ structurally in their origins as solo temple Dasiattam versus Vaishnavite Bhagavata Mela dance-drama. Kuchipudi uniquely retains dramatic Vachika Abhinaya (spoken dialogue/singing by the dancer) and stylized Lokadharmi/Chitrabhinaya feats like the Tarangam.

exp.why: In the early 19th century, the four brothers of the Tanjore Quartet—Chinnayya, Ponnayya, Sivanandam, and Vadivelu—under the patronage of the Maratha rulers of Thanjavur (especially Serfoji II), codified the modern Bharatanatyam concert Margam: Alarippu (invocation), Jatiswaram (melody and rhythm), Shabdam (introductory abhinaya), Varnam (the complex combination of Nritta and Nritya), Padam/Javali (expressive lyrical pieces), and Tillana (pure rhythmic finale).

In the 17th century, the Vaishnavite poet-saint Siddhendra Yogi systematized the Kuchipudi dance-drama tradition in the village of Kuchelapuram (Andhra Pradesh). Drawing inspiration from Narayana Teertha and the Bhagavata Purana, he trained young Brahmin boys (Bhagavathalu) and composed 'Bhamakalapam', centered on the proud consort of Lord Krishna, Satyabhama.

The attributes are reversed between the two dances. Because Kuchipudi evolved from the Yakshagana and Bhagavata Mela dance-drama tradition, the Kuchipudi dancer historically executes Vachika Abhinaya (speaking dialogues and singing on stage) in addition to Angika, Aharya, and Sattvika Abhinaya. Furthermore, 'Tarangam'—where the dancer balances their feet on the rim of a brass plate (Kanchu Thambalam) often with a pot of water (Kindi) on the head, set to verses from Narayana Teertha's 'Krishna Lila Tarangini'—is a hallmark of Kuchipudi, not Bharatanatyam.

ref: Sangeet Natak Akademi Compendium on Classical Dances; CCRT Performing Arts (Bharatanatyam & Kuchipudi)

stem: With reference to the Eastern and North-Eastern classical dance traditions of Odissi and Sattriya, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Odissi represents the Odra-Magadhi style mentioned in the Natyashastra and is structurally built around two contrasting basic postures—the asymmetrical three-bend 'Tribhanga' and the square 'Chowk' stance.

2. While Sattriya was introduced in the fifteenth century by Srimanta Sankardev as part of one-act plays called 'Ankia Naat', the term 'Mati-Akhora' refers to the devotional Sanskrit hymns sung exclusively by female Mahari temple dancers in Odisha.

3. Historically, 'Gotipuas' were celibate male monks who performed ritual dances inside the Vaishnava monasteries (Sattras) of Assam, whereas 'Bhokots' were young boys dressed as females who performed acrobatic dances in Odisha.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Both Odissi and Sattriya are deeply rooted in Vaishnavite Bhakti traditions, yet they evolved within distinct institutional frameworks: Odissi transitioned from female temple Maharis to young acrobatic Gotipua boys in Odisha, whereas Sattriya was institutionalized by Srimanta Sankardev within Assamese Sattras (monasteries) and maintained by celibate male monks (Bhokots) trained in Mati-Akhora.

exp.why: Bharata's Natyashastra identifies 'Odra-Magadhi' as the regional vritti/pravritti of eastern India, which serves as the progenitor of Odissi. The movement grammar of Odissi revolves around two foundational stances: the feminine, sinuous 'Tribhanga' (independent deflection of the head, torso, and hips creating an S-curve) and the masculine, weight-grounded square posture 'Chowk' (symbolizing the iconic form of Lord Jagannath of Puri).

Although Sattriya was indeed introduced in the 15th century by the Neo-Vaishnavite reformer Srimanta Sankardev in Assam as an integral component of 'Ankia Naat' (one-act plays performed in the Brajawali language), 'Mati-Akhora' (literally 'ground exercises') is the foundational physical, gymnastic, and dance-posture grammar of Sattriya taught in the Assamese Sattras—not devotional hymns sung by Odisha's Mahari dancers.

The historical terms are swapped between the two traditions. 'Bhokots' were the celibate male monks living inside the Vaishnava monasteries (Sattras) of Assam who preserved and performed Sattriya as a daily ritual ('Nitya-Prasanga'). Conversely, 'Gotipuas' (literally 'single boy' in Odia) were young boys in Odisha who dressed as female dancers to perform Vaishnavite lyrics and acrobatic Bandha Nritya outside temples when the Mahari (Devadasi) tradition declined.

ref: CCRT Classical Dances of India (Odissi & Sattriya); Sangeet Natak Akademi Guidelines

stem: With reference to the classical dance traditions of Kerala—Kathakali and Mohiniyattam—consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Kathakali, the dancer maintains complete vocal silence on stage, leaving the narrative singing of Manipravalam verses to the vocalists while executing Angika and Sattvika Abhinaya through intricate facial and ocular expressions of the Navarasas.

2. Mohiniyattam blends the formal grace of Bharatanatyam with the expressive vigour of Kathakali, while keeping its movement vocabulary (Atavus) predominantly Lasya-oriented without heavy thumping footwork.

3. Under the traditional Vesham make-up code of Kathakali, 'Kari' (black facial paint) denotes noble, divine, and heroic characters such as Rama and Krishna, whereas 'Pacha' (green facial paint) represents demonic characters and forest huntresses.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Kerala's two classical dances embody complementary aesthetic poles: Kathakali is a stylized, martial-rooted (Kalaripayattu) Tandava-predominant dance-drama with codified gunas-based facial make-up (Vesham), whereas Mohiniyattam is a solo Lasya dance characterized by undulating circular movements (Andolika) resembling swaying palm fronds and gentle ocean waves.

exp.why: In Kathakali, there is a strict division of labour between Vachika (vocal delivery) and Angika/Sattvika Abhinaya. Two backstage vocalists (Ponnani and Sinkidi) sing the Attakatha text—composed in Manipravalam, a literary blend of Sanskrit and Malayalam—accompanied by the percussion instruments Chenda, Maddalam, Chengila (gong), and Ilathalam (cymbals). The actor-dancer never speaks, relying instead on 24 mudras (derived from the Hastalakshana Deepika) and micro-muscular control of the eyes, eyebrows, and cheeks to project the Nine Rasas (Navarasas).

Codified under the patronage of Maharaja Swathi Thirunal of Travancore and Vadivelu (of the Tanjore Quartet) and later revived by Vallathol Narayana Menon at Kerala Kalamandalam, Mohiniyattam combines the structural discipline of Bharatanatyam with the ocular expressiveness of Kathakali. Its roughly 40 foundational movements (Atavus) are strictly Lasya (feminine and graceful), characterized by soft footwork and gentle swaying of the torso without abrupt jerks or loud rhythmic stamping.

The symbolic colour coding of Kathakali's Vesham (make-up) is reversed in this statement. 'Pacha' (emerald green face framed by a white rice-paste ridge called Chutti) signifies Sattvika (noble, divine, and virtuous) characters such as Lord Rama, Lord Krishna, Arjuna, and Nala. Conversely, 'Kari' (carbon-black facial paint) signifies Tamasika characters of the lowest and most ferocious order, such as demonesses (Surpanakha, Putana) and forest huntresses.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art; CCRT Kathakali & Mohiniyattam

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the classical dance forms of Kathak and Manipuri:
items: Statement-I: While Kathak is biomechanically characterized by straight-legged, flat-footed rhythmic footwork (Tatkar), heavy ankle bells (Ghungroos), and rapid pirouettes (Chakkars), Manipuri Raslila is marked by continuous figure-of-eight torso movements (Nagabandha mudra), soft landings on the balls of the feet with flexed knees, and the complete absence of ankle bells.

Statement-II: Manipuri dance completely eschews the masculine Tandava aspect because it originated solely as a secular court entertainment under the eighteenth-century ruler Rajarshi Bhagyachandra, devoid of any ritualistic or martial lineage.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Kathak and Manipuri represent contrasting biomechanical strategies in Indian classical dance: Kathak emphasizes verticality, percussive footwork with heavy Ghungroos, and geometric spins, whereas Manipuri emphasizes fluid, continuous kinetic loops (Nagabandha) and unaccented footfalls without ankle bells to reflect humble Vaishnavite devotion (Bhakti). Yet Manipuri retains a vigorous Tandava counterpart in Pung Cholom, Kartal Cholom, and Thang-Ta.

exp.why: Kathak operates on a vertical axis with knees kept straight (non-flexed), generating complex percussive patterns through flat-footed stamping (Tatkar) amplified by 100–200 ankle bells (Ghungroos) on each leg and punctuated by rapid axial spins (Chakkars) ending in dramatic freezes (Sam). In stark contrast, Manipuri Raslila prohibits ankle bells and hard stamping of the feet against Mother Earth; dancers keep their knees gently bent, alight softly on the toes/balls of the feet first, and weave their body and wrists in continuous figure-of-eight serpentine loops known as the 'Nagabandha' mudra.

Manipuri neither eschews Tandava elements nor originated as a secular court entertainment. First, Manipuri is deeply ritualistic and sacred, evolving from ancient pre-Vaishnavite Meitei 'Lai Haraoba' rituals (performed by Maibis) and later synthesized with Gaudiya Vaishnavism by the 18th-century king Rajarshi Bhagyachandra, who designed the Raslila and the cylindrical Kumil/Potloi costume as an act of religious devotion. Second, Manipuri possesses a dynamic Tandava repertoire alongside Lasya, prominently displayed in 'Pung Cholom' (acrobatic drum dance), 'Kartal Cholom' (cymbal dance) of the Sankirtana tradition, and its organic kinship with the Meitei martial art 'Thang-Ta'.

ref: Sangeet Natak Akademi Monograph on Manipuri & Kathak; CCRT Performing Arts

stem: With reference to the musical, literary, and sculptural synthesis across the Classical Dances of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi are performed to the classical Carnatic system of music, other classical dances employ distinct regional musical traditions such as Sopana Sangeetham in Kathakali and Mohiniyattam, Borgeets in Sattriya, and Odissi Sangita in Odissi.

2. Alongside the sculptural codification of Natyashastra 'Karanas' on the temple walls of Chidambaram and Thanjavur Brihadishvara, Jayadeva's twelfth-century Sanskrit poem 'Gita Govinda' serves as a shared literary anchor across Odissi, Manipuri, Kathakali, and Bharatanatyam.

3. Although Kathak uniquely bridges Hindu temple storytelling (Kathakars) and Persian-Mughal court aesthetics, its patronage under the Mughal emperors and the Nawabs of Awadh led to the complete abandonment of Vaishnavite Radha-Krishna devotional themes in its classical Thumri and Gat-Bhava repertoire.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's eight classical dances share deep pan-Indian structural links—such as the 108 Karanas of the Natyashastra sculpted in Chola temples and the lyrical Ashtapadis of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda—while maintaining distinct musical ecosystems. In North India, Kathak achieved a syncretic fusion where Persian-Mughal court artistry coexisted with, rather than erased, Vaishnavite Radha-Krishna Bhakti.

exp.why: The musical accompaniment of Indian classical dances follows distinct classical and regional streams: Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi strictly utilize the Carnatic raga-tala framework; Kathak utilizes Hindustani classical music (Dhrupad, Tarana, Thumri, Dadra); Kathakali and Mohiniyattam utilize Kerala's indigenous temple vocal tradition 'Sopana Sangeetham' (increasingly blended with Carnatic ragas in Mohiniyattam); Sattriya relies on 'Borgeets' (devotional songs composed by Srimanta Sankardev and Madhavdev in specific ragas and talas accompanied by Khol and cymbals); and Odissi uses 'Odissi Sangita', which integrates elements of both Hindustani and Carnatic music.

Visual and literary canons unify Indian classical dance across regions. Sculpturally, the 108 'Karanas' (coordinated units of hand, foot, and hip movements described in Chapter IV of Bharata's Natyashastra) are carved in stone with accompanying inscriptions on the Gopurams of the Nataraja Temple at Chidambaram and the inner sanctum walls of Rajaraja Chola's Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur. Literarily, the 12th-century poet Jayadeva's Sanskrit 'Gita Govinda' (consisting of 24 Ashtapadis celebrating the love of Radha and Madhava) forms the core repertoire of Odissi, inspired Kerala's 'Krishnanaattam' and Kathakali Padams, and is extensively performed in Manipuri Raslila and Bharatanatyam Abhinaya.
While Kathak evolved from temple storytellers ('Kathakars'—

While Kathak evolved from temple storytellers ('Kathakars'—'Katha kahe so Kathak kahave') and later absorbed Persian-Mughal court aesthetics (such as the upright stance, Chakkars, Aamad, Salami, and Tarana), it never abandoned Vaishnavite Radha-Krishna devotional themes. Under the patronage of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh (who himself composed Thumris under the pen name 'Akhtarpiya' and staged the Rahas/Raslila where he played Krishna) and maestros like Thakur Prasad and Bindadin Maharaj of the Lucknow Gharana, the Radha-Krishna Leela—expressed through Braj-bhasha Thumris, Dadras, Hori, and wordless 'Gat-Bhava' (such as Makhan-Chori and Panghat-ki-Gat)—remained the emotional soul of Kathak's Nritya repertoire.

ref: NCERT Class XI An Introduction to Indian Art; Sangeet Natak Akademi Classical Dance Archives

stem: With reference to the Sanskrit plays attributed to the early classical dramatist Bhasa, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In strict adherence to the dramaturgical rules of Bharata's Natyashastra, Bhasa's plays altogether avoid depicting fatal combat or the death of a principal character directly on the stage.
2. In plays such as Urubhanga and Karnabhara, Bhasa subverts epic conventions by portraying traditional antagonists of the Mahabharata with tragic nobility and moral complexity.
3. Swapnavasavadattam revolves around the political statecraft of Minister Yaugandharayana to restore King Udayana's lost territories in Vatsa through a strategic marital alliance with Magadha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Bhasa predates the rigid enforcement of later classical Sanskrit dramaturgical taboos, famously staging physical combat and the tragic on-stage death of Duryodhana in Urubhanga while elevating epic antagonists into tragic heroes.

exp.why: Bharata's Natyashastra prohibits the direct on-stage depiction of violent battle, siege, or the death of a hero (Nayaka). However, Bhasa famously departs from these classical conventions in plays like Urubhanga (The Breaking of the Thighs) and Abhishekanataka, where fatal combat and the on-stage death of Duryodhana and Vali are directly presented.

In his one-act Mahabharata plays—particularly Urubhanga and Karnabhara—Bhasa reinterprets epic antagonists like Duryodhana and Karna not as villainous archetypes, but as deeply remorseful, magnanimous, and tragic figures confronting fate with dignity.

Swapnavasavadattam (The Vision of Vasavadatta), continuing the plot of Pratijnayaugandharayana, depicts the chief minister Yaugandharayana orchestrating the rumour of Queen Vasavadatta's death in a fire so that King Udayana of Vatsa marries Princess Padmavati of Magadha to secure military backing against his rival Aruni.

ref: A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India (Chapter on Language and Literature); Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India.

stem: With reference to the classical Sanskrit works of Kalidasa, which one of the following statements accurately distinguishes Malavikagnimitram from his other two plays, Abhijnanashakuntalam and Vikramorvashiyam?

opts.A: While Malavikagnimitram is classified as a bourgeois social drama (Prakarana) featuring merchant protagonists, his other two plays are heroic romances (Natakas) featuring royal protagonists.
opts.B: Unlike Abhijnanashakuntalam and Vikramorvashiyam which draw their plots from Vedic and epic-Puranic mythology, Malavikagnimitram is set against the historical political backdrop of the Shunga dynasty.
opts.C: Malavikagnimitram is the only play by Kalidasa composed entirely in Maharashtri Prakrit, whereas Abhijnanashakuntalam and Vikramorvashiyam employ classical Sanskrit exclusively.
opts.D: While Abhijnanashakuntalam and Vikramorvashiyam dispense with the stock comic character (Vidushaka), Malavikagnimitram relies on the Vidushaka to drive its court intrigue.

core: While Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam (from the Mahabharata/Padma Purana) and Vikramorvashiyam (from the Rigveda/Shatapatha Brahmana) adapt mythological lore, Malavikagnimitram uniquely dramatizes historical events of the Shunga period.

exp.why: Option B is correct because Abhijnanashakuntalam derives its narrative from the Adi Parva of the Mahabharata and Vikramorvashiyam from the Rigvedic dialogue hymn (Samvada Sukta) of Pururavas and Urvashi, whereas Malavikagnimitram is set in the historical Shunga court at Vidisha. It centers on King Agnimitra (son of Pushyamitra Shunga) and contains vital historical references to the Shunga-Vidarbha war and Vasumitra's victory over the Indo-Greeks (Yavanas) on the banks of the Sindhu during Pushyamitra's Ashvamedha sacrifice. Option A is incorrect because all three plays have royal heroes and are Natakas/Trotakas, not Prakaranas. Option C is incorrect because all three plays follow classical bilingual dramatic conventions (Sanskrit for upper-caste males and Prakrits for women and subordinate characters). Option D is incorrect because all three plays feature a Vidushaka (Gautama in Malavikagnimitram, Madhavya in Abhijnanashakuntalam, and Manavaka in Vikramorvashiyam).

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 8 & 9; NCERT Class XI Ancient India (R.S. Sharma).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the structural conventions of post-Kalidasa Sanskrit drama:
items: Statement-I: Both Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa and Bhavabhuti's surviving Sanskrit plays (Malatimadhava, Mahaviracharita, and Uttararamacharita) deliberately dispense with the stock comic figure of the Vidushaka (court jester).

Statement-II: While Vishakhadatta excludes comic relief and romantic subplots to maintain an austere focus on political espionage and statecraft between Chanakya and Rakshasa, Bhavabhuti omits the Vidushaka to preserve the uninterrupted aesthetic intensity of the pathetic (Karuna), heroic (Vira), and macabre (Bibhatsa) sentiments.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Both Vishakhadatta and Bhavabhuti break from standard Sanskrit dramatic convention by eliminating the Vidushaka, doing so for distinct dramaturgical purposes: Vishakhadatta to preserve the taut political realism of Mauryan statecraft, and Bhavabhuti to elevate grave emotional rasas (especially Karuna Rasa) without comic dilution.

exp.why: In classical Sanskrit drama, the Vidushaka (a gluttonous, Prakrit-speaking Brahmin companion of the hero) is a ubiquitous stock character. Both Vishakhadatta in Mudrarakshasa and Bhavabhuti across all three of his extant plays (Malatimadhava, Mahaviracharita, and Uttararamacharita) notably omit the Vidushaka.

Statement-II provides the exact dramaturgical reason behind Statement-I. Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa is a purely political drama without a romantic heroine or jester, focusing entirely on the battle of wits, espionage, and psychological warfare by which Chanakya wins over Amatya Rakshasa to Chandragupta Maurya's side. Conversely, Bhavabhuti—renowned for declaring Karuna (pathos) as the fundamental aesthetic sentiment (Eko rasah karuna eva) in Uttararamacharita and evoking grim cremation-ground imagery (Bibhatsa and Raudra rasas) in Malatimadhava—omits the Vidushaka because light-hearted courtly buffoonery would disrupt the solemnity of his emotional registers.

ref: A.B. Keith, The Sanskrit Drama in its Origin, Development, Theory & Practice; A.L. Basham, The Wonder That Was India.

stem: With reference to the Sanskrit dramas of Shudraka and King Harshavardhana, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Categorized as a Prakarana in classical dramaturgy, Shudraka's Mrichchhakatika departs from royal court romances by portraying an impoverished Brahmin merchant, a courtesan, gamblers, and a subaltern political uprising.

2. While Shudraka's Mrichchhakatika dramatizes the Buddhist legend of Prince Jimutavahana's self-sacrifice to protect the Nagas from Garuda, Harshavardhana's Nagananda depicts the overthrow of the tyrannical ruler Palaka of Ujjayini.

3. Harshavardhana's Ratnavali and Priyadarshika are four-act Natikas centered on the courtly romances of King Udayana, with Priyadarshika notably employing the structural device of a 'play-within-a-play' (Garbhanka).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Shudraka's Mrichchhakatika exemplifies the realistic ten-act Prakarana genre weaving urban social life with a political revolt in Ujjayini, whereas Harshavardhana authored two courtly Natikas (Ratnavali and Priyadarshika) and one Buddhist-inspired Nataka (Nagananda).

exp.why: According to the Natyashastra and Dasharupaka, a Prakarana is a ten-act play with an invented plot and a non-royal protagonist (typically a Brahmin, minister, or merchant). Shudraka's Mrichchhakatika (The Little Clay Cart) exemplifies this genre through the love story of the impoverished merchant Charudatta and the cultured courtesan Vasantasena amidst thieves, gamblers, corrupt judges, and political rebels.

The two plots are interchanged. It is Harshavardhana's Nagananda that dramatizes the Buddhist/Vidyadhara legend of the Bodhisattva Prince Jimutavahana offering his own body to the mythical bird Garuda to save the Naga Shankhachuda. Conversely, it is Shudraka's Mrichchhakatika that interweaves its main romance with the political rebellion led by the herdsman Aryaka to overthrow the tyrannical King Palaka of Ujjayini.

Both Ratnavali and Priyadarshika are classical four-act Natikas dealing with the harem intrigues and romances of King Udayana of Vatsa and Queen Vasavadatta. In Act III of Priyadarshika, Harshavardhana introduces the celebrated Garbhanka (embryo-act or play-within-a-play) device, in which a play about Udayana and Vasavadatta's own elopement is staged within the palace.

ref: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, Ch. 9 & 10; Romila Thapar, Early India.

stem: Consider the following pairs of classical Sanskrit aestheticians, their foundational treatises, and the core poetic doctrines associated with them:
items: 1. Bhamaha : Kavyadarsha — Propounded the Riti (poetic style) and Dasha-Guna doctrine
2. Dandin : Dhvanyaloka — Established Dhvani (aesthetic suggestion) as the soul of poetry
3. Vamana : Kavyalankarasutravritti — Declared Riti (diction/style) to be the soul of poetry (Ritir atma kavyasya)
4. Abhinavagupta : Abhinavabharati — Synthesized the Dhvani doctrine with Bharata's Rasa theory through the concept of Rasa-dhvani
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Classical Sanskrit poetics (Kavyashastra) evolved from Bhamaha's Alankara school (Kavyalankara) and Dandin/Vamana's Riti-Guna school (Kavyadarsha and Kavyalankarasutravritti) to Anandavardhana's Dhvani theory (Dhvanyaloka), culminating in Abhinavagupta's Rasa-dhvani synthesis.

exp.why: Bhamaha (c. 7th century CE) was the foundational theorist of the Alankara (figurative ornamentation) school and authored the Kavyalankara, centering poetics around Vakrokti (oblique/figurative expression). The Kavyadarsha, which systematically expounded the Marga/Riti and Dasha-Guna (ten poetic excellences) distinction between the Vaidarbhi and Gaudi styles, was authored by Dandin.

Dandin authored the Kavyadarsha, not the Dhvanyaloka. The Dhvanyaloka was composed by the 9th-century Kashmiri aesthetician Anandavardhana, who established the revolutionary doctrine that Dhvani (suggested or resonant meaning, rather than literal denotation or mere figurative ornament) constitutes the true soul of poetry (Kavyasyatma dhvanih).

Vamana (c. 8th–9th century CE), in his Kavyalankarasutravritti, elevated poetic style or diction (Riti)—defined as a specific arrangement of words characterized by Gunas (excellences)—through his famous aphorism 'Ritir atma kavyasya' (Riti is the soul of poetry).

The Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta (c. 10th–11th century CE), in his monumental commentary Abhinavabharati (on Bharata's Natyashastra) and Lochana (on Anandavardhana's Dhvanyaloka), integrated the Dhvani theory of poetics with Bharata's Rasa theory of dramaturgy, demonstrating that aesthetic emotion (Rasa) cannot be directly stated but is realized strictly through suggestion (Rasa-dhvani).

ref: P.V. Kane, History of Sanskrit Poetics; Sheldon Pollock, A Rasa Reader: Classical Indian Aesthetics.

stem: With reference to historical writing in ancient and early medieval Sanskrit literature, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Unlike Sanskrit court biographies (Charitas) such as Banabhatta's Harshacharita and Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita which function primarily as royal panegyrics, Kalhana's Rajatarangini is recognized as a work of critical historiography that explicitly adopts an ethic of judicial impartiality (ragadveshabahishkrita) and corroborates earlier chronicles against epigraphic land grants (shasanas), coins, and monument inscriptions.

Statement-II: Completed during the reign of the Lohara ruler Jayasimha, the Rajatarangini is structured into eight books (Tarangas) of Sanskrit verse tracing the dynastic history of Kashmir down to the Karkota, Utpala, and Lohara periods.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Kalhana's Rajatarangini (1148–1150 CE) stands out from eulogistic Charita literature because Kalhana was not a salaried court panegyrist and systematically cross-checked eleven earlier chronicles and the Nilamata Purana against epigraphic shasanas and coins under a stated ideal of judicial neutrality.

exp.why: Charita texts like Banabhatta's Harshacharita and Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita were composed by salaried court poets to legitimize and eulogize their royal patrons. In contrast, Kalhana held no office under King Jayasimha and declared in the opening verses of Rajatarangini that a true historian's speech must, like that of a judge, be free from bias or passion (sthemavan ragadveshabahishkritah) in recounting past events. He critically examined eleven earlier royal chronicles alongside the Nilamata Purana and checked their genealogies against edifice inscriptions (pratishthashasanas), land grants (vastushasanas), laudatory tablets (prashastipattas), and coins.

Statement-II is factually correct: the Rajatarangini (River of Kings) was completed in 1148–1150 CE during the reign of the Lohara dynasty ruler Jayasimha of Kashmir and is structured into eight Tarangas (waves/books) of nearly 8,000 Sanskrit verses covering Kashmir's rulers from legendary antiquity through the historical Karkota, Utpala, and First and Second Lohara dynasties.
